Q 4.7·v4 Which statement accurately describes the function of a due-on-sale (alienation) clause in a Hawaii mortgage?
A. It empowers the lender to call in the entire loan balance if the property is sold without consent ✓
B. It requires the buyer to obtain homeowner's insurance before closing
C. It guarantees the buyer the right to assume the existing loan at the same terms
D. It prohibits the lender from ever raising the interest rate on the loan
Answer: A. The due-on-sale clause is an alienation restriction that allows the lender to demand full repayment if the borrower transfers the property without the lender's permission.
Q 4.7·v5 Under a due-on-sale clause, what right does a lender have if a borrower transfers the property without the lender's approval?
A. Demand immediate full repayment of the loan balance ✓
B. File a mechanic's lien against the new owner
C. Impose a penalty equal to 6 months' interest
D. Require the buyer to obtain a new appraisal within 30 days
Answer: A. A due-on-sale clause (alienation clause) gives the lender the right to accelerate the loan and demand full repayment if the property is sold or transferred without lender consent.
Q 4.7·v6 Which statement best describes how a due-on-sale provision protects a lender's interests?
A. It limits the buyer's ability to obtain title insurance on the property
B. It prevents the property from being transferred without the lender's consent and allows acceleration if violated ✓
C. It automatically transfers the property title to the lender upon sale
D. It prevents the borrower from refinancing at a lower interest rate
Answer: B. The due-on-sale clause protects the lender by giving consent rights over property transfer and acceleration rights if the borrower violates the clause.
Q 4.7·v7 A borrower conveys property to a family member without notifying the lender. If the loan contains a due-on-sale clause, what is the lender's primary remedy?
A. Sue the family member for fraud and unjust enrichment
B. Automatically record a lien on the new owner's other property
C. Reduce the interest rate on the existing loan as compensation
D. Call the loan due in full or approve the transfer with amended terms ✓
Answer: D. A due-on-sale clause gives the lender the right to demand acceleration (call the loan) or approve the transfer; it does not automatically create liens or change loan terms.
Q 4.7·v8 In Hawaii real estate transactions, a due-on-sale clause is commonly included in mortgages to:
A. Ensure the seller receives proceeds from the sale
B. Prevent property taxes from being assessed against the lender
C. Give the lender control over property transfers and the right to accelerate if the borrower transfers without consent ✓
D. Allow the lender to assume ownership if property values decline
Answer: C. The due-on-sale clause protects lender interests by requiring lender approval for transfers and allowing acceleration if the borrower violates this restriction.
Q 4.7·v9 When a real estate loan contains an alienation clause, what right does it grant to the lender?
A. The right to adjust the interest rate annually based on market conditions
B. The right to foreclose immediately upon any property improvement
C. The right to prevent the borrower from obtaining homeowner insurance
D. The right to demand full payment if the borrower transfers title without lender approval ✓
Answer: D. An alienation (due-on-sale) clause gives the lender the power to accelerate the loan and demand full repayment if the property is sold or ownership is transferred without the lender's consent.
Q 4.8 PMI is generally required on conventional loans when:
A. Borrower has FICO below 600
B. LTV exceeds 80% ✓
C. Loan exceeds $1M
D. LTV is below 50%
Answer: B. PMI protects lender on high-LTV conventional loans.
Q 4.8·v1 Under what loan-to-value threshold does a conventional borrower typically avoid paying private mortgage insurance?
A. When the borrower has a credit score above 700
B. When LTV exceeds 85%
C. When LTV remains at or below 80% ✓
D. When the purchase price is under $500,000
Answer: C. PMI is not required when LTV is 80% or less on conventional loans; it becomes mandatory when LTV exceeds 80% because the lender's equity cushion drops below 20%.
Q 4.8·v2 A lender will typically require PMI on a conventional mortgage because:
A. The loan-to-value ratio puts the lender at greater risk of loss ✓
B. The property is in a declining market area
C. The loan amount exceeds the county lending limit
D. The borrower is a first-time homebuyer
Answer: A. PMI is risk protection for the lender when the borrower's equity stake is low (high LTV); it compensates the lender if the borrower defaults on a high-LTV conventional loan.
Q 4.8·v3 When does private mortgage insurance become a required cost for a borrower on a conventional loan?
A. Whenever the property appraised value increases year-over-year
B. Whenever the borrower puts down less than 25%
C. Whenever the borrower's debt-to-income ratio exceeds 43%
D. Whenever the borrower finances more than 80% of the property value ✓
Answer: D. PMI is required when LTV exceeds 80%, meaning the borrower is financing more than 80% of the purchase price or appraised value on a conventional loan.
Q 4.8·v4 A conventional loan with an 85% LTV will most likely require the borrower to:
A. Accept a higher interest rate in lieu of down payment
B. Complete a homebuyer education course
C. Pay private mortgage insurance premiums ✓
D. Hold the property in an LLC
Answer: C. At 85% LTV, the borrower exceeds the 80% threshold and therefore must pay PMI to protect the lender's interest in the event of default.
Q 4.8·v5 A lender will typically mandate private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan if the borrower's:
A. Credit score falls within the prime range of 740–760
B. Debt-to-income ratio is below 28%
C. Loan-to-value ratio surpasses 80% ✓
D. Down payment represents 25% or more of the purchase price
Answer: C. PMI is required on conventional loans when LTV exceeds 80%, meaning the borrower's equity is less than 20% and lender risk increases.
Q 4.8·v6 Under what loan condition would a conventional mortgage borrower most likely be required to pay PMI?
A. When the loan principal is under $500,000
B. When the loan amount exceeds 80% of the property's appraised value ✓
C. When the borrower has made timely payments for 24 consecutive months
D. When the borrower puts down 22% of the home's purchase price
Answer: B. Private mortgage insurance protects the lender when LTV exceeds 80%, indicating the borrower has less than 20% equity in the property.
Q 4.8·v7 Which scenario would trigger the requirement for PMI on a conventional residential loan?
A. Borrower makes an initial earnest money deposit of 3%
B. Borrower obtains a fixed-rate 30-year mortgage
C. Borrower finances more than 80% of the property's value ✓
D. Borrower's employment is in a commission-based field
Answer: C. PMI becomes mandatory when LTV exceeds 80% because the lender's risk exposure increases with a lower equity cushion for the borrower.
Q 4.8·v8 On a conventional loan, private mortgage insurance is generally imposed when the:
A. Title search reveals no prior liens or encumbrances
B. Property appraises for less than the purchase price agreed in the contract
C. Borrower's initial equity position falls below 20% of the property value ✓
D. Interest rate is locked in at a rate below the market average
Answer: C. PMI is required when the loan-to-value ratio exceeds 80% (meaning the borrower has less than 20% equity), protecting the lender's interest in a higher-risk loan scenario.
Q 4.8·v9 A lender will typically require private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan if the borrower's loan-to-value ratio reaches what threshold?
A. Exactly 100%
B. 75% or higher
C. 60% or lower
D. Greater than 80% ✓
Answer: D. PMI is mandated by lenders on conventional loans when LTV exceeds 80%, protecting the lender against default risk on high-leverage loans.
Q 4.9 APR is generally:
A. Lower than interest rate
B. Equal to interest rate
C. Higher than interest rate when points charged ✓
D. Always 0%
Answer: C. APR includes points + most fees → higher than nominal interest rate.
Q 4.9·v1 When a lender charges discount points on a loan, how does the APR typically compare to the stated interest rate?
A. The APR exceeds the interest rate due to the inclusion of points and fees ✓
B. The APR is only calculated if no points are charged
C. The APR becomes lower because points reduce the borrower's cost
D. The APR remains identical to the interest rate regardless of points
Answer: A. APR incorporates discount points, origination fees, and closing costs into the calculation, resulting in a rate higher than the nominal interest rate quoted by the lender.
Q 4.9·v2 A borrower sees a loan advertised at 6% interest. After factoring in origination fees and points, the actual APR is most likely to be:
A. Fluctuating between 5% and 6%
B. 6% or lower
C. Exactly 6%
D. Higher than 6% ✓
Answer: D. The APR includes all loan costs (points, fees, closing costs) in its calculation, making it a more comprehensive measure that exceeds the nominal interest rate.
Q 4.9·v3 Under federal truth-in-lending rules, how should an agent explain the relationship between APR and the advertised interest rate to a client?
A. The APR is typically higher because it reflects the total cost of borrowing including points and fees ✓
B. The APR is irrelevant once the interest rate is locked in
C. The APR is always lower when the borrower pays discount points upfront
D. They are the same calculation with different names
Answer: A. APR is mandated by TILA to show the true annual percentage cost of the loan; it includes all finance charges, making it higher than the base interest rate alone.
Q 4.9·v4 If a lender charges 2 discount points on a mortgage loan, which statement best describes the APR?
A. It will be substantially lower than the stated interest rate
B. It will be higher than the interest rate because points are incorporated into the cost ✓
C. It will equal the interest rate since points are a separate line item
D. It cannot be determined without knowing the loan amount
Answer: B. Discount points are factored into APR calculations as part of the total financing cost, causing the APR to exceed the nominal interest rate presented to the borrower.
Q 4.9·v5 When a lender charges discount points on a mortgage loan, how does the APR typically compare to the stated interest rate?
A. The APR is eliminated entirely when points are present
B. The APR is identical to the interest rate regardless of points
C. The APR becomes lower because points reduce the loan balance
D. The APR exceeds the interest rate due to the cost of points and fees ✓
Answer: D. APR (Annual Percentage Rate) includes the nominal interest rate plus the cost of points and other fees expressed as an annualized rate, making it higher than the stated interest rate alone.
Q 4.9·v6 A borrower receives a mortgage quote with a 4% interest rate and 2 discount points. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between APR and the quoted rate?
A. APR will be approximately 4% since points don't affect annual calculations
B. APR will be higher than 4% once points and associated fees are factored in ✓
C. APR will be lower than 4% because points improve the loan terms
D. APR will equal 0% for the first year due to point deductions
Answer: B. The APR reflects the true cost of borrowing by incorporating points, origination fees, and other charges into an annualized percentage, resulting in a rate higher than the nominal interest rate.
Q 4.9·v7 In mortgage financing disclosures, APR and interest rate are typically different values. This difference is most commonly due to:
A. State and federal usury law caps limiting how high interest rates can go
B. The inclusion of points, origination fees, and closing costs in the APR calculation ✓
C. The APR being reset to zero after the loan closing
D. A requirement that APR must always be lower for consumer protection purposes
Answer: B. APR includes discount points, loan origination fees, and other financing charges amortized over the loan term, which raises the APR above the nominal interest rate shown on the promissory note.
Q 4.9·v8 A lender advertises a 3.5% mortgage rate but the APR disclosed on the Loan Estimate is 3.75%. This difference primarily reflects:
A. The cost of points, fees, and other charges included in the APR computation ✓
B. An error in the lender's calculations that must be corrected immediately
C. A penalty applied to borrowers who fail to lock in their rate early
D. The lender's markup on the property appraisal fee only
Answer: A. The higher APR incorporates the cost of discount points, origination fees, title fees, and other financing charges expressed as an annual rate, making the true cost of the loan higher than the stated interest rate.
Q 4.9·v9 When a lender quotes an APR that is higher than the stated interest rate, this difference most likely reflects:
A. Market conditions that will reverse before closing
B. An error in the lender's calculation software
C. The inclusion of points, fees, and other financing costs amortized over the loan term ✓
D. A penalty imposed by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
Answer: C. APR incorporates discount points, origination fees, and other closing costs expressed as an annual percentage, making it typically higher than the nominal interest rate when points are charged.
Q 4.10 RESPA Section 8 prohibits:
A. FHA loans
B. Prepayment
C. Kickbacks among settlement providers ✓
D. High interest rates
Answer: C. RESPA Section 8 bans referral fees / kickbacks.
Q 4.10·v1 Under RESPA, which of the following practices is expressly forbidden in Section 8?
A. Charging origination fees
B. Compensation to a title company for referring business ✓
C. Using an appraisal contingency
D. Requiring hazard insurance
Answer: B. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits kickbacks and referral fees between settlement service providers, making compensation for referrals illegal regardless of the provider type.
Q 4.10·v2 A mortgage lender offers a real estate agent a percentage of the loan origination fee for each client referred to the lender. This violates:
A. Truth in Lending Act (TILA) disclosure requirements
B. Fair Housing Act prohibitions
C. RESPA Section 8 anti-kickback provisions ✓
D. State usury laws
Answer: C. RESPA Section 8 specifically prohibits any payment or thing of value given as consideration for the referral of settlement business, making this referral arrangement illegal.
Q 4.10·v3 Which federal statute's Section 8 makes it unlawful for settlement service providers to give or receive anything of value in exchange for referrals?
A. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
B. Community Reinvestment Act
C. Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) ✓
D. Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Answer: C. RESPA Section 8 is the specific statutory provision that prohibits kickbacks and referral fees among all parties involved in settlement transactions.
Q 4.10·v4 A title insurance company pays an escrow agent $500 for each new customer the escrow agent refers to the title company. This arrangement is most likely prohibited by:
A. The Dodd-Frank Act's consumer protection rules
B. Hawaii's Real Estate Commission licensing requirements
C. State insurance commission regulations on premium rates
D. RESPA Section 8 kickback prohibitions ✓
Answer: D. RESPA Section 8 bans any payment or benefit given as compensation for referrals between settlement service providers, making this direct payment arrangement illegal.
Q 4.10·v5 Under RESPA Section 8, which of the following practices is strictly forbidden in real estate transactions?
A. Receiving compensation for referring a client to a title company ✓
B. Requiring a home inspection before closing
C. Charging a reasonable origination fee for loan processing
D. Disclosing all closing costs on the Closing Disclosure
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 prohibits referral fees and kickbacks between settlement service providers, as these undisclosed payments could inflate costs for consumers.
Q 4.10·v6 A real estate broker is approached by a mortgage lender offering a commission for every loan referral. What does RESPA Section 8 say about this arrangement?
A. It is illegal regardless of whether the referral fee is disclosed ✓
B. It is allowed as long as the fee does not exceed 10% of the loan amount
C. It is acceptable if both parties agree to the arrangement in writing
D. It is permissible if documented in the listing agreement
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees between settlement service providers to prevent inflated costs and maintain transaction integrity.
Q 4.10·v7 Which federal regulation makes it unlawful for settlement service providers to pay each other for generating referrals?
A. RESPA Section 8 ✓
B. The Community Reinvestment Act
C. FIRREA Section 1113
D. Regulation Z of the Truth in Lending Act
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 specifically bans referral fees, kickbacks, and unearned fees among closing service providers to protect consumers from inflated settlement costs.
Q 4.10·v8 A title company offers to pay an escrow agent for each customer referred to them. This transaction would violate:
A. The Fair Housing Act and lending discrimination guidelines
B. Regulation Z disclosure requirements for affiliated business arrangements
C. State licensing laws and appraisal independence standards
D. RESPA Section 8 prohibition on kickbacks and referral fees ✓
Answer: D. RESPA Section 8 prohibits compensation payments between settlement service providers for referrals, as these undisclosed kickbacks artificially increase consumer costs.
Q 4.10·v9 Under RESPA Section 8, which practice is considered an illegal referral arrangement?
A. A title company paying a real estate agent for sending business their way ✓
B. A lender charging origination fees for loan processing
C. A mortgage servicer collecting monthly loan payments
D. A broker requiring earnest money deposits from buyers
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits kickbacks and referral fees between settlement service providers, regardless of the form or justification for the payment.
Q 4.11 A VA-eligible borrower typically:
A. Has no down payment requirement ✓
B. Must put down 20%
C. Cannot use VA twice
D. Pays PMI
Answer: A. VA loans often require no down payment and never PMI.
Q 4.11·v1 Which of the following is a key advantage of VA financing for qualified military veterans?
A. Zero down payment is typically available ✓
B. A minimum 15% equity contribution is required at closing
C. Borrowers must obtain mortgage insurance coverage
D. The loan can only be used once in a lifetime
Answer: A. VA loans are designed to require no down payment and eliminate PMI, making them highly accessible for eligible veterans.
Q 4.11·v2 A borrower with VA loan eligibility would NOT be required to:
A. Pay private mortgage insurance ✓
B. Provide employment verification
C. Disclose the property address to the lender
D. Obtain a VA Certificate of Eligibility
Answer: A. VA loans are exempt from PMI requirements; instead, VA charges a funding fee. All other items are standard loan requirements.
Q 4.11·v3 When comparing VA loans to conventional financing, a VA-eligible borrower typically benefits from:
A. A requirement to maintain an escrow account for taxes and insurance
B. Mandatory hazard insurance at a higher rate than conventional loans
C. Freedom from down payment and mortgage insurance obligations ✓
D. A prepayment penalty that applies for the first five years
Answer: C. VA loans uniquely offer no down payment requirement and no PMI, providing substantial financial advantages over conventional loans.
Q 4.11·v4 A VA-eligible borrower's loan application would MOST LIKELY NOT include a requirement for:
A. A property appraisal
B. Private mortgage insurance ✓
C. A valid Certificate of Eligibility
D. Proof of income and creditworthiness
Answer: B. VA loans are prohibited from requiring PMI; the VA backing and optional funding fee serve as the guarantor, eliminating this cost.
Q 4.11·v5 Which of the following is a key benefit unique to VA loan programs for eligible veterans?
A. Exemption from property inspections
B. Lower interest rates than conventional loans by statute
C. Automatic loan approval regardless of credit
D. No down payment needed in most cases ✓
Answer: D. VA loans typically require zero down payment as a primary benefit to veterans, distinguishing them from conventional and FHA loans that may require 3-20% down.
Q 4.11·v6 A service member with VA eligibility should understand that VA financing generally:
A. Eliminates the down payment requirement ✓
B. Requires 10% minimum down payment
C. Limits borrowers to a single property purchase
D. Mandates mortgage insurance premiums
Answer: A. VA loans feature a zero down payment benefit, which removes the financial barrier of accumulating a large down payment fund required by most other loan types.
Q 4.11·v7 What is a primary distinguishing feature of VA mortgage loans compared to conventional financing?
A. Borrowers pay mortgage insurance annually
B. Down payment is not typically required ✓
C. Interest rates are set by the Department of Veterans Affairs
D. Veterans can only refinance once per year
Answer: B. VA loans uniquely offer no down payment requirement, along with no PMI, making them one of the most affordable financing options available to eligible borrowers.
Q 4.11·v8 An eligible VA borrower reviewing loan terms should expect:
A. No down payment obligation in most transactions ✓
B. A 15% down payment minimum
C. A requirement to pay private mortgage insurance
D. Restrictions on using the benefit for investment property
Answer: A. VA loan programs characteristically waive the down payment requirement for eligible veterans, reducing upfront cash needed to purchase a home compared to other loan programs.
Q 4.11·v9 Which of the following is a key advantage of a VA loan for an eligible veteran?
A. The interest rate is fixed at the federal rate
B. The lender will waive the appraisal requirement
C. Private mortgage insurance premiums are mandatory
D. A down payment is typically not required ✓
Answer: D. VA loans are designed to help veterans by eliminating the down payment requirement and avoiding PMI, making homeownership more accessible.
Q 4.12 On an ARM, the rate equals:
A. Margin only
B. Index − margin
C. Just the index
D. Index + margin ✓
Answer: D. Rate = Index (variable) + Margin (fixed lender spread).
Q 4.12·v1 Which two components, when combined, determine the interest rate charged on an adjustable-rate mortgage?
A. The margin alone, adjusted annually
B. The market index and the lender's margin ✓
C. The appraisal value and the debt-to-income ratio
D. The prime rate and the loan origination fee
Answer: B. An ARM rate is calculated by adding the lender's fixed margin to the variable market index; the index fluctuates while the margin remains constant throughout the loan term.
Q 4.12·v2 A borrower with an ARM wants to understand how her interest rate is calculated. Her lender tells her the current index is 3% and the margin is 2.5%. What is her interest rate?
A. 3% (index only)
B. 5.5% (index plus margin) ✓
C. 0.5% (index minus margin)
D. 2.5% (margin only)
Answer: B. The ARM rate formula is Index + Margin; therefore 3% + 2.5% = 5.5%, demonstrating how the variable index and fixed margin combine to produce the final rate.
Q 4.12·v3 In explaining an ARM to a client, which statement accurately describes the relationship between the index, margin, and the resulting interest rate?
A. The interest rate is determined by adding the index to the margin ✓
B. The interest rate is simply whatever the lender's margin is set at
C. The interest rate equals the margin subtracted from the index
D. The interest rate equals the index regardless of the margin
Answer: A. The correct ARM formula is Rate = Index + Margin; the index changes with market conditions while the margin is a fixed spread set by the lender at origination.
Q 4.12·v4 When discussing ARM mechanics with a consumer, you explain that the interest rate will adjust periodically. The rate adjustment is based on which calculation?
A. The new margin percentage applied to the previous rate
B. The margin value only, with no index component
C. The index divided by the margin
D. The current market index value plus the lender's fixed margin ✓
Answer: D. Each ARM adjustment recalculates using the current index value added to the constant margin; the index may change but the margin component remains fixed.
Q 4.12·v5 When calculating the interest rate on an adjustable-rate mortgage, a lender combines two components. Which of the following correctly identifies those components?
A. The appraisal value and the underwriting adjustment
B. The annual percentage rate and the origination fee
C. The discount point percentage and the loan-to-value ratio
D. The benchmark rate and the lender's markup ✓
Answer: D. An ARM rate is determined by adding the benchmark index (which fluctuates) to the lender's markup or spread, commonly called the margin.
Q 4.12·v6 An ARM borrower wants to understand what makes up their adjustable rate. If the index is currently 2% and the lender's spread is 2.5%, what is the resulting interest rate?
A. 2%
B. 0.5%
C. 2.5%
D. 4.5% ✓
Answer: D. The ARM rate equals the index plus the margin: 2% + 2.5% = 4.5%; the margin remains constant while the index adjusts.
Q 4.12·v7 Which component of an ARM interest rate is set by the lender and does NOT change throughout the loan term?
A. The margin, which is the lender's fixed spread ✓
B. The rate cap, which adjusts annually
C. The initial teaser rate, which is subsidized
D. The index rate, which is tied to market conditions
Answer: A. The margin is the lender's static profit spread that never changes; the index component varies with market conditions and is added to this fixed margin.
Q 4.12·v8 A borrower's ARM adjusts when the index changes. To find the new rate after adjustment, a loan servicer must:
A. Multiply the index by the margin percentage
B. Add the fixed margin to the new index value ✓
C. Use only the published index without any additions
D. Subtract the margin from the current index
Answer: B. The new ARM rate is always calculated by adding the constant margin to the current index; this simple addition formula applies at each adjustment period.
Q 4.12·v9 When calculating the interest rate on an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), which two components must be combined?
A. The index and the points paid at origination
B. The margin alone, adjusted annually
C. The index and the margin ✓
D. The margin and the discount points
Answer: C. An ARM's interest rate is determined by adding the lender's fixed margin to the variable index rate. The index fluctuates with market conditions while the margin remains constant throughout the loan term.
05
Laws of Agency
National portion10 PSI items28 key concepts12 base questions

Agency law governs every relationship between licensee and client. The exam tests it heavily; clients live or die by it.

Chapter Overview

Agency is a legal relationship where one person (the agent) acts on behalf of another (the principal or client) with authority to bind them in dealings with third parties. Real estate agents owe fiduciary duties — the highest duties known to law — to clients but lower duties to customers and third parties. Memorize the acronym COALD: Care, Obedience to lawful instructions, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure. Care plus skill, undivided loyalty, full disclosure of all material facts, accounting for funds, and obedience are the bedrock.

Agency types are organized by scope of authority. A special agent has limited authority for one specific transaction — typical of a listing broker representing a seller for one property sale. A general agent has broader, continuing authority — typical of a property manager handling all aspects of rental management. A universal agent has authority to act in all matters legally allowed — power of attorney territory. Subagency exists when an agent's authority is delegated to another agent (cooperating broker working under listing broker's authority).

Agency creation: An express agency is created by written or oral agreement. An implied agency is created by parties' conduct without explicit agreement — for example, an agent who consistently acts as a buyer's representative may be deemed their agent. Ostensible (apparent) agency arises when a principal's conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe an agency exists, even if it doesn't. Agency by ratification occurs when a principal accepts the benefits of an unauthorized act after the fact.

Designated agency lets one brokerage assign different agents from the same firm to opposite sides of a transaction — keeping the supervising broker as a dual agent but giving each side undivided loyalty from their designated agent. Many states permit this; rules vary. Buyer agency creates a fiduciary relationship with the buyer, contracted by a buyer-broker agreement. Tenant representation similarly creates fiduciary duty to a tenant.

Dual agency occurs when one agent or firm represents both buyer and seller. It's legal in most states only with written informed consent from both parties, and it eliminates undivided loyalty — the agent must act neutrally between the parties. Many states require enhanced disclosure forms before any showing or negotiation. Hawaii recognizes dual agency under HRS 467 with mandatory written consent. Misuse of dual agency — undisclosed self-dealing, biased advice, leaking confidential information — is a leading cause of license revocation and lawsuits.

Fiduciary duties (COALD) explained in depth. Care: act with the diligence and skill a reasonable agent would in similar circumstances. Obedience: follow lawful instructions; refuse unlawful ones (instructions to discriminate, hide defects, etc.). Accounting: maintain accurate records of all funds and property received; deliver client funds promptly. Loyalty: place the client's interests above all others, including the agent's own interests; avoid conflicts. Disclosure: reveal all known material facts that could affect the client's decision.

Agency creates duties to non-clients (customers and third parties) that are lower than fiduciary but still substantial — primarily honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. An agent can never misrepresent a fact regardless of who they represent. "Puffing" (subjective opinion: "this is a great kitchen!") is allowed; misstatement of material fact ("the roof is two years old" when it's twenty) is misrepresentation, actionable as fraud if intentional or negligent.

Termination of agency happens by: expiration of the term, completion of purpose (transaction closes), mutual rescission, breach by either party, destruction of property, death or incompetency of either party (universal agency continues; for special agents, principal's death typically terminates), bankruptcy, or operation of law (changes in legal status). The agent's fiduciary duties continue post-termination for confidentiality of information learned during the agency.

Key Concepts & Definitions
AgentPerson authorized to act for and on behalf of a principal with authority to bind in dealings with third parties.
Principal / clientThe party the agent owes fiduciary duties to.
CustomerThird party in transaction not represented by the agent. Owed honesty + material-fact disclosure.
Fiduciary duties (COALD)Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure. Highest duties known to law.
CareAct with diligence and skill a reasonable agent would use. Negligence is actionable.
ObedienceFollow lawful instructions. Refuse unlawful ones (discrimination, fraud, hiding defects).
AccountingMaintain accurate records of all funds and property; deliver client funds promptly.
LoyaltyPlace client's interests above all others, including agent's own. Avoid conflicts.
Disclosure (fiduciary)Reveal all known material facts affecting client's decision. Including unfavorable info.
Special agentLimited authority for one transaction — typical listing broker.
General agentBroader, continuing authority — typical property manager.
Universal agentAuthority to act in all matters — power of attorney.
SubagencyAgent's authority delegated to another agent. Cooperating broker may be subagent of listing broker.
Designated agencyWithin one brokerage, different agents represent opposite sides. Broker may be dual agent.
Dual agencyOne agent or firm represents both sides. Requires written informed consent. Eliminates undivided loyalty.
Buyer agencyAgent represents buyer's interests exclusively. Buyer-broker agreement creates relationship.
Tenant representationAgent represents tenant. Common in commercial leasing.
Listing agreementContract creating seller-agent relationship.
Buyer-broker agreementContract creating buyer-agent relationship. Often includes compensation.
Express agencyCreated by written or oral agreement.
Implied agencyCreated by parties' conduct without express agreement.
Ostensible / apparent agencyPrincipal's conduct leads third party to reasonably believe agency exists.
Agency by ratificationPrincipal accepts benefits of unauthorized act after the fact, creating retroactive agency.
MisrepresentationFalse statement of material fact. Innocent, negligent, or fraudulent.
PuffingSubjective sales talk ("best house on the street"). Not actionable.
Procuring causeOrigin of unbroken chain producing the sale. Determines commission entitlement in disputes.
Termination by operation of lawDeath, incompetency, bankruptcy, destruction of subject matter, change in legal status.
ConfidentialityAgent's duty to protect client information. Survives agency termination.

Q 5.1 COALD stands for:
A. Confidence, Obedience, Accuracy, Loyalty, Diligence
B. Conduct, Order, Authority, Liability, Documentation
C. Communication, Obligation, Audit, Loyalty, Disclosure
D. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. COALD = the five fiduciary duties.
Q 5.1·v1 Which acronym correctly identifies the five fiduciary duties that a real estate licensee must uphold?
A. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
B. Communication, Obligation, Audit, Loyalty, Disclosure
C. Confidence, Obedience, Accuracy, Loyalty, Diligence
D. Conduct, Order, Authority, Liability, Documentation
Answer: A. COALD represents Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure—the core fiduciary duties required of Hawaii real estate licensees.
Q 5.1·v2 A broker in Hawaii needs to remember her principal fiduciary obligations. Which of the following correctly spells out COALD?
A. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
B. Compliance, Obedience, Authority, Liability, Documentation
C. Care, Organization, Accounting, Law, Disclosure
D. Conduct, Obligation, Audit, Loyalty, Disclosure
Answer: A. COALD is the mnemonic for the five fiduciary duties: Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure that all licensees must perform.
Q 5.1·v3 The five fiduciary duties required of Hawaii real estate agents are best remembered by which acronym?
A. COALD ✓
B. COACH
C. COLD
D. CLAUD
Answer: A. COALD is the standard acronym representing Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure—the fundamental fiduciary obligations in Hawaii real estate practice.
Q 5.1·v4 When explaining fiduciary responsibilities to a new licensee, an instructor outlines Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure. What acronym is being used?
A. COALD ✓
B. COACH
C. COBLA
D. COULD
Answer: A. The acronym COALD directly corresponds to Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure, which are the five essential fiduciary duties.
Q 5.1·v5 Which of the following correctly identifies the five fiduciary duties represented by the acronym COALD?
A. Competence, Obligation, Authority, Liability, Documentation
B. Confidence, Obedience, Accuracy, Loyalty, Diligence
C. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
D. Conduct, Obedience, Audit, Loyalty, Disclosure
Answer: C. COALD is a mnemonic for the five fiduciary duties: Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure. These are the core ethical and legal obligations brokers owe to their clients.
Q 5.1·v6 A real estate licensee must understand COALD, which represents:
A. Conduct, Order, Authority, Liability, Documentation
B. Communication, Obligation, Audit, Loyalty, Disclosure
C. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
D. Competence, Organization, Accuracy, Legal compliance, Diligence
Answer: C. COALD stands for Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure—the five essential fiduciary duties that Hawaii and mainland brokers must fulfill toward their clients.
Q 5.1·v7 In Hawaii real estate practice, the acronym COALD describes the broker's:
A. Confidentiality, Obligation, Authority, Legal duty, Documentation
B. Communication, Obligation, Accountability, Loyalty, Disclosure
C. Conduct, Obedience, Audit, Liability, Diligence
D. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. COALD is the acronym for the five fiduciary duties: Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure. These duties form the foundation of a broker's legal and ethical responsibilities to clients.
Q 5.1·v8 When studying broker responsibilities, what does the acronym COALD stand for?
A. Competence, Obligation, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure
B. Conduct, Obedience, Accuracy, Legal duty, Diligence
C. Confidence, Order, Authority, Loyalty, Documentation
D. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. COALD represents the five fiduciary duties required of real estate brokers: Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, and Disclosure. These are core principles in Hawaii real estate law.
Q 5.1·v9 Which of the following correctly identifies the five fiduciary duties represented by the acronym COALD?
A. Competence, Organization, Authority, Liabilities, Documentation
B. Confidentiality, Obligations, Assessments, Liability, Duties
C. Care, Obedience, Accounting, Loyalty, Disclosure ✓
D. Candor, Oversight, Appraisal, Legal compliance, Diligence

Q 5.2 A property manager is most typically a:
A. General agent ✓
B. Subagent
C. Special agent
D. Universal agent
Answer: A. Property managers have broad continuing authority — general agency.
Q 5.2·v1 Which classification of agent best describes someone hired to oversee the day-to-day operations and maintenance of an apartment complex?
A. Universal agent with unlimited scope
B. Special agent limited to specific transactions
C. General agent with broad, continuing authority ✓
D. Subagent acting under another licensee's supervision
Answer: C. Property managers exercise general agency authority because they manage ongoing operations and make decisions on behalf of the owner within their scope of employment.
Q 5.2·v2 A real estate licensee managing multiple residential units for a landlord, handling rent collection, maintenance requests, and tenant issues, operates primarily as a:
A. General agent ✓
B. Special agent
C. Limited agent
D. Subagent
Answer: A. Property management involves broad, continuing authority over the property's operations, which is the defining characteristic of general agency.
Q 5.2·v3 The authority granted to a property manager to act on behalf of the property owner covers multiple matters and continues over time. This type of agency relationship is known as:
A. Exclusive agency
B. Special agency
C. General agency ✓
D. Transactional agency
Answer: C. General agents possess broad authority to act across multiple property management functions on a continuing basis, unlike special agents limited to single transactions.
Q 5.2·v4 In Hawaii real estate practice, a property manager hired to oversee rental operations, authorize repairs, and collect payments would be classified as what type of agent?
A. Universal agent with all possible powers
B. General agent with authority over multiple matters ✓
C. Subagent acting under a broker's direct control
D. Special agent authorized for one specific purpose
Answer: B. Property managers function as general agents because they exercise broad, ongoing authority over multiple aspects of property management on behalf of the owner.
Q 5.2·v5 Which type of agency relationship best describes the authority held by someone managing residential rental properties on behalf of an owner?
A. Special agent limited to lease negotiations only
B. General agent with broad, continuing powers ✓
C. Universal agent with power of attorney
D. Subagent acting under a broker's supervision
Answer: B. Property managers exercise general agency because they have broad, continuing authority to handle multiple, recurring tasks for the owner over time.
Q 5.2·v6 A person hired to oversee daily operations, collect rent, arrange maintenance, and handle tenant relations for an apartment complex typically functions as a:
A. Special agent
B. Limited power-of-attorney agent
C. Subagent
D. General agent ✓
Answer: D. The scope and duration of property management duties—ongoing authority across multiple property functions—constitute general agency rather than limited or special agency.
Q 5.2·v7 What classification of agent is a property manager who is authorized to act on multiple matters for the property owner on a continuous basis?
A. Special agent for transaction purposes
B. Subagent of the listing broker
C. Universal agent with fiduciary power
D. General agent ✓
Answer: D. General agents possess continuous, broad authority to conduct multiple recurring duties; property managers fit this classification due to their ongoing operational responsibilities.
Q 5.2·v8 An individual employed to manage a condominium complex—including rent collection, maintenance coordination, and tenant screening—exercises which form of agency authority?
A. Subagency under the owner's broker
B. Universal agency over all financial decisions
C. Special agency limited to one specific transaction
D. General agency with continuing broad powers ✓
Answer: D. Property managers hold general agency authority because their role involves broad, continuing power to handle multiple, interconnected property-related functions.
Q 5.2·v9 Which type of agency relationship does a property manager typically hold with their principal?
A. Special agency limited to a single transaction
B. Universal agency with unlimited scope
C. Transactional agency for lease negotiations only
D. General agency with ongoing broad authority ✓
Answer: D. Property managers exercise general agency because they have continuous, wide-ranging authority to act on the principal's behalf across multiple property management duties.
Q 5.3 Dual agency requires:
A. No consent
B. Verbal consent from one party
C. Written consent from buyer only
D. Written informed consent from both parties ✓
Answer: D. Both parties must give written informed consent.
Q 5.3·v1 When representing both the buyer and seller in the same transaction, a licensee must obtain:
A. Verbal permission from the seller's attorney
B. Written informed consent signed by each party acknowledging the dual agency relationship ✓
C. A signed agreement from the listing agent only
D. Oral acknowledgment from both parties that they understand the arrangement
Answer: B. Hawaii real estate law requires written informed consent from both the buyer and seller before a licensee can act as a dual agent. Oral consent or consent from only one party is insufficient.
Q 5.3·v2 Under Hawaii REC regulations, if a salesperson wishes to represent both parties in a real estate transaction, what must occur before proceeding?
A. The licensee must obtain notarized consent from the seller
B. Only the buyer needs to sign an acknowledgment
C. The broker must file a disclosure form with the state
D. Both the buyer and seller must provide written informed consent acknowledging the dual agency ✓
Answer: D. Written informed consent from both parties is the legal requirement for dual agency in Hawaii. Filing with the state, notarization, or single-party consent does not satisfy this requirement.
Q 5.3·v3 A licensee discovers that their client (the buyer) is also represented by the same brokerage as the seller. To legally proceed with this dual agency situation, the licensee should:
A. Request approval from the real estate commission before closing
B. Obtain written informed consent from both the buyer and seller before continuing representation ✓
C. Inform both parties verbally and document it in email later
D. Proceed only if the seller agrees, since they are the listing client
Answer: B. Both parties must give written informed consent before dual agency can proceed. Verbal consent, email documentation alone, or single-party approval does not meet the legal standard.
Q 5.3·v4 What is the mandatory requirement for a real estate licensee engaged in dual agency in Hawaii?
A. Written informed consent must be obtained and signed by both the buyer and the seller ✓
B. Only a phone call disclosure to each party is required
C. The managing broker's verbal approval is sufficient
D. The buyer must consent; seller consent is implied by the listing agreement
Answer: A. Hawaii law mandates written informed consent from both parties before a licensee can act as a dual agent. Implied consent, phone calls, or broker approval alone do not satisfy this requirement.
Q 5.3·v5 When a real estate licensee in Hawaii represents both the seller and the buyer in the same transaction, what is legally required?
A. File a dual agency disclosure with the Hawaii Real Estate Commission before closing
B. Obtain oral acknowledgment from the seller only
C. Obtain documented written consent from each party acknowledging the dual representation ✓
D. Receive written approval from the buyer's lender
Answer: C. Dual agency in Hawaii requires written informed consent from both parties, not just oral acknowledgment or one-sided approval. The licensee must ensure both parties understand and accept the conflict.
Q 5.3·v6 A Hawaii licensee who acts as agent for both parties in a real estate transaction must obtain:
A. A notarized statement from one party only
B. Verbal permission from the party they contacted first
C. Approval from the listing broker before proceeding with the transaction
D. Written informed consent acknowledging dual agency from both the seller and buyer ✓
Answer: D. Both parties must provide written informed consent to the dual agency arrangement; verbal consent or single-party consent is insufficient and does not meet Hawaii's legal requirements.
Q 5.3·v7 To lawfully engage in dual representation, a licensee must:
A. Obtain consent from whichever party has the larger financial stake
B. Secure written informed consent from both parties to the dual agency arrangement ✓
C. Disclose the dual agency to the Hawaii Real Estate Commission in writing before acceptance of offer
D. Inform both parties verbally and document it in the MLS remarks
Answer: B. Written informed consent from both parties is the legal standard for dual agency; verbal disclosure or selective consent does not satisfy Hawaii's statutory requirements.
Q 5.3·v8 In Hawaii, a licensee representing both the seller and buyer in a single transaction must ensure that:
A. The buyer's agent is notified in writing instead of obtaining client consent
B. Both parties sign a written document acknowledging and consenting to the dual agency ✓
C. The seller provides written consent and the buyer provides verbal consent
D. Only the party paying the commission is informed of the dual representation
Answer: B. Both the seller and buyer must provide written consent acknowledging the dual agency; partial consent (one written, one verbal) or notifying third parties does not substitute for full informed consent from both parties.
Q 5.3·v9 When a real estate licensee represents both the buyer and seller in the same transaction, what documentation is required?
A. A single disclosure form signed by the buyer is sufficient
B. Oral permission from the seller and written permission from the buyer
C. No formal documentation if the parties are aware of the arrangement
D. Written acknowledgment of dual agency from each party ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires written informed consent from both parties when a licensee acts as a dual agent, ensuring each party understands the conflict and agrees in writing.
Q 5.4 The agent's duty to a non-represented customer includes:
A. Loyalty
B. Honesty and material-fact disclosure ✓
C. Negotiation on their behalf
D. Confidentiality
Answer: B. Agents owe honesty and disclosure of known material defects to all parties.
Q 5.4·v1 When showing property to an unrepresented buyer, what obligation does the listing agent have?
A. Responsibility to advise the buyer on financing options
B. Duty to disclose all known material facts about the property ✓
C. Obligation to keep all conversations confidential from the seller
D. Fiduciary duty to maximize the buyer's offer
Answer: B. Agents must disclose known material facts to all parties, including unrepresented customers, regardless of representation status.
Q 5.4·v2 An unrepresented customer inquires about a property defect you know exists. Your responsibility is to:
A. Provide honest information and material-fact disclosure about the property condition ✓
B. Demonstrate loyalty by withholding information that might deter their offer
C. Negotiate repairs on their behalf as a goodwill gesture
D. Maintain absolute confidentiality unless the buyer signs a representation agreement
Answer: A. All agents must disclose known material facts honestly to unrepresented parties; this is a universal duty owed to protect the public.
Q 5.4·v3 Which of the following best describes what a licensee owes to a customer without representation?
A. Honesty in all dealings and disclosure of known material information ✓
B. Exclusive loyalty similar to a represented client
C. Commission protection and negotiation assistance
D. Full fiduciary duties including confidentiality and advocacy
Answer: A. Non-represented customers receive honesty and material-fact disclosure but not fiduciary duties like loyalty or confidentiality.
Q 5.4·v4 A broker's salesperson is working with a walk-in customer who has not signed any buyer agency agreement. The agent must:
A. Treat them as a client and provide undivided loyalty
B. Exclusively negotiate in the customer's favor
C. Disclose all known material defects and deal honestly with them ✓
D. Keep information confidential to protect the transaction
Answer: C. Agents owe honesty and disclosure of material facts to all parties, which is a non-negotiable duty regardless of agency status.
Q 5.4·v5 When a licensee interacts with an unrepresented party in a transaction, what obligation does the agent have?
A. Fiduciary loyalty to protect their interests
B. Keeping all transaction details confidential from the seller's agent
C. Disclosure of known material facts and honest dealing ✓
D. Acting as their transaction coordinator without compensation
Answer: C. All agents must disclose material facts honestly to unrepresented parties, even without a client relationship; this is a statutory duty, not a fiduciary one.
Q 5.4·v6 A buyer attends an open house without representation. The listing agent's primary duty to this unrepresented buyer is to:
A. Inform the buyer of material facts about the property that the agent knows ✓
B. Provide exclusive market analysis and comparative pricing
C. Negotiate the best possible price on the buyer's behalf
D. Refrain from disclosing known defects to avoid liability
Answer: A. Agents must disclose known material facts to all parties regardless of representation; this duty of honesty applies universally in Hawaii real estate transactions.
Q 5.4·v7 Which statement correctly describes an agent's responsibilities when working with a non-client?
A. The agent owes them undivided loyalty and confidentiality
B. The agent must act in the customer's best interest above all other parties
C. The agent has no obligations unless there is a signed buyer or seller agreement
D. The agent must honestly disclose material defects and facts about the property ✓
Answer: D. Even without a representation agreement, licensees are required by law to provide honest information and disclose material facts to unrepresented parties.
Q 5.4·v8 An unrepresented seller contacts a listing agent before the property is listed. What is the agent's duty?
A. To withhold opinions about the property's condition to avoid liability
B. To keep all information confidential until a listing agreement is signed
C. To advocate exclusively for the buyer to ensure a fair market price
D. To provide honest disclosure of known material property facts and defects ✓
Answer: D. Licensees must disclose known material facts honestly to all parties, including unrepresented individuals, as a fundamental ethical and legal obligation in Hawaii.
Q 5.4·v9 When working with an unrepresented third party during a transaction, what obligation does a real estate licensee have?
A. Full fiduciary duty identical to represented clients
B. Keeping all transaction details confidential from the other party's agent
C. Acting as a neutral intermediary to negotiate better terms for them
D. Truthful disclosure of known material facts affecting the property ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires licensees to disclose material facts truthfully to all parties, represented or not, though unrepresented parties do not receive fiduciary duties like loyalty or confidentiality.
Q 5.5 Agency by operation of law terminates upon:
A. Property destruction
B. Death of the principal
C. Bankruptcy of the agent
D. All of the above ✓
Answer: D. All three end agency without further action.
Q 5.5·v1 Which of the following events automatically terminates an agency relationship without requiring express notice or formal revocation?
A. The agent's decision to resign with 30 days' notice
B. Death of the principal, destruction of the subject property, or insolvency of the agent ✓
C. Mutual written agreement between agent and principal
D. Expiration of the listing period stated in the listing agreement
Answer: B. Agency by operation of law terminates automatically upon death of the principal, destruction of the property, or bankruptcy of the agent—none require affirmative action to end the relationship.
Q 5.5·v2 A real estate licensee's agency with a property owner ends automatically by operation of law if which of the following occurs?
A. The MLS listing is suspended temporarily
B. The buyer fails to make an offer within the listing period
C. The property is damaged beyond repair, the owner dies, or the licensee becomes insolvent ✓
D. The owner requests a price reduction
Answer: C. Property destruction, principal's death, and agent bankruptcy all terminate agency by operation of law without additional steps or notice requirements.
Q 5.5·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, agency by operation of law is terminated automatically when:
A. The principal becomes deceased, the property is destroyed, or the agent enters bankruptcy ✓
B. The principal files a complaint with the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
C. Either party declines to renew at the end of the contract term
D. Only the agent resigns in writing
Answer: A. Death of the principal, destruction of the subject property, and bankruptcy of the agent all terminate agency by operation of law without any further action needed.
Q 5.5·v4 Which scenario would result in immediate termination of an agency relationship by operation of law?
A. The principal dies, the property is destroyed, or the agent becomes insolvent ✓
B. The agent receives a better job offer elsewhere
C. A title defect is discovered during the marketing period
D. The listing agreement contains a 90-day cancellation clause
Answer: A. Agency terminates by operation of law upon death of the principal, destruction of property, or agent bankruptcy—these occur automatically without requiring notice or consent.
Q 5.5·v5 Which of the following events will automatically terminate an agency relationship without requiring explicit notice or agreement?
A. Mutual written agreement only
B. Expiration of the listing period alone
C. The agent's decision to relocate to another state
D. Death of the principal, destruction of the subject property, and insolvency of the agent ✓
Answer: D. Agency by operation of law terminates automatically upon death of the principal, property destruction, or bankruptcy/insolvency of the agent without further action needed.
Q 5.5·v6 A principal's agency with a broker is terminated by operation of law in which scenario?
A. A buyer makes an unsolicited inquiry
B. The broker receives a competing offer on the property
C. The principal requests a rate reduction
D. The principal becomes incapacitated, the subject property is destroyed, or the broker files for bankruptcy ✓
Answer: D. Agency by operation of law terminates automatically upon principal's incapacity (death), destruction of property, or agent's insolvency without requiring affirmative termination steps.
Q 5.5·v7 Under Hawaii real estate law, which of the following will NOT automatically end an agency relationship by operation of law?
A. Bankruptcy of the agent
B. Passage of time beyond the original listing period ✓
C. Death of the principal
D. Physical destruction of the listed property
Answer: B. Passage of time requires affirmative action or mutual agreement to terminate; death of principal, bankruptcy of agent, and property destruction terminate agency by operation of law automatically.
Q 5.5·v8 A real estate agent's authority to represent a principal terminates automatically by operation of law when:
A. The agent fails to produce a buyer within 30 days
B. Either party expresses dissatisfaction with the agreement
C. The property listing appears on the MLS system
D. The principal dies, the subject property is destroyed, or the agent becomes insolvent ✓
Answer: D. These three occurrences—principal death, property destruction, and agent bankruptcy—are statutory grounds for automatic termination without requiring notice or further action.
Q 5.5·v9 Which of the following events will automatically terminate an agency relationship without requiring notice or further action?
A. The agent's insolvency, the principal's death, or destruction of the subject property ✓
B. The agent's failure to perform marketing duties as promised
C. The expiration of the listing period specified in the contract
D. The principal's request to terminate the listing agreement
Answer: A. Agency by operation of law terminates automatically upon death of the principal, bankruptcy/insolvency of the agent, or destruction of the property—all occur without need for affirmative action or notice. The other options require active steps or are contractual matters, not automatic terminations.
Q 5.6 Which is NOT a fiduciary duty?
A. Obedience
B. Care
C. Loyalty
D. Disclosure to customers ✓
Answer: D. Fiduciary duties are owed to the client, not the customer.
Q 5.6·v1 A real estate licensee owes fiduciary duties to their principal client. Which of the following is owed only to customers, not to clients?
A. Undivided loyalty
B. Accounting of funds
C. Reasonable care and skill
D. Honesty in dealings ✓
Answer: D. Fiduciary duties (loyalty, care, obedience, accounting, disclosure to the client) are owed to principals; honesty in dealings is the standard owed to all parties including customers.
Q 5.6·v2 Under Hawaii real estate law, which duty does a licensee owe to a customer but NOT as a fiduciary obligation to a client?
A. Fair and honest treatment ✓
B. Obedience to lawful instructions
C. Confidentiality of client information
D. Loyalty to the principal's interests
Answer: A. Fair and honest treatment is a general duty owed to all parties, while fiduciary duties (obedience, confidentiality, loyalty) are specific obligations owed only to the principal client.
Q 5.6·v3 A listing agent represents the seller as a client. Which obligation is NOT a fiduciary duty owed to that client?
A. Maintaining undivided loyalty to the seller
B. Following the seller's lawful instructions
C. Providing honest information to unrepresented third parties ✓
D. Accounting for earnest money deposits
Answer: C. Providing honest information to unrepresented third parties is a duty owed to all parties in a transaction, not a fiduciary duty specific to the client.
Q 5.6·v4 Which of the following is a fiduciary duty owed to a principal but would NOT apply to a customer in a non-agency relationship?
A. Loyalty
B. Care
C. Obedience
D. Transparency regarding market conditions ✓
Answer: D. Transparency regarding market conditions is a standard ethical obligation owed to all parties; fiduciary duties (obedience, care, loyalty) are owed exclusively to the client.
Q 5.6·v5 A real estate licensee owes fiduciary duties to their client. Which of the following is a duty owed to customers but NOT a fiduciary duty?
A. Loyalty to the principal
B. Honest and fair dealing
C. Full disclosure of all material facts ✓
D. Accounting for client funds
Answer: C. Fiduciary duties (loyalty, care, obedience, accounting) are owed only to the client/principal. Disclosure of material facts is owed to all parties as a legal obligation, but it is not a fiduciary duty.
Q 5.6·v6 Under Hawaii real estate law, which duty does a broker NOT owe to a customer who is not their client?
A. Care and diligence in performing tasks
B. Obedience to lawful instructions ✓
C. Honesty in all dealings
D. Confidentiality regarding privileged information
Answer: B. Obedience is a fiduciary duty owed exclusively to the client/principal. Customers receive honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts, but not the fiduciary duty of obedience.
Q 5.6·v7 When a licensee represents a buyer as their client, which of the following is NOT among the fiduciary duties owed to that client?
A. Timely disclosure of known defects to all parties ✓
B. Competent and diligent representation
C. Following lawful client instructions
D. Undivided loyalty
Answer: A. Timely disclosure of material facts is a legal duty owed to all parties, not a fiduciary duty reserved for the client. The four fiduciary duties are loyalty, care, obedience, and accounting.
Q 5.6·v8 Which statement best distinguishes a fiduciary duty from a duty owed to the general public?
A. Obedience and care are general duties owed to all transaction parties equally
B. Disclosure of material defects is a fiduciary duty owed exclusively to the principal
C. Customers receive fiduciary duties but at a lower standard than clients
D. Fiduciary duties include accounting and loyalty, which apply only to clients ✓
Answer: D. Fiduciary duties (loyalty, obedience, care, accounting) are owed only to the client/principal. Disclosure to the general public is a legal obligation but not a fiduciary duty.
Q 5.6·v9 A real estate licensee owes fiduciary duties to their principal client. Which of the following is owed only to third parties (customers) and NOT as a fiduciary duty?
A. Undivided loyalty
B. Obedience to lawful instructions
C. Reasonable care and skill
D. Honest and fair dealing ✓
Answer: D. Honest and fair dealing is a duty owed to all parties (customers and clients), but it is not a fiduciary duty. Fiduciary duties—loyalty, care, obedience, and accounting—are owed exclusively to the principal client.
Q 5.7 "This is a great property" is most likely:
A. Puffing ✓
B. Material fact
C. Fraud
D. Misrepresentation
Answer: A. Subjective opinion = puffing, not actionable.
Q 5.7·v1 A listing agent tells a buyer, "You'll absolutely love this home—it's the best value in the neighborhood." What type of statement is this?
A. Material fact that must be disclosed in writing
B. Puffing or sales talk not binding as fact ✓
C. Actionable misrepresentation requiring rescission
D. Fraudulent concealment subject to damages
Answer: B. Subjective praise ('best value,' 'absolutely love') constitutes puffing—opinion-based seller's talk that does not rise to the level of a material fact or misrepresentation.
Q 5.7·v2 During a showing, a salesperson states, "This is a wonderful home with amazing potential." How should this statement be classified?
A. Fraud requiring intent to deceive
B. A fiduciary duty violation
C. Puffery—non-factual opinion language ✓
D. A material fact that affects property value
Answer: C. Terms like 'wonderful' and 'amazing potential' are subjective expressions of opinion (puffery) rather than verifiable facts, and thus are not actionable as misrepresentation.
Q 5.7·v3 When a real estate agent describes a property as "charming and delightful," this statement is most accurately characterized as:
A. An implied warranty of condition
B. A material fact requiring full disclosure
C. Intentional misrepresentation
D. Sales puffing based on subjective opinion ✓
Answer: D. Adjectives describing aesthetic appeal ('charming,' 'delightful') reflect personal opinion rather than verifiable facts, making them puffing rather than actionable misrepresentation.
Q 5.7·v4 A broker's statement that "this is one of the finest properties I've ever listed" most likely constitutes:
A. Breach of the duty of honest dealing
B. Material nondisclosure of a latent defect
C. Puffing—subjective opinion not binding as fact ✓
D. Fraudulent inducement due to exaggeration
Answer: C. Subjective evaluations of quality or personal impression ('finest properties') are classic examples of puffing, which is permissible sales rhetoric and not legally binding.
Q 5.7·v5 A listing agent tells a prospective buyer, "You'll love the views from this lanai." This statement is best classified as:
A. A material misrepresentation subject to rescission
B. Fraudulent concealment
C. A breach of fiduciary duty
D. Puffing or seller's talk ✓
Answer: D. Subjective expressions of opinion or value (like 'love the views') are puffing and not actionable misrepresentation because they are not presented as verifiable facts.
Q 5.7·v6 During a showing, a broker says, "This is one of the finest homes in the neighborhood." From a legal standpoint, this statement would most likely be deemed:
A. An express warranty of condition
B. Non-actionable puffery ✓
C. Fraudulent inducement
D. Fraud requiring criminal intent
Answer: B. General laudatory statements about quality or desirability are considered puffing—harmless opinions that buyers are expected to disregard or verify independently.
Q 5.7·v7 Which of the following statements by a real estate agent would be protected as non-actionable opinion rather than actionable misrepresentation?
A. "The roof was inspected last year and passed." (when it was not)
B. "The property has never flooded." (when it has)
C. "This is a wonderful investment opportunity." ✓
D. "The zoning allows commercial use." (when it does not)
Answer: C. Only subjective assessments of value, desirability, or quality constitute puffing; false statements about specific facts, conditions, or legal matters are misrepresentations.
Q 5.7·v8 A salesperson states, "This is a fantastic property at a great price." If a buyer relied on this statement and later sued, the court would most likely classify it as:
A. Negligent misrepresentation requiring proof of damages
B. Seller puffery and opinion, not legally actionable ✓
C. Innocent misrepresentation voiding the contract
D. Actionable fraud due to false statements of material fact
Answer: B. Vague, subjective praise about a property's quality or value is recognized as puffing—ordinary sales talk that reasonable buyers are expected to evaluate skeptically rather than rely on as fact.
Q 5.7·v9 A listing agent tells a prospective buyer that a home has "the best views in the neighborhood." This statement is most appropriately classified as:
A. A material fact that must be disclosed in writing
B. Puffing or sales talk that is not legally actionable ✓
C. Non-disclosure of a latent defect
D. Fraudulent misrepresentation requiring rescission
Answer: B. Subjective praise and comparative opinions ('best,' 'great') constitute puffing—non-actionable seller talk rather than factual misrepresentation or fraud.
Q 5.8 A buyer-broker agreement creates:
A. A fiduciary relationship with the buyer ✓
B. No legal relationship
C. Subagency only
D. A customer relationship
Answer: A. Buyer-broker agreement = express agency with buyer as principal.
Q 5.8·v1 When a real estate licensee enters into a written buyer-broker agreement with a consumer, what type of relationship is established?
A. An express agency relationship where the buyer is the principal ✓
B. A non-agency customer relationship with limited duties
C. A dual agency relationship with both buyer and seller
D. A transactional coordination role with no fiduciary obligations
Answer: A. A buyer-broker agreement creates an express agency relationship, making the buyer the principal and establishing fiduciary duties of loyalty, disclosure, and care.
Q 5.8·v2 Which statement best describes the legal consequence of signing a buyer-broker agreement?
A. The broker owes fiduciary duties to the buyer as the broker's client ✓
B. The broker becomes a subagent of the seller's agent
C. The relationship remains undefined until an offer is made
D. The broker acts as a transaction facilitator with no agency duties
Answer: A. A buyer-broker agreement establishes a fiduciary relationship where the broker owes the buyer duties of loyalty, honesty, and full disclosure as a client, not a customer.
Q 5.8·v3 A buyer signs a buyer-broker agreement with an agent. This agreement primarily establishes:
A. A fiduciary duty-based relationship between agent and buyer ✓
B. That the buyer is a customer with no legal protections
C. That the agent is compensated by the multiple listing service
D. That the agent represents the seller exclusively
Answer: A. The buyer-broker agreement creates an agency relationship where the broker/agent has fiduciary obligations to the buyer, who becomes the principal in the relationship.
Q 5.8·v4 Under Hawaii real estate law, when a buyer executes a buyer-broker agreement, the broker:
A. Retains only transactional duties without agency obligations
B. Functions as a neutral third party with no allegiance to either party
C. Assumes a fiduciary position with the buyer as principal ✓
D. Represents the seller and owes duties to the seller only
Answer: C. A buyer-broker agreement creates express agency with fiduciary duties running from the broker to the buyer as the principal.
Q 5.8·v5 When a real estate licensee and a prospective buyer execute a buyer-broker agreement, what legal relationship is established between them?
A. A dual agency arrangement requiring written consent from all parties
B. A fiduciary duty owed by the broker to the buyer as principal ✓
C. A transactional facilitator role with no agency duties
D. An independent contractor relationship with limited liability
Answer: B. A buyer-broker agreement creates express agency, establishing fiduciary duties owed by the broker to the buyer who is the principal in the relationship.
Q 5.8·v6 A buyer signs a representation agreement with a broker. This agreement results in:
A. A non-agency customer arrangement with disclosure requirements
B. Mutual obligations with no agency duties on either party
C. Fiduciary obligations running from the broker to the buyer ✓
D. The broker acting as a subagent of the listing agent only
Answer: C. Buyer representation agreements create express agency wherein the broker owes fiduciary duties to the buyer as the client and principal.
Q 5.8·v7 Which best describes the relationship created when a buyer enters into a written agreement with a broker to represent the buyer's interests in a real estate transaction?
A. Limited agency with shared responsibilities between broker and buyer
B. Customer status with the broker acting as a transaction facilitator
C. Subagency of the seller's broker with divided loyalty
D. Principal-agent relationship with fiduciary duties owed to the buyer ✓
Answer: D. A written buyer-broker agreement creates a principal-agent relationship where the broker becomes the agent owing fiduciary duties to the buyer as principal.
Q 5.8·v8 A buyer executes a buyer-broker agreement. The legal consequence is that the broker:
A. Becomes a transaction coordinator without fiduciary responsibility
B. Acts as the seller's subagent in all matters
C. Functions as a neutral third party with no agency authority
D. Owes fiduciary duties to the buyer as the broker's client ✓
Answer: D. A buyer-broker agreement creates express agency, making the buyer the broker's client to whom fiduciary duties are owed.
Q 5.8·v9 When a real estate licensee and a buyer execute a buyer-broker agreement, what legal relationship is established between them?
A. A limited agency relationship with the seller as the primary principal
B. The buyer is classified as a customer with no agency protection
C. The broker owes fiduciary duties to the buyer as the client ✓
D. The licensee becomes a transaction coordinator with limited liability
Answer: C. A buyer-broker agreement creates express agency, making the broker a fiduciary bound to the buyer (the principal), not a limited or transaction-only service provider.
Q 5.9 When an agent's authority is delegated to another agent in a different brokerage, it's called:
A. Subagency ✓
B. Universal agency
C. Dual agency
D. Implied agency
Answer: A. Subagency = delegated authority. Cooperating broker as subagent of listing broker.
Q 5.9·v1 A listing broker authorizes a cooperating broker from another firm to represent the seller in a transaction. This relationship is best described as:
A. Subagency ✓
B. Non-delegable fiduciary duty
C. Expressed agency
D. Transactional brokerage
Answer: A. Subagency occurs when a listing broker delegates authority to a cooperating broker in a different brokerage to act on behalf of the principal.
Q 5.9·v2 If Broker A transfers her authority to Broker B, who works for a separate real estate company, what type of agency relationship exists between Broker A and Broker B?
A. Limited agency
B. Subagency ✓
C. Dual agency
D. Ostensible agency
Answer: B. Subagency is the delegation of real estate authority from one broker to another broker in a different brokerage to act as agent for the original principal.
Q 5.9·v3 Under the traditional MLS cooperation model, when a cooperating broker from a different firm helps a listing broker sell property, the cooperating broker acts as:
A. A dual agent
B. A principal
C. An independent contractor without authority
D. A subagent of the listing broker ✓
Answer: D. The cooperating broker receives delegated authority from the listing broker and becomes a subagent, representing the same principal through the original broker's authorization.
Q 5.9·v4 When authority is passed down from one brokerage to another brokerage in a real estate transaction, this delegation creates a relationship known as:
A. Designated agency
B. Subagency ✓
C. General agency
D. Power of attorney
Answer: B. Subagency is specifically the term for delegated authority granted by one broker to another broker in a different firm to act on behalf of the original principal.
Q 5.9·v5 A listing broker transfers the power to act on the seller's behalf to an agent at another brokerage firm. This relationship is best described as:
A. Subagency ✓
B. Designated agency
C. Ostensible agency
D. Implied agency
Answer: A. Subagency occurs when a broker delegates authority to another broker or agent outside their firm to represent the same principal. This is a formal delegation of the original agent's authority.
Q 5.9·v6 When a cooperating broker accepts the authority to represent a seller through delegation from the listing broker, what is this agent relationship called?
A. Subagency ✓
B. Transactional agency
C. Limited agency
D. General agency
Answer: A. Subagency is the delegation of an agent's authority to another agent in a different brokerage firm, creating a chain of authority back to the original principal.
Q 5.9·v7 An agent from Broker A authorizes an agent from Broker B to perform acts on behalf of their mutual client. This arrangement is known as:
A. Subagency ✓
B. Power of attorney
C. Dual agency
D. Fiduciary agency
Answer: A. Subagency is the delegation of authority from one agent to another agent in a different brokerage; the subagent owes fiduciary duties to the original principal through the delegating agent.
Q 5.9·v8 If a listing agent's brokerage delegates its authority to represent a seller to an agent at a different firm, the delegated agent holds what type of agency?
A. Coupled agency
B. Subagency ✓
C. Undisclosed agency
D. Exclusive agency
Answer: B. Subagency is the formal delegation of an agent's authority to another agent at a different brokerage, allowing the subagent to act as an authorized representative of the principal.
Q 5.9·v9 A listing broker transfers their authority to represent the seller to a cooperating broker in another firm. This relationship is known as:
A. Transactional brokerage
B. Designated agency
C. Implied agency
D. Subagency ✓
Answer: D. Subagency occurs when a broker delegates their fiduciary authority to another broker in a different firm to act on behalf of the principal. The cooperating broker becomes the subagent of the listing broker.
Q 5.10 A power of attorney typically creates a:
A. Universal agency ✓
B. Special agency
C. General agency
D. Subagency
Answer: A. POA = authority to act in all (legal) matters = universal agency.
Q 5.10·v1 When a principal executes a power of attorney document, what type of agency relationship is established?
A. Limited agency restricted to a single transaction
B. Subagency created through a broker relationship
C. Special agency confined to real estate transactions only
D. Universal agency with broad authority over all matters ✓
Answer: D. A power of attorney grants the agent authority to act on behalf of the principal in all legal matters, creating a universal agency relationship with comprehensive powers.
Q 5.10·v2 A principal who grants a power of attorney to an attorney-in-fact is creating which classification of agency?
A. General agency
B. Special agency for a particular task
C. Universal agency ✓
D. Exclusive agency
Answer: C. A POA establishes universal agency because it authorizes the agent to represent the principal in all legal and financial matters, not just specific transactions.
Q 5.10·v3 What type of agency relationship results when an individual executes a power of attorney?
A. Subagency through broker delegation
B. Special agency for defined purposes
C. General agency limited to business transactions
D. Universal agency with comprehensive authority ✓
Answer: D. A power of attorney creates a universal agency because it grants the agent plenary authority to act in virtually all matters on behalf of the principal.
Q 5.10·v4 If a principal signs a power of attorney document, the agent receives which type of agency status?
A. Bilateral agency
B. Universal agency ✓
C. Special agency restricted in scope
D. Limited agency for single transactions
Answer: B. A POA creates a universal agency, meaning the agent has broad authority to represent the principal across all legal and financial matters within the document's scope.
Q 5.10·v5 When a principal grants a power of attorney to an agent, what type of agency relationship is established?
A. Ostensible agency based solely on apparent authority
B. Universal agency with broad authority across all legal matters ✓
C. Limited agency restricted to real estate transactions only
