D. Exclusive agency preventing the principal from acting independently
Answer: B. A power of attorney grants the agent broad authority to act in all legal matters on behalf of the principal, creating a universal agency relationship.
Q 5.10·v6 Which agency classification best describes the relationship created by executing a power of attorney document?
A. Special agency for designated transactions
B. Subagency
C. Dual agency with disclosed principals
D. Universal agency ✓
Answer: D. POA grants comprehensive legal authority across all matters, establishing a universal agency rather than limited or special agency authority.
Q 5.10·v7 A principal executes a power of attorney giving an agent authority to handle financial, legal, and personal affairs. This creates what type of agency?
A. Special agency for specific enumerated powers
B. Fiduciary agency requiring court approval
C. General agency limited to business transactions
D. Universal agency with comprehensive delegated authority ✓
Answer: D. Authority to manage financial, legal, and personal affairs demonstrates universal agency—the broadest form of delegated authority covering all legal matters.
Q 5.10·v8 Under Hawaiian real estate law, when a client grants a power of attorney to another person, the resulting agency is classified as:
A. Universal agency encompassing authority over all legal and business matters ✓
B. Implied agency created by conduct rather than document
C. Probate agency requiring estate administration approval
D. Special agency tied to one specific property transaction
Answer: A. A power of attorney is the legal instrument that establishes universal agency, granting the agent sweeping authority to act in all legal matters on the principal's behalf.
Q 5.10·v9 When a principal executes a power of attorney document, what type of agency relationship is established?
A. Limited agency restricted to financial transactions only
B. Designated agency covering only property management duties
C. Universal agency with broad authority over all legal matters ✓
D. Transactional agency for a single real estate closing
Answer: C. A power of attorney grants the agent (attorney-in-fact) broad authority to act on behalf of the principal in all legal matters, which constitutes universal agency rather than limited or specific agency types.
Q 5.11 Confidentiality duty:
A. Ends at closing
B. Applies only to commercial transactions
C. Applies only to written information
D. Continues after agency termination ✓
Answer: D. Confidentiality survives agency termination.
Q 5.11·v1 A real estate agent's duty to maintain client confidentiality:
A. Persists indefinitely, even after the agency relationship dissolves ✓
B. Only extends to conversations documented in writing
C. Lapses upon execution of the purchase agreement
D. Is limited to residential sales and excludes commercial property
Answer: A. The confidentiality duty is fiduciary in nature and survives the termination of the agency relationship, continuing to protect client information indefinitely.
Q 5.11·v2 When does an agent's obligation to keep client information confidential end?
A. When the listing period expires, regardless of sale status
B. Only for oral disclosures; written documents become public record
C. At the time escrow closes and funds transfer
D. It does not end; confidentiality obligations extend beyond agency termination ✓
Answer: D. Confidentiality is a fiduciary duty that transcends the termination of the brokerage relationship and remains binding on the agent perpetually.
Q 5.11·v3 Which statement correctly describes the scope and duration of an agent's confidentiality duty in Hawaii real estate transactions?
A. It applies to all transaction types and survives the end of the agency relationship ✓
B. It covers only documented communications and ends when the broker-client relationship is discharged
C. It applies only to residential properties and terminates at settlement
D. It is limited to information disclosed verbally and expires upon contract ratification
Answer: A. Confidentiality applies across all property types and transaction structures, and remains in effect after the agency relationship concludes as a continuing fiduciary obligation.
Q 5.11·v4 After a real estate agency relationship terminates, which obligation continues without interruption?
A. Duty to maintain confidentiality of client information ✓
B. Duty to attend open houses and showings
C. Duty to market the property on active listing services
D. Duty to provide monthly market analysis reports
Answer: A. The confidentiality duty is a fiduciary obligation that persists beyond agency termination, unlike other duties that end when the relationship dissolves.
Q 5.11·v5 After a real estate agency relationship is terminated, an agent's duty of confidentiality:
A. Expires immediately upon termination
B. Only applies to transactions valued above $500,000
C. Covers only oral statements made during the listing period
D. Persists indefinitely with respect to client information ✓
Answer: D. Confidentiality is a fiduciary duty that survives the termination of agency; agents remain bound to protect client confidences after the relationship ends.
Q 5.11·v6 Which statement correctly describes the scope of an agent's confidentiality obligation in Hawaii?
A. It only protects information disclosed in writing by the client
B. It terminates when the purchase and sale agreement is executed
C. It applies exclusively to residential properties, not commercial ones
D. It extends beyond the conclusion of the agency relationship ✓
Answer: D. Confidentiality duty persists after agency termination and protects all client information regardless of how it was disclosed or the property type involved.
Q 5.11·v7 An agent receives confidential information from a client during a listing engagement. Once the listing expires and the agency terminates, the agent:
A. Is released from all duties except those required by written contract
B. Only remains bound to keep information secret if it pertains to the physical property condition
C. May disclose the information to prospective buyers or other parties
D. Must continue to protect the confidential information ✓
Answer: D. The duty of confidentiality persists after agency termination and requires agents to maintain client secrets even after the relationship concludes.
Q 5.11·v8 Regarding confidentiality obligations, a licensee's duty to keep client information private:
A. Applies only to factual disclosures, not to opinions or observations
B. Is waived if the information becomes public knowledge through other sources
C. Lasts only until the transaction closes
D. Continues even after the agent-client relationship is dissolved ✓
Answer: D. Confidentiality is a post-termination fiduciary duty that survives agency dissolution and obligates licensees to protect client confidences indefinitely.
Q 5.11·v9 A real estate agent's duty to maintain confidentiality of client information:
A. Must be disclosed to all third parties upon request
B. Only applies to residential properties and not commercial deals
C. Is limited to facts known in writing before the transaction closes
D. Persists even after the agency relationship has been dissolved ✓
Answer: D. The confidentiality duty is fiduciary in nature and survives the termination of agency, protecting client information indefinitely after the relationship ends.
Q 5.12 A seller tells the agent the basement floods. The agent is asked by a buyer about water issues. The agent must:
A. Disclose the known defect ✓
B. Refer the buyer to the seller only
C. Honor seller wishes and stay silent
D. Disclose only if buyer asks twice
Answer: A. Material defects must be disclosed to all parties; agent has independent duty.
Q 5.12·v1 During a listing appointment, the seller discloses to the agent that the roof has a history of leaks during heavy rain. When the agent shows the property to a prospective buyer, the buyer does not inquire about the roof condition. What is the agent's obligation?
A. Voluntarily disclose the known roof defect regardless of whether the buyer asks ✓
B. Document the disclosure only if the buyer signs an acknowledgment form
C. Wait for the buyer to ask specifically about roof leaks before mentioning the issue
D. Suggest the buyer hire an inspector and avoid commenting on known defects
Answer: A. Agents have an independent fiduciary duty to disclose known material defects to all prospective buyers, even without direct questioning. Staying silent to protect the seller violates Hawaii's disclosure requirements.
Q 5.12·v2 An agent discovers through the seller that the property's electrical system has been repeatedly repaired for code violations. A buyer submits an offer without asking about electrical issues. The agent should:
A. Advise the seller to repair the violations before showing the property again
B. Disclose the electrical history as a material defect that could affect property value and safety ✓
C. Only mention the electrical issue if the buyer specifically includes it on the inspection contingency
D. Remain neutral and allow the inspection process to uncover the problem later
Answer: B. Material defects known to the agent must be affirmatively disclosed to buyers as part of the agent's duty of honesty and fair dealing, regardless of buyer inquiry.
Q 5.12·v3 A listing agent learns that the property experienced significant mold remediation in the kitchen two years ago. A buyer views the property and makes an offer. When asked about the property's history, what must the agent do?
A. Inform the buyer that the remediation was completed, so no current disclosure is needed
B. Mention mold only if the buyer's inspector requests historical records
C. Suggest the buyer request all documentation directly from the seller's attorney
D. Disclose the mold remediation history because it is a material fact affecting the property ✓
Answer: D. Prior remediation of a significant defect like mold is a material fact that must be disclosed by the agent, as it informs the buyer of the property's condition and potential risk.
Q 5.12·v4 At a listing presentation, the seller reveals to the agent that the foundation has visible cracks and a structural engineer previously recommended monitoring. Later, a buyer tours the property without commenting on structural concerns. The agent's responsibility is to:
A. Let the buyer's own structural inspector identify the cracks during the inspection period
B. Provide the structural engineer's report only if the buyer requests it in writing
C. Tell the buyer to consult with the seller directly about any structural matters
D. Initiate disclosure of the known foundation issue as a material defect ✓
Answer: D. An agent cannot withhold known material defects based on a buyer's lack of inquiry. The duty to disclose is affirmative and independent of buyer questions or inspection results.
Q 5.12·v5 During a transaction, a listing agent becomes aware that the property has experienced recurring moisture intrusion in the crawl space. When preparing marketing materials, the agent should:
A. Mention it only to buyers who specifically inquire about foundation conditions
B. Allow the seller to decide whether disclosure is necessary
C. Include this information in all disclosures provided to prospective buyers ✓
D. Wait for the buyer's inspector to discover it independently
Answer: C. Real estate agents have an affirmative duty to disclose known material defects to all potential buyers regardless of whether they ask; this duty is independent of the seller's preferences.
Q 5.12·v6 An agent lists a home where the owner mentions that the roof leaks during heavy rains. A prospective buyer asks if there are any known structural issues. The agent's obligation is to:
A. Suggest the buyer obtain a professional inspection before asking further questions
B. Disclose the known roof leak because it is a material defect ✓
C. Refer the buyer directly to the seller for all property condition questions
D. Disclose the defect only if the buyer appears interested in making an offer
Answer: B. Agents must disclose known material facts about the property's condition to all parties; the roof leak is a material defect that directly affects property value and insurability.
Q 5.12·v7 A seller confides in the listing agent that the home's electrical system has intermittent failures. Later, a buyer asks general questions about the property's systems. The agent must:
A. Keep the seller's confidential information private unless the buyer specifically asks about electricity
B. Suggest the buyer hire an electrician if they have concerns
C. Provide honest disclosure of the known electrical issue ✓
D. State that all systems appear to be in working order
Answer: C. Material defects must be affirmatively disclosed as a matter of law and professional ethics; an agent cannot withhold known defects even when the seller requests confidentiality.
Q 5.12·v8 While preparing a property listing, the agent learns that the home has had significant termite damage in the past. When a buyer tours the property and asks if there are any pest-related concerns, the agent should:
A. Avoid the topic unless the buyer specifically mentions termites by name
B. State that current pest control reports are available for the buyer to review
C. Acknowledge the prior termite damage and disclose this material fact ✓
D. Explain that the seller's pest control company can discuss any history
Answer: C. An agent's duty to disclose material defects includes known past structural damage from pests; this information directly affects property value and the buyer's decision-making.
Q 5.12·v9 During a listing appointment, the seller mentions that the property has experienced water intrusion in the crawl space during heavy rains. When a prospective buyer's agent inquires about the foundation and structural condition, the listing agent should:
A. Allow the seller to decide whether to volunteer this information directly to the buyer
B. Affirmatively disclose the known water intrusion problem to protect all parties ✓
C. Wait for the buyer to submit a formal inspection request before mentioning any water issues
D. Suggest the buyer hire a professional inspector without commenting on known defects
Answer: B. Agents have an independent fiduciary duty to disclose material defects known to them, regardless of seller preference or buyer inquiry method; water intrusion is a material defect affecting property value and habitability.
06
Mandated Disclosures
National portion7 PSI items23 key concepts12 base questions

Disclosure failures create more lawsuits than any other licensee mistake. When in doubt — disclose.

Chapter Overview

Sellers in nearly every state must disclose known material defects in writing on a state-mandated form. The form typically asks about plumbing, electrical, roof, structural, environmental hazards, prior repairs, neighborhood conditions, and any pending claims. The agent's role is to facilitate accurate disclosure, not to certify the property's condition. If the agent has actual knowledge of a defect — water in the basement, an undisclosed addition, a foundation crack — the agent must disclose it independently, even if the seller refuses. Misrepresentation by silence is just as actionable as a lie.

A material fact is anything a reasonable buyer or seller would consider important in deciding whether and at what price to transact. The standard is objective: would this matter to a typical buyer? If yes, it's material and must be disclosed if known. Material facts include known defects, boundary disputes, pending litigation, planned road construction, sex-offender notifications (Megan's Law), past flooding, prior fires, prior deaths or stigmatizing events (rules vary by state).

Federal law mandates a Lead-Based Paint Disclosure (the Lead Hazard Information Pamphlet plus the Lead Disclosure Form) for all residential housing built before 1978. Buyers receive a 10-day right to inspect for lead-based paint hazards (which can be waived in writing). Failure to disclose carries per-violation federal penalties. Asbestos, radon, mold, formaldehyde, underground storage tanks, electromagnetic fields, and methamphetamine contamination are increasingly addressed via state-specific forms or general material-fact duties.

Stigmatized property is property where a non-physical event (death, suicide, murder, alleged paranormal activity, criminal activity) has occurred. State rules on disclosure vary widely. Some states require disclosure if asked, others affirmatively, others not at all. HIV/AIDS-related deaths have specific federal protection — generally not disclosable. A licensee's safest stance is disclose-when-asked unless state law clearly says otherwise.

An agent who relays a seller's statement is generally not liable, unless the agent knew or should have known the statement was false. The duty to investigate "red flags" — visible signs of potential problems like water stains, sloping floors, recent paint over one wall — is real. Agents are not inspectors and don't certify, but they can't willfully ignore obvious signs.

"As-is" sales do not eliminate disclosure obligations. The seller is still required to disclose known material defects; the buyer simply accepts the property in its current condition, waiving the right to demand repairs. As-is is about repair allocation, not information disclosure. Many disputes arise when sellers think "as-is" means they don't have to talk about problems — that's wrong.

Latent defects (hidden, not discoverable on reasonable inspection) and patent defects (obvious) have different treatment. Latent defects must be disclosed if known. Patent defects are presumed observed by the buyer; failure to point them out is generally not actionable. The line between latent and patent is a frequent dispute.

Caveat emptor ("let the buyer beware") was the historical rule in real estate. Modern state disclosure statutes have largely supplanted it for residential transactions. Commercial transactions still operate closer to caveat emptor, but professional duties of honesty and material-fact disclosure remain.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Material factA fact a reasonable buyer or seller would consider important in deciding whether and at what price to transact.
MisrepresentationFalse statement of material fact. Can be innocent, negligent, or fraudulent.
Innocent misrepresentationFalse statement made without knowledge of falsity. Still actionable for rescission.
Negligent misrepresentationFalse statement that should have been verified. Damages available.
Fraudulent misrepresentationIntentional false statement. Punitive damages possible.
Misrepresentation by silenceFailure to disclose a known material fact. Actionable as fraud.
PuffingSubjective sales talk ("this is the best house"). Not actionable.
Lead-Based Paint DisclosureFederal law requires for pre-1978 housing. Buyer gets 10-day inspection window + EPA pamphlet + disclosure form.
Megan's LawSex offender registration disclosure. State rules vary on agent duty.
Stigmatized propertyProperty with non-physical issue (death, crime, alleged haunting). State rules vary on disclosure.
Caveat emptor"Let the buyer beware." Largely supplanted by mandatory disclosure laws for residential.
Caveat venditor"Let the seller beware." Modern leaning — sellers must disclose.
Latent defectHidden defect not discoverable on reasonable inspection. Must be disclosed if known.
Patent defectObvious defect visible on reasonable inspection. Generally presumed observed by buyer.
Red flagA visible condition prompting inquiry — water stains, sloping floor, recent isolated paint. Triggers duty to investigate or recommend inspection.
As-is saleBuyer takes property in current condition. Does NOT eliminate disclosure obligations.
CERCLA / SuperfundFederal environmental cleanup law. Strict, joint and several liability.
Mold disclosureRequired in many states. Toxic mold (Stachybotrys) is a major concern.
Radon disclosureNaturally occurring radioactive gas. Federal pamphlet recommended.
AsbestosCommon in pre-1980 construction. Federal AHERA rules for schools; private property has fewer.
Underground storage tankCommon environmental issue on commercial property. RCRA regulated.
Mello-Roos / special districtsTax districts for new development infrastructure (CA term; analogous in other states). Disclosable.
Property condition disclosureState-mandated form listing known material facts about property condition.
Question Bank — Mandated Disclosures
Q 6.1 A licensee learns the basement floods every winter. The seller insists on not disclosing. The agent must:
A. Disclose to buyers anyway ✓
B. Disclose only if asked
C. Resign the listing only
D. Honor seller wishes
Answer: A. Agent has independent duty to disclose known material defects.
Q 6.1·v1 During a property showing, a licensee becomes aware that the roof requires immediate repair due to water damage discovered in the attic. The seller explicitly forbids mentioning this issue to prospective buyers. What is the licensee's obligation?
A. Document the seller's refusal and proceed without disclosure
B. Disclose only structural defects, not cosmetic repairs
C. Wait for the buyer's inspector to find the problem independently
D. Fulfill the affirmative duty to disclose all material facts known to the agent ✓
Answer: D. A licensee has an independent fiduciary duty to disclose all known material defects regardless of seller objections or buyer inquiry.
Q 6.1·v2 A real estate agent representing a seller discovers that the property's septic system failed its last inspection and requires replacement. The owner requests confidentiality about this condition. The agent should:
A. Suggest the seller hire a contractor to fix it before showing
B. Only mention the septic issue if a buyer specifically asks about the system
C. Respect the seller's privacy wishes and remain silent
D. Make the mandatory disclosure of this material defect to all prospective buyers ✓
Answer: D. Agents cannot be bound by seller instructions to withhold material facts; disclosure of known defects is a non-delegable duty.
Q 6.1·v3 While preparing a listing, an agent learns that the home's electrical system has a documented history of circuit failures requiring repeated repairs. The seller states, 'Don't tell anyone about that—we just fixed it.' What must the agent do?
A. Honor the seller's request since the system was recently repaired
B. List the property as-is and let buyers assume all risk
C. Disclose this material defect to buyers despite the seller's objection ✓
D. Only disclose if a buyer's offer includes an inspection contingency
Answer: C. An agent's obligation to disclose known material defects is independent of the seller's wishes and cannot be overridden by recent repairs or seller instructions.
Q 6.1·v4 An agent becomes aware that a property has had multiple insurance claims for mold damage in the past three years. The seller pressures the agent not to include this information in marketing materials or share it with buyers. The licensee must:
A. Disclose the material fact of known mold history to all potential buyers ✓
B. Advise the buyer to conduct their own mold testing instead
C. Comply with the seller's directive to protect the listing
D. Include the information only in the detailed property disclosures, not verbal conversations
Answer: A. Licensees cannot comply with seller instructions to conceal material defects; affirmative disclosure duties exist independently of seller consent.
Q 6.1·v5 During a property showing, a licensee discovers that the roof has persistent leak damage. The seller explicitly forbids disclosure of this condition to prospective buyers. What is the licensee's legal obligation?
A. Keep the information confidential per the listing agreement
B. Document the seller's refusal and proceed with marketing
C. Disclose the known material defect regardless of seller objection ✓
D. Reveal only the defect's existence, not its severity
Answer: C. A licensee has an independent fiduciary and statutory duty to disclose known material defects to potential buyers, regardless of seller preferences or instructions.
Q 6.1·v6 A broker's agent becomes aware that a property has a history of termite infestation. When the agent attempts to include this in the disclosure, the seller threatens to fire the brokerage and work with another agent. The broker should:
A. Allow the buyer to request a termite inspection at their own expense
B. Advise the agent to comply with the seller's demand to maintain the listing
C. Ensure the material defect is disclosed to all prospective buyers ✓
D. Suggest the seller hire a separate pest control company first
Answer: C. The broker and licensee cannot be coerced into non-disclosure; they must fulfill their independent duty to disclose known material facts affecting property value or desirability.
Q 6.1·v7 An agent has personal knowledge that the property's foundation has cracks caused by soil settlement. The seller states that disclosure could tank the sale and asks the agent to keep silent. Which action is permissible under Hawaii real estate law?
A. File a complaint with the REC and withdraw from the transaction
B. Affirmatively disclose the known material defect to all interested parties ✓
C. Wait for the buyer's home inspection to reveal the problem naturally
D. Honor the seller's request and only disclose if a buyer specifically asks about foundation issues
Answer: B. An agent's duty to disclose known material defects is affirmative and independent of seller instructions or buyer inquiries, protecting the integrity of the transaction.
Q 6.1·v8 While listing a property, a licensee learns from neighbors that the home experiences mold growth every summer due to poor drainage. The seller denies there is a problem and instructs the agent not to mention it. The agent must:
A. Obey the seller's directive to remain in their fiduciary role
B. Require the seller to obtain a mold inspection before proceeding
C. Disclose this known material defect to prospective buyers despite the seller's prohibition ✓
D. List the property 'as-is' and let the buyer's inspector discover any issues
Answer: C. Licensees cannot subordinate their duty to disclose known material defects to seller pressure; disclosure is mandatory and protects both buyers and the integrity of the market.
Q 6.1·v9 During a listing presentation, the licensee discovers that the roof leaks during heavy rains—a fact the seller wants kept confidential. What is the licensee's obligation?
A. Suggest the seller repair the roof before listing
B. Wait for a buyer's inspector to find the defect
C. Affirmatively disclose the known material defect to prospective buyers ✓
D. Respect the seller's confidentiality and remain silent
Answer: C. A real estate licensee has an independent fiduciary duty to disclose known material facts affecting property value, regardless of seller instructions or buyer inquiries.
Q 6.2 Lead-based paint disclosure applies to housing built before:
A. 1965
B. 1972
C. 1986
D. 1978 ✓
Answer: D. Pre-1978 residential housing.
Q 6.2·v1 Under federal law, which properties require mandatory lead-based paint disclosures during the sales transaction?
A. Residential structures built prior to 1978 ✓
B. Commercial buildings erected before 1985
C. All residential properties constructed after 1980
D. Single-family homes built after 1990
Answer: A. Federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements apply to residential properties constructed before 1978, when lead paint was commonly used.
Q 6.2·v2 A seller is required to disclose the potential presence of lead-based paint in a home. The disclosure obligation applies when the property was built in:
A. 1975 ✓
B. 1992
C. 1983
D. 2001
Answer: A. Lead-based paint disclosures are mandatory for homes built before 1978; homes built after that year fall outside the disclosure requirement.
Q 6.2·v3 In a real estate transaction, lead-based paint disclosure becomes necessary when dealing with residential property constructed:
A. Between 1975 and 1985
B. Between 1970 and 1980
C. Any year prior to 1978 ✓
D. After 1970 but before 1990
Answer: C. The cut-off year for lead-based paint disclosure requirements is 1978; any residential property built before that date requires disclosure.
Q 6.2·v4 Which timeframe establishes when a residential property is presumed to potentially contain lead-based paint and triggers disclosure requirements?
A. Construction completed before January 1, 1978 ✓
B. Pre-1980 residential development
C. Any structure built prior to 1975
D. Pre-1960 construction
Answer: A. Federal regulations establish 1978 as the threshold year; properties built before that date fall under lead-based paint disclosure requirements.
Q 6.2·v5 Under federal law, residential housing built before a certain year requires disclosure of potential lead-based paint hazards. Housing built before which year is covered?
A. 1970
B. 1978 ✓
C. 1988
D. 1982
Answer: B. The federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement applies to all residential properties constructed before 1978, making 1978 the cutoff year for mandatory disclosure obligations.
Q 6.2·v6 A real estate licensee in Hawaii is listing a single-family home constructed in 1960. Which statement correctly identifies the lead-based paint disclosure requirement?
A. The property was built before the federal lead-based paint disclosure threshold and requires disclosure ✓
B. Disclosure is waived for homes older than 50 years
C. Disclosure applies only to properties built after 1980
D. Disclosure is required only if the property has been tested for lead
Answer: A. Federal law requires lead-based paint disclosure for all residential properties built before 1978, regardless of testing status or age category.
Q 6.2·v7 Which of the following residential properties would trigger a mandatory lead-based paint disclosure requirement?
A. A single-family home built in 1990
B. A townhouse built in 1979
C. A multi-family rental built in 1977 ✓
D. A condominium built in 1985
Answer: C. Pre-1978 construction requires lead-based paint disclosure; the 1977 multi-family rental is the only property built before the 1978 cutoff date.
Q 6.2·v8 A property transaction involves a home originally constructed in 1973. What federal real estate disclosure requirement applies to this transaction?
A. Asbestos encapsulation documentation
B. Lead-based paint hazard disclosure ✓
C. Mold remediation certification
D. Radon gas testing and disclosure only
Answer: B. Properties built before 1978 are subject to federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements; the 1973 construction date falls within the regulated period.
Q 6.2·v9 Under federal law, which properties require a lead-based paint disclosure when being sold or leased?
A. Residential structures built in or before 1977 ✓
B. Commercial buildings and multi-unit dwellings only
C. All residential properties constructed after 1980
D. Single-family homes built between 1970 and 1985
Answer: A. Federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements apply to housing built in 1978 or earlier (pre-1978 residential housing), making 1977 and prior the applicable cutoff date for disclosure obligations.
Q 6.3 "This house has the best view on the street" is most likely:
A. Misrepresentation
B. Fraud
C. Puffing ✓
D. A material fact
Answer: C. Subjective opinion = puffing, allowed.
Q 6.3·v1 A listing agent tells a prospective buyer, "This is the most beautiful home in the neighborhood." This statement would most accurately be classified as:
A. Actionable misrepresentation
B. Fraudulent concealment
C. Puffing or seller's talk ✓
D. A material fact subject to verification
Answer: C. Statements of subjective beauty, aesthetics, or superiority are considered puffing—harmless exaggeration and opinion that the law permits in real estate sales.
Q 6.3·v2 When a seller states, "You won't find a nicer lot anywhere in this area," this claim is most likely to be considered:
A. A legally actionable misstatement of fact
B. Puffing or seller's puffery ✓
C. Fraud requiring proof of intent to deceive
D. A breach of the duty of disclosure
Answer: B. Comparative value judgments and hyperbolic opinions about property quality are classic examples of puffing, which are not actionable misrepresentation under Hawaii real estate law.
Q 6.3·v3 A real estate agent's claim that "This property offers the best investment potential in the subdivision" is best characterized as:
A. A violation requiring rescission
B. Fraud if the agent believes it is false
C. Puffery or non-actionable opinion ✓
D. Misrepresentation of a material fact
Answer: C. Subjective predictions about investment performance and superiority constitute puffing, not material misrepresentation, as they represent opinion rather than verifiable fact.
Q 6.3·v4 If a broker tells clients, "This is the finest home you'll ever see," this statement would most accurately be deemed:
A. Actionable fraud requiring reliance damages
B. Harmless puffing or exaggerated opinion ✓
C. A fact claim subject to the statute of frauds
D. A material misrepresentation if any buyer disputes it
Answer: B. Superlative descriptions regarding aesthetic appeal or general quality are puffing—permitted rhetorical exaggeration that buyers are expected to discount rather than rely upon.
Q 6.3·v5 A listing agent tells a buyer, "This is the most beautiful kitchen in the neighborhood." This statement is best classified as:
A. A breach of fiduciary duty
B. A material fact that must be disclosed
C. Fraudulent misrepresentation
D. Puffing or sales talk ✓
Answer: D. Statements of subjective aesthetic quality (beauty, attractiveness) are opinion-based puffing, which is permissible in real estate sales and does not constitute actionable misrepresentation.
Q 6.3·v6 During an open house, an agent says, "You won't find a better location anywhere in this area." How should this statement be characterized?
A. Fraud requiring rescission
B. Harmless puffery or exaggeration ✓
C. Concealment of a material defect
D. Actionable misrepresentation
Answer: B. Comparative value judgments and superlative claims about location desirability are considered puffing—subjective opinions that buyers are expected to evaluate independently.
Q 6.3·v7 A seller's agent describes the property as "stunning" and "the nicest home in the subdivision." Which category best describes these statements?
A. Misrepresentation requiring monetary damages
B. Omission of a material fact
C. Puffing or seller's talk ✓
D. Active fraud
Answer: C. Subjective characterizations of aesthetic appeal and comparative quality are classic examples of puffing, which is generally not legally actionable in real estate transactions.
Q 6.3·v8 A listing includes the phrase: "This property has the most desirable curb appeal on the block." What is the proper legal classification of this language?
A. Puffing or exaggerated sales talk ✓
B. A factual assertion about comparative market value
C. Material misrepresentation subject to rescission
D. Fraudulent concealment
Answer: A. Statements about subjective qualities like desirability and curb appeal are opinion-based puffery, not factual representations, and therefore constitute permitted sales talk in Hawaii real estate practice.
Q 6.3·v9 A listing agent tells a prospective buyer that a property has "the most beautiful landscaping in the neighborhood." This statement would most appropriately be classified as:
A. Actionable misrepresentation requiring damages
B. Fraudulent concealment of defects
C. A material fact that must be disclosed in writing
D. Permissible puffing or sales talk ✓
Answer: D. Subjective aesthetic judgments about beauty, views, or landscaping are considered puffing—exaggerated opinions that buyers expect in real estate sales and are not actionable misrepresentations.
Q 6.4 A defect not visible on reasonable inspection is:
A. Functional
B. Cosmetic
C. Latent ✓
D. Patent
Answer: C. Latent defects are hidden; agents must disclose if known.
Q 6.4·v1 Which type of property defect would NOT be discovered during a standard walk-through inspection?
A. Hidden water damage inside the walls ✓
B. Obvious structural damage to the roof
C. Broken window panes
D. Peeling paint on exterior surfaces
Answer: A. Hidden defects that cannot be seen without invasive inspection are latent defects; disclosure is required if the agent has knowledge of them.
Q 6.4·v2 A real estate licensee discovers that a home has termite damage behind the walls, undetectable without opening the structure. This is classified as a:
A. Cosmetic defect
B. Patent defect
C. Structural enhancement
D. Latent defect ✓
Answer: D. Latent defects are concealed or hidden conditions not apparent upon ordinary observation; agents must disclose known latent defects to buyers.
Q 6.4·v3 An underground septic system malfunction that shows no external signs would be considered:
A. A latent flaw ✓
B. A patent flaw
C. A minor surface flaw
D. An aesthetic flaw
Answer: A. Latent defects are hidden defects not discoverable by reasonable inspection; subsurface issues like septic problems must be disclosed if known.
Q 6.4·v4 Which property condition is NOT readily apparent to a buyer during a visual inspection?
A. Cracked glass in sliding doors
B. Faded exterior paint
C. Chipped tile on the bathroom floor
D. Faulty electrical wiring concealed within walls ✓
Answer: D. Latent defects are defects that are not visible or apparent under normal circumstances; agents must disclose any known latent defects to potential buyers.
Q 6.4·v5 Which category of property defect is characterized by being concealed from view and discoverable only through specialized inspection or disclosure?
A. Obvious defect
B. Structural defect
C. Hidden defect ✓
D. Aesthetic defect
Answer: C. Hidden defects (latent defects) are not apparent during normal inspection and must be disclosed if the agent has actual knowledge of them.
Q 6.4·v6 A homebuyer tours a property and observes no water damage, mold, or foundation issues. However, the seller's agent knows there is significant termite damage behind the walls. This damage would be classified as a:
A. Latent defect ✓
B. Manifest defect
C. Disclosed defect
D. Minor defect
Answer: A. Termite damage behind walls is a latent defect—not visible during a reasonable inspection—and the agent's knowledge triggers a disclosure obligation.
Q 6.4·v7 Under Hawaii real estate law, a defect that cannot be discovered through ordinary observation or reasonable inspection is considered:
A. Latent ✓
B. Trivial
C. Conditional
D. Patent
Answer: A. Latent defects are hidden from ordinary view and do not become apparent except upon close investigation or specialized testing; they must be disclosed if known.
Q 6.4·v8 A licensee learns that a property has a known subsurface issue that would not be visible during a standard walkthrough. This is an example of a:
A. Latent defect ✓
B. Conspicuous defect
C. Readily apparent defect
D. Surface defect
Answer: A. Subsurface problems are latent defects because they are not discoverable through reasonable inspection and must be disclosed if the agent has actual knowledge.
Q 6.4·v9 Which term describes a property defect that cannot be discovered through a standard walk-through or visual inspection?
A. Obvious defect
B. Superficial defect
C. Concealed defect ✓
D. Apparent defect
Answer: C. Concealed (latent) defects are hidden from ordinary view and must be disclosed by the agent if known; this is the same concept as latent defects.
Q 6.5 An "as-is" clause:
A. Does NOT eliminate disclosure of known material defects ✓
B. Bars all buyer claims
C. Eliminates seller disclosure duty
D. Eliminates agent disclosure duty
Answer: A. As-is does not override disclosure laws.
Q 6.5·v1 When a property is marketed with an "as-is" condition, which statement is accurate regarding Hawaii disclosure requirements?
A. The seller is relieved of all obligations to disclose latent defects
B. The as-is condition voids the buyer's right to conduct inspections
C. The real estate agent may withhold known material defects from the buyer
D. Known material defects must still be disclosed to the buyer despite the as-is clause ✓
Answer: D. An as-is clause does not exempt sellers or agents from disclosing known material defects; Hawaii law requires disclosure of material facts regardless of property condition language.
Q 6.5·v2 A broker lists a property with an "as-is" provision. What is the broker's legal obligation?
A. Disclose all known material defects to prospective buyers ✓
B. Allow only licensed inspectors to identify defects without agent involvement
C. Limit disclosure to cosmetic conditions only
D. Avoid disclosing any structural issues to protect the seller's interests
Answer: A. The broker must disclose known material defects to prospective buyers; the as-is clause does not eliminate this fiduciary and statutory disclosure duty.
Q 6.5·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, an as-is sale clause:
A. Does not override the requirement to disclose known material facts ✓
B. Protects the buyer from liability for defects discovered after closing
C. Absolves the agent from disclosing any known defects
D. Permits the seller to avoid disclosing environmental hazards
Answer: A. As-is language is not a blanket exemption from disclosure laws; sellers and agents must still disclose known material defects to comply with Hawaii disclosure requirements.
Q 6.5·v4 A buyer signs a purchase agreement containing an as-is clause. Which of the following remains true?
A. Material defects known to the seller or agent must still be disclosed to the buyer ✓
B. The listing agent is absolved of disclosure responsibilities regarding known issues
C. The buyer forfeits the right to request any seller repairs or credits
D. The seller's prior knowledge of foundation damage need not be disclosed
Answer: A. Even with an as-is clause, disclosure laws mandate that known material defects be revealed; the as-is condition addresses post-closing liability, not pre-sale disclosure obligations.
Q 6.5·v5 When a property is marketed with an "as-is" condition clause, what effect does this have on the seller's responsibility to disclose known defects?
A. It allows the seller to conceal latent defects discovered during inspection
B. It does not relieve the seller from disclosing known material defects ✓
C. It transfers all disclosure liability solely to the buyer's agent
D. It completely waives all disclosure requirements under Hawaii law
Answer: B. An as-is clause addresses the condition of the property but does not override statutory disclosure obligations; sellers must still reveal known material defects regardless of as-is language.
Q 6.5·v6 A broker represents a seller who insists on including an "as-is" provision in the listing. Which statement accurately reflects the broker's disclosure obligations?
A. The broker is exempt from the fiduciary duty to disclose defects known to the broker
B. The as-is clause permits the broker to withhold information about structural issues
C. The broker's duties end once the as-is language is added to the contract
D. The broker must still disclose known material facts about the property condition ✓
Answer: D. Brokers cannot hide behind as-is clauses; they retain their duty to disclose known material defects even when a property is sold as-is.
Q 6.5·v7 A buyer signs a purchase agreement containing an "as-is" clause. Which of the following is true regarding what the seller must disclose?
A. The seller is required to disclose known material defects despite the as-is language ✓
B. The seller must disclose known material defects unless the as-is clause was prominently displayed
C. The as-is clause eliminates the seller's liability for non-disclosure
D. The seller has no obligation to reveal any property conditions
Answer: A. The as-is clause does not eliminate disclosure obligations; sellers must still disclose known material defects as required by Hawaii law and fiduciary duties.
Q 6.5·v8 How does an "as-is" condition clause interact with Hawaii's disclosure requirements?
A. It eliminates the need for the seller to provide a property condition disclosure form
B. It permits the agent to withhold information about known defects from the buyer
C. It supersedes all statutory disclosure rules and contractual obligations
D. It does not negate the obligation to disclose known material defects ✓
Answer: D. An as-is clause addresses the buyer's acceptance of visible condition but does not override the legal duty to disclose known material defects.
Q 6.5·v9 When a property is sold under an "as-is" condition clause, which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the seller's legal obligations?
A. The seller is relieved of all responsibility to disclose latent defects discovered during inspection
B. The real estate agent may withhold information about defects if the contract includes an as-is provision
C. The buyer assumes all risk and waives the right to pursue any legal remedies for discovered problems
D. The seller must still reveal known material facts about the property despite the as-is language ✓
Answer: D. An as-is clause does not override Hawaii's mandatory seller disclosure requirements for known material defects; sellers and agents must still disclose what they know regardless of the as-is language in the contract.
Q 6.6 Lead-based paint buyer's right to inspect is:
A. 3 days
B. 30 days
C. 14 days
D. 10 days ✓
Answer: D. 10-day right to inspect; can be waived in writing.
Q 6.6·v1 Under federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements, how many days does a buyer have to conduct an inspection for lead hazards before closing?
A. 21 days
B. 7 days
C. 45 days
D. 10 days ✓
Answer: D. Federal law provides a 10-day inspection period for lead-based paint; this timeline can be shortened or waived if the buyer agrees in writing.
Q 6.6·v2 A seller receives an offer on a pre-1978 home. The buyer requests time to have the property inspected for lead-based paint. What is the standard inspection period allowed?
A. 10 days ✓
B. 20 days
C. 5 days
D. 15 days
Answer: A. The lead-based paint inspection period is 10 days; buyers may waive this right in writing if they choose not to inspect.
Q 6.6·v3 Which timeframe represents the buyer's inspection opportunity for lead-based paint hazards on properties built before 1978?
A. 8 days from offer acceptance
B. 12 days from offer acceptance
C. 6 days from offer acceptance
D. 10 days from offer acceptance ✓
Answer: D. Buyers have a 10-day right to inspect for lead-based paint; they may waive this right in writing to expedite the transaction.
Q 6.6·v4 If a buyer wants to exercise their right to inspect a pre-1978 property for lead-based paint, they must do so within what period?
A. 18 days of the purchase agreement
B. 10 days of the purchase agreement ✓
C. 3 days of the purchase agreement
D. 14 days of the purchase agreement
Answer: B. The federal lead-based paint inspection period is 10 days from acceptance of the offer; this period can be waived in writing by the buyer.
Q 6.6·v5 Under federal lead-based paint disclosure rules, how long does a purchaser have to conduct an inspection for lead hazards before becoming obligated to proceed with the transaction?
A. 5 business days
B. 21 calendar days
C. 10 calendar days ✓
D. 45 calendar days
Answer: C. Buyers have a 10-day inspection period for lead-based paint; this timeframe applies to all residential properties built before 1978 and can be shortened or waived by mutual written agreement.
Q 6.6·v6 A seller provides a lead-based paint disclosure to a buyer on a pre-1978 home. The buyer wishes to have the property inspected for lead. What is the maximum inspection window allowed?
A. 14 days from disclosure
B. 7 days from disclosure
C. 30 days from closing
D. 10 days from disclosure ✓
Answer: D. The federal lead-based paint inspection period is 10 days from receipt of the disclosure; buyers may waive this right in writing if they choose to proceed without an inspection.
Q 6.6·v7 In a transaction involving a residential structure constructed before 1978, the buyer's inspection contingency for lead-based paint typically allows:
A. 20 days to obtain a lead-free certification
B. 15 days to complete all lead remediation
C. 10 days to arrange and conduct inspections ✓
D. 3 business days for testing and results
Answer: C. Federal regulations provide a 10-day period for lead-based paint inspection in pre-1978 homes; the buyer may waive this right in writing at any time.
Q 6.6·v8 A licensee is assisting with a property sale built in 1975. The buyer asks how long they have after receiving the lead disclosure to inspect for lead-based paint hazards without penalty. What should the licensee state?
A. The buyer has only 3 days before the contract becomes binding
B. The buyer has until closing to arrange any lead testing
C. The buyer has 10 days to request and complete an inspection ✓
D. The buyer waives inspection rights unless demanded within 5 days
Answer: C. Federal law grants a 10-day inspection period for lead-based paint in pre-1978 homes, which begins upon receipt of the disclosure and may be waived in writing by the buyer.
Q 6.6·v9 Under federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements, what is the standard timeframe a purchaser has to conduct an inspection for lead hazards before contract contingencies expire?
A. 10 calendar days ✓
B. 45 calendar days
C. 21 calendar days
D. 5 business days
Answer: A. Federal law provides a 10-day inspection period for lead-based paint hazards; buyers may voluntarily waive this right in writing if they choose.
Q 6.7 A reasonable buyer would consider it important = the fact is:
A. Patent
B. Material ✓
C. Stigmatizing
D. Puffing
Answer: B. Materiality standard is "would a reasonable party consider it important?"
Q 6.7·v1 Under Hawaii real estate law, a fact is considered significant enough to disclose if a prudent buyer would regard it as important. This standard is known as:
A. Materiality ✓
B. Misrepresentation
C. Caveat emptor
D. Latent defect
Answer: A. The materiality standard requires disclosure of facts that a reasonable person would consider important to a purchase decision, regardless of whether they are hidden or obvious.
Q 6.7·v2 When evaluating whether a property condition must be disclosed to a prospective buyer, the key legal question is whether a typical buyer would find the information:
A. Significant to their decision to buy or price offered ✓
B. Fraudulent in nature
C. Obviously visible on inspection
D. Protected by the statute of limitations
Answer: A. The materiality test applies significance based on what a reasonable buyer would consider important, not on visibility or legal protection categories.
Q 6.7·v3 A seller's agent must disclose information about a property defect if it meets which standard?
A. The defect affects the structural integrity only
B. The buyer specifically asks about it first
C. A reasonable person in the buyer's position would consider it important ✓
D. The defect is intentionally concealed
Answer: C. Materiality is the standard applied—whether a reasonable person would find the fact important to their transaction decision—independent of other factors.
Q 6.7·v4 In a real estate transaction, information must be disclosed if it would influence a prudent purchaser's decision. This requirement is based on the concept of:
A. Stigmatized property status
B. Express warranty
C. Materiality ✓
D. Licensee liability
Answer: C. Materiality is the standard that determines disclosure obligations based on whether a reasonable buyer would regard the information as important to the transaction.
Q 6.7·v5 In Hawaii real estate disclosure law, a fact that a prudent buyer would want to know before purchasing is considered:
A. Material ✓
B. Latent
C. Superficial
D. Speculative
Answer: A. Material facts are those a reasonable person would consider important in deciding whether to buy or the price to pay; this is the standard test for disclosure obligations.
Q 6.7·v6 When determining whether a property defect must be disclosed, the legal standard asks: would an ordinary, prudent buyer regard this as significant? This describes the test of:
A. Fraudulent concealment
B. Apparent defect
C. Caveat emptor
D. Materiality ✓
Answer: D. The materiality test is whether a reasonable person would consider the fact important in their purchase decision or financing; it is the benchmark for mandatory disclosure.
Q 6.7·v7 A real estate licensee must disclose information about a property defect if a reasonable person in the buyer's position would consider it important to their transaction. This criterion is known as:
A. The materiality standard ✓
B. The puffery exception
C. The stigmatized property test
D. The patent defect rule
Answer: A. Materiality is the foundational standard—facts are material if they would influence a reasonable person's decision or affect the property's value or desirability.
Q 6.7·v8 A seller's agent learns that the property experiences occasional flooding during heavy rains. When deciding if this must be disclosed, the agent applies the test of whether a typical, reasonable buyer would find this fact significant. This is the:
A. Innocent misrepresentation threshold
B. Obvious defect exemption
C. Fiduciary disclosure duty
D. Material fact standard ✓
Answer: D. The material fact standard asks whether a reasonable party would consider the information important in making a buying decision; flooding history clearly meets this threshold.
Q 6.7·v9 Under Hawaii real estate disclosure laws, a fact that a reasonable person in the buyer's position would regard as significant in making a purchase decision is classified as:
A. Caveat emptor
B. Latent
C. Immaterial
D. Material ✓
Answer: D. Materiality is defined by what a reasonable buyer would consider important or significant to their decision-making; this is the legal standard for determining disclosure obligations in Hawaii.
Q 6.8 A statement made without knowing it is false but that should have been verified is:
A. Fraudulent misrepresentation
B. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
C. Innocent misrepresentation
D. Puffing
Answer: B. Negligent = should have known.
Q 6.8·v1 A real estate agent describes a property's condition based on information that was not properly researched or verified. The agent made this statement in good faith but failed to exercise reasonable diligence. This represents:
A. Puffing or sales talk
B. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
C. Fraudulent misrepresentation with intent to deceive
D. Innocent misrepresentation due to lack of information
Answer: B. Negligent misrepresentation occurs when someone makes a statement they should have verified through reasonable effort, even without intent to deceive. The failure to investigate constitutes negligence.
Q 6.8·v2 An agent tells a buyer that a property has never had foundation issues, but the agent did not review the inspection reports or title history. What type of misrepresentation is this?
A. Fraudulent misrepresentation
B. Puffing
C. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
D. Innocent misrepresentation
Answer: C. This is negligent misrepresentation because the agent had a duty to verify material facts about the property and failed to do so, even though there was no intentional deception.
Q 6.8·v3 When a licensee makes a factual statement about a property without actual knowledge of its truth but with the belief it is true, and the licensee failed to conduct reasonable investigation, this is classified as:
A. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
B. Innocent misrepresentation
C. Puffing or opinion
D. Fraudulent misrepresentation with scienter
Answer: A. Negligent misrepresentation is defined by the agent's failure to verify information that they should have investigated, regardless of their subjective belief in the statement's accuracy.
Q 6.8·v4 A property manager states that the rental income is consistent without checking the actual lease agreements or payment history. The manager believed the statement was true but did not verify it. This is an example of:
A. Puffing or exaggeration within industry standards
B. Fraudulent misrepresentation
C. Innocent misrepresentation caused by third-party information
D. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
Answer: D. Negligent misrepresentation applies when a licensee should have verified material facts through reasonable investigation but failed to do so, creating liability despite lack of intent to defraud.
Q 6.8·v5 A real estate licensee states a property fact that turns out to be false. The licensee did not know it was false at the time but failed to conduct a reasonable investigation that would have revealed the truth. This is best classified as:
A. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
B. Puffing or sales talk
C. Innocent misrepresentation
D. Fraudulent misrepresentation with intent to deceive
Answer: A. Negligent misrepresentation occurs when a party makes a false statement without knowledge of its falsity but should have known through reasonable investigation or due diligence.
Q 6.8·v6 An agent represents that a home's roof was recently replaced, but this claim was never verified. The agent genuinely believed the statement was true when made. Under Hawaii real estate law, this unverified assertion most likely constitutes:
A. Innocent misrepresentation only
B. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
C. Actionable puffery
D. Fraudulent misrepresentation
Answer: B. Because the agent made the statement without verifying it despite having the opportunity and obligation to do so, this represents negligent misrepresentation—a failure to exercise reasonable care in confirming facts.
Q 6.8·v7 Which type of misrepresentation involves a false statement that the speaker did not know was false but reasonably should have discovered through proper inquiry?
A. Innocent misrepresentation
B. Harmless exaggeration
C. Fraudulent misrepresentation
D. Negligent misrepresentation ✓
Answer: D. Negligent misrepresentation is defined by the speaker's failure to exercise reasonable care or verify information before stating it as fact, even without actual knowledge of falsity.
Q 6.8·v8 A licensee tells a buyer that the property has not had foundation issues based on a casual conversation with the seller, without ordering an inspection or reviewing public records. The statement proves false. This represents:
A. Innocent misstatement with no liability
B. Negligent misrepresentation due to lack of reasonable verification ✓
C. Opinion stated as fact that is protected by law
D. Fraud requiring proof of intentional deception
Answer: B. The licensee failed to verify a material fact through reasonable methods available to them, making this negligent misrepresentation rather than innocent (which requires no duty to investigate) or fraudulent (which requires intent).
Q 6.8·v9 An agent makes a statement about property conditions that turns out to be false. The agent did not deliberately lie, but a reasonable person in the real estate profession would have investigated the claim before making it. This constitutes:
A. Fraudulent misrepresentation with intent to deceive
B. Innocent misrepresentation without duty to investigate
C. Negligent misrepresentation due to failure to verify ✓
D. Puffery regarding general market conditions
Answer: C. Negligent misrepresentation occurs when a statement is made without actual knowledge of falsity but the agent failed to exercise reasonable care or verification that a professional should have performed.
Q 6.9 The historical "let the buyer beware" doctrine is:
A. Caveat venditor
B. Quid pro quo
C. Caveat emptor ✓
D. Statute of frauds
Answer: C. Caveat emptor = buyer beware.
Q 6.9·v1 Which Latin maxim embodies the principle that a purchaser assumes the risk of inspecting property and bears responsibility for their own due diligence?
A. Caveat venditor
B. Caveat emptor ✓
C. Statute of frauds
D. Res ipsa loquitur
Answer: B. Caveat emptor (buyer beware) places the burden on the purchaser to investigate property condition and assume risk unless otherwise protected by law or contract.
Q 6.9·v2 In traditional real estate law, the doctrine requiring buyers to conduct their own inspections and accept property 'as-is' unless expressly warranted is known as:
A. Caveat emptor ✓
B. Caveat venditor
C. Quid pro quo
D. Merger doctrine
Answer: A. Caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) is the historical common-law principle that shifts inspection and disclosure responsibility primarily to the buyer.
Q 6.9·v3 Which of the following best describes the 'buyer beware' concept in historical real estate transactions?
A. The broker is liable for any undisclosed property conditions
B. The buyer assumes the risk of discovering defects through reasonable inspection ✓
C. The seller warrants the condition of all structural components
D. The seller must disclose all known defects to protect the buyer
Answer: B. Caveat emptor places the onus on buyers to investigate and discover defects themselves rather than relying on seller disclosures.
Q 6.9·v4 The principle that historically placed the burden of property inspection and risk assumption on the purchaser rather than the seller is termed:
A. Caveat emptor (buyer beware) ✓
B. Accord and satisfaction
C. Lis pendens
D. Caveat venditor (seller beware)
Answer: A. Caveat emptor is the Latin maxim meaning 'buyer beware,' reflecting the doctrine that buyers must verify property condition through their own diligence.
Q 6.9·v5 Under the traditional real estate principle known as 'buyer beware,' a purchaser is generally responsible for conducting due diligence on a property. What is the Latin term for this doctrine?
A. Quid pro quo
B. Caveat venditor
C. Statute of frauds
D. Caveat emptor ✓
Answer: D. Caveat emptor is the Latin phrase meaning 'buyer beware,' placing the onus on the purchaser to inspect and verify property conditions.
Q 6.9·v6 Which of the following Latin legal principles historically placed the burden of inspection and verification on the purchaser rather than the seller?
A. Caveat venditor
B. Statute of frauds
C. Res ipsa loquitur
D. Caveat emptor ✓
Answer: D. Caveat emptor ('buyer beware') is the doctrine that transfers responsibility to the buyer to examine property and assume risk of defects.
Q 6.9·v7 A real estate instructor explains that under common law, buyers were expected to discover property defects themselves rather than rely on seller disclosures. This principle is known as:
A. Good faith and fair dealing
B. Caveat emptor ✓
C. Caveat venditor
D. Estoppel
Answer: B. Caveat emptor means 'let the buyer beware' and historically required purchasers to conduct their own investigation of property conditions.
Q 6.9·v8 In contrast to modern mandatory seller disclosure laws, the historical 'as-is' approach to real estate transactions was governed by which Latin doctrine?
A. Quid pro quo
B. Lis pendens
C. Caveat emptor ✓
D. Caveat venditor
Answer: C. Caveat emptor ('buyer beware') was the historical default principle requiring buyers to assess property conditions without seller obligation to disclose defects.
Q 6.9·v9 Which Latin maxim reflects the principle that a purchaser assumes responsibility for inspecting property and accepting it in its present condition without reliance on the seller's representations?
A. Statute of frauds
B. Caveat emptor ✓
C. Quid pro quo
D. Caveat venditor
Answer: B. Caveat emptor (buyer beware) is the doctrine placing the burden on the buyer to investigate property condition and negotiate protections rather than relying on seller warranties. This principle, though modified by modern disclosure laws, remains foundational to real estate transactions.
Q 6.10 A licensee notices fresh paint over one wall in a basement and water stains nearby. The licensee should:
A. Investigate or recommend inspection ✓
B. Tell only the listing broker
C. Wait for the buyer to ask
D. Ignore — buyer's problem
Answer: A. Red flag = duty to inquire or recommend inspection.
Q 6.10·v1 During a property showing, a licensee observes peeling paint, a musty odor, and efflorescence on a basement wall. What is the licensee's appropriate course of action?
A. Report the findings exclusively to the listing agent without discussing with the buyer
B. Document observations in writing and recommend the buyer obtain a professional inspection ✓
C. Mention the condition only if the buyer directly asks about the basement
D. Assume the seller has already disclosed any moisture issues
Answer: B. A licensee must take reasonable steps to investigate or recommend professional inspection when observable conditions suggest potential problems, fulfilling duty of disclosure.
Q 6.10·v2 A licensee showing a property notices a large water-stained ceiling patch covered with new drywall tape and spackle in an upstairs bedroom. The licensee's responsibility is to:
A. Assume it was cosmetic repair and proceed with the showing
B. Note the condition and advise the buyer to have a professional inspector evaluate it ✓
C. Decline to show the property until the seller explains the damage
D. Discuss the finding only with other agents during broker meetings
Answer: B. Observable evidence of past or potential moisture/structural issues triggers a licensee's duty to inform the buyer and recommend professional inspection rather than overlook or minimize the observation.
Q 6.10·v3 While inspecting a property on behalf of a client, a licensee spots fresh caulking around a basement window frame and visible mold spots on adjacent framing. The licensee should:
A. Consider the repairs evidence of responsible maintenance and assure the buyer there are no issues
B. Remain silent unless the buyer specifically requests information about water intrusion
C. Report concerns to the seller's agent and wait for written clarification before mentioning anything to the buyer
D. Promptly alert the buyer and suggest engaging a qualified home inspector or structural specialist ✓
Answer: D. A licensee who observes suspicious or concerning conditions must take affirmative steps to investigate or recommend professional inspection, not wait passively for buyer inquiries.
Q 6.10·v4 A licensee notices a basement wall has been freshly painted and there are rust stains on metal shelving stored nearby. When asked by the buyer about the basement condition, the licensee should:
A. State that the fresh paint indicates the seller has maintained the property well
B. Suggest the buyer contact the seller directly if they have concerns, as the licensee cannot comment on unpermitted repairs
C. Explain that cosmetic updates are common and do not warrant further investigation
D. Acknowledge the observed conditions and recommend a professional home inspection to identify any underlying moisture or structural concerns ✓
Answer: D. When a licensee observes red flags suggesting possible defects—even during a direct buyer question—the appropriate response is to disclose the observation and recommend professional inspection.
Q 6.10·v5 During a showing, a licensee observes discolored drywall and newly applied caulk around a basement window frame. What is the licensee's appropriate action?
A. Assume the seller has already disclosed any issues and proceed with the showing
B. Document the observation and actively investigate or suggest a professional inspection ✓
C. Allow the buyer to discover and address any concerns independently
D. Report findings only to the seller's agent for private handling
Answer: B. Visible signs of potential water damage or structural issues trigger a duty to investigate further or recommend professional inspection to protect all parties.
Q 6.10·v6 A licensee spots cracked paint and efflorescence (white mineral deposits) on a basement wall. The licensee's best practice is to:
A. Suggest cosmetic repairs to cover the affected area before closing
B. Inform only the listing side and let them decide whether to disclose
C. Stay silent unless the buyer specifically asks about basement conditions
D. Recommend the buyer obtain a professional inspection or conduct further investigation ✓
Answer: D. Visible indicators of moisture or foundation issues create an obligation to recommend inspection or further inquiry to fulfill fiduciary duties.
Q 6.10·v7 At an open house, you notice recently painted drywall adjacent to dark staining that suggests prior water intrusion. What should you do?
A. Relay your concerns exclusively to your broker for internal documentation
B. Encourage prospective buyers to hire an inspector and disclose or investigate the condition ✓
C. Request the homeowner's written explanation before mentioning it to any prospective buyer
D. Consider it a cosmetic issue and focus the showing on other property features
Answer: B. Signs of concealment or water damage—such as fresh paint over stains—obligate the licensee to recommend inspection or conduct due diligence.
Q 6.10·v8 While conducting a pre-listing walkthrough, you observe new paint covering what appears to be water-damaged drywall in the basement. Your responsibility is to:
A. Accept the owner's assurance that repairs were completed and list the property as-is
B. Identify the red flag and recommend further inspection or investigation before marketing ✓
C. Note it privately but only share with the buyer's agent if asked directly
D. Withhold the observation from any disclosure and let the buyer's inspector find it
Answer: B. Fresh paint over suspicious stains is a red flag requiring investigation or professional inspection to ensure proper disclosure and protect all parties.
Q 6.10·v9 During a showing, a salesperson observes peeling paint in a bedroom closet and discovers mold spots on the adjacent wall. What is the licensee's appropriate course of action?
A. Report the findings exclusively to the listing agent without discussing with the buyer
B. Assume the seller will disclose this issue on the disclosure form
C. Document observations and recommend the buyer obtain a professional mold inspection ✓
D. Mention the issue only if the buyer directly asks about mold or moisture
Answer: C. A licensee encountering visible defects or red flags must proactively investigate or recommend professional inspection to fulfill the duty of inquiry and care.
Q 6.11 A seller refuses to complete the property condition disclosure form. The licensee should:
A. Submit the listing without it
B. Only disclose to buyers who ask
C. Insist on completion or decline the listing ✓
D. Complete it themselves
Answer: C. Most states require completed seller disclosure; refusal often means walking away.
Q 6.11·v1 A licensee receives a listing where the owner will not provide a completed property condition disclosure. What should the licensee do?
A. Market the property as-is and note in the listing remarks that no disclosure was provided
B. Decline the listing or require the seller to complete the disclosure ✓
C. Fill out the disclosure form based on public records and MLS data
D. Proceed with marketing and let the buyer's inspector find any issues
Answer: B. Hawaii law requires seller disclosures; a licensee cannot proceed with a listing if the seller refuses to complete required disclosure forms. The licensee must either obtain completion or decline the engagement.
Q 6.11·v2 When a seller resists providing a property condition disclosure, a real estate agent's appropriate response is to:
A. Require the disclosure or terminate the listing relationship ✓
B. Prepare the disclosure on behalf of the seller to expedite the transaction
C. List the property contingent on buyer acceptance of unknown conditions
D. Accept the listing with a clause stating the buyer waives disclosure review
Answer: A. A licensee has a professional and legal duty to ensure required disclosures are completed; accepting a listing without it violates REC regulations and exposes the licensee to liability.
Q 6.11·v3 A seller tells their agent, 'I don't want to fill out that condition form—just sell the house.' The licensee should:
A. Complete the disclosure form themselves based on their own observations
B. Allow the buyer to waive the disclosure requirement before closing
C. Honor the seller's preference and submit the listing immediately
D. Explain that the disclosure is mandatory and either obtain it or withdraw from the listing ✓
Answer: D. Licensees cannot ignore mandatory seller disclosure requirements, regardless of seller preference. The licensee must insist on compliance or decline the listing.
Q 6.11·v4 Which action is improper when a seller adamantly refuses to complete a property condition disclosure?
A. Proceeding with the listing and allowing disclosure to be withheld ✓
B. Consulting with the broker about the seller's obligations before listing
C. Requesting the seller sign a statement acknowledging the disclosure requirement
D. Declining to accept the listing and referring the seller to another agent
Answer: A. Moving forward without a completed mandatory disclosure violates Hawaii REC rules and real estate law; the licensee must enforce the requirement or withdraw.
Q 6.11·v5 During a listing appointment, the seller states they will not fill out the property condition disclosure required by Hawaii law. What is the licensee's most appropriate response?
A. Proceed with listing and note that disclosure is pending
B. Ask the seller to initial a waiver instead of completing the full form
C. Market the property without disclosure and let the buyer's inspector find issues
D. Decline the listing or require the seller to complete the disclosure form ✓
Answer: D. Licensees cannot bypass mandatory seller disclosure requirements; refusing to complete it is grounds to decline representation to protect both parties and comply with law.
Q 6.11·v6 A property owner tells their real estate agent that completing a property condition disclosure form is too time-consuming and wants to list without it. The agent should:
A. Contact the broker to get written permission to skip the disclosure
B. Obtain a signed statement from the seller acknowledging they refuse to disclose and proceed with listing
C. Prepare the disclosure based on publicly available information and the seller's verbal statements
D. Require completion of the disclosure or terminate the listing agreement ✓
Answer: D. Licensees must enforce disclosure compliance as a condition of representation; accepting a refusal without consequences violates fiduciary duty and regulatory requirements.
Q 6.11·v7 When a seller declines to complete the mandatory property condition disclosure, which action best protects the licensee and client?
A. Modify the disclosure to include only positive features the seller confirms
B. Refuse to take the listing until the disclosure is properly completed ✓
C. Allow the sale to proceed contingent on buyer discovery and inspection
D. Request the seller sign a form acknowledging their refusal and continue marketing
Answer: B. A licensee's professional obligation is to insist on compliance with disclosure laws; proceeding without it exposes the licensee to liability and violates consumer protection standards.
Q 6.11·v8 A licensee encounters a seller who explicitly refuses to complete a required property condition disclosure statement. The licensee's proper course of action is to:
A. Advise the buyer that disclosure is not available and reduce the offer price accordingly
B. Create a simplified disclosure form that summarizes only the seller's known defects
C. Require the seller to complete the disclosure or decline representation of that listing ✓
D. File a complaint with the Hawaii Real Estate Commission and then list the property
Answer: C. Licensees must uphold disclosure requirements; if a seller will not comply, the licensee must choose not to represent them rather than circumvent legal obligations.
Q 6.11·v9 During listing intake, a seller states they will not complete the property condition disclosure required by Hawaii law. As the listing agent, what is your most appropriate response?
A. Prepare a summary disclosure based on your own inspection and have the seller initial it
B. Have the seller sign a waiver exempting them from the disclosure requirement
C. Decline the listing unless the seller agrees to provide the completed disclosure form ✓
D. Proceed with marketing the property and note in the MLS that disclosure is pending
Answer: C. Hawaii law requires sellers to provide accurate property condition disclosures; a licensee cannot ethically list a property or circumvent this requirement, and must decline the listing if the seller refuses compliance.
Q 6.12 Stigmatized property disclosure rules:
A. Only apply to murder
B. Vary by state ✓
C. Don't exist
D. Are uniform federally
Answer: B. State-specific. Some require, some don't.
Q 6.12·v1 A real estate agent in Hawaii is asked about disclosure obligations for a property where a suicide occurred five years ago. Which statement best describes the legal framework for such disclosures?
A. Federal law establishes a uniform national standard for all stigmatizing events
B. Hawaii law prohibits any disclosure of non-death-related stigmatizing events
C. Requirements differ depending on which state the property is located in ✓
D. Disclosure is only mandatory if the death was violent
Answer: C. Stigmatized property disclosure laws vary significantly by state; there is no uniform federal requirement, and some states mandate disclosure while others do not.
Q 6.12·v2 When counseling a seller about a property involved in a highly publicized crime, an agent should understand that:
A. Only homicides trigger disclosure obligations under real estate law
B. The Federal Trade Commission sets national standards for all stigma-related disclosures
C. Each state has its own rules—some require disclosure, others do not ✓
D. Disclosure requirements apply uniformly across all U.S. states and territories
Answer: C. Stigmatized property disclosure requirements are state-specific; there is no federal mandate, and states have adopted varying approaches from mandatory disclosure to no requirement.
Q 6.12·v3 Which of the following correctly describes the legal status of stigmatized property disclosures in real estate?
A. State laws govern whether and how stigmatizing information must be disclosed ✓
B. A national standard created by the National Association of REALTORS® applies in all states
C. Federal housing law requires disclosure of all stigmatizing events nationwide
D. Disclosure is only required when a property is involved in criminal activity
Answer: A. Stigmatized property disclosure is regulated at the state level with no uniform federal requirement; states determine their own disclosure obligations.
Q 6.12·v4 A broker is handling a listing for a property with a concerning history. Regarding disclosure obligations for stigmatizing factors, the broker should know:
A. Disclosure applies only to properties where deaths occurred
B. HUD establishes binding disclosure rules that apply everywhere
C. There are no legal disclosure requirements for any stigmatizing information
D. Disclosure requirements are determined individually by each state and vary widely ✓
Answer: D. Stigmatized property disclosure laws vary by state—some require it, some forbid it, and some are silent, creating a patchwork of state-specific rules with no national standard.
Q 6.12·v5 When advising a client about disclosure obligations for a property where a suicide occurred, a Hawaii real estate agent should understand that:
A. Hawaii law prohibits any disclosure of stigmatized property information to buyers
B. Disclosure requirements for stigmatized properties differ from state to state ✓
