C. Only deaths resulting from criminal acts must be disclosed in every state
D. Federal law mandates identical disclosure requirements nationwide for all stigmatized properties
Answer: B. Stigmatized property disclosure rules vary significantly by state; some states require disclosure while others do not, and the time periods and types of events differ.
Q 6.12·v6 A real estate licensee in Hawaii is asked whether a property where a felony occurred must be disclosed to potential buyers. The correct response is:
A. Stigmatized property disclosures are only required for properties involved in drug manufacturing
B. Disclosure requirements depend on which state the property is located in, as rules are not uniform ✓
C. Federal regulations override all state laws regarding stigmatized property disclosure
D. All states have adopted the same stigmatized property disclosure statute
Answer: B. Each state sets its own rules on what events trigger stigmatized property disclosure requirements, meaning requirements are not consistent across jurisdictions.
Q 6.12·v7 Which statement accurately describes how Hawaii real estate law handles stigmatized property disclosure?
A. State laws control stigmatized property disclosure requirements; they are not standardized federally ✓
B. Stigmatized property rules apply equally to all property types and circumstances across the country
C. The National Association of REALTORS® has established a single nationwide standard that all agents must follow
D. Only events causing death require disclosure, and this requirement is uniform in all states
Answer: A. Stigmatized property disclosure obligations are determined by individual state law, not by federal mandate or national standards, resulting in significant variations.
Q 6.12·v8 When a Hawaii agent encounters a property with a negative history, the agent should recognize that requirements to disclose such stigmatizing information:
A. Are nonexistent in all jurisdictions as a matter of public policy
B. Apply exclusively to properties where violent crimes occurred within the past year
C. Follow a federal template that applies identically in all 50 states
D. Differ from state to state based on each state's specific statutory framework ✓
Answer: D. Stigmatized property disclosure laws vary by state; some jurisdictions require disclosure while others do not, and the scope of what must be disclosed differs widely.
Q 6.12·v9 A Hawaii real estate licensee is advising a seller about potential disclosure obligations related to a property's negative history. Which statement best describes how stigmatized property laws function?
A. Each state establishes its own rules regarding what must be disclosed about a property's stigmatized status ✓
B. Hawaii has no legal framework addressing disclosure of properties with negative events or reputations
C. Disclosure is required only when a death occurred on the property within the past year
D. Federal law provides a single standard that all states must follow for disclosure
Answer: A. Stigmatized property disclosure requirements vary significantly by state; Hawaii and other states each set their own rules about which negative events require disclosure, making this a state-level determination rather than a uniform federal mandate.

Contracts
National portion10 PSI items39 key concepts12 base questions

Real estate transactions are governed by contract from offer to closing. Know what makes a contract valid and what voids it.

Chapter Overview

A valid contract requires four essential elements: mutual agreement (offer + acceptance, also called "meeting of the minds"), consideration (something of value exchanged), legal capacity of all parties, and lawful purpose. Real estate contracts must additionally satisfy the Statute of Frauds — they must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Verbal agreements to transfer interests in land are generally unenforceable, with narrow exceptions for partial performance.

An offer must be a definite, communicated proposal showing intent to be bound on acceptance. It must include the essential terms: parties, property, price, and any unique conditions. An invitation to make offers (a listing on MLS) is not itself an offer. Acceptance must be unconditional and communicated to the offeror; until then, the offeror can revoke. Conditional acceptance — accepting with changed terms — is a counteroffer that rejects and replaces the original offer.

Listing agreements come in three flavors. Exclusive Right to Sell — broker earns commission no matter who finds the buyer (including the seller themselves). Exclusive Agency — broker earns commission unless the seller personally finds the buyer, in which case the broker earns nothing. Open Listing — broker earns only if their efforts produced the sale; seller can have multiple open listings simultaneously. Net listings (broker keeps everything above a stated price) are discouraged or banned in most states because of the inherent conflict of interest.

Purchase agreements bind buyer and seller. Standard contingencies (escape clauses) include financing (buyer must obtain a loan within X days), inspection (right to inspect and request repairs or terminate), appraisal (property must appraise at or above purchase price), sale of buyer's current home, title (must be marketable), and sometimes attorney review. A contingency must be satisfied or waived by its deadline; otherwise the contract terminates and the deposit is typically returned.

"Time is of the essence" makes contract deadlines strict — a single day late is a breach giving the non-breaching party remedies. Without this language, courts may grant reasonable extensions. Most modern real estate contracts include time-is-of-the-essence language; agents should never assume otherwise.

Breach gives the non-breaching party remedies: specific performance (court orders the actual conveyance — typical for buyers because real estate is considered unique and damages don't fully substitute), monetary damages (lost profits, out-of-pocket costs), liquidated damages (pre-agreed amount, typically the earnest money — common for seller's remedy when buyer breaches), or rescission (cancel + restore parties to original positions). Mitigation duty: the non-breaching party must take reasonable steps to minimize damages.

Modification, assignment, and termination. A bilateral modification requires consideration on both sides. Assignment transfers contract rights (and usually duties) to a third party — generally allowed unless the contract bars it or the duties are personal. Novation substitutes a new party or new contract with all parties' consent, releasing the original obligor. Mutual rescission ends a contract by agreement; unilateral termination usually requires a contractual or legal basis.

Defenses to contract enforcement: lack of capacity (minors, incompetents, intoxication), duress (improper pressure), undue influence (excessive psychological pressure by trusted person), fraud, mistake (mutual or unilateral material mistake), illegality, statute of frauds violation, statute of limitations expired, and impossibility/frustration of purpose. Voidable contracts can be avoided by the harmed party (minor's contract); void contracts have no legal effect from the start (illegal purpose).

Key Concepts & Definitions
Statute of FraudsReal estate contracts must be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
Mutual agreementOffer + acceptance. "Meeting of the minds" on essential terms.
OfferDefinite proposal communicated with intent to be bound on acceptance.
AcceptanceUnconditional agreement to all material terms. Communication required.
CounterofferConditional acceptance (changed terms). Rejection + new offer. Cancels original.
ConsiderationSomething of value exchanged. Money, property, services, promises.
CapacityLegal ability to contract. Minors, incompetents, intoxicated have limited capacity.
Lawful purposeObject of contract must be legal. Illegal contracts are void.
Bilateral contractBoth parties make promises. Most real estate contracts.
Unilateral contractOne party makes a promise; other accepts by performance (e.g., reward).
Express contractTerms stated in words (written or oral).
Implied contractTerms inferred from conduct.
Executory contractNot yet fully performed.
Executed contractFully performed.
Valid contractHas all elements; enforceable.
Void contractNo legal effect from inception. Illegal purpose, lack of capacity.
Voidable contractOne party can rescind. Minor's contract; contract induced by fraud.
Unenforceable contractValid in form but court won't enforce. Statute of frauds violation, statute of limitations.
Exclusive Right to SellBroker earns commission regardless of who produces the buyer.
Exclusive AgencyBroker earns unless seller personally finds the buyer.
Open ListingBroker earns only if their efforts cause the sale. Multiple brokers possible.
Net ListingBroker keeps amount above seller's stated minimum. Disfavored or illegal.
Multiple Listing Service (MLS)Cooperative database where listing brokers share listings with cooperating brokers.
Earnest moneyBuyer's good-faith deposit, typically held in trust by escrow or broker.
ContingencyCondition that must be met for the contract to proceed. Failure = termination.
Specific performanceCourt orders actual conveyance. Common remedy for breach by seller because real estate is unique.
Liquidated damagesPre-agreed damages amount, usually the earnest money. Avoids fact-finding.
Compensatory damagesActual losses (lost profits, costs). Available for breach.
RescissionTermination of contract returning parties to pre-contract position.
Mutual rescissionBoth parties agree to cancel.
NovationSubstitution of new party or new contract by all parties' consent. Releases original obligor.
AssignmentTransfer of contract rights to a third party. Generally allowed unless barred.
Time is of the essenceDeadlines strictly enforced. Late performance = breach.
MitigationNon-breaching party must take reasonable steps to minimize damages.
Option contractRight (not obligation) to buy at stated price within stated time. Optionee pays consideration for option.
Right of first refusalRight to match a bona fide third-party offer before owner accepts it.
DuressImproper pressure invalidating consent. Voidable.
Undue influenceExcessive psychological pressure by trusted person. Voidable.
MistakeMaterial misunderstanding of facts. Mutual mistake → rescission. Unilateral generally not.
Question Bank — Contracts
Q 7.1 A buyer's offer is accepted by the seller's verbal "OK." Is there a contract?
A. Yes
B. Yes if earnest money posted
C. Yes if witnessed
D. No — Statute of Frauds requires writing ✓
Answer: D. Real estate contracts must be in writing to be enforceable.
Q 7.1·v1 A seller orally agrees to sell their residential property to a buyer over the phone. The buyer immediately sends a text confirming the conversation. Is this oral agreement enforceable as a valid real estate contract in Hawaii?
A. Yes, if the text message is saved and printed within 24 hours
B. Yes, if the buyer has already scheduled a home inspection
C. Yes, because both parties agreed and there was prompt confirmation
D. No, because the Statute of Frauds requires a signed written instrument ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii real estate law, based on the Statute of Frauds, requires all contracts for the sale of land to be evidenced by a written document signed by the party being charged—oral agreements alone are unenforceable.
Q 7.1·v2 During a negotiation, a seller verbally tells a real estate agent, 'Yes, I will accept $450,000 for my home.' The agent relays this to the buyer's agent, who immediately notifies the buyer. At this point, is there a binding and enforceable contract?
A. Yes, verbal acceptance combined with agent communication creates a binding contract
B. No—a written, signed agreement is required for any real estate sales contract ✓
C. Yes, if both agents co-sign a memorandum of their conversation
D. Yes, but only if the earnest money deposit has been delivered to escrow
Answer: B. Real estate contracts must be in writing and signed by the seller to satisfy the Statute of Frauds; mere verbal acceptance, even when communicated through agents, does not create an enforceable contract.
Q 7.1·v3 A buyer and seller shake hands and verbally agree on all material terms of a residential sale in Honolulu, including price, closing date, and contingencies. No written document is prepared that day. Does this handshake agreement constitute a valid, enforceable real estate contract?
A. Yes, if the buyer has provided identification and proof of funds
B. Yes, but only if a neutral third party witnessed the handshake
C. No—Hawaii law requires a written contract signed by the seller to be enforceable ✓
D. Yes, if both parties genuinely intended to be bound by their spoken words
Answer: C. Even when parties intend to be bound and have agreed on all material terms, a real estate contract is not enforceable without a written instrument complying with the Statute of Frauds.
Q 7.1·v4 A property seller emails a buyer saying 'I accept your offer at the stated price and terms.' However, neither the email nor any other document has been signed by the seller. Is this acceptance sufficient to create an enforceable real estate contract?
A. Yes, if the buyer immediately deposits earnest money upon receiving the email
B. No, because the Statute of Frauds requires a signed written agreement for real estate sales ✓
C. Yes, email communication satisfies the Statute of Frauds requirement
D. Yes, if the email is printed out and notarized within 10 days
Answer: B. Although an email may constitute writing, it must be signed by the party to be charged to satisfy the Statute of Frauds; an unsigned electronic acceptance alone cannot create an enforceable real estate contract.
Q 7.1·v5 A seller orally agrees to sell residential property to a buyer over the phone. Both parties shake hands later and agree to proceed. Is this arrangement enforceable as a real estate contract in Hawaii?
A. No, because Hawaii law requires real estate contracts to be documented in writing ✓
B. Yes, if the buyer immediately deposits earnest money into escrow
C. Yes, because both parties agreed and shook hands
D. Yes, if a third party witnessed the oral agreement
Answer: A. The Statute of Frauds mandates that contracts for the sale of real property must be in writing to be enforceable, regardless of witness or earnest money.
Q 7.1·v6 During a property showing, a seller verbally tells a prospective buyer, "I accept your offer." The buyer leaves satisfied that a binding agreement exists. What is the legal status of this transaction?
A. Unenforceable because the agreement lacks written documentation ✓
B. Binding only if the buyer provides proof of earnest money deposit
C. Enforceable if both parties later acknowledge it in front of witnesses
D. Binding and fully enforceable as a valid contract
Answer: A. Without a written instrument, no enforceable real estate contract exists under the Statute of Frauds, even if both parties intended to be bound.
Q 7.1·v7 Two parties negotiate the sale of a lot in Hawaii. The seller sends an email saying "I accept your terms," but no formal purchase agreement document is ever signed by either party. Do the parties have an enforceable contract?
A. Yes, if earnest money has been exchanged between the parties
B. Yes, the email constitutes written acceptance
C. No, a formal written purchase agreement signed by the party to be charged is required ✓
D. Yes, provided both parties have proof of the negotiation discussions
Answer: C. While an email may satisfy the writing requirement in some jurisdictions, a formalized purchase agreement typically signed by the party to be charged is required to create an enforceable real estate contract.
Q 7.1·v8 A buyer makes an offer for a condominium and the seller responds with a verbal counteroffer at a social gathering, saying "I'll sell for that price." The buyer agrees verbally on the spot. Which statement accurately reflects the legal enforceability of this transaction?
A. It is enforceable if the parties later confirm the terms via telephone conversation with a witness
B. It is enforceable if the buyer can produce written notes documenting the conversation
C. It is fully enforceable because both parties made mutual assent and consideration was present
D. It is not enforceable; Hawaii's Statute of Frauds requires real estate sales contracts to be in writing ✓
Answer: D. Oral agreements for the sale of real estate cannot be enforced, no matter how clear the mutual intent, because the Statute of Frauds requires a written contract.
Q 7.1·v9 A seller orally agrees to sell residential property to a buyer over the phone. Both parties clearly understand the terms and price. Is this oral agreement enforceable as a real estate contract in Hawaii?
A. Yes, if the buyer deposits earnest money within 24 hours
B. No, because Hawaii law requires all real estate sales contracts to be evidenced by a signed written document ✓
C. Yes, if a real estate licensee was present during the conversation
D. Yes, if both parties are competent and agree on material terms
Answer: B. The Statute of Frauds mandates that real estate contracts must be in writing and signed to be legally enforceable, regardless of oral agreement or witness presence.
Q 7.2 In an exclusive-agency listing, the seller pays the broker:
A. Only if seller produces buyer
B. Always
C. Unless seller produces the buyer ✓
D. Never
Answer: C. Exclusive agency = broker earns UNLESS the seller themselves found the buyer.
Q 7.2·v1 Under an exclusive-agency agreement, when does the listing broker NOT earn a commission?
A. When the sale closes after the listing expires
B. When the seller independently locates and produces the buyer ✓
C. When the property sells through any source
D. When another broker brings an offer
Answer: B. Exclusive agency allows the seller to avoid paying commission only if the seller themselves finds the buyer; the broker earns in all other situations.
Q 7.2·v2 A property is listed under an exclusive-agency agreement. The seller's neighbor expresses interest and purchases the home directly from the seller without broker involvement. Who owes commission?
A. Neither party owes commission since the seller produced the buyer ✓
B. The seller owes commission because any sale requires payment
C. The listing broker owes commission to the MLS
D. The buyer owes commission to the listing broker
Answer: A. In exclusive agency, the seller's right to sell without paying commission applies specifically when the seller personally finds and produces the buyer, which is the case here.
Q 7.2·v3 An exclusive-agency listing broker will receive compensation in all scenarios EXCEPT when:
A. A cooperating broker brings an offer that closes
B. The sale occurs after marketing by the broker
C. The property sells within the listing period
D. The seller themselves source the buyer ✓
Answer: D. Exclusive agency creates one exception to the broker's automatic commission right: when the seller, not the broker, is responsible for finding the buyer.
Q 7.2·v4 Which situation would result in NO commission owed to the listing broker under an exclusive-agency listing agreement?
A. Another brokerage introduces the successful buyer
B. The seller personally negotiates with an interested party and completes the sale ✓
C. The property sells through the local MLS database
D. The seller contacts a prospect from the broker's advertising and that person buys
Answer: B. Exclusive agency permits the seller to circumvent the commission obligation only when the seller is the source of the buyer; broker involvement from any other source triggers the commission obligation.
Q 7.2·v5 When a seller signs an exclusive-agency listing agreement, the broker's compensation is NOT earned if:
A. Another broker brings a qualified offer
B. The sale closes within 60 days of listing
C. The seller locates and procures the buyer themselves ✓
D. The property remains on the market for more than 30 days
Answer: C. Under exclusive agency, the broker foregoes commission only when the seller, not the broker or another agent, finds the buyer; in all other scenarios, the broker is entitled to compensation.
Q 7.2·v6 Which statement correctly describes the broker's right to commission under an exclusive-agency listing?
A. The broker is paid a commission regardless of who brings the buyer
B. The broker is only paid if they are the sole source of the buyer
C. The broker earns commission except when the seller personally produces the buyer ✓
D. The broker forfeits all compensation if the property sells within the listing period
Answer: C. Exclusive agency protects the seller's right to avoid paying commission if they independently find their own buyer, but the broker receives commission in all other buyer-source scenarios.
Q 7.2·v7 A seller enters into an exclusive-agency listing with Broker Chen. Broker Chen should expect to receive compensation:
A. Whenever a sale closes, with no exceptions
B. Unless the seller personally identifies and brings the buyer to closing ✓
C. When any licensed agent procures an offer, even if the seller found them first
D. Only if Broker Chen's agents show the property to the eventual buyer
Answer: B. The defining feature of exclusive agency is that the broker retains the right to commission in most scenarios, except when the seller themselves (not any agent or third party) produces the buyer.
Q 7.2·v8 Under an exclusive-agency listing arrangement, the broker's entitlement to commission is contingent on which factor?
A. Whether someone other than the seller was the procuring cause of the buyer ✓
B. Whether the transaction includes both a buyer's and seller's agent
C. Whether the listing period extends beyond 90 days
D. Whether the property appraises at or above the listing price
Answer: A. Exclusive agency allows the broker to earn commission from any buyer source except the seller themselves; if the seller is the procuring cause, no commission is due.
Q 7.2·v9 Under an exclusive-agency listing agreement, when is the broker NOT entitled to a commission?
A. When another broker brings the buyer
B. When the listing period expires without a sale
C. When the seller procures the buyer without broker assistance ✓
D. When the property is sold through the MLS
Answer: C. In exclusive agency, the broker earns commission on all sales except those directly procured by the seller themselves; this is the defining exception to the broker's commission guarantee.
Q 7.3 A counteroffer:
A. Voids the listing
B. Must be accepted
C. Cancels the original offer ✓
D. Locks in the original price
Answer: C. A counteroffer rejects + replaces the original offer.
Q 7.3·v1 When a seller presents a counteroffer to a buyer's initial proposal, what happens to the original offer?
A. It is terminated and replaced by the counteroffer ✓
B. It is suspended until the counteroffer expires
C. It becomes a backup offer with reduced terms
D. It remains valid and the buyer may accept either offer
Answer: A. A counteroffer constitutes a rejection of the original offer and substitutes new terms in its place; the original offer no longer exists.
Q 7.3·v2 Under Hawaii real estate law, if a seller rejects a buyer's offer and submits modified contract terms instead, the buyer's original offer is:
A. Enforceable as a secondary contingency
B. Extinguished and superseded by the counteroffer ✓
C. Held in escrow pending the counteroffer outcome
D. Still binding on both parties unless formally withdrawn
Answer: B. The act of countering an offer constitutes a rejection of the original terms, eliminating that offer and creating a new negotiation point.
Q 7.3·v3 A buyer submits an offer on a property. The seller responds with a counteroffer containing different price and closing date. What is the status of the buyer's initial offer?
A. Automatically dead upon the seller's counteroffer ✓
B. Enforceable if the counteroffer is rejected within 48 hours
C. Converted to a contingent backup agreement
D. Active until expressly revoked in writing by the buyer
Answer: A. By presenting a counteroffer, the seller has rejected the original offer, which ceases to exist as a binding or enforceable agreement.
Q 7.3·v4 In a real estate transaction, a counteroffer differs from a rejection in that a counteroffer:
A. Proposes alternative terms while eliminating the previous offer ✓
B. Preserves the buyer's earnest money deposit from the initial offer
C. Requires the listing agent's approval before the original offer expires
D. Allows the original offer to remain open for acceptance
Answer: A. A counteroffer rejects the original proposal and simultaneously introduces new contract terms; the original offer is extinguished in this process.
Q 7.3·v5 When a seller presents a counteroffer to a buyer's initial offer, what happens to the original offer?
A. It is held in escrow pending the seller's decision
B. It is terminated and replaced by the counteroffer ✓
C. It becomes a contingent offer
D. It remains valid until the counteroffer is rejected
Answer: B. A counteroffer legally rejects and supersedes the original offer; the two cannot coexist simultaneously.
Q 7.3·v6 An offeree who responds with different terms than those proposed in the original offer has:
A. Made a counteroffer that extinguishes the original offer ✓
B. Preserved both offers for later comparison
C. Accepted the original offer conditionally
D. Requested mediation under Hawaii's real estate law
Answer: A. Presenting modified terms constitutes a counteroffer, which automatically rejects and replaces the prior offer.
Q 7.3·v7 If a buyer submits an offer at $500,000 and the seller responds with different price terms, the seller's response:
A. Cancels the original offer and creates a new negotiating point ✓
B. Keeps both offers active simultaneously
C. Requires the buyer to pay the difference immediately
D. Extends the inspection period by law
Answer: A. The seller's response with different terms is a counteroffer that terminates the buyer's original offer.
Q 7.3·v8 Under Hawaii real estate practice, when a seller issues a counteroffer with modified conditions, the buyer's original offer:
A. Automatically converts to a backup offer
B. Is no longer available for acceptance ✓
C. Gains legal priority over the counteroffer
D. Must be notarized before the counteroffer takes effect
Answer: B. A counteroffer rejection destroys the original offer, so the buyer can no longer accept it—they must respond to the counteroffer instead.
Q 7.3·v9 When a seller presents a counteroffer to a buyer's initial offer, what is the legal effect on the original offer?
A. It becomes a binding backup offer if the counteroffer is declined
B. It continues in effect alongside the counteroffer until closing
C. It is terminated and replaced by the new counteroffer terms ✓
D. It remains valid until the counteroffer is formally rejected in writing
Answer: C. A counteroffer constitutes a rejection of the original offer and replaces it with new terms; the original offer ceases to exist once the counteroffer is made.
Q 7.4 Specific performance is most often sought by:
A. Listing brokers
B. Lenders
C. Buyers ✓
D. Insurers
Answer: C. Buyers can compel conveyance because real estate is unique.
Q 7.4·v1 When a seller refuses to close on a purchase agreement for residential property, which party is most likely to file a lawsuit seeking specific performance?
A. The listing agent's broker
B. The title insurance company
C. The purchaser ✓
D. The mortgagee holding a construction loan
Answer: C. Buyers seek specific performance because real estate is considered unique property that cannot be adequately replaced by monetary damages alone.
Q 7.4·v2 In a real estate dispute, a court is most likely to award specific performance to satisfy the claims of:
A. A buyer seeking to compel the owner to convey the property ✓
B. A real estate agent claiming lost commission
C. An escrow officer demanding fee payment
D. A lender attempting to recover loss reserves
Answer: A. Specific performance compels conveyance because each parcel of land is unique and irreplaceable, making it the appropriate remedy for a buyer's breach claim.
Q 7.4·v3 Which party in a real estate transaction typically pursues specific performance as their remedy for breach of a sales contract?
A. Property managers
B. The buyer ✓
C. Insurance underwriters
D. Closing attorneys representing the title company
Answer: B. Buyers pursue specific performance because land and buildings are unique assets where no two properties are identical, making monetary damages insufficient.
Q 7.4·v4 Specific performance as a remedy in Hawaii real estate law is most commonly invoked by:
A. Buyers compelling sellers to complete the sale ✓
B. Homeowners associations enforcing CC&Rs
C. Brokers seeking to enforce listing agreement terms
D. Appraisers challenging valuation disputes
Answer: A. Buyers invoke specific performance because real property's unique nature means a breach cannot be remedied by damages; only actual conveyance satisfies the buyer's interest.
Q 7.4·v5 When a seller refuses to close and transfer title, which party has the strongest legal basis to request specific performance in Hawaii court?
A. The purchaser under the sales contract ✓
B. The title insurance company
C. The listing agent's employing broker
D. The mortgage lender holding the promissory note
Answer: A. A buyer can pursue specific performance because real property is considered unique and cannot be adequately replaced with monetary damages alone.
Q 7.4·v6 In a real estate dispute where the seller breaches the purchase agreement, specific performance is typically the remedy of choice for:
A. Lenders seeking foreclosure authority
B. Brokers seeking compensation for lost commissions
C. Buyers seeking to force conveyance of the property ✓
D. Sellers seeking to recover earnest money deposits
Answer: C. Buyers invoke specific performance because each parcel of real estate is unique; money damages cannot replicate the specific property the buyer contracted to purchase.
Q 7.4·v7 Which party to a real estate transaction would most likely ask a court to compel the other party to perform the actual deed transfer rather than accept monetary compensation?
A. A hazard insurance provider
B. A bank financing the property purchase
C. A prospective owner who signed a binding purchase agreement ✓
D. A managing broker seeking commission enforcement
Answer: C. The buyer has the strongest claim for specific performance because real estate's unique nature makes it impossible to substitute with damages; the buyer wants the actual property conveyed.
Q 7.4·v8 Specific performance as a contractual remedy in Hawaii real estate law is pursued most commonly by:
A. Real estate brokers collecting earned commissions
B. Escrow agents protecting earnest money
C. Sellers defending against breach claims
D. Purchasers seeking to enforce a binding sales agreement ✓
Answer: D. Purchasers use specific performance to force the actual conveyance of the real property because land is inherently unique and its loss cannot be compensated adequately through money damages.
Q 7.4·v9 When a seller refuses to close on a valid purchase agreement, which party is most likely to pursue specific performance in court?
A. The real estate appraiser
B. The escrow agent
C. The purchaser ✓
D. The title insurance company
Answer: C. Purchasers seek specific performance to force the seller to convey the property because real estate is considered unique and irreplaceable, making monetary damages an inadequate remedy.
Q 7.5 Time is of the essence means:
A. Closing must be within 30 days
B. The seller controls timing
C. Deadlines are strictly enforced ✓
D. Negotiations should be fast
Answer: C. Strict performance is required by the deadline.
Q 7.5·v1 In a Hawaii real estate contract, when a clause states 'time is of the essence,' what legal consequence does this create?
A. Both parties are encouraged to complete the transaction quickly but have flexibility
B. Failure to perform by the specified date constitutes a material breach ✓
C. The listing agent has authority to adjust closing deadlines as needed
D. The buyer may extend the closing date once without penalty
Answer: B. When time is of the essence, the deadline becomes a critical contractual term, and missing it is a material breach rather than a minor delay. This creates strict enforceability of the stated completion date.
Q 7.5·v2 A buyer and seller execute a purchase contract that includes the phrase 'time is of the essence.' What does this language require?
A. Prompt negotiation of repairs and credits between inspection and closing
B. Strict adherence to all dates and deadlines specified in the agreement ✓
C. The transaction must close by the end of the calendar month
D. All parties must communicate within 24 hours of any contract change
Answer: B. This language makes performance on or before the specified deadline a binding obligation; failure to meet deadlines becomes grounds for default rather than acceptable delay.
Q 7.5·v3 Which statement best describes the legal effect of including 'time is of the essence' in a real estate purchase agreement?
A. It requires the transaction to occur within a mutually agreed-upon general timeframe
B. It permits either party to walk away without penalty if deadlines slip by a few days
C. It allows the seller to unilaterally extend closing if repairs are incomplete
D. It makes timely performance a condition that must be satisfied to avoid breach ✓
Answer: D. This clause transforms deadlines from guidelines into strict contractual conditions; failure to perform by the deadline constitutes a material breach of contract.
Q 7.5·v4 A Hawaii real estate contract states 'time is of the essence.' A buyer misses the earnest money deposit deadline by three business days. What is the likely outcome?
A. The parties should negotiate a reasonable extension without legal consequences
B. The seller must accept the late deposit as long as it arrives within one week
C. The buyer's failure to meet the deadline is a material breach of contract ✓
D. The earnest money deadline is waived if the buyer communicates intent to close
Answer: C. With 'time is of the essence' language, even relatively minor delays in meeting specified deadlines constitute material breaches because the contract has established that timely performance is essential.
Q 7.5·v5 In a real estate contract, when a clause states 'time is of the essence,' what legal obligation does this create?
A. Performance must occur by the specified date or the contract may be breached ✓
B. Either party can request a 15-day extension without cause
C. The buyer may delay closing without penalty if market conditions change
D. The transaction timeline becomes a suggestion rather than a requirement
Answer: A. This clause makes the deadline a material term of the contract; failure to perform by the stated date constitutes a breach.
Q 7.5·v6 A seller's agent includes 'time is of the essence' in the purchase agreement. What does this language primarily accomplish?
A. It establishes that failure to close by the deadline is a material breach ✓
B. It allows the escrow company to set closing dates unilaterally
C. It prevents either party from requesting inspection contingencies
D. It encourages buyers to make quick offers during negotiation
Answer: A. The phrase makes timeliness a critical contract obligation; parties cannot disregard deadlines without risking breach of contract.
Q 7.5·v7 Which statement best explains the legal effect of including 'time is of the essence' in a Hawaii real estate purchase contract?
A. Negotiations must conclude within a specific timeframe set by the MLS
B. The real estate commission may issue a fine if closing is delayed
C. Strict compliance with stated deadlines becomes a contractual obligation ✓
D. The closing agent must schedule settlement within 20 business days
Answer: C. This clause converts the closing date and other time-sensitive terms into mandatory contract requirements rather than flexible guidelines.
Q 7.5·v8 A buyer's attorney advises that 'time is of the essence' language in the offer should be carefully negotiated. Why is this contract language significant?
A. It reduces the number of days allowed for title search and review
B. It makes the deadline a material term, and missing it can trigger contract default ✓
C. It grants the seller authority to proceed with other offers if closing is one day late
D. It automatically waives the buyer's right to conduct inspections
Answer: B. Including this clause means the parties have explicitly agreed that deadlines are binding; breach of the deadline may justify rescission or damages.
Q 7.5·v9 When a real estate contract includes the clause 'time is of the essence,' what legal obligation does this create for the parties?
A. The buyer may request a reasonable extension without penalty
B. The listing agent has authority to extend closing by up to 10 business days
C. Both parties are encouraged to complete the transaction promptly but flexibility is allowed
D. Performance must occur by the specified date or the contract may be breached ✓
Answer: D. This clause makes the deadline a material condition of the contract; failure to perform by the stated date constitutes a breach, with no automatic right to extension.
Q 7.6 Net listings are:
A. Most common for new construction
B. Disfavored or prohibited in most states ✓
C. Encouraged by NAR
D. Required by law
Answer: B. Net listings create conflict-of-interest risk.
Q 7.6·v1 A net listing arrangement, where the seller retains all proceeds above a set price and the broker keeps the difference, is generally regarded by most state regulators as:
A. Problematic due to inherent conflicts of interest ✓
B. The preferred method for commercial properties
C. An arrangement explicitly recommended by the National Association of REALTORS®
D. A standard practice compliant with fiduciary duties
Answer: A. Net listings create a conflict of interest because the broker's compensation increases if the sale price rises, incentivizing the broker to prioritize personal profit over the client's best interest; most states restrict or prohibit them.
Q 7.6·v2 Which statement accurately reflects how net listings are treated under real estate law and professional standards?
A. They are widely prohibited or disfavored due to conflict-of-interest concerns ✓
B. They are required by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission before listing any property
C. They are the most efficient pricing method for luxury homes
D. They are mandated in all residential transactions
Answer: A. Net listings inherently create a perverse incentive structure where the agent benefits more from higher sale prices, undermining the agent's fiduciary obligation to the seller; most states and professional organizations discourage or ban them.
Q 7.6·v3 In a net listing, the broker's commission is determined by the amount above a predetermined net price the seller will receive. What is the primary regulatory concern with this arrangement?
A. It reduces transparency and increases broker liability for disclosure violations
B. It establishes a financial incentive that conflicts with undivided loyalty to the client ✓
C. It creates an undisclosed dual agency situation
D. It violates the Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Answer: B. Net listings create a problematic incentive where the broker's profit grows with the sale price, creating a conflict of interest that undermines the broker's duty to represent the client's interests; this structural flaw is why they are disfavored or prohibited in most jurisdictions.
Q 7.6·v4 A broker proposes a net listing structure to a prospective seller, claiming it will maximize the seller's proceeds. From a regulatory and ethical standpoint, how are net listings typically addressed?
A. They are permitted without limitation as long as both parties consent in writing
B. They are restricted or prohibited in most states due to inherent conflict-of-interest problems ✓
C. They are actively promoted by state real estate commissions as consumer-friendly
D. They are the standard arrangement for properties listed under $500,000
Answer: B. Net listings are disfavored or prohibited because the broker's compensation incentive misaligns with fiduciary duty—the agent profits more by negotiating a higher price, creating a conflict that many jurisdictions restrict to protect consumers.
Q 7.6·v5 In Hawaii and most U.S. states, a net listing arrangement is generally:
A. Subject to strict regulation or outright prohibition due to ethical concerns ✓
B. Mandated by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission for all residential transactions
C. The preferred method for commercial property sales
D. Recommended by the National Association of REALTORS® as a best practice
Answer: A. Net listings are disfavored or prohibited in most states because they create inherent conflicts of interest between the agent's personal profit motive and the seller's interest in maximizing net proceeds.
Q 7.6·v6 Why would a Hawaii real estate licensee face regulatory scrutiny when entering into a net listing with a seller?
A. The arrangement creates a significant risk of agent self-dealing and undisclosed conflicts of interest ✓
B. Net listings reduce transaction costs and are considered industry standard practice
C. Federal law mandates that all listings must include a net price floor
D. Net listings are explicitly required by Hawaii statute for all residential properties
Answer: A. Net listings inherently incentivize the agent to keep any amount above the net price for themselves, rather than seeking the best possible price for the seller, creating a problematic conflict of interest.
Q 7.6·v7 Which statement accurately reflects the regulatory position on net listings in most states?
A. They are generally discouraged or prohibited because the listing agent's personal profit motive may override the seller's interests ✓
B. They are most frequently used in new construction and commercial development markets
C. They are encouraged by real estate commissions as a way to align broker and seller incentives
D. They are required by law whenever a seller requests a guaranteed sale price
Answer: A. Most states restrict or prohibit net listings due to the inherent conflict of interest: the agent benefits by keeping the difference between the sale price and the net price, rather than advocating for the highest possible price for the seller.
Q 7.6·v8 A seller asks a Hawaii licensee: 'Can we set up a net listing where you get to keep anything above $500,000?' The licensee should understand that this arrangement is:
A. Compliant with NAR Code of Ethics requirements
B. Problematic due to the conflict of interest it creates between the agent's compensation and the seller's best interest ✓
C. A common structure for listing agreements in residential real estate
D. Permissible under Hawaii law and standard industry practice
Answer: B. Net listings create an unacceptable conflict of interest because the agent profits directly from keeping the spread above the net price, rather than being motivated to achieve the highest possible sale price for the seller.
Q 7.6·v9 In Hawaii and most U.S. states, a net listing arrangement is generally viewed with caution or restricted because:
A. It is mandated by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission for all exclusive listings
B. It is the fastest way to sell residential properties in competitive markets
C. It creates an inherent conflict of interest between broker compensation and seller's best interest ✓
D. It guarantees the seller receives a minimum net amount regardless of sale price
Answer: C. Net listings are problematic because the broker's commission increases with the sale price above the net, incentivizing the broker to prioritize their own gain over maximizing the seller's proceeds, creating an ethical conflict.
Q 7.7 A contract signed under improper pressure is:
A. Voidable ✓
B. Unenforceable
C. Void
D. Executed
Answer: A. Duress makes a contract voidable at the harmed party's election.
Q 7.7·v1 If a seller coerces a buyer into signing a purchase agreement through threats, what is the legal status of that agreement?
A. It remains fully enforceable despite the coercion
B. It is automatically void from the moment of signing
C. It is voidable at the discretion of the coerced party ✓
D. It becomes executed upon the buyer's acceptance of duress
Answer: C. Duress renders a contract voidable, meaning the injured party may choose to either enforce or reject it; the contract is not void ab initio but gives the harmed party an election.
Q 7.7·v2 A broker obtains a listing agreement from an elderly owner after threatening to file a complaint with the REC if they don't sign. What is the contract status?
A. Voidable ✓
B. Void
C. Rescinded
D. Executed
Answer: A. A contract induced by coercion or improper pressure is voidable at the option of the wronged party, giving them the power to affirm or disaffirm.
Q 7.7·v3 Which term best describes a real estate contract that was signed after one party applied unlawful pressure to the other?
A. Unilaterally executed
B. Void ab initio
C. Voidable at the election of the coerced party ✓
D. Ratified
Answer: C. Improper pressure or duress makes a contract voidable rather than void, allowing the harmed party to choose whether to enforce or reject it.
Q 7.7·v4 A property manager signs a property management agreement under threat of eviction. The contract is:
A. Voidable by the threatened party ✓
B. Fully binding and enforceable
C. Ratified by operation of law
D. Automatically void
Answer: A. Duress makes a contract voidable, meaning the coerced party has the right to affirm or disaffirm it; it is not automatically void but rather subject to the victim's election.
Q 7.7·v5 When a real estate agent coerces a seller into signing a listing agreement through threats, the contract is most accurately described as:
A. Void ab initio
B. Fully executed and binding
C. Rescindable only with court approval
D. Voidable ✓
Answer: D. Duress renders a contract voidable, meaning the injured party may elect to affirm or disaffirm it, but the contract is not automatically void.
Q 7.7·v6 A buyer who signs a purchase agreement after being threatened with legal action if she does not comply has entered into a contract that is:
A. Automatically rescinded
B. Void and unenforceable against either party
C. Voidable at the buyer's election ✓
D. Valid but subject to rescission by the seller
Answer: C. A contract procured through duress is voidable—the threatened party has the right to void it, but only that party may exercise this option.
Q 7.7·v7 Which statement best describes a contract executed under undue influence or coercion?
A. It is void from its inception and never creates binding obligations
B. It is suspended until a court determines the extent of the pressure applied
C. It is unenforceable unless both parties later ratify it in writing
D. It is voidable, and the injured party may choose to enforce or disaffirm it ✓
Answer: D. Duress makes a contract voidable—the harmed party has the unilateral right to void it, though the contract is not inherently void.
Q 7.7·v8 A lessor pressures a tenant to sign an extension by threatening eviction based on a false claim of lease violation. The resulting extension agreement is:
A. Valid and enforceable unless the tenant files a complaint with the REC
B. Voidable at the tenant's discretion ✓
C. Enforceable against the tenant but not the lessor
D. Null and void from the moment of signing
Answer: B. Contracts procured through duress or improper pressure are voidable, meaning the injured party may disaffirm them, but they are not void ab initio.
Q 7.7·v9 A buyer executes a real estate purchase agreement after the seller threatens legal action if the buyer does not sign immediately. What is the legal status of this agreement?
A. It is enforceable because both parties signed the document
B. It is unenforceable only if the buyer can prove emotional distress
C. It is void from inception and cannot be ratified by either party
D. It is voidable by the injured party at their discretion ✓
Answer: D. Duress through threats renders a contract voidable, meaning the coerced party may choose to void it or enforce it; the contract is not automatically void.
Q 7.8 Substitution of a new party with all parties' consent is:
A. Novation ✓
B. Rescission
C. Reformation
D. Assignment
Answer: A. Novation releases the original obligor and substitutes a new one.
Q 7.8·v1 When a real estate contract is modified to replace the original buyer with a qualified third party and all parties agree to the change, this legal process is known as:
A. Novation ✓
B. Estoppel
C. Reformation
D. Delegation
Answer: A. Novation is the substitution of a new obligor with the consent of all parties, effectively releasing the original obligor from liability.
Q 7.8·v2 In a lease transaction, if the landlord, original tenant, and new tenant all consent to replace the original tenant with the new tenant, the substitution is accomplished through:
A. Novation ✓
B. Assignment with reservation of liability
C. Discharge by performance
D. Offset
Answer: A. Novation creates a new contract with a substitute obligor and releases the original obligor; it requires the express consent of all parties involved.
Q 7.8·v3 A seller's agent negotiates a deal where an original buyer backs out and is replaced by another buyer with the seller's approval. The seller also agrees to release the first buyer from any obligations. This substitution is:
A. Accord and satisfaction
B. Novation ✓
C. Waiver
D. Assumption
Answer: B. Novation involves replacing one obligated party with another and obtaining mutual consent from all parties to release the original party from further obligations.
Q 7.8·v4 Which contract modification technique specifically requires consent from all parties and extinguishes the original party's liability by substituting a new obligor?
A. Assignment
B. Subrogation
C. Novation ✓
D. Waiver
Answer: C. Novation is the only modification method that completely releases the original obligor while substituting a new one, and it demands express agreement from all involved parties.
Q 7.8·v5 When a contract requires all parties to agree to replace one obligor with another party, the legal process is called:
A. Novation ✓
B. Delegation
C. Rescission
D. Reformation
Answer: A. Novation is the mutual agreement by all parties to substitute a new obligor for the original one, discharging the original party's liability.
Q 7.8·v6 A seller, buyer, and lender all consent to replace the original buyer with a new buyer in a real estate transaction. This mutual substitution is known as:
A. Modification
B. Assumption of liability
C. Novation ✓
D. Assignment of contract
Answer: C. Novation requires consent from all parties and creates a new contract with the substituted party, releasing the original obligor entirely.
Q 7.8·v7 Which contractual remedy involves the complete substitution of one party for another with full consent of all remaining parties?
A. Assignment
B. Rescission
C. Novation ✓
D. Estoppel
Answer: C. Novation discharges the original party and creates a new obligation with the substitute party, requiring unanimous consent from all parties to the contract.
Q 7.8·v8 If a real estate contract party wants to be completely released from all obligations by having another party take their place with everyone's approval, this is accomplished through:
A. Subordination
B. Novation ✓
C. Contract interpretation
D. Transfer of title
Answer: B. Novation is the only mechanism that allows a party to be fully released from contractual obligations while a new party assumes them, provided all parties consent.
Q 7.8·v9 When all parties agree to replace an original contracting party with a completely new party, thereby releasing the original obligor from liability, this legal process is known as:
A. Rescission and restatement
B. Reformation of the contract terms
C. Novation ✓
D. Assignment of contractual rights
Answer: C. Novation is the substitution of a new obligor with consent of all parties, which extinguishes the original party's obligations. Assignment, by contrast, transfers rights but does not release the original obligor.
Q 7.9 An option contract requires:
A. A 30-day exercise period
B. Notarization
C. Consideration paid by optionee for the option ✓
D. Equal exchange
Answer: C. Optionee must pay something to keep the option open.
Q 7.9·v1 What element is essential to make an option contract binding and enforceable in Hawaii real estate transactions?
A. A written agreement signed by both parties
B. Recording with the Bureau of Conveyances
C. Payment or other valuable consideration from the optionee to the optionor ✓
D. A specific expiration date within 60 days
Answer: C. An option contract requires the optionee to provide consideration (money or value) to the optionor to secure the right to purchase the property within a specified timeframe.
Q 7.9·v2 In a real estate option agreement, the optionee's primary obligation is to:
A. Provide compensation to the optionor in exchange for the right to purchase ✓
B. Accept the property exactly as disclosed in the inspection report
C. Register the option with the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. Complete the purchase within 45 days or forfeit all rights
Answer: A. The optionee must pay consideration (a fee or deposit) to hold the option open and secure the seller's promise to sell at a specified price if exercised.
Q 7.9·v3 Which of the following is a legal requirement for a valid option contract in Hawaii real estate?
A. The option period must align with the standard real estate transaction timeline
B. The optionee must give something of value to support the option ✓
C. The optionor must be a licensed real estate broker
D. Both parties must appear before a notary public
Answer: B. Consideration from the optionee is essential to create a binding option; without payment or value, there is no enforceable contract right.
Q 7.9·v4 A real estate option becomes legally binding when the optionee:
A. Files the option contract with the county recorder
B. Signs the agreement in the presence of the optionor
C. Submits a purchase agreement to the seller's agent
D. Provides consideration to the optionor for the right to purchase ✓
Answer: D. An option requires the optionee to pay or provide value to the optionor; this consideration makes the optionor's offer to sell irrevocable for the option period.
Q 7.9·v5 What essential element must the optionee provide to establish a valid option contract in Hawaii?
A. Proof of financing approval
B. A mutual agreement to exchange properties
C. Money or valuable consideration to bind the option ✓
D. A written appraisal of the property
Answer: C. An option contract requires the optionee to pay consideration (money or other valuable benefit) to the optionor to keep the option right alive and enforceable.
Q 7.9·v6 Which of the following is NOT required for an enforceable option contract?
A. An option fee or deposit held by the optionor
B. Payment or other value from the optionee
C. A specific exercise period lasting at least 60 days ✓
D. Consideration moving from optionee to optionor
Answer: C. While consideration is essential, there is no mandated minimum duration for the option period; parties may agree to any timeframe, including shorter periods.
Q 7.9·v7 A real estate option contract becomes binding when:
A. The property is formally appraised and recorded
B. The optionee delivers consideration to the optionor for the right to purchase ✓
C. Both parties execute a sales contract within the option period
D. The optionor signs a statement acknowledging receipt of earnest money
Answer: B. An option contract is created when the optionee gives consideration (typically a fee or deposit) to the optionor in exchange for the right to purchase the property at a specified price within a set time.
Q 7.9·v8 Under Hawaii real estate law, what must the optionee provide to secure an option contract?
A. Equal value in the form of a counter-option
B. Verification that all liens will be satisfied at closing
C. Cash or something of value paid to the optionor ✓
D. Notarized consent from the property owner's spouse
Answer: C. The optionee must pay consideration to create a binding option contract; this payment gives the optionee the exclusive right to purchase within the agreed-upon time period.
Q 7.9·v9 What essential element must the optionee provide to establish a valid option agreement in Hawaii real estate?
A. Monetary or valuable consideration to the optionor ✓
B. A binding commitment to purchase within 60 days
C. Proof of financing approval
D. A written appraisal of the property
Answer: A. The optionee must pay consideration (money or something of value) to secure the optionor's promise to keep the property available for a specified period. Without consideration, there is no enforceable option contract.
Q 7.10 A contingency that fails:
A. Generally terminates the contract with deposit returned ✓
B. Triggers liquidated damages
C. Voids the listing
D. Forces the contract to close anyway
Answer: A. Failed contingency typically allows termination and deposit return.
Q 7.10·v1 When a buyer's financing contingency is not satisfied by the deadline, what is the typical legal outcome?
A. The buyer may terminate the contract and recover the earnest money deposit ✓
B. The contract automatically converts to a cash sale
C. The property listing becomes void and must be re-listed
D. The seller may force specific performance to proceed to closing
Answer: A. An unsatisfied contingency generally permits contract termination with return of the buyer's deposit; the contract does not automatically continue or convert.
Q 7.10·v2 A home inspection contingency is not satisfied by the inspection deadline. What typically happens to the purchase contract?
A. The seller's license is suspended for allowing the contingency to lapse
B. The contract may be terminated by the buyer, and the deposit is usually returned ✓
C. The buyer forfeits the entire deposit as liquidated damages
D. The parties must proceed to closing regardless of inspection results
Answer: B. When a contingency expires unused, the buyer generally loses that protection but may still terminate; the deposit return depends on contract language and whether default occurred.
Q 7.10·v3 In a real estate purchase agreement, if an appraisal contingency condition is not met, the most likely outcome is:
A. The contract terminates and the buyer receives the earnest money back ✓
B. The sale must close at the appraised value regardless of purchase price
C. Liquidated damages are assessed against the buyer
D. The real estate license of the listing agent is placed on probation
Answer: A. A failed appraisal contingency typically allows either party to terminate, with the earnest money returned unless the buyer is in default of the contract.
Q 7.10·v4 Under Hawaii real estate law, when a contingency in a purchase contract cannot be fulfilled by the specified deadline, the expected outcome is:
A. The buyer must pay penalties equal to the contingency amount
B. The property automatically becomes subject to new listing requirements
C. The contract remains binding and the deposit is held in escrow indefinitely
D. The contract may be terminated and the earnest money is generally released to the buyer ✓
Answer: D. A contingency that fails permits contract termination, typically with deposit return to the buyer, unless the buyer caused the failure or waived the contingency.
Q 7.10·v5 When a buyer's financing contingency is not satisfied by the deadline, what is the typical consequence?
A. The buyer becomes obligated to close without a loan
B. The seller may immediately pursue specific performance
C. The contract is usually dissolved and the earnest money deposit is released to the buyer ✓
D. The listing agent receives a commission adjustment
Answer: C. A failed contingency generally allows the buyer to terminate without penalty and recover their earnest money deposit, as the contingency condition was not met.
Q 7.10·v6 Under Hawaii real estate law, if an inspection contingency expires unresolved, the likely outcome is:
A. Contract termination with the deposit returned to the buyer ✓
B. Automatic forfeiture of the buyer's earnest money to the seller
C. The parties must renegotiate the purchase price
D. The property reverts to the broker's trust account indefinitely
Answer: A. When a contingency fails to be satisfied, the contract typically terminates and the earnest money is returned to the buyer unless the buyer waives the contingency.
Q 7.10·v7 A buyer includes a homeowner's association approval contingency in the purchase agreement. The HOA denies approval. What is the standard contract result?
A. The seller may force closing despite the denial
B. Both parties split the earnest money as a settlement fee
C. The buyer must seek arbitration before any release of funds
D. The contract is terminated and the buyer recovers their earnest money deposit ✓
Answer: D. A failed contingency allows the party relying on it to terminate the contract and recover their earnest money, as the contingency condition was not satisfied.
Q 7.10·v8 If a contingency in a real estate contract is not met prior to the contingency deadline, the most common legal effect is:
A. Liquidated damages become immediately due to the seller
B. Contract termination occurs and the buyer's deposit is returned ✓
C. The title company holds all funds in escrow indefinitely
D. The contract converts to a binding lease agreement
Answer: B. When a contingency fails, the contract is generally terminated without penalty and the earnest money is returned to the buyer, as the contingency protection has been triggered.
Q 7.10·v9 When a buyer's inspection contingency is not satisfied and the condition is not waived, what is the typical legal consequence?
A. The seller may force the buyer to close the transaction
B. The listing agreement is automatically canceled
C. The buyer forfeits the entire down payment as penalty
D. The contract is usually dissolved and the buyer's earnest money deposit is released ✓
Answer: D. A failed contingency generally allows the non-breaching party to terminate the contract and recover their earnest money deposit, as the condition precedent was not met.
Q 7.11 A right of first refusal allows the holder to:
A. Refuse all offers
B. Force a sale
C. Buy at any price
D. Match a bona fide third-party offer ✓
Answer: D. ROFR = right to match the deal someone else has offered.
Q 7.11·v1 When a property owner grants a right of first refusal to a tenant, what right does the tenant acquire?
A. The automatic ownership of the property upon lease termination
B. The opportunity to match any acceptable offer the owner receives from a third party ✓
C. The ability to purchase the property at below-market rates
D. An exclusive listing agreement preventing the owner from showing the property
Answer: B. A right of first refusal gives the holder the chance to match an offer that the owner has actually received from another buyer; it does not guarantee a price, prevent other offers, or transfer ownership.
Q 7.11·v2 Which statement best describes the mechanics of exercising a right of first refusal?
A. The holder can demand the owner sell at a price the holder determines
B. The holder gains control over all marketing and sale decisions the owner makes
C. The holder automatically receives legal title to the property without negotiation
D. The holder must be notified of a legitimate third-party offer and given the chance to accept those same terms ✓
Answer: D. ROFR requires notification of a real third-party offer and allows the holder to match that offer's terms; it does not grant pricing power, control over operations, or automatic title.
Q 7.11·v3 A beneficiary of a right of first refusal is in a position to:
A. Prevent the owner from listing the property for sale
B. Step into the shoes of a third-party buyer by matching the offer the owner received ✓
C. Purchase the property whenever they wish at any negotiated price
D. Veto any sale the property owner wishes to make
Answer: B. ROFR allows the holder to match a bona fide third-party offer the owner has received; it is not a veto right, an unlimited purchase option, or a listing restriction.
Q 7.11·v4 Under a right of first refusal clause, the property owner must:
A. Grant the ROFR holder exclusive permission to find buyers before listing publicly
B. Notify the ROFR holder of an acceptable offer from another buyer and allow the holder to match it ✓
C. Sell only to the ROFR holder at a price determined by the holder
D. Accept the first offer made by any prospective buyer without negotiation
Answer: B. ROFR obligates the owner to inform the holder of a genuine third-party offer and permit the holder to match those terms; it does not surrender pricing control, require acceptance of the first offer, or grant exclusive listing rights.
Q 7.11·v5 When a property owner grants a right of first refusal to a tenant, what action is the tenant entitled to take if the owner receives an acceptable offer from a third party?
A. Negotiate the purchase price downward without the owner's consent
B. Reject the sale entirely and block any future transactions
C. Match the terms of the third-party offer before it can be accepted ✓
D. Demand a lease extension at no additional cost
Answer: C. A right of first refusal gives the holder the opportunity to accept or match the exact terms of a bona fide offer from another buyer, not to modify terms or block sales.
Q 7.11·v6 Which statement best describes the practical benefit of holding a right of first refusal on a property?
A. The right provides an opportunity to match an actual offer before the owner accepts from someone else ✓
B. The right eliminates the owner's ability to sell the property to anyone
C. The right allows the holder to purchase without a formal appraisal or inspection
D. The right guarantees the holder can purchase at any price they choose
Answer: A. ROFR works by allowing the holder to meet the same terms a third party has offered, giving them a chance to step in before the transaction closes with an outside buyer.
Q 7.11·v7 If a seller receives a legitimate purchase offer from Buyer A, and that seller has previously granted a right of first refusal to Buyer B, what must happen next?
A. The seller can immediately accept Buyer A's offer and ignore Buyer B's rights
B. The seller must void Buyer A's offer and renegotiate with Buyer B at a lower price
C. The seller must offer Buyer B the same terms Buyer A presented to match or decline ✓
D. Buyer B can force the seller to accept any counteroffer from Buyer B
Answer: C. The holder of a right of first refusal must be given the opportunity to match the bona fide third-party offer's terms; the owner cannot bypass this right by immediately accepting another buyer's offer.
Q 7.11·v8 A real estate agent representing a property owner learns that the property carries a right of first refusal in favor of the current lessee. When a third-party cash offer arrives, what is the correct procedure?
A. Notify the lessee of the offer terms and allow them to match before the owner accepts ✓
B. Reject the third-party offer because the lessee's right prevents any outside sale
C. Present the third-party offer to the owner, who can accept it immediately since cash is superior
D. Inform the owner that the lessee automatically has the right to purchase at any negotiated price
Answer: A. Even with a strong third-party offer, the owner must honor the right of first refusal by giving the lessee the chance to accept the same terms before the owner can sell to the outside party.
Q 7.11·v9 Under a right of first refusal, if the property owner receives an acceptable offer from a third party, the ROFR holder must be given the opportunity to:
A. Accept the same terms as the third-party offer ✓
B. Veto any sale to that particular buyer
C. Extend the contract indefinitely
D. Negotiate the purchase price down by at least 10%
Answer: A. A right of first refusal entitles the holder to match (accept on the same terms) the bona fide offer the property owner has received from another party, not to renegotiate, reject all offers, or block sales indefinitely.
Q 7.12 A minor's contract is generally:
A. Voidable by the adult
B. Unenforceable
C. Voidable by the minor ✓
D. Void
Answer: C. Minors can affirm or disaffirm; protection runs to the minor.
Q 7.12·v1 Under Hawaii real estate law, what is the legal status of a contract entered into by a person under 18 years of age?
A. Immediately void and cannot be ratified
B. Enforceable only if a parent co-signs the agreement
C. Subject to disaffirmance at the minor's election ✓
D. Fully binding and enforceable against both parties
Answer: C. Minors have the right to disaffirm (cancel) contracts; this protection is a one-way right that belongs to the minor, not the adult party.
Q 7.12·v2 A 16-year-old signs a real estate purchase agreement without parental consent. Which statement best describes the contract's enforceability?
A. Voidable only if the adult party objects within 30 days
B. Absolutely void and cannot be ratified under any circumstances
C. Valid and binding unless the minor obtains a court order of rescission
D. Capable of being disaffirmed by the minor upon reaching majority or before ✓
Answer: D. Contracts with minors are voidable at the minor's option; the minor retains the power to affirm or disaffirm, but the adult cannot force the minor to perform.
Q 7.12·v3 When a minor executes a real estate transaction without proper authorization, the resulting contract is best characterized as:
A. Unenforceable against both parties until the minor reaches age of majority
B. Binding on the minor but not on the adult seller or buyer
C. Capable of being avoided by the minor through disaffirmance ✓
D. Null and void from inception with no possibility of enforcement
Answer: C. Minors' contracts are voidable (not void), meaning the minor has the right to disaffirm; this protects the minor's interests while allowing ratification upon reaching majority.
Q 7.12·v4 A 17-year-old broker applicant enters into a listing agreement on behalf of a client. What is the legal nature of this contract from the minor's perspective?
A. Enforceable against the minor but subject to the adult's withdrawal
B. Permanently invalid and cannot be performed by anyone
C. Disaffirmable at the minor's discretion, giving the minor an out ✓
D. Void ab initio unless a licensed guardian approves in writing
Answer: C. A minor's contract is voidable by the minor alone; the minor may disaffirm (reject) the contract, but only the minor has this power of avoidance.
Q 7.12·v5 When a party to a real estate transaction discovers they were a minor at the time of signing, what is the legal status of that contract?
A. Subject to disaffirmance at the minor's election ✓
B. Absolutely void and cannot be ratified under any circumstances
C. Valid only if the minor's parent provides written consent retroactively
D. Binding on the minor but voidable by the adult party
Answer: A. Minors have the legal right to disaffirm (cancel) their contracts; the law protects the minor's interests, not the adult's.
Q 7.12·v6 A 17-year-old signs a purchase agreement for a condominium in Honolulu without parental consent. Which statement best describes the contract's enforceability?
A. It is void if the seller did not know the buyer was underage
B. It is enforceable against both parties equally
C. It is voidable at the minor's discretion only ✓
D. It may be ratified by the minor once they reach age 18
Answer: C. The minor has the power to disaffirm or affirm the contract; only the minor benefits from this protection, not the adult party.
Q 7.12·v7 In a Hawaii real estate transaction, if one party is a minor, the contract is typically:
A. Voidable at the option of the minor party ✓
B. Enforceable only with a guardian ad litem's approval
C. Void ab initio regardless of the minor's later wishes
D. Voidable at the option of the non-minor party
Answer: A. Contract law protects minors by giving them alone the right to disaffirm; the adult party has no such right of avoidance.
Q 7.12·v8 A teenager enters into a lease agreement for a residential property without understanding all terms. After turning 18, the former minor seeks to cancel the lease. What legal principle applies?
A. The lease is voidable by the minor but cannot be disaffirmed after age of majority
B. The lease is void and was never valid
C. The lessor can force performance because the minor benefited from occupancy
D. The minor had the right to disaffirm before or after reaching majority ✓
Answer: D. Minors retain the power to disaffirm contracts and may exercise this right during minority or within a reasonable time after reaching adulthood.
Q 7.12·v9 Under Hawaii law, when a person under the age of majority enters into a purchase agreement for real property, the contract is best characterized as:
A. Valid and binding unless a court determines it unfair
B. Capable of being disaffirmed solely at the minor's election ✓
C. Capable of being disaffirmed by either party
D. Absolutely void from inception
Answer: B. A minor has the unilateral right to disaffirm (void) a contract upon reaching majority or during minority; the adult party cannot similarly disaffirm based on the minor's age alone.
08
Transfer of Title
National portion4 PSI items34 key concepts12 base questions

Title transfers happen at closing. Master the deed types, recording, and escrow.

Chapter Overview

A deed is the document that transfers title from grantor to grantee. To be valid, a deed requires: a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, a recital of consideration, words of conveyance ("grant," "convey," "sell"), an adequate legal description, the signature of the grantor (not the grantee), delivery, and acceptance. Notarization isn't required for validity but is required for recording. Recording protects the grantee's interest against later claims by giving constructive notice to all subsequent parties.

Deed types differ by warranties. A General Warranty Deed offers the strongest protection — the grantor warrants against all defects of title back to the property's origin, including those before the grantor owned it. The four typical covenants: seisin (grantor owns it), against encumbrances (no undisclosed liens), quiet enjoyment (buyer won't be disturbed by superior claim), and warranty forever (grantor will defend title). A Special (Limited) Warranty Deed warrants only against defects arising during the grantor's ownership. A Bargain and Sale Deed implies the grantor has title but offers no express warranties. A Quitclaim Deed conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with zero warranty — common for clearing title clouds, transferring between family members, divorce settlements.

Title at death passes by will (testate) or by state intestate succession statute (intestate). A testator must have testamentary capacity (sound mind, knowledge of property and natural heirs). Intestate succession follows a statutory order: spouse, children, parents, siblings, more distant relatives. Probate court oversees the transfer, validates wills, settles claims against the estate, and issues letters testamentary or letters of administration to the personal representative who deeds the property.

Joint tenancy property passes by survivorship outside probate — no will needed for the share to pass to surviving joint tenants. Property held in trust passes per trust terms (avoiding probate). A life estate ends at the measuring life's death and either reverts to grantor or remains to a named remainderman.

Title insurance protects against title defects existing at the time of closing. Two policies: an owner's policy (one-time premium, protects buyer for as long as they own) and a lender's policy (required by lender, covers loan amount, decreases as loan balance does). Standard exclusions: defects created or known by the insured, government regulations, eminent domain proceedings, mining claims, and matters not of record. Extended coverage can be purchased for some excluded items via endorsements.

Chain of title is the recorded history of ownership. A title search examines the chain back to a marketable starting point. A title abstract is the summary report. Clouds are defects or unresolved claims affecting marketability — old liens not released, unsigned deeds, gaps in chain, conflicting recordings. A suit to quiet title is a court action to resolve clouds and confirm ownership.

Closing combines the buyer's funds, the loan proceeds, and the deed into a single coordinated transfer. An escrow agent (or attorney in attorney-state closings) holds funds and documents and disburses on satisfaction of all conditions. Closing statements detail every credit and debit. The federal Closing Disclosure form replaced the HUD-1 for most residential mortgage loans.

Prorations split shared items at the closing date — taxes, rent, HOA dues, insurance, utilities. Methods vary by state and contract: 360-day "banker's" year (12 × 30) or actual 365-day year. The day of closing is allocated by contract — sometimes seller pays through closing, sometimes buyer owns from closing. Conveyance/transfer taxes and recording fees are charged based on the deed value.

Key Concepts & Definitions
DeedDocument transferring title from grantor to grantee.
Grantor / GranteeGrantor = transferor (signs deed). Grantee = recipient.
Words of conveyance"Grant, sell, convey..." — required to make a deed effective.
Habendum clause"To have and to hold" — defines extent of estate granted.
Granting clauseStates the conveyance and consideration.
Consideration recitalStatement of value exchanged. May be nominal ("$10 and other valuable consideration").
Legal descriptionPrecise identification of property: metes and bounds, lot and block, government rectangular survey.
AcknowledgmentNotarized statement that signature was made voluntarily. Required for recording, not validity.
Delivery and acceptanceDeed must be delivered with intent to convey; grantee must accept. No transfer until both occur.
General warranty deedStrongest deed. Five covenants. Warranties run back to property's origin.
Special / limited warranty deedWarrants only against defects arising during grantor's ownership.
Bargain and sale deedImplies grantor has title; no express warranties.
Quitclaim deedConveys whatever interest grantor has; no warranties. Used to clear title clouds.
Sheriff's deedTransfers title from foreclosure sale or judgment execution.
Tax deedTransfers title from tax foreclosure sale.
RecordingFiling the deed with the county recorder. Provides constructive notice.
Constructive noticeLegal presumption everyone is on notice of recorded documents.
Actual noticeSubjective knowledge of fact.
Inquiry noticeNotice imputed when facts would prompt a reasonable person to investigate.
Title insuranceProtects against title defects existing at closing. Owner's + lender's policies.
Chain of titleRecorded history of ownership.
Title abstractSummary report of chain of title.
Title commitmentInsurer's preliminary report identifying issues to clear before closing.
Cloud on titleDefect or unresolved claim affecting marketability.
Suit to quiet titleCourt action to resolve clouds and confirm ownership.
