Marketable titleTitle free of significant clouds, acceptable to a reasonable buyer.
ProbateCourt process administering a deceased person's estate.
Testate / intestateTestate = died with valid will. Intestate = without one.
Intestate successionStatutory order of heirs when no will.
Letters testamentary / administrationCourt documents authorizing personal representative to act.
Escrow agentNeutral third party holding funds + documents and disbursing per instructions.
Closing DisclosureFederal form summarizing loan + closing costs. Replaced HUD-1 for most residential.
Conveyance tax / transfer taxState or local tax on real property transfers.
ProrationSplitting shared expenses at closing.
Question Bank — Transfer of Title
Q 8.1 Which deed offers the most protection to the buyer?
A. Special warranty
B. General warranty ✓
C. Quitclaim
D. Bargain and sale
Answer: B. General warranty deed warrants the entire chain of title.
Q 8.1·v1 A buyer wants maximum protection regarding title defects throughout the property's entire history. Which type of deed should the buyer request?
A. General warranty deed ✓
B. Bargain and sale deed
C. Quitclaim deed
D. Special warranty deed
Answer: A. General warranty deed provides the broadest protection by warranting title against all defects from the beginning of ownership, not just during the grantor's period of ownership.
Q 8.1·v2 If a buyer is concerned about title issues that may have existed before the current owner acquired the property, which deed provides the best safeguard?
A. Quitclaim deed
B. Special warranty deed
C. Bargain and sale deed
D. General warranty deed ✓
Answer: D. General warranty deed warrants the entire chain of title, protecting the buyer against defects regardless of when they originated in the property's history.
Q 8.1·v3 Which of the following deeds contains covenants that extend back to the original source of title?
A. General warranty deed ✓
B. Special warranty deed
C. Bargain and sale deed
D. Quitclaim deed
Answer: A. General warranty deed includes covenants that warrant the entire title chain from the beginning, providing comprehensive protection to the grantee.
Q 8.1·v4 A buyer purchasing residential property in Hawaii wants assurance against title defects from any prior owner. Which deed offers this comprehensive coverage?
A. Bargain and sale deed
B. Special warranty deed
C. General warranty deed ✓
D. Quitclaim deed
Answer: C. General warranty deed warrants title against all defects in the entire chain of ownership, making it the most protective deed for a buyer's interests.
Q 8.1·v5 A buyer in Hawaii wants maximum title protection and representation of clear ownership. Which deed type should the seller be required to provide?
A. General warranty deed ✓
B. Bargain and sale deed
C. Quitclaim deed
D. Special warranty deed
Answer: A. General warranty deed provides the broadest protection because the grantor warrants title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor acquired the property.
Q 8.1·v6 If a buyer needs a deed that covers potential title defects throughout the entire history of the property, which instrument provides the most comprehensive protection?
A. Special warranty deed
B. Bargain and sale deed
C. General warranty deed ✓
D. Quitclaim deed
Answer: C. General warranty deed warrants title for the entire chain of ownership and protects against defects that may have existed before the current owner took possession.
Q 8.1·v7 A buyer is reviewing deed options and wants to minimize risk exposure from prior title claims. Which deed provides the strongest guarantee?
A. Statutory warranty deed
B. Special warranty deed
C. Quitclaim deed
D. General warranty deed ✓
Answer: D. General warranty deed offers the strongest guarantee by warranting against all title defects in the entire chain of title, not just defects created during the grantor's ownership.
Q 8.1·v8 Which of the following deeds would a buyer prefer when financing a Hawaii property because it offers the most recourse against the grantor for hidden title defects?
A. Bargain and sale deed
B. General warranty deed ✓
C. Quitclaim deed
D. Special warranty deed
Answer: B. General warranty deed provides the most extensive recourse because the grantor warrants the title against defects from the beginning of the chain, not just during their period of ownership.
Q 8.1·v9 A buyer is concerned about potential title defects from previous owners. Which type of deed would provide the strongest legal recourse if an undisclosed claim arises from the property's history?
A. General warranty deed, which guarantees title from the original owner to the present ✓
B. Quitclaim deed, which releases only the grantor's claims to the property
C. Bargain and sale deed, which transfers all grantor's interests without warranties
D. Special warranty deed, which covers only the grantor's period of ownership
Answer: A. General warranty deed provides the broadest protection by warranting the entire chain of title back to the original owner, allowing the buyer to pursue claims against the grantor for any title defects regardless of when they originated.
Q 8.2 A quitclaim deed:
A. Guarantees clear title
B. Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranty ✓
C. Cannot be recorded
D. Is used only for first-time conveyances
Answer: B. Quitclaim is "as-is" with no warranties.
Q 8.2·v1 When a grantor executes a quitclaim deed, what is the extent of the grantor's obligation regarding the title being conveyed?
A. The grantor warrants the title is marketable and insurable
B. The grantor transfers only whatever rights or interest the grantor actually possesses, without any warranty of ownership ✓
C. The grantor guarantees the property is free from all liens and encumbrances
D. The grantor must defend the title against all subsequent claims
Answer: B. A quitclaim deed conveys the grantor's interest as-is with no warranties of title, ownership, or freedom from defects.
Q 8.2·v2 Which statement accurately describes the nature and effect of a quitclaim deed in Hawaii real estate practice?
A. It requires a title search and title insurance before recording
B. It is typically used only in commercial transactions between sophisticated parties
C. It releases whatever claim or interest the grantor may have without guaranteeing the grantor actually owns anything ✓
D. It provides the grantee with full covenants and warranties of title
Answer: C. A quitclaim deed is a minimal-warranty instrument that merely releases the grantor's claim or interest without affirming ownership or quality of title.
Q 8.2·v3 A buyer receives a quitclaim deed from the seller. What protection does the buyer have if the seller did not actually own the property?
A. The buyer has no recourse against the seller based on the deed itself, as quitclaim deeds contain no title warranties ✓
B. Title insurance automatically covers any defect in the grantor's ownership
C. The Hawaii REC will void the deed and return the buyer's money
D. The buyer is protected by the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment in all Hawaii deeds
Answer: A. A quitclaim deed provides no warranties; if the grantor had no interest to convey, the grantee receives nothing and has no warranty claim.
Q 8.2·v4 How does a quitclaim deed differ from a general warranty deed in terms of the grantor's liability?
A. A quitclaim deed contains no warranties of title, while a general warranty deed includes covenants protecting the grantee against title defects ✓
B. A quitclaim deed imposes greater liability on the grantor than a general warranty deed
C. Both deeds impose identical liability regardless of the grantor's intent or knowledge
D. A quitclaim deed is legally binding only if recorded within 30 days
Answer: A. A quitclaim deed is a no-warranty instrument passing only the grantor's interest, whereas a general warranty deed warrants the title against defects.
Q 8.2·v5 Which statement best describes the legal effect of a quitclaim deed in Hawaii?
A. It transfers title subject to any liens or encumbrances the grantor may have held ✓
B. It is valid only when the grantor has already obtained a warranty deed first
C. It provides the grantee with title insurance protection against prior claims
D. It requires a full property survey before recording is permitted
Answer: A. A quitclaim deed conveys only the interest the grantor possessed, without warranties of title or clear ownership, meaning encumbrances transfer with it.
Q 8.2·v6 When a grantor executes a quitclaim deed, what does the grantee actually receive?
A. Whatever ownership rights or claims the grantor held at the time of conveyance, with no assurances about quality ✓
B. A legal promise that the property is unencumbered and marketable
C. Only the right to occupy the property for a specified lease term
D. A guaranteed fee simple title free of all defects
Answer: A. Quitclaim deeds are 'as-is' instruments that pass only what the grantor has, with zero warranties regarding title quality or defects.
Q 8.2·v7 A real estate licensee is explaining deed types to a buyer. Which characteristic most accurately reflects a quitclaim deed?
A. It releases whatever interest the grantor possesses without representing the validity or extent of that interest ✓
B. It is the most secure form of conveyance and includes full covenants of title
C. It must be delivered by a title company and cannot be handed directly to the grantee
D. It is automatically void if the property has any outstanding property taxes or assessments
Answer: A. A quitclaim deed simply conveys the grantor's interest—whatever it may be—without any warranties or representations about its validity.
Q 8.2·v8 From a risk perspective, a grantee accepting a quitclaim deed should understand that:
A. The Hawaii REC guarantees the title is free from defects within 30 days of recording
B. The deed is not legally binding unless the grantor has previously obtained a certified title report
C. The grantor makes no warranties about the quality, extent, or freedom from encumbrances of the interest being transferred ✓
D. Title insurance is automatically included and paid for by the grantor under state law
Answer: C. Quitclaim deeds provide no warranties, meaning the grantee accepts the risk that the grantor's interest may be defective, limited, or encumbered.
Q 8.2·v9 When a grantor executes a quitclaim deed, what exactly is being transferred to the grantee?
A. The grantor's equitable interest, but not legal title
B. Only the grantor's legal interest in the property, with full warranty of title
C. Whatever right, title, or interest the grantor possesses at the time of conveyance, without any guarantees ✓
D. A fee simple absolute interest, provided the property has no liens
Answer: C. A quitclaim deed transfers only the grantor's existing interest with no warranties or representations about title quality, marketability, or freedom from defects.
Q 8.3 For a deed to be valid, it must be:
A. Notarized
B. In a court order
C. Recorded
D. Delivered and accepted ✓
Answer: D. Delivery + acceptance is essential. Recording protects but isn't required for validity.
Q 8.3·v1 Which of the following is an essential requirement for a deed to become legally binding and effective?
A. Physical transfer of possession to the grantee
B. Filing with the county assessor's office
C. Actual delivery to and acceptance by the grantee ✓
D. Approval by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
Answer: C. Delivery and acceptance are the critical elements for a deed to be valid and enforceable. Recording and other formalities provide protection but are not essential to the deed's validity.
Q 8.3·v2 A grantor executes a properly signed and notarized deed but fails to deliver it to the grantee. Under Hawaii law, is the deed valid?
A. No, because delivery and acceptance have not occurred ✓
B. Yes, because the grantor's intent to transfer is sufficient
C. Yes, because it was notarized by a public officer
D. Yes, because it was recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances
Answer: A. Without delivery to and acceptance by the grantee, a deed lacks the essential element needed for validity, regardless of notarization or execution formality.
Q 8.3·v3 Which element is NOT required for a deed to be valid in Hawaii?
A. The grantor's intent to transfer the property
B. Delivery of the deed to the grantee
C. Recording the document with the county recorder ✓
D. Acceptance by the intended grantee
Answer: C. Recording is a protective measure that creates constructive notice but is not a prerequisite for a deed's validity; delivery and acceptance are the essential requirements.
Q 8.3·v4 A deed is prepared, signed, and notarized. For this deed to become legally valid and effective, what must still occur?
A. It must be delivered to the grantee and accepted by them ✓
B. The deed must be recorded within 30 days
C. The county tax assessor must acknowledge receipt
D. The title company must issue an insurance commitment
Answer: A. Delivery and acceptance constitute the final, essential step for deed validity; all other steps are procedural protections or formalities that follow after the deed is already valid.
Q 8.3·v5 Which of the following is an essential requirement for a deed to have legal effect and transfer title?
A. Physical transfer of the document to the grantee and their acceptance of it ✓
B. Approval by a probate court
C. Filing with the county assessor's office
D. Obtaining a title insurance commitment
Answer: A. Delivery to the grantee and acceptance by the grantee are fundamental requirements for title transfer. Recording, title insurance, and court approval are separate matters that do not affect the deed's legal validity.
Q 8.3·v6 A deed fails to transfer property if it lacks:
A. Proper delivery to and acceptance by the grantee ✓
B. An attorney's signature as a witness
C. County recorder's stamp and filing date
D. A certified copy filed at the state level
Answer: A. Delivery and acceptance are the critical elements that make a deed effective. Without them, title does not pass regardless of notarization, recording, or attorney involvement.
Q 8.3·v7 Which element is absolutely necessary for a deed to become legally valid and binding?
A. Recordation in the public record
B. Registration with the Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources
C. Acknowledgment before a notary public
D. Delivery of the deed to the grantee with the grantee's acceptance ✓
Answer: D. Delivery and acceptance are essential substantive requirements for deed validity. Recording and notarization are procedural safeguards but are not required for the deed itself to be valid.
Q 8.3·v8 A grantor signs and has a deed notarized. For the deed to be valid and effectively transfer title, what must also occur?
A. The deed must be approved by the local zoning board
B. The deed must be delivered to the grantee and accepted by the grantee ✓
C. The deed must be recorded within 30 days
D. The deed must be reviewed by a title company
Answer: B. Notarization alone does not create validity; delivery and acceptance are the non-negotiable requirements for a deed to transfer title. Recording protects interests but is not a prerequisite for validity.
Q 8.3·v9 Which of the following is a requirement for a deed to have legal validity in Hawaii?
A. The grantor must physically transfer the deed to the grantee, and the grantee must accept it ✓
B. The deed must be filed with the county assessor within 30 days
C. The deed must contain a legal description that has been surveyed by a licensed surveyor
D. The grantor must obtain title insurance before signing
Answer: A. Delivery by the grantor and acceptance by the grantee are essential elements for deed validity; recording and surveying are protective measures but not required for the deed itself to be valid.
Q 8.4 A person dies without a will. Their property passes by:
A. Public auction
B. Quitclaim deed
C. Eminent domain
D. Operation of law via intestate succession ✓
Answer: D. Intestate succession statutes determine heirs.
Q 8.4·v1 When an individual passes away intestate in Hawaii, the transfer of real property to heirs occurs through which mechanism?
A. Government taking via condemnation proceedings
B. Automatic transfer by quitclaim deed
C. Statutory intestate succession laws ✓
D. Probate court auction to the highest bidder
Answer: C. Intestate succession statutes automatically determine which heirs inherit and in what order when someone dies without a valid will.
Q 8.4·v2 A decedent with no testamentary document leaves behind titled real property. How does legal title transfer to the rightful heirs?
A. Through the application of intestacy statutes ✓
B. By exercise of the government's right to take private property
C. By competitive public sale of the estate
D. Via a general warranty deed prepared by the county
Answer: A. Intestacy laws establish the legal succession chain and automatically vest property rights in qualified heirs without requiring a will or additional conveyance instruments.
Q 8.4·v3 When someone dies intestate, which of the following determines who receives their real property?
A. State laws governing intestate succession ✓
B. The probate court's discretionary judgment
C. A non-binding quitclaim deed filed posthumously
D. The public trustee's authority to distribute assets
Answer: A. Intestate succession statutes, not judicial discretion or voluntary conveyance documents, establish the predetermined order and shares of inheritance for heirs.
Q 8.4·v4 Property of a decedent who left no will passes to the next of kin by what legal process?
A. Adverse possession by the county government
B. Conversion through a special purpose deed instrument
C. Intestate succession as prescribed by statute ✓
D. Forced liquidation and redistribution by the state
Answer: C. Intestate succession statutes provide the legal mechanism by which property automatically transfers to heirs according to a predetermined order of kinship when no will exists.
Q 8.4·v5 When a Hawaii resident passes away intestate, which mechanism governs the distribution of their real property to heirs?
A. Probate court auction procedures
B. Automatic transfer via warranty deed
C. State acquisition through escheat powers
D. Statutory intestate succession laws ✓
Answer: D. Intestate succession statutes automatically determine who inherits when no will exists; this is a matter of law, not deed transfer or auction.
Q 8.4·v6 If an individual dies without executing a valid will, their real estate property will be transferred according to:
A. State laws governing descent and distribution ✓
B. Judicial condemnation proceedings
C. The decedent's prior quitclaim deeds
D. The county assessor's title determination
Answer: A. State descent and distribution laws (intestate succession) dictate property transfer when no will exists; these are statutory rules, not deed-based or condemnation mechanisms.
Q 8.4·v7 An owner of Hawaii property dies without a testamentary document. By what legal process does ownership transfer to heirs?
A. Operation of intestacy statutes ✓
B. Competitive public sale at auction
C. Filing a special warranty deed with the registry
D. Petition for eminent domain by the state
Answer: A. Intestacy statutes operate automatically by law to pass property to legal heirs; this occurs without deed action, condemnation, or auction.
Q 8.4·v8 When a property owner in Hawaii dies intestate, the transfer of real property to heirs occurs through:
A. Transfer by gift deed to designated beneficiaries
B. Foreclosure sale procedures
C. Application of intestate succession laws ✓
D. Execution of a new deed by the executor
Answer: C. Intestate succession laws determine heirs and property distribution automatically when no will exists; this is distinct from deed execution, foreclosure, or gift transfers.
Q 8.4·v9 When an individual passes away intestate in Hawaii, what legal mechanism governs the distribution of their real property to heirs?
A. Transfer under the state's right of condemnation
B. Competitive sealed bidding at county auction
C. A warranty deed executed by the probate court
D. Statutory intestate succession laws ✓
Answer: D. Intestate succession statutes automatically determine which heirs inherit property when there is no valid will; no deed or auction is required.
Q 8.5 Recording a deed provides:
A. No notice
B. Actual notice
C. Constructive notice ✓
D. Inquiry notice
Answer: C. Recording = constructive notice to all subsequent parties.
Q 8.5·v1 When a property owner files a deed in the public record, what type of notice is provided to the world regarding that transaction?
A. Inquiry notice requiring investigation of the property title
B. Personal notice delivered directly to all interested parties
C. Presumptive notice based on the grantor's reputation
D. Constructive notice available through the public record system ✓
Answer: D. Recording a deed in the public record creates constructive notice, which means all subsequent parties are deemed to have knowledge of the recorded interest, whether or not they actually inspected the records.
Q 8.5·v2 A buyer's lender requires title insurance before funding a mortgage loan. The lender relies on the fact that recording the deed will establish what form of notice?
A. Implied notice based on the buyer's possession of the property
B. Constructive notice through the recordation system ✓
C. Express notice through personal notification
D. Statutory notice automatically provided by the county
Answer: B. Recording creates constructive notice, which protects the lender by ensuring that all future parties searching the title records will be charged with knowledge of the lender's interest.
Q 8.5·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, the primary purpose of recording a deed in the appropriate county office is to provide:
A. Judicial notice requiring court approval of the transaction
B. Constructive notice to all subsequent parties who search the records ✓
C. Actual notice to the immediate parties to the transaction only
D. Apparent notice based on visible improvements to the property
Answer: B. Recording provides constructive notice to the world, meaning anyone conducting a proper title search will be charged with knowledge of the recorded deed, even if they never actually read it.
Q 8.5·v4 If an agent advises a client that their recently recorded deed will protect their ownership interest against future claims, what legal concept is the agent relying upon?
A. Lis pendens notice filed in pending litigation
B. Constructive notice created by proper recordation ✓
C. Estoppel notice preventing the other party from denying the transaction
D. Actual notice obtained through personal service of documents
Answer: B. Constructive notice is the legal principle that makes recording effective—it charges all subsequent parties with knowledge of the recorded deed without requiring actual delivery or personal notice to each individual.
Q 8.5·v5 When a property deed is properly recorded in the Hawaii Bureau of Conveyances, what type of notice is created for all future purchasers and lienholders?
A. Implied notice from neighborhood conditions
B. Actual notice requiring personal delivery of documents
C. Constructive notice through the public record system ✓
D. Inquiry notice requiring personal investigation
Answer: C. Recording creates constructive notice, which means the public record system itself provides legal notice to all subsequent parties without requiring actual knowledge or personal contact.
Q 8.5·v6 A buyer searches the recorded documents at the Bureau of Conveyances and discovers a prior mortgage on the property. This discovery represents which form of notice?
A. Constructive notice because the information was available in the public record ✓
B. Inquiry notice because the buyer had to investigate the chain of title
C. Statutory notice issued by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. Actual notice because the buyer personally reviewed the documents
Answer: A. Constructive notice arises from the recording system itself; once a document is recorded, all parties are legally charged with knowledge of its contents regardless of whether they actually reviewed it.
Q 8.5·v7 Which of the following BEST describes the legal effect of recording a deed in Hawaii?
A. It puts the world on notice of the transaction through the public record system ✓
B. It requires all subsequent buyers to personally contact the current owner
C. It transfers possession of the property to the grantee immediately upon filing
D. It guarantees the grantor's title is free from all defects
Answer: A. Recording provides constructive notice, placing the world on legal notice of the recorded interest through the public record system, even if parties never actually read the document.
Q 8.5·v8 A deed is recorded but a third party claims they had no knowledge of it. Under Hawaii law, what notice has been provided to that third party?
A. Actual notice because the recording officer must provide personal notification
B. Constructive notice; recording in the public record provides legal notice regardless of actual knowledge ✓
C. No notice; only actual knowledge counts in real estate disputes
D. Inquiry notice; the party should have searched before entering the transaction
Answer: B. Recording creates constructive notice to all parties, meaning the law presumes notice through the public record system exists even if the party never actually knew about or reviewed the recorded deed.
Q 8.5·v9 When a buyer searches the public record and finds a properly recorded deed, what type of notice has been established?
A. Constructive notice through the recording system ✓
B. Actual notice requiring personal knowledge of the grantor
C. Inquiry notice based on visible conditions of the property
D. Statutory notice under Hawaii's adverse possession laws
Answer: A. Recording a document in the public record creates constructive notice to anyone who searches or should search those records, regardless of whether they actually reviewed them.
Q 8.6 Title insurance protects against:
A. Property damage
B. Future title problems
C. Defects existing at closing ✓
D. Loan default
Answer: C. Title insurance covers title defects existing at closing time.
Q 8.6·v1 Which of the following is covered by a title insurance policy?
A. Hidden liens and ownership claims that existed before closing ✓
B. Boundary disputes that arise after the policy is issued
C. Structural defects discovered during property inspection
D. Natural disasters affecting the insured property
Answer: A. Title insurance protects against pre-existing defects in the chain of title, such as undisclosed liens, encumbrances, and ownership claims that existed at or before closing.
Q 8.6·v2 A homeowner purchases title insurance at closing. The policy protects the owner against:
A. Future zoning changes that reduce property value
B. Loss of the property due to foreclosure
C. Maintenance and repair costs for structural issues
D. Defects in the title that existed prior to the closing date ✓
Answer: D. Title insurance is designed to indemnify the owner against losses arising from title defects that were in existence at or before the time of closing, not future events.
Q 8.6·v3 When a real estate transaction closes, the title insurance policy issued at that time covers:
A. Environmental contamination discovered years later
B. Increases in property taxes assessed after the purchase
C. Claims by creditors against the new owner
D. Pre-existing conditions affecting the legal ownership of the property ✓
Answer: D. Title insurance provides coverage for defects that existed in the title at the time of closing, protecting against historical ownership and lien issues.
Q 8.6·v4 Which scenario would be covered under a standard title insurance policy?
A. A previous owner's unpaid property tax bill discovered after closing ✓
B. A mortgage default by the current property owner
C. A neighbor's encroachment onto the property after the policy is issued
D. A flood that damages the home six months after purchase
Answer: A. Title insurance covers defects existing at closing time, including unpaid taxes and liens from prior ownership that were not discovered before the transaction closed.
Q 8.6·v5 Which of the following is covered under a standard owner's title insurance policy?
A. Pre-existing title defects present at the time of closing ✓
B. Liens and encumbrances discovered after the sale closes
C. Unpaid property taxes assessed in future years
D. Natural disasters affecting the property structure
Answer: A. Title insurance protects the owner against defects in title that existed at the time of closing, not future occurrences or physical damage to the property.
Q 8.6·v6 A buyer purchases a home and receives a title insurance commitment. What risk is the insurer primarily protecting the buyer against?
A. Hidden title defects that existed before the closing date ✓
B. Flood damage or other casualty losses
C. Changes in property value or market conditions
D. Maintenance repairs needed within the first year
Answer: A. Title insurance is designed to protect against defects in ownership that existed at the time of purchase, not future market changes or physical damage to the property.
Q 8.6·v7 An owner's title insurance policy provides protection for:
A. Structural deficiencies discovered during inspection
B. Claims arising from future boundary disputes
C. Defects in the chain of title existing at closing ✓
D. Mortgage payment defaults by the property owner
Answer: C. Title insurance covers defects in title that existed at the time of closing, such as undisclosed liens, missing heirs, or forgery in the chain of title.
Q 8.6·v8 Which situation would typically be covered under a standard title insurance policy?
A. A previous owner files a claim six months after closing
B. The property suffers water damage from a burst pipe
C. The borrower fails to make scheduled loan payments
D. A title defect from an earlier owner discovered at or before closing ✓
Answer: D. Title insurance protects against defects in title that existed on or before the closing date, regardless of when they are discovered.
Q 8.6·v9 When a title insurance policy is issued at closing, what is its primary purpose in protecting the buyer?
A. Ensuring the seller's mortgage is paid off after settlement
B. Covering hidden liens and ownership claims that existed before closing ✓
C. Guaranteeing the property will increase in value
D. Protecting against future natural disasters affecting the property
Answer: B. Title insurance protects against defects and claims that existed before or at the time of closing, such as undisclosed liens, easements, or ownership disputes that may surface later.
Q 8.7 A lender's title policy:
A. Is optional
B. Covers the lender for loan amount ✓
C. Replaces homeowner's insurance
D. Covers the buyer
Answer: B. Lender's policy covers the loan amount and decreases as loan is paid down.
Q 8.7·v1 Which statement accurately describes the scope and purpose of a lender's title insurance policy in Hawaii?
A. It protects the property owner against title defects up to the purchase price
B. It is always bundled with the owner's policy and cannot be purchased separately
C. It protects the mortgagee's financial interest in the loan amount, which diminishes as the loan balance decreases ✓
D. It provides coverage for physical damage to the property caused by title disputes
Answer: C. A lender's policy insures the lender's security interest for the outstanding loan amount, decreasing proportionally as the borrower pays down the mortgage principal.
Q 8.7·v2 A mortgagee in Hawaii requires a lender's title policy as a condition of financing. What is the primary benefit to the lender?
A. The policy covers the lender against losses arising from title defects, with coverage limited to the outstanding mortgage balance ✓
B. The policy compensates the lender if the borrower defaults on the monthly payment
C. The policy guarantees that the borrower will maintain homeowner's insurance for the duration of the loan
D. The policy transfers all ownership risks to a third-party escrow holder
Answer: A. The lender's policy specifically insures the lender's loan security against title defects, with the coverage amount equaling the loan balance at any given time.
Q 8.7·v3 In a typical Hawaii real estate transaction, how does a lender's title insurance policy differ from an owner's policy?
A. The lender's policy is mandatory while the owner's policy is optional
B. The lender's policy covers both the buyer and the lender equally
C. The lender's policy protects only the mortgagee's interest up to the loan amount, whereas the owner's policy protects the buyer's equity ✓
D. The lender's policy lasts indefinitely while the owner's policy expires after ten years
Answer: C. The lender's policy insures the lender's loan amount security and decreases as the loan is paid, while the owner's policy protects the buyer's ownership interest.
Q 8.7·v4 A borrower obtains financing for a $500,000 purchase price with a $400,000 mortgage. Which party is covered by the lender's title insurance policy, and to what extent?
A. The real estate agent is covered for any commission disputes related to title defects
B. The borrower is covered for the full $500,000 purchase price
C. Both the borrower and lender share equal coverage of $450,000
D. The lender is covered for its security interest in the $400,000 loan amount, declining as the mortgage is paid down ✓
Answer: D. A lender's policy protects the mortgagee specifically for the loan amount outstanding, with coverage decreasing as principal is paid and eventually terminating when the mortgage is satisfied.
Q 8.7·v5 Which statement accurately describes the scope and purpose of a lender's title insurance policy in Hawaii?
A. It protects the property owner against all title defects throughout the loan term
B. It is mandatory for all residential transactions and cannot be waived
C. It indemnifies the mortgagee for the outstanding loan balance and diminishes as the loan principal is repaid ✓
D. It covers both the lender and borrower equally under a single combined policy
Answer: C. A lender's policy insures the lender's interest (the loan amount) and the coverage amount decreases proportionally as the mortgage principal is paid down.
Q 8.7·v6 A lender requires title insurance as a condition of funding the mortgage. What is the primary protection this lender's policy provides?
A. Protection against future property tax assessments and special assessments
B. Protection of the lender's financial interest in an amount equal to the loan balance outstanding ✓
C. Protection of the buyer's equity and ownership rights against title defects
D. Protection that remains constant at the original purchase price regardless of loan payoff
Answer: B. The lender's policy covers the mortgagee's interest, which equals the loan amount owed, and this coverage amount reduces as the borrower pays down the principal balance.
Q 8.7·v7 In a typical Hawaii real estate transaction, the lender's title insurance policy differs from an owner's policy in that it:
A. Is paid for by the seller instead of the buyer
B. Provides broader coverage and includes all physical property defects
C. Extends indefinitely even after the mortgage has been satisfied
D. Protects an amount of coverage that decreases in proportion to the loan paydown ✓
Answer: D. The lender's policy amount tracks the outstanding loan balance; as the borrower pays down the mortgage, the insured amount decreases accordingly, unlike an owner's policy which remains constant.
Q 8.7·v8 A mortgagee insists on a title insurance policy before releasing loan funds. This lender's policy protects against title defects up to an amount equal to:
A. The unpaid principal balance of the mortgage loan at any given time ✓
B. A flat minimum amount set by Hawaii real estate commission rules
C. The appraised value of the property at the time of closing
D. The original sales price stated in the purchase agreement
Answer: A. A lender's title policy insures the mortgagee's interest for the loan amount, with coverage declining as the principal balance is paid down over the life of the loan.
Q 8.7·v9 Which statement accurately describes the scope and purpose of a lender's title insurance policy?
A. It protects the property owner against defects in title
B. It provides coverage that increases as the mortgage principal is paid down
C. It is a mandatory requirement that can never be waived by the borrower
D. It insures the lender's interest up to the outstanding loan balance ✓
Answer: D. A lender's title policy protects the lender's financial interest in the property up to the loan amount, with coverage that decreases as the borrower pays down the principal balance.
Q 8.8 Property held in joint tenancy passes at death:
A. To the trustee
B. By intestate succession
C. By survivorship outside probate ✓
D. Through probate
Answer: C. Joint tenancy avoids probate via right of survivorship.
Q 8.8·v1 When a joint tenant dies, what happens to their interest in the property?
A. It must be probated through the decedent's estate
B. It automatically transfers to the surviving joint tenant(s) without court involvement ✓
C. It passes according to Hawaii's rules of intestate succession
D. It reverts to the state as abandoned property
Answer: B. Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship, which allows the property to pass directly to surviving joint tenants outside the probate process.
Q 8.8·v2 Which of the following best describes the probate treatment of property owned in joint tenancy?
A. Subject to probate administration and the decedent's debts
B. Controlled by a court-appointed guardian during estate settlement
C. Exempt from probate due to the right of survivorship ✓
D. Passed through probate only if the will specifies joint tenancy property
Answer: C. Joint tenancy with right of survivorship bypasses probate entirely, allowing immediate transfer to the surviving joint tenant(s) upon death.
Q 8.8·v3 A property owner in Hawaii holds real property in joint tenancy with another person. Upon the owner's death, the property will most likely:
A. Be held in trust by the decedent's personal representative
B. Be distributed according to Hawaii's intestacy statutes
C. Go through a formal probate process as part of the estate
D. Pass directly to the surviving joint tenant outside of probate ✓
Answer: D. The right of survivorship inherent in joint tenancy ensures the property transfers automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), completely avoiding probate.
Q 8.8·v4 Compared to sole ownership, what is a key advantage of holding property in joint tenancy regarding estate disposition?
A. The property avoids estate taxes through a stepped-up basis
B. The property is automatically subject to a recorded deed of trust
C. The surviving joint tenant receives the property without probate proceedings ✓
D. The surviving joint tenant must file an affidavit with the probate court
Answer: C. Joint tenancy's right of survivorship allows seamless transfer to the surviving co-owner(s) upon death, bypassing the probate system entirely.
Q 8.8·v5 When a joint tenant dies, how does their interest in the property transfer to the surviving joint tenant?
A. Automatically by operation of law, without probate proceedings ✓
B. Through the probate court system
C. To a designated beneficiary named in a deed
D. Via the decedent's will or the state intestacy statute
Answer: A. Joint tenancy with right of survivorship transfers property directly to surviving co-owners outside the probate process upon death.
Q 8.8·v6 Which statement correctly describes what happens to jointly held real property when one joint tenant passes away?
A. Title automatically vests in the surviving joint tenant(s) outside probate ✓
B. The property must be transferred by court order following intestate succession laws
C. Ownership transfers to the county recorder's office until heirs claim it
D. The deceased's share goes to their estate and is distributed through probate
Answer: A. Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship, which causes the property to pass automatically to surviving joint tenants without probate involvement.
Q 8.8·v7 A property is titled in joint tenancy between two individuals. Upon the death of one joint tenant, the surviving joint tenant's interest in the property is determined by:
A. Creditors' claims filed during the probate period
B. The provisions of the decedent's last will and testament
C. The right of survivorship inherent in the joint tenancy arrangement ✓
D. State laws governing probate administration and estate settlement
Answer: C. The right of survivorship is a fundamental characteristic of joint tenancy that automatically passes the deceased's share to the surviving co-owner(s) outside probate.
Q 8.8·v8 If real estate is owned in joint tenancy and one owner dies, which of the following best describes the transfer of that owner's property interest?
A. It passes according to the decedent's intestate succession plan
B. It transfers immediately to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law ✓
C. It is held in trust for the heirs until probate is completed
D. It becomes part of the probate estate and is subject to court administration
Answer: B. Joint tenancy creates an automatic transfer mechanism—the right of survivorship—that bypasses probate entirely and vests the property directly in surviving co-owners.
Q 8.8·v9 When a joint tenant dies, how does their interest in the property transfer to the surviving joint tenant?
A. Automatically by operation of law without probate proceedings ✓
B. Through the probate court system with a will requirement
C. By quitclaim deed filed with the county recorder
D. Through the Hawaii intestate succession statutes
Answer: A. Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship, which automatically transfers the deceased's interest to surviving joint tenants outside the probate process by operation of law.
Q 8.9 A "cloud on title" is:
A. A type of warranty
B. A federal lien
C. An unresolved title claim or defect ✓
D. A weather event
Answer: C. Cloud = title defect or unresolved claim.
Q 8.9·v1 Which of the following best describes what a title professional means by a "cloud on title"?
A. A type of title insurance policy endorsement
B. A period of overcast weather that delays closing
C. An outstanding claim or encumbrance that casts doubt on ownership ✓
D. A recorded easement benefiting adjacent property
Answer: C. A cloud on title is any defect or unresolved claim that impairs the seller's ability to convey clear ownership to the buyer.
Q 8.9·v2 In Hawaii real estate transactions, when a seller's title report shows a potential "cloud," this typically indicates:
A. The property is located in a flood zone
B. The buyer must obtain a survey before closing
C. There is a questionable claim or unresolved defect affecting ownership ✓
D. The property has an existing deed of trust that may be assumed
Answer: C. A cloud on title represents any issue—such as a competing claim, old lien, or improperly released mortgage—that clouds the marketability of the title.
Q 8.9·v3 A real estate licensee should advise a buyer that a "cloud on title" means:
A. There is an unresolved title issue or adverse claim that needs to be cleared ✓
B. The property cannot be financed by conventional lenders
C. The seller holds only a life estate rather than fee simple ownership
D. The property is subject to a homeowners association lien
Answer: A. A cloud on title is any defect or competing claim that impairs clear title and must typically be resolved before or at closing.
Q 8.9·v4 Which situation would most likely create a "cloud on title" that a title search might reveal?
A. The current owner holds a mortgage with a reputable institutional lender
B. The property is assessed for property taxes annually
C. The property is zoned for residential use in an urban area
D. A previous owner's unpaid judgment lien remains recorded against the property ✓
Answer: D. A cloud on title consists of unresolved claims or defects—such as judgment liens, unreleased mortgages, or competing ownership claims—that cloud marketability.
Q 8.9·v5 When a title search reveals a 'cloud on title,' what does this indicate?
A. A mechanic's lien has been placed on the property by a contractor
B. The property has been registered with the Hawaii Land Court system
C. There is an outstanding claim or defect that impairs the seller's ability to transfer clear ownership ✓
D. The property is located in a flood zone requiring additional insurance
Answer: C. A cloud on title is any claim, lien, or defect that creates uncertainty or impairs ownership rights; it must be resolved before a clean title transfer.
Q 8.9·v6 Which of the following best describes a 'cloud on title' in real estate transactions?
A. A covenant requiring disclosure of property defects to future buyers
B. An easement granted by the state of Hawaii for public utility purposes
C. An unresolved or questionable claim against the property that affects marketability ✓
D. A title insurance policy that limits coverage to specific risks
Answer: C. A cloud on title is a defect or unresolved claim that makes the title unmarketable; it must be cleared through legal action or settlement.
Q 8.9·v7 A title company discovers a 'cloud on title' during a preliminary examination. What does this mean?
A. The property deed must be recorded with the state tax assessor
B. The property is subject to deed restrictions that limit future use
C. The owner has failed to pay property taxes for the current fiscal year
D. There exists an outstanding claim, prior lien, or other defect that affects clear ownership transfer ✓
Answer: D. A cloud on title represents any unresolved title defect or claim that compromises the seller's ability to convey marketable title.
Q 8.9·v8 In Hawaii real estate practice, a 'cloud on title' refers to:
A. An unresolved title defect or questionable claim that must be resolved before clear title passes ✓
B. A preliminary assessment required by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
C. A requirement to obtain title insurance before closing escrow
D. A notice from the Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources regarding property boundaries
Answer: A. A cloud on title is any defect, lien, or claim that creates doubt about ownership; it impairs marketability until resolved.
Q 8.9·v9 When a title examiner discovers a "cloud on title," what does this mean for the property owner?
A. The property is located in a flood-prone area requiring additional insurance
B. The seller must provide a title commitment within 10 days
C. There is a potential dispute or encumbrance that may affect ownership rights ✓
D. A mechanic's lien has been recorded against the property
Answer: C. A cloud on title refers to any unresolved claim, defect, or potential dispute that casts doubt on clear ownership—distinct from specific liens or weather conditions.
Q 8.10 A deed must be signed by:
A. Both parties
B. Grantor only ✓
C. A notary only
D. Grantee only
Answer: B. Only the grantor signs the deed.
Q 8.10·v1 Which party is responsible for executing (signing) a warranty deed?
A. The title company representative
B. Both the transferor and recipient together
C. The transferor of the property ✓
D. The recipient of the property
Answer: C. The transferor (grantor) executes the deed by signing it; the grantee does not need to sign for the deed to be valid.
Q 8.10·v2 When preparing a quitclaim deed for a real estate transaction, whose signature is required on the document?
A. Only the person receiving the property must sign
B. Only the person conveying the property must sign ✓
C. A licensed Hawaii attorney must sign as witness
D. Both the grantor and grantee must sign
Answer: B. Only the grantor (person conveying) needs to sign the deed; the grantee's signature is not a legal requirement for deed validity.
Q 8.10·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, a deed requires the signature of:
A. The grantee and grantor in equal capacity
B. The grantor alone ✓
C. The escrow agent and title company officer
D. A notary public acting as principal
Answer: B. The grantor's signature alone is sufficient to execute a valid deed; the grantee does not sign the deed.
Q 8.10·v4 Which of the following statements about deed execution in Hawaii is correct?
A. Both parties must appear together to sign before a notary
B. Only the grantor is required to sign a deed ✓
C. The grantor's agent can sign without the grantor's presence
D. The grantee must countersign the deed for it to be recordable
Answer: B. A deed requires only the grantor's signature; the grantee is not a party to the execution of the deed.
Q 8.10·v5 In Hawaii real estate transactions, which party is responsible for executing the deed by adding their signature?
A. The person transferring the property ✓
B. Both the transferor and transferee
C. The person receiving the property
D. The title company representative
Answer: A. The grantor (person transferring property) is the only party required to sign the deed; the grantee's signature is not necessary for a valid deed.
Q 8.10·v6 Which of the following is a requirement for executing a valid deed in Hawaii?
A. Signature of the grantor only ✓
B. Signature of the grantee alone
C. Signature of the grantee and grantor together
D. Signature of a licensed escrow officer
Answer: A. Only the grantor must sign the deed; the grantee is not a signatory party to the instrument transferring title.
Q 8.10·v7 When closing a real estate transaction in Hawaii, whose signature makes a deed legally binding?
A. Signatures from both parties equally
B. The recorder's signature upon filing
C. The grantor's signature only ✓
D. The grantee's signature and acknowledgment
Answer: C. The grantor's signature is what executes the deed and transfers title; the grantee does not sign the deed itself.
Q 8.10·v8 A seller is preparing to transfer property to a buyer through a warranty deed. Who must sign this document?
A. The seller and buyer together
B. Only the real estate agent handling the transaction
C. Only the seller ✓
D. Only the buyer
Answer: C. The seller, as the grantor, is the only required signatory on the deed; the buyer (grantee) does not execute the deed.
Q 8.10·v9 When preparing a warranty deed for recording in Hawaii, whose signature is legally required on the document?
A. The person receiving the property
B. The county recorder
C. The person transferring the property ✓
D. Both the transferor and transferee
Answer: C. Only the grantor (person transferring the property) must sign a deed. The grantee does not sign the deed, though they may sign other closing documents.
Q 8.11 The federal closing form for most residential mortgage loans is:
A. HUD-1
B. Settlement Statement
C. Truth in Lending
D. Closing Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. CD replaced HUD-1 for TRID loans.
Q 8.11·v1 Under the TRID rule, which document must lenders provide to borrowers at closing for residential real estate transactions?
A. Uniform Settlement Statement
B. Final Loan Estimate
C. Truth in Lending Act Disclosure
D. Closing Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. The Closing Disclosure is the mandatory TRID closing document that replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement for federally regulated residential mortgage transactions.
Q 8.11·v2 Which of the following is the current official closing document required by federal law for most home purchase loans?
A. RESPA Accounting Form
B. Loan Origination Statement
C. Closing Disclosure ✓
D. HUD-1 Settlement Statement
Answer: C. The Closing Disclosure replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement when the TRID rule took effect, and is now the required federal closing document for residential mortgage loans.
Q 8.11·v3 A borrower is closing on a residential mortgage loan subject to federal TRID requirements. What form must the lender provide at the closing table?
A. Promissory Note and Security Instrument
B. Good Faith Estimate and HUD-1
C. Closing Disclosure ✓
D. Settlement Agreement and Title Insurance Commitment
Answer: C. The Closing Disclosure is the federally mandated form that lenders must provide at closing for TRID-covered residential loans, replacing the earlier HUD-1.
Q 8.11·v4 Since implementation of the TRID rule, the standard federal disclosure document provided at closing for residential home loans has been:
A. Uniform Settlement Statement
B. Loan Estimate only
C. HUD-1 or its equivalent
D. Closing Disclosure ✓
Answer: D. The Closing Disclosure became the required federal closing document under TRID, superseding the HUD-1 Settlement Statement for residential mortgage transactions.
Q 8.11·v5 Under the TRID rule, which document must be provided to borrowers at closing for a federally-regulated residential mortgage transaction?
A. Loan Estimate (final version)
B. HUD-1 Settlement Statement
C. Closing Disclosure ✓
D. Truth in Lending Statement
Answer: C. The Closing Disclosure is the mandatory federal closing document required by TRID regulations for most residential mortgage loans, replacing the older HUD-1 form.
Q 8.11·v6 A mortgage lender in Hawaii must provide borrowers with which official federal closing document three business days before settlement?
A. Promissory Note
B. Good Faith Estimate
C. Closing Disclosure ✓
D. Settlement Statement
Answer: C. The Closing Disclosure is the TRID-required federal form that lenders must deliver at least three business days before closing for residential mortgage transactions.
Q 8.11·v7 Which of the following replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement as the standard federal closing disclosure form for most home loans?
A. Affiliated Business Arrangement Disclosure
B. Final Truth in Lending Act Notice
C. Closing Disclosure ✓
D. Uniform Closing Dataset
Answer: C. The Closing Disclosure superseded the HUD-1 form under the TRID rule to provide consumers with a clearer, more standardized federal closing document.
Q 8.11·v8 In a typical residential mortgage closing subject to federal regulations, the lender must provide the borrower with:
A. A Closing Disclosure that itemizes loan terms and closing costs ✓
B. A Truth in Lending disclosure at the time of closing
C. A completed HUD-1 form signed by all parties
D. A Settlement Statement within 24 hours after closing
Answer: A. The Closing Disclosure is the federally-mandated TRID form that lenders must provide to show loan terms and itemized closing costs for residential mortgage transactions.
Q 8.11·v9 Under TRID requirements, which document must a lender provide to a borrower at least three business days before closing on a residential mortgage transaction?
A. Initial Escrow Statement
B. Closing Disclosure ✓
C. HUD-1 Settlement Statement
D. Truth in Lending Act Disclosure
Answer: B. The Closing Disclosure is the mandatory federal form required under TRID that replaced the HUD-1 and must be delivered to borrowers at least three business days before loan consummation.
Q 8.12 "To have and to hold" language is the:
A. Acknowledgment
B. Granting clause
C. Habendum clause ✓
D. Recital
Answer: C. Habendum defines the extent of estate granted.
Q 8.12·v1 In a Hawaii deed, the clause that uses the phrase 'to have and to hold' and describes the type and duration of the estate being transferred is called the:
A. Granting clause
B. Covenant of seisin
C. Acknowledgment clause
D. Habendum clause ✓
Answer: D. The habendum clause specifies the nature and extent of the estate granted, using traditional language 'to have and to hold.'
Q 8.12·v2 Which of the following deed provisions contains 'to have and to hold' language and defines the scope of the property interest being conveyed?
A. Habendum ✓
B. Consideration clause
C. Recital
D. Attestation
Answer: A. The habendum clause is the portion of a deed that defines the extent and duration of the estate, traditionally beginning with 'to have and to hold.'
Q 8.12·v3 A grantor in Hawaii includes 'to have and to hold' language in a deed to establish and clarify the:
A. Legal authority to execute the document
B. Consideration paid for the property
C. Validity of the grantor's title
D. Type and duration of the estate conveyed ✓
Answer: D. The habendum clause, which contains 'to have and to hold' language, specifies the nature, extent, and duration of the estate being transferred.
Q 8.12·v4 In Hawaii real estate documents, 'to have and to hold' phrasing is a defining characteristic of which deed clause?
A. Testimonium clause
B. Warranty clause
C. Description clause
D. Habendum clause ✓
Answer: D. The habendum clause traditionally uses 'to have and to hold' language and establishes the extent and terms of the property interest granted.
Q 8.12·v5 In a Hawaii deed, which clause contains the phrase 'to have and to hold' and specifies the type and duration of the estate being transferred?
A. Consideration clause
B. Testimonium clause
C. Habendum clause ✓
D. Recital clause
Answer: C. The habendum clause defines the nature and extent of the estate granted and traditionally includes 'to have and to hold' language.
Q 8.12·v6 A grantor uses the words 'to have and to hold' in a deed. What is the name of the deed section that contains this language?
A. Habendum clause ✓
B. Acknowledgment
C. Granting clause
D. Description of property
Answer: A. The habendum clause is the traditional location for 'to have and to hold' language and establishes the extent of the estate transferred.
Q 8.12·v7 Which of the following deed provisions is characterized by the phrase 'to have and to hold' and determines the scope of ownership rights being conveyed?
A. The testimonium
B. The recital
C. The habendum clause ✓
D. The acknowledgment
Answer: C. The habendum clause contains 'to have and to hold' language and defines the precise nature and duration of the estate granted to the grantee.
Q 8.12·v8 When reviewing a deed document, your client asks you to identify where the 'to have and to hold' language appears and what function it serves. You should direct them to the:
A. Recital, which states the consideration
B. Habendum clause, which defines the estate and its duration ✓
C. Acknowledgment, which authenticates the grantor's signature
D. Granting clause, which conveys the property
Answer: B. The habendum clause is the deed section containing 'to have and to hold' language and it specifies the extent and type of estate being granted.
Q 8.12·v9 Which deed clause contains the phrase 'to have and to hold' and specifies the nature and extent of the estate being transferred?
A. The habendum clause ✓
B. The acknowledgment clause
C. The consideration clause
D. The warranty clause
Answer: A. The habendum clause uses 'to have and to hold' language to define the type and duration of the estate granted to the grantee.
09
The Practice of Real Estate
National portion12 PSI items27 key concepts12 base questions

How licensees actually operate — trust funds, fair housing, ads, supervision, antitrust. License-revocation territory.

Chapter Overview

Trust accounts hold other people's money — earnest money deposits, security deposits, rents collected. Commingling personal and trust funds is a license-law violation in every state. So is conversion (using trust funds for the broker's own benefit, even temporarily). Trust accounts must be properly identified ("Trust Account" or "Client Trust Account"), held at a state-approved depository, reconciled regularly (typically monthly), and with records retained for the period state law requires (commonly 3 years). Even accidental commingling — depositing a personal check that should have gone elsewhere — can trigger disciplinary action.

The Federal Fair Housing Act (1968) and its amendments prohibit discrimination in housing on the basis of seven protected classes: race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status (presence of children under 18), and disability. Hawaii and many other states add additional protected classes — Hawaii's HRS 515 includes ancestry, age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, HIV/AIDS status, and source of income. Civil Rights Act of 1866 separately protects race in all property transactions.

Discriminatory practices that violate fair housing: refusal to sell or rent, different terms or conditions, false statements about availability, blockbusting (inducing sales by representing protected-class entry), steering (channeling buyers to or away from neighborhoods based on protected class), redlining (refusing to lend or insure in certain areas), discriminatory advertising. ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) covers accessibility in commercial property.

Advertising rules require: identifying the firm by name, distinguishing "agent" from "broker" titles per state law, avoiding misleading claims, not falsely advertising as the listing broker, never soliciting a property currently under exclusive agreement with another broker. "Truth in advertising" applies equally to print, MLS, internet, social media, and email. Many states require specific language for licensees ("each office independently owned and operated").

Supervision: brokers are responsible for the acts of their licensees. Failure to supervise can revoke the broker's license even if the agent's violation was unilateral. Independent contractor status (typical in real estate for tax purposes) does NOT reduce the broker's license-law supervisory duty. Brokers must have written policies covering trust accounts, advertising, fair housing, dispute resolution, and ongoing training.

Antitrust law (the federal Sherman Act) bans price fixing — brokers agreeing on commission rates is a per se violation, no defenses. Market allocation (geographic carve-ups: "you take the east side, I'll take the west") is also per se illegal. Group boycotts (brokers agreeing to refuse dealings with another firm) are per se illegal. Tying arrangements (forcing customers to buy one product to get another) are scrutinized. The phrase "What's the going commission rate?" must be answered with "commissions are negotiable" — a market-rate quote could be construed as evidence of conspiracy.

Procuring cause is the agent who initiated the unbroken chain leading to a sale. Determines commission entitlement when more than one agent has been involved. The party that "introduced" the buyer to the property is generally the procuring cause, but the chain can be broken by abandonment, by the buyer's genuine independent action, or by the listing broker's acceptance of cooperation from a different agent.

Ethics: NAR Code of Ethics binds REALTOR® members (a voluntary professional designation), not all licensees. State license law sets the legal floor; NAR Code is generally higher. Practicing within area of competence is a near-universal duty. Avoiding the unauthorized practice of law (UPL) is critical — agents can fill in standard form blanks but cannot draft contracts, give legal advice, or interpret legal documents.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Trust accountSeparate account holding client/customer funds. No commingling. Subject to audit.
ComminglingMixing personal and trust funds. License-law violation everywhere.
ConversionUsing trust funds for personal benefit. Felony in many states.
ReconciliationPeriodic verification (typically monthly) that trust account balance matches owed amounts.
Fair Housing Act (1968 + amendments)Federal law banning discrimination in housing on 7 protected bases.
Civil Rights Act of 1866Prohibits race discrimination in all property transactions. No exceptions.
Protected class (federal)Race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability.
Protected class (Hawaii HRS 515)Federal + ancestry, age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, HIV, source of income.
Familial statusPresence of children under 18 (or pregnant). Senior housing has narrow exception.
SteeringChanneling buyers to/away from neighborhoods based on protected class. Illegal.
BlockbustingInducing sales by representing protected-class entry. Illegal.
RedliningRefusing to lend or insure in protected-class areas. Illegal.
Discriminatory advertisingAds suggesting preference for/against any protected class. Illegal.
ADAAmericans with Disabilities Act. Accessibility in public accommodations and commercial.
Sherman Antitrust ActFederal antitrust. Price fixing, market allocation, group boycotts are per se illegal.
Price fixingBrokers agreeing on commission rates. Per se Sherman violation.
Market allocationBrokers agreeing to divide territory or customers. Per se illegal.
Group boycottBrokers agreeing to refuse dealings with another firm. Per se illegal.
Tying arrangementForcing customer to buy product B to get product A. Antitrust scrutiny.
Independent contractorAgent classified for tax purposes; broker still supervises for license law.
Failure to superviseBroker liability for licensee's violations. Can revoke broker license.
NAR Code of EthicsVoluntary professional code; binding on REALTOR® members; not state law.
Procuring causeAgent who initiated the unbroken chain leading to a sale. Determines commission entitlement.
Unauthorized practice of law (UPL)Drafting contracts, giving legal advice, interpreting documents — agent must avoid.
Truth in advertisingAds must accurately reflect property, firm, and licensee status.
Continuing educationOngoing training required for license renewal. Hours and topics vary by state.
RESPA Section 8Bans kickbacks and unearned fees among settlement service providers.
Question Bank — The Practice of Real Estate
Q 9.1 Steering means:
A. Negotiating price
B. Offering homestaging advice
C. Channeling buyers based on protected class ✓
D. Encouraging a buyer to use your lender
Answer: C. Steering is a textbook fair housing violation.
Q 9.1·v1 Which practice constitutes steering in real estate?
A. Suggesting a specific appraisal method to expedite closing
B. Directing prospects toward or away from neighborhoods based on race or national origin ✓
C. Recommending a property inspection company to a buyer
D. Advising clients on staging to improve marketability
Answer: B. Steering involves directing buyers or sellers to or away from particular areas based on protected characteristics, which is a violation of the Fair Housing Act.
Q 9.1·v2 A licensee would be engaged in steering if they:
A. Required the use of a specific title company
B. Provided comparable market analysis to justify listing price
C. Explained different financing options available in the market
D. Selectively showed properties to clients based on their race or familial status ✓
Answer: D. Selectively showing properties based on protected class characteristics is a classic example of steering, a prohibited fair housing practice under Hawaii REC rules.
Q 9.1·v3 Under Hawaii fair housing law, steering occurs when a real estate agent:
A. Coordinates with home inspectors to schedule property examinations
B. Explains property tax implications of a purchase
C. Channels prospective tenants away from certain buildings due to their religion ✓
D. Assists clients in obtaining pre-approval letters from lenders
Answer: C. Steering based on protected class status—including religion—violates fair housing protections and is strictly prohibited in Hawaii real estate practice.
Q 9.1·v4 Which of the following best describes steering in a real estate context?
A. Providing multiple listing options within the buyer's stated budget
B. Recommending energy-efficient upgrades during a listing presentation
C. Negotiating HOA fees on behalf of a buyer
D. Influencing where buyers or renters can live based on protected class membership ✓
Answer: D. Steering is the practice of directing prospects toward or away from properties based on their membership in a protected class, constituting a fair housing violation.
Q 9.1·v5 Under Hawaii fair housing law, which practice constitutes steering?
A. Recommending a property inspection company to a client
B. Directing buyers away from certain areas based on their race or national origin ✓
C. Advising a seller on comparable market analysis
D. Showing properties in neighborhoods where the buyer's income qualifies
Answer: B. Steering—directing or discouraging buyers based on protected characteristics—is a direct violation of fair housing laws in Hawaii and federally.
Q 9.1·v6 A licensee commits steering when they:
A. Provide a list of approved contractors for home repairs
B. Subtly discourage an applicant from purchasing in a particular neighborhood due to their familial status ✓
C. Explain closing costs and loan terms to a client
D. Limit property showings to areas where a buyer can afford based on financing
Answer: B. Steering based on protected class characteristics (including familial status) is illegal. Limiting showings by affordability or providing contractor referrals are legitimate business practices.
Q 9.1·v7 Which scenario best describes steering as a fair housing violation?
A. A salesperson refers buyers to mortgage lenders for pre-qualification
B. An associate broker recommends title insurance and escrow services
C. A broker encourages a client to put down a larger deposit for a stronger offer
D. An agent channels prospective buyers away from specific communities because of their religion ✓
Answer: D. Steering involves steering buyers away from or toward properties based on protected class status; recommending financial services or negotiating terms are lawful activities.
Q 9.1·v8 In Hawaii real estate practice, steering is prohibited because it:
A. Limits consumers' free choice by channeling them based on protected class membership ✓
B. Reduces the number of properties shown to each client
C. Requires additional paperwork at closing
D. Increases transaction costs for the brokerage
Answer: A. Steering violates fair housing by restricting buyer choice and opportunity based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability—not for administrative or transaction reasons.
Q 9.1·v9 Under Hawaii fair housing law, which practice constitutes steering?
A. Advising a seller to accept a competitive offer
B. Recommending a property inspection company to a client
C. Suggesting mortgage pre-approval before showing properties
D. Directing prospective buyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on their race or national origin ✓
Answer: D. Steering is the unlawful practice of influencing buyers or renters to favor certain properties or neighborhoods based on protected class characteristics. It is a direct violation of the Fair Housing Act and Hawaii REC rules.
Q 9.2 A broker uses earnest money to pay office rent. This is:
A. Procuring cause
B. Allowed if reimbursed
C. Commingling only
D. Conversion ✓
Answer: D. Conversion = using trust funds for own benefit.
Q 9.2·v1 A broker deposits client earnest money into the operating account and withdraws funds to cover monthly overhead expenses. What violation has occurred?
A. Conversion of client funds ✓
B. Commingling with subsequent accounting
C. Improper trust account designation
D. Breach of fiduciary duty
Answer: A. Conversion is the unauthorized use of client trust funds for the broker's own business purposes, regardless of intent to repay. Using earnest money for overhead expenses constitutes conversion.
Q 9.2·v2 Under Hawaii real estate law, if a broker takes earnest money received from a buyer and uses it to pay for advertising costs for the brokerage, this action is best described as:
A. Proper trust account management
B. Negligent record-keeping
C. Commingling
D. Conversion ✓
Answer: D. Conversion occurs when a broker misappropriates client funds for personal or business use. Using earnest money for the broker's advertising expenses is conversion, not merely commingling.
Q 9.2·v3 A broker receives earnest money from a transaction and deposits it into a mixed account containing both client funds and broker operating funds. The broker then withdraws the earnest money amount to pay utilities for the real estate office. This constitutes:
A. Lawful use if documented properly
B. Conversion of client funds ✓
C. Commingling and breach of trust account rules
D. Record-keeping violations only
Answer: B. The unauthorized taking and use of earnest money for business expenses is conversion, the most serious violation. Commingling may also be present, but conversion is the primary violation.
Q 9.2·v4 When a broker receives earnest money from a client and applies those funds to pay the broker's personal business obligations without authorization, this action is:
A. Procuring cause
B. A minor commingling issue
C. Conversion ✓
D. Acceptable if the broker maintains detailed records
Answer: C. Conversion is the misappropriation of client trust funds for the broker's own use or benefit. Record-keeping does not excuse the unauthorized use of client money for broker obligations.
Q 9.2·v5 A broker deposits client earnest money into a trust account, then withdraws funds to cover the broker's personal business expenses. What violation has occurred?
A. Misappropriation of commingled funds
B. Conversion of trust account monies ✓
C. Breach of fiduciary duty without conversion
D. Failure to maintain proper escrow accounting
Answer: B. Conversion occurs when a broker uses client trust funds for personal benefit, regardless of intent to repay. This is a serious violation of Hawaii REC trust account rules.
Q 9.2·v6 Which of the following scenarios represents an illegal use of earnest money deposits?
A. Depositing earnest money in a non-interest bearing trust account
B. Commingling earnest money with other client funds in one account
C. Using earnest money to pay the broker's monthly office utilities ✓
D. Holding earnest money for 30 days before disbursing per closing instructions
Answer: C. Using client trust funds for broker business expenses constitutes conversion, the unauthorized appropriation of another's property for personal use.
Q 9.2·v7 A real estate broker receives earnest money on a transaction and places it in the trust account. The broker then withdraws a portion to pay salesperson commissions owed from a previous sale. This action is best described as:
A. Failure to follow proper escrow procedures
B. Conversion of client funds ✓
C. Commingling of earnest money with operating funds
D. Improper trust accounting with correctable deficiencies
Answer: B. Converting trust account funds to pay broker or salesperson obligations—even legitimate business expenses—is conversion because the funds belong to clients and must not be used for broker benefit.
Q 9.2·v8 If a broker temporarily uses earnest money held in trust to pay office expenses with a written plan to repay within 30 days, the broker has committed:
A. Negligent trust account management
B. A technical violation requiring a corrective notice
C. Commingling that requires trust account remediation
D. Conversion of trust monies ✓
Answer: D. Conversion is using trust funds for personal benefit—the intent to repay does not cure conversion because the funds were misappropriated when withdrawn, not borrowed.
Q 9.2·v9 A broker deposits earnest money into the firm's operating account and withdraws funds to cover monthly office expenses. What violation has occurred?
A. Breach of fiduciary duty that is curable upon repayment
B. Conversion of trust account funds ✓
C. Commingling of client and broker funds
D. Unauthorized practice of real estate
Answer: B. Conversion occurs when a broker uses client trust funds (earnest money) for personal or business expenses, which constitutes misappropriation regardless of intent to repay. This is distinct from commingling, which is improper account management but may not involve actual use of funds.
Q 9.3 Two competing brokers agree to charge 6% on all listings. This is:
A. Standard practice
B. A market efficiency
C. Price negotiation
D. Price fixing — antitrust violation ✓
Answer: D. Sherman Act violation; commissions are negotiable.
Q 9.3·v1 Three brokers in the same MLS area secretly agree to maintain a uniform 6% commission rate across all their listings. What legal issue does this create?
A. A collaborative market standard that benefits consumers
B. A reasonable industry custom that promotes transparency
C. Unfair competition under Hawaii's Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act
D. Horizontal price-fixing in violation of antitrust law ✓
Answer: D. Broker agreements to fix commission rates constitute per se antitrust violations under the Sherman Act; commissions must remain independently negotiable.
Q 9.3·v2 A broker overhears a competitor mention using a 6% flat fee on residential sales and decides to adopt the same rate. If both brokers' rates are identical, is this legal?
A. Yes, only if they document the decision in writing
B. No, because matching competitors' commissions always violates antitrust law
C. No, because any uniform rate structure is considered per se illegal
D. Yes, because independent pricing decisions are lawful even if they coincide ✓
Answer: D. Independent, unilateral pricing decisions are legal under antitrust law; illegality arises only from agreement or conspiracy to fix prices.
Q 9.3·v3 During a broker association meeting, Broker A proposes that all members commit to a minimum 6% commission to protect market stability. Broker B agrees verbally. This proposal is:
A. Permissible under the Realtor® Code of Ethics
B. Legal collaborative pricing in a professional association context
C. A standard practice recognized by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. An illegal cartel arrangement violating Sherman Act Section 1 ✓
Answer: D. Commission agreements between competing brokers, even within professional organizations, constitute illegal price-fixing under antitrust law.
Q 9.3·v4 Broker X and Broker Y compete in the same market. They exchange information about their commission structures and then both implement identical 6% rates on comparable properties. The brokers claim they arrived at this rate independently. What is the likely legal outcome?
A. The arrangement is legal as long as it doesn't exceed the state-mandated maximum
B. The brokers are protected because each set their rate independently
C. Courts may infer an unlawful agreement from the exchange of price information and parallel conduct ✓
D. Hawaii Real Estate Commission approval eliminates any antitrust exposure
Answer: C. Parallel pricing combined with evidence of communication regarding commissions can establish an illegal agreement; the exchange of rate information suggests conspiracy, not independent decision-making.
Q 9.3·v5 A group of three real estate firms in the same market decide together to uniformly charge 5.5% commission on all residential transactions. What legal issue does this create?
A. Fair competition practice
B. Compliance with Hawaii Real Estate Commission guidelines
C. Violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act ✓
D. A reasonable market stabilization agreement
Answer: C. Competitors agreeing on commission rates constitutes price fixing, a per se Sherman Act violation; commissions must remain independently negotiable by each broker.
Q 9.3·v6 Four brokers in Honolulu meet and collectively decide to charge no less than 6% commission on all listings in their market area. This agreement is:
A. An acceptable trade association standard
B. Required by Hawaii Real Estate Commission rules
C. An illegal restraint of trade under federal antitrust law ✓
D. A customary industry practice
Answer: C. Horizontal agreements among competitors to set minimum commission rates violate antitrust law; each broker must independently set their own commission rates.
Q 9.3·v7 If brokers in the same geographic area conspire to establish a uniform 6% commission structure across all their firms, they are engaging in:
