A. Consumer protection
B. Predictable market behavior
C. Price fixing—a federal antitrust violation ✓
D. Standard industry coordination
Answer: C. Such collusion constitutes illegal price fixing under the Sherman Act; commission rates must be determined independently by each broker without agreement or coordination.
Q 9.3·v8 Two brokers discuss and agree to charge identical 6% commissions on all their listings to avoid 'destructive competition.' This arrangement violates:
A. The Sherman Antitrust Act ✓
B. Local board of REALTORS® bylaws
C. Hawaii Revised Statutes on brokerage operations
D. Hawaii real estate licensing renewal requirements
Answer: A. Commission rates are individually negotiable; competitors cannot agree on commission levels or structure as this constitutes illegal price fixing under federal antitrust law.
Q 9.3·v9 Three real estate brokers in the same market decide together to maintain a uniform 6% commission rate across all properties. What legal issue does this arrangement create?
A. Violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act through horizontal price fixing ✓
B. An acceptable industry custom that benefits consumers through predictability
C. Compliance with Hawaii real estate industry standards
D. A legitimate cooperative marketing agreement
Answer: A. Brokers agreeing to set commissions at a fixed rate constitutes illegal price fixing under antitrust law; commissions must be independently determined and negotiable with clients.
Q 9.4 Federal Fair Housing's 7 protected classes include:
A. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability ✓
B. Race and religion only
C. Income and credit score
D. Race only
Answer: A. These are the seven federal classes; states (including Hawaii) add more.
Q 9.4·v1 Under the Fair Housing Act, which of the following represents the complete list of federally protected classes?
A. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and disability only
B. Race, color, and religion only
C. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and age
D. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
Answer: D. Federal Fair Housing law protects these seven specific classes; age is a protected class in some states like Hawaii but not federally under Fair Housing Act.
Q 9.4·v2 A real estate licensee in Hawaii must understand that the federal Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on which categories?
A. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
B. Race, gender, and family composition only
C. Employment history and financial status
D. Sexual orientation and marital status
Answer: A. The seven federal protected classes are enumerated in the Fair Housing Act; sexual orientation and marital status are protected under Hawaii state law but not the federal act.
Q 9.4·v3 When discussing fair housing compliance with clients, you should know that federal law specifically protects individuals in which of these categories?
A. Socioeconomic status and educational background
B. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
C. Race and color only
D. National origin, familial status, and disability
Answer: B. The Fair Housing Act lists exactly seven protected classes; socioeconomic status and education are not federally protected categories.
Q 9.4·v4 Which statement correctly identifies the scope of federal Fair Housing Act protections?
A. Federal law protects only against race discrimination; states add other categories
B. Protection covers only race and national origin
C. Protection applies to race, color, and religion, plus four additional protected classes ✓
D. Protection applies to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and political affiliation
Answer: C. Federal Fair Housing protects seven specific classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability; political affiliation is not a federally protected class.
Q 9.4·v5 Which of the following represents the complete list of protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act?
A. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and disability only
B. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and marital status
C. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability ✓
D. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and sexual orientation
Answer: C. The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on exactly these seven protected classes; Hawaii and other states may add additional protections beyond federal law.
Q 9.4·v6 A real estate agent must be aware that federal fair housing law prohibits discrimination based on membership in which groups?
A. Sexual orientation and gender identity only
B. Religion and national origin only
C. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
D. Employment history and credit rating
Answer: C. These seven classes are the federal baseline for protected-class status; additional protections may exist under state or local law, but federal law covers these specific categories.
Q 9.4·v7 Under the federal Fair Housing Act, which combination of protected classes is legally prohibited from being used as a basis for discrimination in housing transactions?
A. Race, color, familial status, and disability only
B. National origin and familial status only
C. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
D. Religion, sex, disability, and sexual orientation only
Answer: C. Federal fair housing law protects these seven distinct classes; Hawaii may recognize additional protected classes, but the federal requirement covers all seven.
Q 9.4·v8 If a Hawaii licensee is training on federal Fair Housing Act compliance, they should know the seven protected classes are which of the following?
A. Race, color, age, disability, sexual orientation, and religion
B. Race, color, religion, and national origin only
C. Sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and marital status
D. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
Answer: D. These are the exact seven protected classes established by the federal Fair Housing Act; states and counties may add protections, but these seven form the federal foundation.
Q 9.4·v9 Under the federal Fair Housing Act, which of the following represents the complete list of protected classes?
A. Income level, employment history, credit rating, and financial status
B. Sex and disability only
C. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability ✓
D. Race, color, and religion only
Answer: C. The Fair Housing Act protects these seven federal classes; Hawaii state law adds additional protected classes beyond the federal minimum.
Q 9.5 A broker who pays an undisclosed referral fee to a settlement service provider violates:
A. RESPA Section 8 ✓
B. ECOA
C. Truth in Lending
D. Statute of Frauds
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks and unearned referral fees.
Q 9.5·v1 Which federal law prohibits a real estate broker from accepting hidden compensation from a title company in exchange for steering clients to that company?
A. Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act compliance standards
B. Equal Credit Opportunity Act
C. RESPA Section 8 ✓
D. Fair Housing Act
Answer: C. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees for referrals of settlement services, regardless of whether they are disclosed.
Q 9.5·v2 A broker receives a payment from an escrow company for referring a client but does not disclose this arrangement to the client. This broker has violated which regulation?
A. RESPA antiKickback provisions ✓
B. California Fair Housing laws
C. TRID disclosure requirements
D. Dodd-Frank Act consumer protections
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 prohibits all undisclosed referral fees and kickbacks for settlement services; disclosure does not cure the violation.
Q 9.5·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law and federal regulations, paying an undisclosed fee to a settlement service provider for client referrals violates which of the following?
A. Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy standards
B. RESPA Section 8 ✓
C. Truth in Savings Act
D. Community Reinvestment Act
Answer: B. RESPA Section 8 bans all kickbacks and unearned referral fees to settlement service providers, whether disclosed or not.
Q 9.5·v4 A broker agrees with a title company to share fees for referred clients without informing the clients of this arrangement. Which federal statute has been violated?
A. RESPA Section 8 antiKickback rule ✓
B. Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
C. Federal Trade Commission Act Section 5
D. Homeowners Protection Act
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 prohibits undisclosed referral fees and kickbacks between service providers; secrecy about the arrangement is a core element of the violation.
Q 9.5·v5 Which federal law prohibits a real estate broker from accepting hidden compensation from a title company in exchange for referring clients to that company?
A. RESPA Section 8 ✓
B. Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act disclosure requirements
C. Equal Credit Opportunity Act
D. Fair Housing Act
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 specifically prohibits kickbacks and undisclosed referral fees between settlement service providers and brokers.
Q 9.5·v6 A broker receives a payment from an appraisal company for steering transactions to them without disclosing this arrangement to clients. This violates:
A. Regulation Z
B. The Dodd-Frank Act
C. Hawaii Real Estate Commission compensation rules only
D. RESPA Section 8 ✓
Answer: D. RESPA Section 8 prohibits undisclosed referral fees and kickbacks between settlement service providers, including appraisers and brokers.
Q 9.5·v7 When a broker fails to disclose that they received compensation from a lender for referring a borrower, which law has most likely been violated?
A. Truth in Lending Act
B. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
C. Community Reinvestment Act
D. RESPA Section 8 ✓
Answer: D. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits undisclosed kickbacks and referral fees paid by settlement service providers to brokers or other referral sources.
Q 9.5·v8 A settlement agent pays a broker a concealed fee for referrals without the client's knowledge. This practice violates:
A. The Fair Credit Reporting Act
B. RESPA Section 8 ✓
C. Regulation B
D. The Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
Answer: B. RESPA Section 8 bans undisclosed payments between settlement service providers and referral sources as unearned kickbacks.
Q 9.5·v9 Which federal statute is violated when a real estate broker secretly compensates a title company employee for referring business to that settlement service?
A. RESPA Section 8 ✓
B. Hawaii Residential Tenancies Law
C. Regulation Z
D. Fair Housing Act
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 explicitly prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees paid to settlement service providers for referrals, whether disclosed or undisclosed.
Q 9.6 "Familial status" protection includes:
A. Senior citizens only
B. Married couples only
C. Households with children under 18 or pregnant ✓
D. Adults only
Answer: C. Familial status = children under 18, with narrow senior-housing exception.
Q 9.6·v1 Under Hawaii fair housing law, which group receives protection based on familial status?
A. Retired persons aged 62 and older in all residential settings
B. Single individuals without children or dependents
C. Only married couples with biological children
D. Families with dependent children under age 18 and expectant mothers ✓
Answer: D. Familial status protection covers households with children under 18 and pregnant women; senior housing has limited exceptions but is not broadly protected under familial status.
Q 9.6·v2 A real estate licensee cannot discriminate based on familial status. This protected class encompasses:
A. Elderly individuals living in age-restricted communities only
B. Parents or guardians of minors and women who are pregnant ✓
C. Heterosexual married couples exclusively
D. Childless couples planning to have children in the future
Answer: B. Familial status protection applies to households with children under 18 and pregnant individuals; future parenthood plans and age restrictions are separate issues.
Q 9.6·v3 Which of the following is protected under the familial status provision of fair housing law?
A. A couple married 25 years with adult children over 21
B. A pregnant woman applying for an apartment ✓
C. A divorced parent over age 55 without custody
D. A bachelor seeking a rental in a building marketed to families
Answer: B. Familial status protection explicitly covers pregnant women; familial status does not protect unmarried individuals, post-child-rearing parents, or age-based preferences alone.
Q 9.6·v4 If a landlord refuses to rent to an applicant due to familial status, the protected group would likely include:
A. Married individuals regardless of whether they have children
B. All senior citizens seeking affordable housing
C. Households with children under 18 and expectant mothers ✓
D. Couples without children who are unable to conceive
Answer: C. Familial status protection covers children under 18 and pregnant women; it does not protect based on marital status alone, age, or fertility status.
Q 9.6·v5 Under Hawaii's fair housing laws, which group receives explicit protection under the familial status classification?
A. Couples without children regardless of marital status
B. Retirees and individuals over age 62
C. Families with minors under age 18 and expectant mothers ✓
D. Unmarried domestic partners with shared income
Answer: C. Familial status protection specifically covers households with children under 18 and pregnant individuals; age-based senior protections are limited to specific senior housing exemptions.
Q 9.6·v6 A landlord cannot discriminate based on familial status. This protection applies to:
A. Owner-occupied buildings with fewer than four units
B. Prospective tenants who are pregnant or have children under 18 ✓
C. Tenants who are legally married
D. Properties with at least one resident over age 55
Answer: B. Familial status discrimination protections extend to households with children under 18 and pregnant individuals; owner-occupied and certain senior housing have different exemptions.
Q 9.6·v7 Which scenario would constitute a violation of familial status protection under Hawaii fair housing law?
A. Refusing to rent to an elderly couple over age 70
B. Requiring higher income from unmarried applicants
C. Denying housing to a family with a child aged 12 ✓
D. Excluding single applicants from a property
Answer: C. Refusing housing based on the presence of a child under 18 violates familial status protections, which is the core definition of this protected class.
Q 9.6·v8 Familial status as a protected class in Hawaii real estate transactions covers:
A. Households with combined family income above the state median
B. Parents or guardians with dependent children under 18, plus pregnant women ✓
C. Residents in multi-generational living situations
D. All individuals living in family-style arrangements
Answer: B. The familial status protection specifically targets discrimination against households with minor children under 18 and expectant mothers, excluding other family configurations.
Q 9.6·v9 Under Hawaii fair housing law, which of the following groups receives protection based on familial status?
A. Individuals age 55 and older in any residential setting
B. Unmarried cohabitating partners
C. Families expecting a child or raising children younger than 18 years old ✓
D. Divorced parents without current custody arrangements
Answer: C. Familial status protection covers households with children under 18 and pregnant women; it does not protect based on marital status, age alone, or custody status except where children under 18 are present.
Q 9.7 When a broker says "What is the going commission rate?", the proper answer is:
A. "6%"
B. "Industry standard 7%"
C. "Commissions are negotiable" ✓
D. "Whatever others charge"
Answer: C. Quoting "going rate" risks antitrust evidence; commissions are negotiable.
Q 9.7·v1 A broker asks you, "What commission percentage should I be charging to stay competitive?" What is the most legally appropriate response?
A. "Check what the top firms in your market are charging."
B. "Each broker sets their own commission rates independently." ✓
C. "The standard rate in Hawaii is 6%."
D. "Most brokers are charging between 5% and 6% right now."
Answer: B. Brokers must set commissions independently; discussing or coordinating rates with competitors violates antitrust law.
Q 9.7·v2 During a board meeting, a broker inquires, "What's the typical commission percentage in our area these days?" How should this question be handled?
A. Cite the average commission charged by the five largest brokerages.
B. Reference the published Hawaii Real Estate Commission fee guidelines.
C. Provide historical data from the local MLS about prevailing rates.
D. Explain that each brokerage determines its own commission structure. ✓
Answer: D. Discussing what competitors charge or endorsing a common rate creates antitrust liability; each firm must independently decide its compensation.
Q 9.7·v3 A real estate licensee asks a broker, "What rate do other offices charge so I know what to recommend to clients?" The correct guidance is:
A. "Most successful brokers are staying at the traditional 5% rate."
B. "Check the National Association of REALTORS® national averages."
C. "Commission rates are individually determined by each brokerage." ✓
D. "Around 6% to 7%, based on regional benchmarks."
Answer: C. Referencing competitor rates or 'typical' percentages invites antitrust scrutiny; proper guidance is that each broker sets its own rates.
Q 9.7·v4 When discussing compensation structures with other brokers at a conference, you are asked, "What percentage are you using for commissions?" The legally sound approach is to:
A. Suggest that brokers in the area should align on a standard percentage.
B. Indicate that most listings in Hawaii settle around 6% commission.
C. Decline to discuss specific rates and explain that commissions are negotiated individually by each firm. ✓
D. Share your rate and ask what they charge to identify market trends.
Answer: C. Price-fixing discussions, even informal sharing of rates, breach antitrust law; commissions must remain independently determined.
Q 9.7·v5 A broker asks you, "What rate are most agents charging for their services in this market?" How should you respond?
A. "Most agents charge between 5% and 6% in our area."
B. "I can tell you what competing brokers advertise online."
C. "Each broker sets their own commission structure; rates are negotiable." ✓
D. "The typical market rate is around 6%, which is what we should all charge."
Answer: C. Discussing what competitors charge or implying a standard rate constitutes potential antitrust violation; the correct approach is to explain that commissions are always negotiable between parties.
Q 9.7·v6 During a training session, an experienced agent states, "New agents should know the prevailing commission in our area is 6%." What is your professional obligation?
A. Ask the agent to email all staff the agreed-upon rate.
B. Clarify that commission rates are subject to negotiation and not set by industry consensus. ✓
C. Use this figure as the baseline for all future client negotiations.
D. Agree and reinforce this as the standard going forward.
Answer: B. Commission rates cannot be standardized or agreed upon across the industry; they must remain freely negotiable between broker and client to comply with antitrust laws.
Q 9.7·v7 A client asks your broker, "What do other real estate companies typically charge?" The broker should respond:
A. "Commission rates vary by brokerage and are open to negotiation; I'd be happy to discuss our fee structure." ✓
B. "The market standard is 6%, though we occasionally negotiate down."
C. "Most firms in Hawaii charge between 5% and 7% depending on the transaction type."
D. "That information is proprietary; just know our rate is competitive."
Answer: A. Brokers must avoid discussing or implying industry-standard rates; instead, they should acknowledge that rates are individually negotiable and discuss only their own firm's structure.
Q 9.7·v8 At a broker meeting, agents discuss what fees they should quote to sellers. The safest legal response is:
A. "Let's establish a firm policy of 6% to stay competitive."
B. "We should match whatever the top brokerages in the area are charging."
C. "Commission rates are determined individually with each client and are fully negotiable." ✓
D. "The Hawaii Real Estate Commission publishes a recommended rate we should follow."
Answer: C. Establishing a uniform rate or matching competitors' rates violates antitrust principles; commissions must be negotiated independently with each client.
Q 9.7·v9 A broker asks you, "What commission should I charge my clients?" You should respond:
A. "Set your own rate—commissions are negotiable between broker and client." ✓
B. "Follow the rate card posted by the local Board of REALTORS®."
C. "Use the standard 6% that most firms in Hawaii charge."
D. "Check what the local MLS reports as typical."
Answer: A. Commissions must be individually negotiated; discussing or implying a "standard" or "typical" rate constitutes illegal price-fixing under antitrust law.
Q 9.8 NAR Code of Ethics:
A. Is state law
B. Binds REALTOR® members voluntarily ✓
C. Replaces license law
D. Binds all licensees
Answer: B. NAR Code is voluntary professional designation; license law is state-mandatory.
Q 9.8·v1 Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the NAR Code of Ethics and REALTOR® membership?
A. It is enforced by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
B. Members agree to follow it as a condition of their REALTOR® designation ✓
C. It supersedes all state licensing requirements
D. All Hawaii real estate licensees must comply with it by law
Answer: B. The NAR Code of Ethics is a voluntary professional standard that REALTOR® members adopt upon joining NAR, not a legal mandate for all licensees.
Q 9.8·v2 A salesperson who is NOT a REALTOR® member has what obligation regarding the NAR Code of Ethics?
A. Must follow it if working in Hawaii
B. Must comply with all provisions or lose their license
C. Must adopt it within one year of licensing
D. No obligation, as it applies only to REALTOR® members ✓
Answer: D. The NAR Code of Ethics binds only those who voluntarily join NAR and become REALTOR® members; non-members are governed by state license law instead.
Q 9.8·v3 How does the NAR Code of Ethics differ from Hawaii's real estate license law?
A. License law is state-mandated for all licensees; the Code is a voluntary professional standard for REALTOR® members ✓
B. The Code of Ethics is mandatory for all licensees; license law is not
C. Both are enforced equally by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. License law is voluntary; the Code of Ethics is mandatory
Answer: A. State license law is mandatory for all licensees, while the NAR Code of Ethics is a voluntary professional commitment made by REALTOR® members only.
Q 9.8·v4 A broker asks a new salesperson, 'Are you bound by the NAR Code of Ethics?' The correct response is:
A. Only if I choose to join NAR and become a REALTOR® ✓
B. Yes, the Real Estate Commission requires it
C. Yes, all licensees in Hawaii must follow it
D. No, it only applies to brokers, not salespersons
Answer: A. The NAR Code of Ethics applies only to those who voluntarily seek REALTOR® membership; it is not a mandatory requirement of state licensure.
Q 9.8·v5 Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the NAR Code of Ethics and Hawaii real estate licensing requirements?
A. The NAR Code applies only to brokers, not salespersons
B. The NAR Code supersedes all state statutory provisions governing real estate conduct
C. Adherence to the NAR Code is required exclusively of those who hold the REALTOR® designation ✓
D. The NAR Code is mandatory for all Hawaii licensees regardless of membership status
Answer: C. The NAR Code of Ethics is a voluntary professional standard binding only REALTOR® members; state licensing law remains the mandatory baseline for all licensees.
Q 9.8·v6 A Hawaii licensee who is not a REALTOR® member would be bound by:
A. Both the NAR Code and state law equally, regardless of REALTOR® membership
B. The NAR Code of Ethics as a condition of their license
C. State license law and rules set by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission, but not the NAR Code ✓
D. Only the NAR Code of Ethics, since it is the industry standard
Answer: C. Non-REALTOR® licensees must comply with state-mandated license law and REC rules; the NAR Code binds only those who voluntarily join NAR as REALTOR® members.
Q 9.8·v7 The NAR Code of Ethics differs from Hawaii real estate license law in that the Code:
A. Establishes the minimum standards that satisfy Hawaii statutory requirements
B. Applies voluntarily to REALTOR® members rather than being a state-mandated requirement for all licensees ✓
C. Is enforceable by the state through license suspension or revocation
D. Takes precedence over state statutes and administrative rules
Answer: B. The NAR Code is a voluntary professional commitment for REALTOR® members only, whereas state license law is mandatory for all licensees; they are distinct regulatory frameworks.
Q 9.8·v8 When a Hawaii real estate licensee joins the National Association of REALTORS®, they become subject to:
A. The NAR Code of Ethics in addition to their state licensing obligations ✓
B. Neither state law nor the NAR Code, as REALTOR® status exempts them from regulation
C. The NAR Code instead of state license law, which is replaced upon membership
D. State license law only, which now incorporates NAR standards
Answer: A. REALTOR® membership adds the voluntary NAR Code of Ethics to existing state-mandated compliance; it does not replace or exempt from state licensing requirements.
Q 9.8·v9 Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the National Association of REALTORS® Code of Ethics and Hawaii real estate licensure?
A. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission enforces the NAR Code of Ethics as part of state licensing law
B. NAR Code of Ethics is a mandatory state regulatory requirement that supersedes HRS Chapter 467
C. Membership in NAR and adherence to its Code of Ethics is an optional professional commitment for REALTOR® members ✓
D. All Hawaii real estate licensees must comply with NAR Code of Ethics as a condition of their license
Answer: C. NAR Code of Ethics applies only to REALTOR® members who voluntarily join NAR; it is not mandatory state law for all licensees, and the REC enforces HRS Chapter 467, not the NAR Code.
Q 9.9 Brokers must reconcile trust accounts:
A. Never
B. Quarterly
C. Typically monthly ✓
D. Annually
Answer: C. Most states require monthly trust account reconciliation.
Q 9.9·v1 Under Hawaii real estate regulations, how frequently should a broker verify the balance of client trust funds?
A. Semi-annually during tax season
B. Once per calendar year at year-end
C. Only when deposits or withdrawals occur
D. On a monthly basis ✓
Answer: D. As in most jurisdictions, industry best practice is for brokers to reconcile trust accounts monthly to ensure accuracy and client fund protection.
Q 9.9·v2 A broker receives a notice from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission regarding trust account procedures. The notice emphasizes reconciliation frequency to maintain compliance. How often must this reconciliation occur?
A. Upon closing of each transaction
B. Every month ✓
C. Bi-annually
D. Every quarter
Answer: B. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the standard requirement for brokers to ensure proper accounting controls and prevent misappropriation of client funds.
Q 9.9·v3 Which statement best describes the trust account reconciliation requirements for a Hawaii-licensed broker?
A. Reconciliation frequency depends on the broker's discretion
B. Reconciliation is required annually with an external auditor
C. Quarterly reconciliation is mandated by all state commissions
D. Monthly reconciliation is the typical regulatory standard ✓
Answer: D. Monthly reconciliation is the typical requirement for broker trust accounts to maintain fiduciary responsibility and comply with state licensing standards.
Q 9.9·v4 A brokerage firm is establishing its internal accounting procedures for managing client escrow funds. According to Hawaii real estate licensing rules, what reconciliation schedule should the firm implement?
A. Reconcile trust balances only when requested by clients
B. Reconcile trust balances each month ✓
C. Reconcile trust balances every 6 months
D. Reconcile trust balances annually before license renewal
Answer: B. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the standard regulatory requirement to ensure continuous monitoring and proper safeguarding of client funds.
Q 9.9·v5 How frequently should a Hawaii real estate broker perform a reconciliation of client trust accounts?
A. At the broker's discretion, no set frequency
B. Only when a client requests it
C. Twice per year during audit season
D. Every month, at minimum ✓
Answer: D. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the industry standard to ensure accuracy and compliance with fiduciary duties.
Q 9.9·v6 A broker maintains a client trust account. What is the standard requirement for reconciliation frequency?
A. Each calendar month ✓
B. Every six months
C. Only if there is a discrepancy discovered
D. Annually, at fiscal year-end
Answer: A. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the standard practice to maintain proper accounting controls and fiduciary accountability.
Q 9.9·v7 According to Hawaii real estate regulations, trust account reconciliation should occur:
A. On a monthly basis ✓
B. Quarterly, as part of standard business practice
C. Annually, with certified public accountant verification
D. When the broker determines it is necessary
Answer: A. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the industry standard to verify that account balances match client records and prevent misappropriation of funds.
Q 9.9·v8 Which statement accurately describes the reconciliation schedule for broker-maintained client trust accounts in Hawaii?
A. Reconciliation only occurs when a broker application is reviewed
B. Monthly reconciliation is the typical requirement ✓
C. Reconciliation frequency is determined by each brokerage firm independently
D. Reconciliation is required annually with a third-party auditor
Answer: B. Industry best practice is for brokers to reconcile trust accounts monthly to ensure proper accounting and protection of client funds.
Q 9.9·v9 How frequently should a Hawaii real estate broker perform reconciliation of their escrow trust account to ensure compliance with REC regulations?
A. On a monthly basis ✓
B. Only upon audit request by the REC
C. Semiannually, at minimum
D. Whenever a transaction closes
Answer: A. Monthly reconciliation of trust accounts is the industry standard to maintain accurate records and detect discrepancies promptly. This standard protects client funds and ensures regulatory compliance.
Q 9.10 A broker drafts a custom addendum modifying a standard contract's default terms. This may be:
A. Required by license law
B. Permitted always
C. Antitrust
D. Unauthorized practice of law ✓
Answer: D. Drafting custom legal language is UPL territory; agents fill blanks, lawyers draft.
Q 9.10·v1 A real estate agent creates a new clause to replace language in the seller's standard purchase agreement. Which statement best describes this action?
A. It violates unauthorized practice of law unless the agent is also a licensed attorney ✓
B. It constitutes a restraint of trade under antitrust law
C. It must be pre-approved by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. It is always acceptable under Hawaii broker regulations
Answer: A. Composing novel contract language goes beyond filling in blanks and crosses into legal document drafting, which is the unauthorized practice of law unless performed by a licensed attorney.
Q 9.10·v2 When a broker substantially rewrites portions of a standard form contract to suit a specific transaction, this conduct potentially constitutes:
A. An approved modification under HRS 467
B. A routine brokerage practice
C. Unauthorized practice of law ✓
D. Permissible customization within broker authority
Answer: C. Material drafting of contractual provisions—beyond mechanically completing pre-printed blanks—crosses the line into legal practice and requires an attorney, not a broker.
Q 9.10·v3 A broker is asked by a buyer to insert unique language into a purchase agreement that does not appear on any standard form. The broker's response should be:
A. Recommend the buyer consult an attorney rather than draft custom terms ✓
B. Draft the language directly to serve the buyer's interest
C. Include it under the broker's implied authority to negotiate
D. Submit it to the Hawaii Real Estate Commission for pre-approval
Answer: A. Drafting original contract language is unauthorized practice of law; the broker should direct the client to legal counsel rather than compose novel contractual provisions.
Q 9.10·v4 If a broker creates new contractual language outside standard addenda forms to address a buyer's special request, this action may expose the broker to liability for:
A. License suspension under the general duty to transact fairly
B. Competitive interference under antitrust statutes
C. Breach of fiduciary duty to competing agents
D. Unauthorized practice of law ✓
Answer: D. Composing original legal provisions—rather than merely completing or selecting from approved forms—constitutes the unauthorized practice of law and is beyond a broker's authorized scope.
Q 9.10·v5 When a real estate broker creates original contractual language to adjust the terms of a purchase agreement, this action most likely constitutes:
A. Unauthorized practice of law ✓
B. A standard brokerage practice covered by the broker's license
C. Compliance with Hawaii Real Estate Commission rules
D. A fiduciary duty owed to the buyer
Answer: A. Drafting novel legal language and contract modifications is the practice of law, which requires a law license. Brokers may only fill in blanks on pre-approved forms.
Q 9.10·v6 A broker receives a request from a client to write a special rider that changes key contract provisions not covered in the standard form. The broker should:
A. Complete the rider under the brokerage's general real estate license
B. Refer the client to an attorney, as drafting custom legal language exceeds broker authority ✓
C. File the custom rider with the Hawaii Real Estate Commission for approval
D. Proceed, as this falls within the broker's fiduciary duty
Answer: B. Customizing legal language in contracts is the practice of law and requires attorney involvement. Brokers lack authority to draft original legal provisions.
Q 9.10·v7 Which of the following best describes the legal boundary between a broker's permissible contract work and unauthorized practice of law?
A. Brokers may create custom contract terms if the transaction amount is under $500,000
B. Brokers may draft addenda only if approved by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
C. Brokers may modify any standard form if they include a disclaimer
D. Brokers may complete pre-printed forms but cannot draft original contractual language ✓
Answer: D. The legal boundary is clear: brokers fill blanks and use pre-approved forms, but creating novel legal language crosses into the unauthorized practice of law.
Q 9.10·v8 A sales associate asks a broker whether she can prepare a custom amendment to modify specific performance obligations in a standard purchase contract. The broker's correct response should be:
A. No, this requires legal expertise and the client should consult an attorney ✓
B. Yes, this is part of normal brokerage operations under the real estate license
C. Yes, but only if the amendment is filed with the seller's broker first
D. Yes, provided the associate has been licensed for more than two years
Answer: A. Drafting custom legal modifications is unauthorized practice of law; the broker must direct the associate to refer clients to attorneys for contract language that is not pre-approved.
Q 9.10·v9 A real estate broker creates new contract language to replace provisions in the seller's standard purchase agreement. This practice is most likely to constitute:
A. A permitted broker duty under HI license law
B. A required broker function in all transactions
C. Unauthorized practice of law ✓
D. An antitrust violation if done competitively
Answer: C. Composing novel contract provisions is the practice of law; brokers may only use pre-approved forms or direct clients to legal counsel. Creating custom legal language exceeds broker authority.
Q 9.11 A failure-to-supervise charge can revoke:
A. Only the agent's license
B. Both broker and agent licenses ✓
C. Neither
D. Only the broker's license
Answer: B. Both can be sanctioned; broker for failure to supervise, agent for the underlying violation.
Q 9.11·v1 When a Hawaii broker fails to properly supervise a licensee who commits a violation, regulatory action could result in:
A. License revocation for both the supervising broker and the offending agent ✓
B. Revocation of the broker's license only, with the agent remaining unaffected
C. A fine against the brokerage firm but no license sanctions
D. Suspension of the agent's license only
Answer: A. Both the broker and agent can face license revocation; the broker for inadequate supervision and the agent for the underlying misconduct.
Q 9.11·v2 Under Hawaii real estate law, if a broker's failure to supervise results in a licensee's illegal activity, which licenses are at risk of revocation?
A. Only the broker's license, as the agent bears no responsibility
B. The agent's license and the broker's trust account license
C. Both the broker's and agent's licenses ✓
D. The broker's license only if the agent's conduct was intentional fraud
Answer: C. Both licenses can be revoked; the broker for supervisory failure and the agent for the underlying violation, regardless of intent.
Q 9.11·v3 A real estate commission investigation determines that inadequate office supervision allowed an agent to mishandle client funds. What disciplinary outcome is possible?
A. No action against either party, as the funds were eventually returned
B. Revocation of the agent's license only, with the broker receiving a fine
C. Revocation of both the broker's and agent's licenses ✓
D. Disciplinary action against the broker only, with a warning to the agent
Answer: C. Both the broker and agent can have licenses revoked; the broker for failure to supervise and the agent for the financial misconduct.
Q 9.11·v4 Which of the following best describes the potential license consequences when a Hawaii broker fails to adequately supervise a salesperson who violates real estate law?
A. Only the broker's license is at stake; the agent is exempt as a salesperson
B. License revocation applies only if the violation was intentional by both parties
C. The broker faces suspension while the agent faces revocation
D. Both the broker and the agent may have their licenses revoked ✓
Answer: D. Both broker and agent licenses can be revoked as a result of the broker's supervisory failure and the agent's underlying violation.
Q 9.11·v5 Under Hawaii real estate law, when a broker fails to properly supervise a salesperson who commits a violation, which licenses are subject to revocation?
A. Both the broker's and salesperson's licenses ✓
B. The broker's license only, never the salesperson's
C. Neither license can be revoked for supervisory failures
D. The salesperson's license only
Answer: A. Both the broker and the salesperson face potential license revocation; the broker for inadequate supervision and the salesperson for the underlying conduct violation.
Q 9.11·v6 A Hawaii Real Estate Commission investigation reveals that a broker failed to adequately oversee an agent's unlicensed practice activities. What are the possible licensing consequences?
A. Revocation of the broker's license exclusively
B. Revocation of the agent's license exclusively
C. Revocation of both the broker's and agent's licenses ✓
D. No license revocations are possible in supervisory violations
Answer: C. Both parties can face revocation: the broker for failing its supervisory duty and the agent for the underlying unlicensed practice.
Q 9.11·v7 If the Hawaii REC determines that a managing broker failed to supervise, resulting in violations by licensed agents under the broker, what is the maximum scope of license revocation?

10
Real Estate Calculations
National portion7 PSI items19 key concepts12 base questions

Roughly 7-10 exam questions are math. Memorize the formulas and the scenario-types repeat.

Chapter Overview

Areas: Rectangle = Length × Width. Triangle = ½ × Base × Height. Circle = π × radius². Trapezoid = ½ × (a + b) × height. One acre = 43,560 square feet. One section = 640 acres = 1 square mile. Many exam questions test conversion between square feet and acres or between acres and sections.

Percentages: Part = Whole × Rate. The same equation rearranges to find any one variable. Commission = Sale Price × Commission Rate. Then split between listing and selling brokerages, and again between brokers and individual agents per their internal split.

LTV (Loan-to-Value) = Loan Amount ÷ Property Value. Down Payment = Value − Loan. Discount points: each point = 1% of loan amount, each typically reduces interest rate roughly 0.25%. APR vs interest rate: APR includes points + most fees, so APR > nominal rate when points are charged.

Prorations split shared expenses at closing. Most exams use a 360-day "banker's" year (12 × 30-day months), though some contracts use actual 365-day year. Daily amount = annual amount ÷ 360 (or monthly ÷ 30). Whoever owns the day of closing typically pays for that day (varies by jurisdiction; the exam will specify or assume).

Tax calculations: Property Tax = Assessed Value × Mill Rate ÷ 1,000. (One mill = $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.) Some jurisdictions express tax as a percentage of value instead. Special assessments are added separately.

Capitalization: Value = NOI ÷ Cap Rate. Solve for any of three variables. Net Operating Income = Effective Gross Income − Operating Expenses. Effective Gross Income = Potential Gross Income − Vacancy and Collection Loss + Other Income. Mortgage P&I is NOT an operating expense for NOI.

GRM = Sale Price ÷ Monthly Gross Rent. GIM = Sale Price ÷ Annual Gross Income. Quick screen: comparables show GRM = 120; a property renting for $2,000/month suggests ~$240,000 value before adjustments.

Mortgage math: Monthly P&I payments are computed via the mortgage amortization formula or looked up in payment tables. For exam purposes, often you're given a payment factor: payment per $1,000 of loan × (loan amount ÷ 1,000) = monthly P&I. Total interest paid over loan life = total payments − principal. For partial-year interest: Annual interest = Loan × Rate; daily interest = annual ÷ 360 (or 365 depending on convention).

Closing math: Total money buyer needs at closing = down payment + closing costs + prorations owed to seller − any seller credits. Seller proceeds = sale price − payoff loans − commissions − closing costs − prorations owed to buyer. Conveyance/transfer tax often calculated as a rate per $1,000 of sale price.

Profit and percentage problems: % Profit = (Gain ÷ Original Cost) × 100. Selling Price for Target Profit = Cost × (1 + Profit %). Gross Profit Margin = (Sale Price − Cost) ÷ Sale Price.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Acre43,560 square feet.
Section640 acres = 1 square mile = 5,280 ft × 5,280 ft.
Square foot ↔ square yard1 sq yard = 9 sq ft.
Triangle area½ × Base × Height.
Circle areaπ × radius² (≈ 3.14 × r²).
Commission formulaSale Price × Commission Rate = Total Commission. Then split.
LTV formulaLoan ÷ Value.
Down paymentValue − Loan.
Discount point1% of loan amount. Reduces rate roughly 0.25% per point.
NOIEffective Gross Income − Operating Expenses (no debt service).
Cap rate formulaNOI ÷ Value. Solve for any variable.
GRM formulaSale Price ÷ Monthly Rent.
GIM formulaSale Price ÷ Annual Gross Income.
Proration (360-day)Annual ÷ 360 = daily; multiply by days owed. Used in many contracts.
Proration (365-day)Annual ÷ 365 = daily; some contracts use actual day count.
Mill rateProperty tax = Assessed Value × Mills ÷ 1,000. One mill = $1 per $1,000.
Daily interestLoan × Rate ÷ 360 (or 365). Used for partial-period interest calculations.
Profit percentage(Sale Price − Cost) ÷ Cost × 100.
Conveyance taxOften calculated as rate per $1,000 of sale price.
