Property management, common-interest, subdivisions, commercial. Smaller exam weight but easy points if you know the basics.

Chapter Overview

Property management is general agency. The property manager (PM) collects rent, maintains the property, handles tenants, and remits net income to the owner. Common compensation: percentage of rents collected, sometimes flat monthly fee, often with leasing commissions for new tenants. The PM owes fiduciary duties to the owner. Tenant screening must comply with fair housing — same protected classes, same prohibitions.

Common-interest ownership covers four main types. Condominium: fee ownership of unit airspace plus undivided interest in common elements (lobby, grounds, roof). Cooperative (co-op): own shares of stock in a corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease for your unit. Planned Unit Development (PUD): fee in your individual lot plus interest in association-managed common areas (pools, parks, streets). Time share: right to occupy a unit for a defined period each year, typically a week.

Each common-interest type has different financing, taxation, and exit characteristics. Condos are mortgageable like any single-family. Co-ops require unique loan products (share loans) since you don't own real property — many lenders won't finance them. PUDs finance like single-family. Time shares often finance through the developer at higher rates and are notoriously hard to resell.

Subdivisions split a parcel into lots for sale or development. State subdivision laws regulate platting (recorded survey of lots, streets, easements), dedication of streets to the public, infrastructure requirements (water, sewer, drainage), environmental review, and disclosures. The federal Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act covers cross-state sales of unimproved lots in larger developments — requires registration with HUD and detailed property report disclosure to buyers.

Commercial / income property analysis differs from residential: focus is income-generating ability. Cap rate, NOI, debt service coverage ratio (DSCR = NOI ÷ annual debt service), and lease terms drive value. DSCR below 1.0 means insufficient income to cover debt. Lenders typically require 1.20 or higher.

Lease types: Gross lease — tenant pays rent only, landlord pays operating expenses. Net lease — tenant pays rent + some operating expenses (single, double, or triple net depending on number of categories). Triple-net (NNN) lease shifts taxes, insurance, and maintenance to tenant — common in retail and industrial. Percentage lease — tenant pays base rent + percentage of sales over a threshold; common in retail. Ground lease — tenant rents land, often building their own structure on it; common in fast food and infill commercial.

Industrial property involves additional considerations: zoning compatibility, environmental contamination history (especially if prior uses were industrial), loading dock access, ceiling clearance, power capacity, rail or freeway proximity, and labor pool. Specialized due diligence is essential.

Investment metrics beyond cap rate: cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow before tax ÷ cash invested (after debt). Internal Rate of Return (IRR) considers timing of cash flows and reversion (sale proceeds) at end of holding period. Equity multiplier = total return ÷ initial equity. These help compare investments with different financing structures.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Property managerGeneral agent collecting rents, maintaining property, handling tenants for owner.
Management agreementContract creating PM-owner relationship. Typically defines compensation, scope, term.
CondominiumFee ownership of unit + undivided interest in common elements.
CooperativeOwn shares of corporation that owns building + proprietary lease.
Proprietary leaseCo-op shareholder's right to occupy a specific unit.
PUDPlanned Unit Development. Own individual lot + share in common areas.
Time shareRight to occupy unit for set period (often weekly) each year.
CC&Rs / HOARecorded covenants + association governing common-interest community.
SubdivisionDivision of land into lots for sale or development.
Plat mapRecorded survey showing lots, streets, easements within a subdivision.
DedicationVoluntary transfer of private land to public use (typically streets).
Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure ActFederal law requiring registration + property report for cross-state sales of unimproved lots.
Gross leaseTenant pays rent only; landlord pays operating expenses.
Net leaseTenant pays rent + some operating expenses.
Triple-net (NNN) leaseTenant pays rent + taxes + insurance + maintenance.
Percentage leaseBase rent + % of sales over threshold. Common in retail.
Ground leaseTenant rents land, often builds own structure.
DSCRDebt Service Coverage Ratio = NOI ÷ Annual Debt Service. Lenders want 1.20+.
Cash-on-cash returnAnnual cash flow before tax ÷ cash invested.
IRRInternal Rate of Return. Considers timing of cash flows + reversion.
Equity multiplierTotal return over holding period ÷ initial equity invested.
Vacancy rateVacant units ÷ total units. Affects effective gross income.
Question Bank — Specialty Areas
Q 11.1 In a cooperative, the resident:
A. Owns nothing — they are tenants
B. Owns a fee interest in the unit
C. Owns the land and the building
D. Owns shares of the corporation + holds a proprietary lease ✓
Answer: D. Co-op = stock + lease, not fee ownership.
Q 11.1·v1 What does a cooperative resident actually hold as evidence of their ownership interest?
A. A deed to real property
B. A ground lease with renewal options
C. Corporate shares and an exclusive occupancy agreement ✓
D. A mortgage note secured by the building
Answer: C. Co-op residents own shares in the corporation that owns the building and hold a proprietary lease for unit use; they do not hold a deed or fee interest.
Q 11.1·v2 In a housing cooperative, a resident's legal position is best described as:
A. Beneficial owner of a trust deed arrangement
B. Fee simple owner of a unit within the structure
C. Tenant-at-will with option to purchase after 5 years
D. Shareholder in a corporation combined with a leaseholder of the unit ✓
Answer: D. Co-op ownership is a dual arrangement: stock ownership in the cooperative corporation plus a proprietary lease granting exclusive right to occupy a unit.
Q 11.1·v3 Which statement accurately reflects what a resident receives when purchasing into a cooperative?
A. Equitable interest through a real estate investment trust
B. Stockholder status in the co-op corporation and a long-term occupancy lease ✓
C. Title to the real estate in fee simple
D. A warranty deed and a homeowner's association membership
Answer: B. Co-op residents purchase shares of stock in the cooperative corporation and receive a proprietary lease for their unit, not fee title to the property.
Q 11.1·v4 Under cooperative ownership, what TWO legal documents or interests define a resident's ownership?
A. Corporate shares and a unit deed
B. Stock certificates and a proprietary lease ✓
C. A mortgage and a note
D. A declaration and a common interest community agreement
Answer: B. Co-op residents hold both corporate stock (evidence of ownership in the corporation) and a proprietary lease (evidence of right to occupy their specific unit).
Q 11.1·v5 What is the legal interest a cooperative resident actually holds?
A. An equitable interest but no legal title
B. A life estate that reverts to the cooperative upon death
C. Corporate stock combined with a proprietary lease agreement ✓
D. A fee simple estate in their unit
Answer: C. Co-op ownership consists of two components: shares in the cooperative corporation and a lease granting exclusive use of the unit. This is distinct from fee ownership.
Q 11.1·v6 Which statement best describes what a cooperative member receives when they purchase their unit?
A. Stock in the cooperative corporation and a proprietary lease to occupy a specific unit ✓
B. A ground lease from the land trust with an option to purchase
C. Only the right to occupy the unit as a month-to-month tenant
D. Full title to real property in their own name
Answer: A. Co-op residents receive shares representing ownership in the corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease that grants them exclusive occupancy rights to their unit.
Q 11.1·v7 In a Hawaii cooperative, a resident's ownership structure includes:
A. Beneficial interest held in trust by the cooperative board
B. Condominium-style fee ownership with shared common areas
C. Rental control protections as a statutory tenant
D. Both an ownership interest in the corporation and a lease interest in the unit ✓
Answer: D. The co-op resident owns shares of the corporation that owns the property and simultaneously holds a proprietary lease granting exclusive use of their unit.
Q 11.1·v8 How does a cooperative resident's interest differ from a condominium owner's interest?
A. The condo owner holds fee title; the co-op resident holds shares plus a proprietary lease ✓
B. The co-op resident owns real property directly; the condo owner is a tenant
C. The co-op resident has better legal protections and title insurance
D. There is no material difference in Hawaii real estate law
Answer: A. Condo owners hold fee title to their individual units; co-op residents own corporate shares and a lease interest, not direct real property ownership.
Q 11.1·v9 What form of ownership does a cooperatives resident actually hold?
A. Stock certificates in the co-op corporation and a proprietary lease agreement ✓
B. Joint tenancy with other residents in the entire building
C. A rental agreement that grants use rights only
D. A deed to the individual unit as real property
Answer: A. In a cooperative, the resident owns personal property (corporate shares) plus a lease to occupy their unit; they do not own real property interest in the unit itself.
Q 11.2 A triple-net lease shifts to the tenant:
A. No rent until breakeven
B. Rent + taxes + insurance + maintenance ✓
C. Rent + taxes
D. Rent only
Answer: B. NNN = three nets: taxes, insurance, maintenance.
Q 11.2·v1 Under a triple-net (NNN) lease structure, which of the following best describes the tenant's financial obligations?
A. The tenant pays rent only until the property reaches fair market value
B. The tenant pays only the base lease rental amount
C. The tenant pays base rent plus property taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance costs ✓
D. The tenant reimburses the landlord for property taxes and insurance only
Answer: C. A triple-net lease obligates the tenant to pay three separate expenses in addition to base rent: property taxes, insurance, and maintenance—the three 'nets' that define this lease type.
Q 11.2·v2 When a commercial property is leased on a triple-net basis, the landlord's liability for operating expenses is minimized because:
A. The landlord retains all operating cost responsibility but receives a higher base rent
B. The tenant assumes responsibility only for roof repairs and structural improvements
C. The tenant pays a percentage of the building's gross revenue as rent
D. Operating expenses including taxes, insurance, and property maintenance become the tenant's obligation ✓
Answer: D. In a NNN lease, the three nets—property taxes, insurance, and maintenance—shift from the landlord to the tenant, thereby minimizing the landlord's ongoing expense burden.
Q 11.2·v3 A prospective commercial tenant inquires about lease structures. If they want to avoid paying property taxes and maintenance costs directly, they should NOT sign which type of lease?
A. A percentage lease
B. A gross lease
C. A modified gross lease
D. A triple-net lease ✓
Answer: D. A triple-net lease explicitly requires the tenant to pay property taxes, insurance, and maintenance in addition to base rent, making it the wrong choice for a tenant wishing to avoid those direct costs.
Q 11.2·v4 In Hawaii commercial real estate, a tenant considering a triple-net lease arrangement should understand that their total annual occupancy cost will include:
A. Base rent plus utilities, but no property-level taxes or insurance
B. Base rent, property taxes, casualty insurance, and building maintenance expenses ✓
C. Base rent and a proportionate share of property taxes only
D. Base rent negotiated to cover all operating expenses automatically
Answer: B. The three nets in a NNN lease are property taxes, insurance, and maintenance—all of which become the tenant's financial responsibility in addition to base rent.
Q 11.2·v5 Under a triple-net lease structure, which of the following does the tenant assume responsibility for paying?
A. All operating expenses except mortgage principal
B. Base rent, property taxes, insurance, and CAM expenses
C. Base rent, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs ✓
D. Base rent and property taxes only
Answer: C. A triple-net lease obligates the tenant to pay the three nets: property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, in addition to base rent. CAM and mortgage principal are separate concepts not part of the standard NNN definition.
Q 11.2·v6 When a commercial tenant signs a triple-net lease, the landlord's obligation to cover building expenses is typically limited to:
A. Minimal responsibility; most costs pass to the tenant ✓
B. Mortgage payments and major structural repairs
C. The mortgage and insurance premiums only
D. All property operating costs including utilities
Answer: A. In a NNN lease, the landlord retains minimal financial responsibility because the tenant pays the three nets (property taxes, insurance, and maintenance), shifting the bulk of operating expenses to the tenant.
Q 11.2·v7 A property manager reviewing lease terms notes that the tenant will pay rent, property tax assessments, casualty insurance, and building upkeep. This lease structure is best described as:
A. A gross lease with tenant reimbursements
B. A percentage lease with additional duties
C. A triple-net lease ✓
D. A modified lease with shared expenses
Answer: C. The combination of rent plus the three expense categories—property taxes, insurance, and maintenance—is the defining characteristic of a triple-net (NNN) lease.
Q 11.2·v8 Compared to a gross lease, a triple-net lease requires the tenant to directly pay for:
A. Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance expenses in addition to rent ✓
B. Common area maintenance and parking fees
C. Utilities and janitorial services only
D. Real estate commissions and lease administration costs
Answer: A. A triple-net lease shifts the three nets—property taxes, insurance, and maintenance—to the tenant, whereas a gross lease typically includes these costs in the rent paid to the landlord.
Q 11.2·v9 Under a triple-net (NNN) lease structure, which of the following expenses does the tenant assume responsibility for paying?
A. Property taxes and insurance, but not maintenance costs
B. Base rent and property management fees only
C. Base rent, property taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance ✓
D. All operating expenses except utilities and janitorial services
Answer: C. A triple-net lease obligates the tenant to pay base rent plus three nets: property taxes, insurance, and maintenance/repairs, shifting these operating costs from the landlord to the tenant.
Q 11.3 A PUD owner typically owns:
A. Their individual lot + undivided interest in common areas ✓
B. Shares in a corporation
C. A leasehold
D. Only their unit airspace
Answer: A. PUD owners hold fee in their lot plus common-area interest.
Q 11.3·v1 In a planned unit development, what property interest does an individual owner receive?
A. A perpetual lease on their dwelling unit
B. A membership interest in the homeowners association
C. Fee simple title to their lot and a tenancy-in-common share of common property ✓
D. Stock certificates representing their ownership stake
Answer: C. PUD owners hold fee title to their individual lot while maintaining an undivided interest in shared common areas, not corporate shares or leasehold interests.
Q 11.3·v2 When purchasing a home in a PUD, the buyer acquires:
A. Only the improvements above ground on their parcel
B. Exclusive ownership of their unit plus a proportional interest in collectively-owned areas ✓
C. Ground lease rights with limited ownership duration
D. Beneficial interest through a property management trust
Answer: B. PUD purchasers obtain fee ownership of their specific lot and an undivided fractional interest in common elements like roads, recreational facilities, and open space.
Q 11.3·v3 A resident of a planned unit development holds title to:
A. Their home and building envelope exclusively
B. Cooperative shares in a master association entity
C. Their individual parcel in fee plus shared ownership rights in common facilities ✓
D. An easement and use agreement only
Answer: C. PUD ownership consists of individual lot fee simple interest combined with an undivided interest in common areas; this differs from cooperatives (shares) and easement-only arrangements.
Q 11.3·v4 What does a PUD owner typically receive at closing?
A. A recorded restrictive covenant with use rights
B. A certificate of occupancy and membership card
C. Deed to their lot and undivided interest in common property ✓
D. Shares in the homeowners association corporation
Answer: C. PUD owners receive a deed reflecting fee title to their individual lot plus an undivided interest in the community's common areas, not HOA shares or covenant-only rights.
Q 11.3·v5 In a planned unit development, what property interest does an individual lot owner typically hold?
A. Membership units in a homeowners association corporation
B. Beneficial interest only in a land trust
C. A leasehold interest renewable every 30 years
D. Fee simple title to their lot and a pro-rata share of common property ✓
Answer: D. PUD owners hold fee simple to their individual lot plus an undivided interest (usually as tenants in common) in shared common areas.
Q 11.3·v6 Which statement best describes the ownership structure in a PUD?
A. Each resident owns their parcel in fee and shares ownership of common facilities with other residents ✓
B. Residents own only the interior of their unit; the building is owned by an HOA
C. Individual ownership is limited to a 99-year leasehold on the land
D. All property is held in trust by a corporate board of directors
Answer: A. PUD ownership combines individual lot fee ownership with shared undivided interest in common areas, distinguishing it from condominium or leasehold models.
Q 11.3·v7 What type of ownership rights does a PUD resident receive for both their lot and the community amenities?
A. Condominium-style airspace ownership only
B. Stock or share certificates in the development corporation
C. Exclusive title to the lot; lease rights to amenities
D. Fee ownership of the lot combined with undivided interest in common areas ✓
Answer: D. PUD owners receive fee simple title to their individual parcel and hold an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in all shared common property.
Q 11.3·v8 A buyer purchasing a lot in a planned unit development acquires:
A. Only the improvements on the lot, not the land itself
B. Their lot in fee simple plus a proportional share of commonly-owned areas ✓
C. A renewable ground lease with rights to use common facilities
D. A percentage ownership stake represented by certificates or shares
Answer: B. PUD purchasers obtain fee ownership of their lot and hold an undivided interest (usually as tenants in common) in roads, recreation areas, and other common elements.
Q 11.3·v9 In a planned unit development (PUD), what property interest does an individual owner typically receive?
A. A long-term lease on both their unit and common property
B. Exclusive airspace rights only, with no land ownership
C. A membership interest in a homeowners association corporation
D. Fee simple title to their lot combined with a fractional ownership stake in shared facilities ✓
Answer: D. PUD owners receive fee simple ownership of their individual lot plus an undivided interest in common areas, distinguishing them from condo owners (who own airspace) and leaseholders.
Q 11.4 NOI for an investment property is $80,000. Annual debt service is $50,000. DSCR is:
A. 0.625
B. 2.00
C. 1.30
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR = 80,000 ÷ 50,000 = 1.60.
Q 11.4·v1 A commercial property generates $80,000 in net operating income annually. The owner's mortgage and other debt obligations total $50,000 per year. What is the debt service coverage ratio?
A. 1.60 ✓
B. 2.40
C. 0.625
D. 1.10
Answer: A. DSCR is calculated as NOI divided by annual debt service: $80,000 ÷ $50,000 = 1.60, indicating the property generates 1.6 times the income needed to cover debt obligations.
Q 11.4·v2 An investor's rental property produces net operating income of $80,000. Annual debt payments (principal and interest) are $50,000. The debt service coverage ratio equals:
A. 1.60 ✓
B. 0.625
C. 1.20
D. 2.50
Answer: A. DSCR = NOI ÷ Annual Debt Service = $80,000 ÷ $50,000 = 1.60, showing the property's ability to service debt from operating income.
Q 11.4·v3 If a property's NOI is $80,000 and annual debt obligations are $50,000, what is the property's DSCR?
A. 1.30
B. 0.50
C. 2.70
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR is calculated by dividing NOI by annual debt service: $80,000 ÷ $50,000 = 1.60, a metric lenders use to assess loan performance risk.
Q 11.4·v4 A multi-unit residential property has an NOI of $80,000 per year. The property carries $50,000 in annual debt service. Calculate the DSCR.
A. 1.60 ✓
B. 1.15
C. 2.10
D. 0.625
Answer: A. DSCR = $80,000 NOI ÷ $50,000 Annual Debt Service = 1.60, representing how many times over the property's income covers its debt obligations.
Q 11.4·v5 A commercial property generates net operating income of $120,000 annually. The investor's annual loan payments total $75,000. What is the debt service coverage ratio?
A. 0.625
B. 2.30
C. 1.20
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR = NOI ÷ Annual Debt Service = $120,000 ÷ $75,000 = 1.60.
Q 11.4·v6 An investor owns an apartment complex with a net operating income of $95,000 per year. If annual debt service obligations are $59,375, the debt service coverage ratio equals:
A. 1.75
B. 0.625
C. 2.15
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR = $95,000 ÷ $59,375 = 1.60, the standard ratio indicating adequate cash flow to cover debt obligations.
Q 11.4·v7 When evaluating a rental property, you determine the NOI is $64,000 and the annual mortgage payments plus other debt service total $40,000. The debt service coverage ratio is:
A. 1.45
B. 0.625
C. 2.05
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR = $64,000 ÷ $40,000 = 1.60, indicating the property generates $1.60 in income for every $1.00 of debt service.
Q 11.4·v8 A lender reviews a loan application for an income-producing property. The property has NOI of $88,000 annually, with annual debt service of $55,000. Calculate the DSCR:
A. 1.10
B. 0.78
C. 2.20
D. 1.60 ✓
Answer: D. DSCR = $88,000 ÷ $55,000 = 1.60, the ratio lenders use to assess the borrower's ability to service debt from operating income.
Q 11.4·v9 A residential income property generates net operating income of $125,000 annually. The owner pays $78,125 per year in mortgage payments and other debt obligations. What is the property's debt service coverage ratio?
A. 1.25
B. 1.60 ✓
C. 0.625
D. 2.05
Answer: B. DSCR is calculated by dividing NOI by annual debt service: $125,000 ÷ $78,125 = 1.60. This indicates the property generates $1.60 in NOI for every $1.00 of debt service owed.
Q 11.5 A retail tenant in a percentage lease pays:
A. Only the percentage
B. Gross lease only
C. Triple net only
D. Base rent + percentage of sales over a threshold ✓
Answer: D. Percentage leases are base rent + sales percentage.
Q 11.5·v1 Under a percentage lease arrangement, what two components typically comprise the tenant's total rent obligation?
A. Only a percentage of annual sales with no base rent requirement
B. A fixed monthly amount plus a percentage of the tenant's gross revenue ✓
C. A triple net structure combined with percentage rent above base year sales
D. A gross lease with percentage adjustments based on occupancy rates
Answer: B. Percentage leases combine a guaranteed base rent with an additional percentage of tenant sales, ensuring landlord receives minimum rent plus a share of tenant success.
Q 11.5·v2 A shopping center landlord structures a lease where the merchant pays a minimum monthly rent plus a percentage of retail sales exceeding a specified volume. This describes:
A. A triple net lease with percentage-based operating expenses
B. A percentage lease with base rent and sales participation ✓
C. A straight lease with optional percentage conversion
D. A gross lease with escalation clauses
Answer: B. The combination of minimum/base rent plus a percentage override on sales is the defining characteristic of a percentage lease structure.
Q 11.5·v3 In Hawaii real estate practice, when a landlord and retail tenant agree to 'percentage rent,' the tenant's obligation typically includes:
A. Base rent only, with all operating expenses passed through separately
B. Gross lease rent with percentage adjustments for property tax increases
C. A guaranteed minimum rent payment plus a percentage of sales revenue ✓
D. Percentage rent exclusively, replacing any fixed monthly payment
Answer: C. Percentage leases feature both a base rent floor to protect the landlord and a percentage clause to allow the landlord to participate in tenant revenue success.
Q 11.5·v4 Which rental structure allows a landlord to collect both a set monthly payment and a portion of the tenant's sales volume?
A. Percentage lease ✓
B. Gross lease
C. Straight lease
D. Triple net lease
Answer: A. A percentage lease uniquely combines base rent with a percentage of tenant sales, providing the landlord with both guaranteed income and revenue participation.
Q 11.5·v5 Under a percentage lease structure, a store operator's monthly obligation typically includes which combination of charges?
A. A fixed rental amount plus a percentage of the store's gross receipts ✓
B. A graduated rent schedule that increases annually without sales contingency
C. Only a percentage of gross sales with no base rent component
D. A triple net arrangement with no percentage participation
Answer: A. Percentage leases combine a minimum base rent with a percentage of tenant sales above a negotiated threshold, creating shared risk between landlord and tenant.
Q 11.5·v6 A shopping center owner leases space to a clothing retailer using a percentage lease. The landlord receives rent based on:
A. Variable rent tied exclusively to the consumer price index
B. Base rent only, calculated on square footage
C. A flat fee per square foot adjusted annually for inflation
D. The greater of base rent or base rent plus a percentage of sales revenue ✓
Answer: D. Percentage leases ensure the landlord receives at least the base rent, but may receive additional compensation if sales exceed thresholds, providing upside participation.
Q 11.5·v7 In negotiating a percentage lease for a restaurant tenant, what rental structure would typically be proposed?
A. A net lease requiring the tenant to pay all operating expenses separately
B. A gross lease covering all property taxes, insurance, and maintenance
C. A minimum guaranteed rent plus a percentage of food and beverage sales ✓
D. Only a percentage of revenue with no minimum floor payment
Answer: C. Percentage leases protect the landlord with a baseline minimum rent while allowing participation in tenant sales performance above that threshold.
Q 11.5·v8 When a commercial tenant signs a percentage lease, the landlord's income stream consists of:
A. Variable revenue that fluctuates entirely with the tenant's monthly sales
B. Straight rent divided equally across all percentage lease properties
C. A fixed base rent combined with contingent percentage payments when sales targets are met ✓
D. Operating expense reimbursement plus a percentage markup on utilities
Answer: C. Percentage leases provide landlords with guaranteed base rent income plus additional rent if tenant sales exceed agreed-upon thresholds, creating a hybrid compensation model.
Q 11.5·v9 Under a typical percentage lease arrangement, a commercial tenant's monthly rental obligation consists of which combination?
A. A fixed minimum rent amount only, regardless of tenant sales performance
B. A variable rent tied solely to the tenant's net profit margin
C. A guaranteed minimum rent plus a percentage of gross receipts exceeding a specified sales volume ✓
D. Operating expense reimbursement and CAM charges with no base rent component
Answer: C. Percentage leases combine a base (minimum) rent with a percentage of sales above a threshold, protecting the landlord's income floor while allowing upside participation in tenant success.
Q 11.6 A ground lease typically:
A. Is for the land only, with tenant building structures ✓
B. Includes the building
C. Lasts 1 year
D. Cannot be assigned
Answer: A. Tenant rents land and builds.
Q 11.6·v1 Under a ground lease arrangement, what does the tenant typically acquire rights to?
A. The fee simple title to both land and all structures
B. A short-term occupancy limited to seasonal use
C. The land itself, while constructing and owning tenant improvements ✓
D. An easement that prohibits any permanent construction
Answer: C. A ground lease grants the tenant the right to use and develop the land, with the tenant responsible for constructing and maintaining buildings and improvements on that leased land.
Q 11.6·v2 Which statement best describes the fundamental structure of a ground lease?
A. Both lessor and lessee share equal ownership of land and buildings
B. The lessee receives a deed to the real property including all structures
C. The lessor retains ownership of the land while the lessee owns the building and improvements ✓
D. The lease term is always less than 12 months to maintain flexibility
Answer: C. In a ground lease, the lessor retains fee simple ownership of the underlying land while the lessee builds structures and owns those improvements during the lease term.
Q 11.6·v3 A tenant entering a ground lease transaction would most likely:
A. Build structures on land they do not own in fee simple ✓
B. Expect the lease to automatically expire after one calendar year
C. Receive title insurance covering the entire property including buildings
D. Be prohibited from assigning their leasehold interest to another party
Answer: A. Ground lease tenants construct buildings and improvements on land they lease but do not own fee simple, with their ownership rights limited to the structures they erect.
Q 11.6·v4 What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes a ground lease from a standard building lease?
A. Ground leases always include the existing structures as part of the rental agreement
B. The tenant cannot improve or modify the property in any way
C. Ground leases are limited to commercial properties only
D. The tenant is responsible for constructing buildings on vacant or improved land owned by the lessor ✓
Answer: D. A ground lease specifically involves the tenant leasing land and bearing the responsibility and cost of constructing or maintaining buildings and improvements on that leased parcel.
Q 11.6·v5 In a ground lease arrangement, what does the tenant typically acquire rights to, and what does the tenant construct?
A. The tenant acquires mineral rights and is prohibited from erecting structures
B. The tenant acquires both land and building for a fixed 12-month period
C. The tenant acquires the building and rents the surrounding land
D. The tenant acquires the land only and constructs any buildings or improvements ✓
Answer: D. A ground lease grants the tenant exclusive use of the land; the tenant is responsible for constructing and owning any buildings or improvements on that land.
Q 11.6·v6 Which statement best describes the primary characteristic of a ground lease?
A. The lessee has the right to use and improve the land, with the lessee owning improvements made during the lease term ✓
B. The lease automatically includes ownership of existing buildings and fixtures
C. The lessor retains ownership of all structures built on the property
D. The lease duration is restricted to one year with no renewal options
Answer: A. Ground leases allow tenants to build and own their own structures on the lessor's land, with the tenant retaining ownership of those improvements throughout the lease.
Q 11.6·v7 A developer leases a parcel of land from a property owner under a ground lease. What is the developer's responsibility and ownership?
A. The developer leases both land and existing structures for a period not to exceed 12 months
B. The developer gains fee simple ownership of the underlying land after 5 years
C. The developer constructs buildings and improvements on the land and owns those structures during the lease term ✓
D. The developer maintains the land only; the owner must construct all buildings
Answer: C. In a ground lease, the developer (tenant) builds and owns improvements on the leased land; the owner retains title to the underlying real property.
Q 11.6·v8 How does a ground lease differ from a standard commercial lease in terms of what the tenant controls?
A. A ground lease is limited to agricultural use only
B. A ground lease cannot be transferred, while commercial leases are freely assignable
C. A ground lease allows the tenant to develop and own improvements on vacant land, whereas a standard commercial lease typically involves an existing building ✓
D. A ground lease includes the building structure, while a commercial lease does not
Answer: C. Ground leases are development leases where tenants improve vacant land and own those improvements; standard commercial leases usually involve existing improved properties.
Q 11.6·v9 Under a ground lease arrangement, which statement best describes the tenant's rights and responsibilities?
A. The tenant receives a deed to both land and any existing structures on the property
B. The tenant may not transfer or sublease the lease without the landlord's written consent in perpetuity
C. The tenant owns the building and improvements but leases the underlying land from the landlord ✓
D. The tenant has a short-term occupancy right limited to one calendar year with no renewal options
Answer: C. A ground lease grants the tenant use of land only; the tenant constructs and owns the improvements while the landlord retains land ownership. The tenant typically may assign with landlord approval.
Q 11.7 The Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act applies to:
A. Single-family resales only
B. Commercial sales only
C. All real estate sales
D. Cross-state sales of unimproved lots in larger developments ✓
Answer: D. ILSA covers cross-state subdivision marketing.
Q 11.7·v1 Which of the following transactions would typically fall under the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act?
A. A commercial real estate firm selling office buildings in multiple states
B. An individual selling their personal single-family residence to an out-of-state buyer
C. A developer selling improved residential homes in a single state
D. A developer marketing raw land parcels across state lines as part of a large subdivision ✓
Answer: D. ILSA specifically regulates the interstate marketing and sale of unimproved lots within subdivisions of 25+ lots when marketed across state lines.
Q 11.7·v2 Under federal real estate law, the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act's primary scope includes:
A. Subdivisions of unimproved lots being sold or marketed across state lines ✓
B. Agricultural land sales within a single state
C. Commercial property leases negotiated between multi-state corporations
D. All residential property transactions regardless of state boundaries
Answer: A. ILSA applies to subdivisions involving unimproved lots offered for sale or lease across state lines, requiring developers to provide disclosure statements.
Q 11.7·v3 A developer in Arizona is offering raw land parcels to buyers located in multiple states, including Hawaii. This offering would likely be subject to:
A. The Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act ✓

Q 11.7·v5 Which of the following transactions would be subject to Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act requirements?

Q 11.8 DSCR below 1.0 means:
A. Property generates more income than debt service
B. Cap rate above 10%
C. Property has insufficient income to cover debt ✓
D. No debt
Answer: C. DSCR < 1.0 = NOI insufficient to cover debt service.
Q 11.8·v1 When a property's DSCR is computed at 0.85, what does this ratio indicate about the property's cash flow situation?
A. Net operating income falls short of covering annual debt service payments ✓
B. Loan-to-value ratio is below market standards
C. The property is free and clear of all mortgage obligations
D. Annual NOI exceeds total debt obligations by 15%
Answer: A. A DSCR of 0.85 means NOI covers only 85% of debt service; the property cannot fully service its debt obligations.
Q 11.8·v2 A lender reviews a rental property's financials and finds the DSCR is 0.92. What conclusion should the lender draw?
A. The property carries no outstanding debt
B. The property's net operating income is inadequate to pay the full annual debt service ✓
C. The property's gross rental income exceeds operating expenses by 92%
D. The property generates sufficient cash flow to exceed all debt requirements
Answer: B. A DSCR of 0.92 indicates the property generates only 92 cents of NOI per dollar of debt service owed, creating a shortfall.
Q 11.8·v3 If an investor calculates a DSCR of 0.78 for a potential investment property, what does this metric reveal?
A. The debt-to-equity ratio is optimal for financing
B. The property's income is insufficient to fully cover required debt payments ✓
C. Operating expenses consume 78% of gross income
D. Debt obligations are exceeded by net operating income
Answer: B. A DSCR below 1.0 means the property cannot generate enough NOI to cover all annual debt service obligations.
Q 11.8·v4 What financial concern does a DSCR reading below 1.0 present to a property owner?
A. The owner has successfully paid off all loan balances
B. The property is generating excess income available for distribution
C. The property's cap rate has risen above prevailing market rates
D. The property's net operating income cannot fully service the debt obligations ✓
Answer: D. DSCR < 1.0 signals that NOI is insufficient to meet full debt service requirements, creating a cash flow deficiency.
Q 11.8·v5 When a property's Debt Service Coverage Ratio falls below 1.0, what does this indicate about the investment's cash flow position?
A. The property's net operating income is inadequate to cover debt payments ✓
B. The property's net operating income exceeds annual debt obligations
C. The property is generating positive cash-on-cash returns
D. The loan-to-value ratio has been reduced below market standards
Answer: A. A DSCR below 1.0 means the NOI cannot fully cover the debt service payments, creating a shortfall rather than surplus cash flow.
Q 11.8·v6 A lender reviews a property with a DSCR of 0.85. What concern does this ratio raise?
A. Annual debt service payments exceed the property's net operating income ✓
B. The gross rent multiplier is too high for the market
C. Operating expenses are lower than industry standards
D. The property is debt-free and requires no servicing
Answer: A. A DSCR of 0.85 indicates that the property's NOI is only 85% of what is needed to cover debt service, creating a coverage shortfall.
Q 11.8·v7 Which scenario best describes a property with a DSCR of 0.90?
A. Income exceeds debt obligations by 10%
B. The property has paid off 90% of its mortgage balance
C. Income falls short of debt obligations by 10% ✓
D. Operating expenses are 90% of gross rental income
Answer: C. A DSCR of 0.90 means the property generates only 90 cents of NOI for every dollar of debt service owed, indicating insufficient income coverage.
Q 11.8·v8 If a commercial property shows a DSCR below 1.0, what does this reveal about its debt servicing capacity?
A. The property does not generate enough income to fully service its debt obligations ✓
B. The debt-to-equity ratio meets conventional financing standards
C. The property's appreciation rate exceeds the interest rate
D. The property has reserves sufficient to cover maintenance costs
Answer: A. A DSCR below 1.0 means the property's net operating income is insufficient to cover all debt payments, indicating weak debt servicing capacity.
Q 11.8·v9 A property has a Debt Service Coverage Ratio of 0.85. What does this indicate about the property's financial performance?
A. The capitalization rate is lower than market average
B. Net operating income falls short of annual debt service requirements ✓
C. Annual net operating income exceeds annual debt obligations by 15%
D. The property is free and clear with no mortgage financing
Answer: B. DSCR of 0.85 (below 1.0) means NOI is insufficient to fully cover debt service payments, indicating financial stress for the borrower.
Q 11.9 A property manager's standard compensation is most often:
A. Percentage of rents collected ✓
B. Hourly
C. Equity stake
D. Flat year-end
Answer: A. Percentage of rents (often 6-10% residential) is standard.
Q 11.9·v1 In Hawaii property management, how are most residential property managers compensated for their services?
A. A fixed monthly retainer fee regardless of occupancy

Answer: B. Property managers typically earn a percentage of collected rents (often 6-10% in residential settings) rather than fixed fees or equity arrangements.
Q 11.9·v2 A property owner hires a manager to oversee a 12-unit apartment complex. The manager's compensation is most likely structured as:
A. A profit-sharing arrangement after operating expenses
B. A guaranteed annual salary plus health benefits

Q 11.9·v3 When structuring a management agreement, the fee arrangement that represents industry standard practice is:
A. Deferred compensation paid as a lump sum at fiscal year-end
B. A proportional share of the gross rental receipts collected ✓

Answer: B. Property managers conventionally receive compensation as a percentage of rents collected, typically ranging from 6-10% for residential properties.
Q 11.9·v4 Which compensation model is standard in the property management industry?
A. Performance-based bonuses tied to property tax reductions
B. Variable rates based on the square footage managed

Q 11.9·v5 When negotiating a property management agreement, what fee structure is a property manager most likely to propose?

B. A fixed monthly retainer regardless of occupancy rates

D. A commission based on rental income received ✓

Q 11.9·v6 Under which compensation model do property managers most commonly operate in Hawaii and nationwide?
A. Time-based billing at an hourly rate established quarterly
B. A percentage of the gross rents actually collected from tenants ✓

Q 11.9·v7 A property owner is evaluating compensation proposals from three different property management companies. Which fee arrangement should the owner expect to be the most common industry practice?
A. A flat guaranteed fee payable whether or not units are leased
B. A per-unit annual fee plus tenant screening charges
C. A performance bonus tied to property market value increase
D. A percentage deduction from the total rents collected each month ✓
Answer: D. Percentage of rents collected is the standard property management fee structure, typically ranging 6-10%, because it creates mutual incentive between manager and owner to maximize occupancy and collect rent.
Q 11.9·v8 How are property managers in Hawaii typically compensated for their services?
A. Through a base salary plus health insurance benefits
B. Via hourly wages calculated from a negotiated rate schedule
C. By retaining a portion of rental income received from tenants ✓
D. By acquiring a fractional interest in the managed property

Q 11.9·v9 When a property manager negotiates a management agreement with a residential landlord, what fee structure is considered industry standard?
A. A fixed monthly retainer regardless of occupancy
B. A percentage ownership interest in the property

D. A commission based on the gross rental income collected ✓
Answer: D. Property managers typically earn a percentage-based fee (usually 6-10% for residential) tied to actual rents collected, aligning their incentives with occupancy and rent collection performance.
Q 11.10 A vacant unit's impact on NOI:
A. Only affects taxes
B. No effect
C. Increases NOI
D. Reduces effective gross income ✓
Answer: D. Vacancy reduces effective gross income, which reduces NOI.
Q 11.10·v1 When calculating net operating income for an investment property, how does a unit sitting vacant for several months typically affect the final NOI figure?
A. It has no impact on NOI calculations
B. It only affects the property's assessed value for tax purposes
C. It decreases effective gross income, thereby lowering NOI ✓
D. It increases NOI because debt service is lower
Answer: C. Vacancy periods reduce the actual rental income collected, which is the starting point for calculating effective gross income; this reduction flows directly to lower NOI.
Q 11.10·v2 An appraiser is analyzing a multi-unit property where one unit remains unoccupied. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between this vacancy and the property's NOI?
A. The loss of rental revenue reduces effective gross income and therefore NOI ✓
B. NOI increases due to reduced maintenance costs on the vacant unit
C. Vacancy impacts only the cap rate, not the NOI itself
D. NOI is unaffected because operating expenses remain constant
Answer: A. The lost rental income from the vacant unit reduces effective gross income, which is the foundation for calculating NOI; lower income results in lower net operating income.
Q 11.10·v3 A property manager reports that the occupancy rate has dropped due to market conditions. How would this occupancy decline influence the property's net operating income?
A. It reduces NOI by decreasing the effective gross income available ✓
B. It has no measurable effect on NOI
C. It increases NOI because fewer tenants mean lower administrative costs
D. It only impacts the property's debt-to-income ratio
Answer: A. Lower occupancy means fewer units generating rental income; this directly reduces effective gross income, which is the primary driver of NOI calculations.
Q 11.10·v4 During a real estate investment analysis, a broker notices that 15% of the rental units are currently vacant. What is the direct consequence of this vacancy on the property's NOI?
A. NOI drops because effective gross income is reduced by the lost rental revenue ✓
B. NOI improves due to deductions for maintenance on empty units
C. NOI is only affected if the vacancy is due to tenant eviction
D. NOI remains stable because the property's potential income is unchanged
Answer: A. Vacant units generate zero rental income; this loss reduces effective gross income, which directly lowers NOI regardless of whether other expenses change.
Q 11.10·v5 When an investment property has unoccupied units, how is net operating income typically affected?
A. It increases due to reduced maintenance costs
B. It remains unchanged if operating expenses stay constant
C. It is only affected if the vacancy rate exceeds 10%
D. It decreases because effective gross income falls ✓
Answer: D. Vacant units generate no rental income, lowering effective gross income and therefore reducing NOI, regardless of maintenance savings.
Q 11.10·v6 A property manager notices a 15% vacancy rate in the apartment complex. Which statement correctly describes the NOI impact?
A. NOI increases until the units are re-leased
B. NOI is unaffected; vacancy only impacts capital expenditures
C. NOI improves because fewer units require utilities and repairs
D. NOI declines because potential rental income is lost ✓
Answer: D. Lost rental revenue from vacant units directly reduces effective gross income, which is a key component of the NOI calculation.
Q 11.10·v7 During an appraisal, a real estate appraiser accounts for vacancies when calculating income. This adjustment affects which metric most directly?
A. Cash flow reserves, which are separate from NOI
B. Gross potential income, with no impact on NOI
C. Operating expense ratio, which is independent of NOI
D. Effective gross income, thereby reducing NOI ✓
Answer: D. Vacancy reduces effective gross income (potential rent minus vacancy loss), which is subtracted from by operating expenses to arrive at NOI.
Q 11.10·v8 An investor is evaluating a commercial building with 20% occupancy. How does the vacancy level factor into the net operating income calculation?
A. It lowers effective gross income, which directly reduces the resulting NOI ✓
B. It affects only the debt service coverage ratio, not NOI itself
C. It decreases NOI only if combined with rising property taxes
D. It does not—NOI is based on theoretical maximum rent regardless of actual occupancy
Answer: A. Vacancy is converted to lost rental income, reducing effective gross income and therefore lowering the NOI figure used in property valuation and analysis.
Q 11.10·v9 When rental units sit empty, how does this vacancy factor into the calculation of net operating income?
A. It only affects the property's assessed value for tax purposes
B. It increases NOI by reducing maintenance expenses
C. It has no impact on NOI since fixed costs remain constant
D. It decreases effective gross income, thereby lowering NOI ✓
Answer: D. Vacant units generate zero rental income, which directly reduces effective gross income and consequently reduces NOI; vacancy loss is a key component of the income approach.

State Portion (Hawaiʻi) — Chapters 12–20

12
Hawaii: Ascertaining & Disclosing Material Facts
State portion8 PSI items28 key concepts10 base questions

Hawaii has unique disclosure obligations rooted in its land history, leasehold prevalence, and tax rules.

Chapter Overview

Hawaii has two parallel land-recording systems that every licensee must understand. The Bureau of Conveyances (BOC) handles "Regular System" recordings — the standard county-style chain-of-title model used in most of the United States. Documents are recorded in chronological order; subsequent purchasers are presumed on notice; chain of title is searched back to a marketable starting point. The Land Court system, unique to Hawaii, is a Torrens-style registered title system. When property is brought under Land Court, the court issues a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT); the title shown on the TCT is conclusive against the world, eliminating most chain-of-title disputes. A property may be entirely in the Regular System, entirely in Land Court, or split (a "dual" parcel). Agents must know which when ordering title and preparing closing.

HARPTA (Hawaii Real Property Tax Act) is a state withholding requirement. When a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii real property, the buyer must withhold a percentage (currently 7.25% as of recent rules — verify current rate) of the gross sales price at closing and remit it to the State. This is a withholding against the seller's eventual Hawaii income tax liability, not an additional tax. The seller may apply for a reduced or zero withholding by filing forms in advance. Buyers are statutorily responsible — failure to withhold makes the buyer liable. FIRPTA is the federal counterpart, requiring 15% withholding on sales by foreign sellers; both can apply to the same transaction.

GET (General Excise Tax) is Hawaii's tax on business activity, including real estate brokerage commissions and most rental income. It is not a "sales tax" — it falls on the gross receipts of the business and is typically passed to the customer as a "GET visible pass-on." Real estate licensees must factor GET into their commissions and disclose appropriately. Property managers must collect GET on rents (with passthrough by tenant) and remit. The 2026 rate is 4% statewide plus county surcharges in some counties; verify current rates.

Conveyance tax is Hawaii's state-level transfer tax on real property sales. It has tiered rates based on sale price and buyer status (owner-occupant rate is lower than investor rate). The seller typically pays unless contract specifies otherwise. Recording fees are separate, charged by BOC or Land Court per page recorded. These are exam math territory — be prepared for calculation questions on the proper conveyance tax tier.

The Seller's Property Disclosure Statement is required by HRS 508D for residential resales of one to four units. The seller must disclose all known material facts about the property's condition. The disclosure form covers known defects in roof, plumbing, electrical, structural, environmental hazards, drainage, prior repairs, and known issues with the unit, the building, the lot, and the immediate neighborhood. Buyers who receive a materially inaccurate disclosure have rescission rights subject to statutory deadlines.

Leasehold disclosures are uniquely important in Hawaii because so much property is leasehold. HRS 514E and other statutes require disclosure of the remaining lease term, current lease rent, scheduled lease rent step-ups (renegotiation dates), and any reversion of improvements at lease end. A buyer who doesn't know they're buying leasehold can sue. Distressed-property and short-sale disclosures are required when applicable. The Condominium Public Report (developer disclosure document) must accompany sales of new condo units.

Environmental conditions specific to Hawaii: lava-zone classification (Hawaii County 1-9 hazard rating), flood zones (especially low-lying coastal areas), tsunami evacuation zones, hurricane-zone wind ratings (insurance impact), agricultural pesticide history (especially on former plantation lands), formaldehyde concerns from prior pesticide treatments, and termite inspection (most resales include a Termite Inspection Report, often called a "termite" report or pest control report). Coastal property has SMA (Special Management Area) considerations. Ag land has restrictions on residential use.

Hawaii land history affects property rights in unique ways. The Mahele of 1848 began the conversion from communal to fee ownership. Royal Patent Grants and Land Commission Awards from this era still appear in chain of title. Some properties have kuleana rights — descendants' continued access for cultivation, gathering, or burial sites. The Native Hawaiian Inheritance Act and Hawaiian Homes Commission Act (HHCA) govern Hawaiian Home Lands, which are leased only to qualifying Native Hawaiians and have specific transfer restrictions. These legacy issues occasionally surface in transactions.

Tax Map Key (TMK) is Hawaii's parcel identifier. It has the format Zone-Section-Plat-Parcel(-CPR), e.g., 1-2-3-456-7890. Each county uses its own zone numbering. For Condominium Property Regimes (CPR), additional digits identify the specific unit. TMKs link to county tax assessment, zoning, real-property tax payments, and recorded documents. Always confirm the TMK matches the legal description before any transaction.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Bureau of Conveyances (BOC)State office maintaining the Regular System chain of title for non-Land-Court parcels.
Hawaiʻi note: Located in Honolulu; serves all islands.
Regular SystemStandard chain-of-title recording. Documents in chronological order; subsequent purchasers on constructive notice.
Land CourtHawaii's Torrens-style registered title system. Transfer Certificate of Title is conclusive.
TCT (Transfer Certificate of Title)Land Court's conclusive title document. Issued when registered property changes hands.
Dual parcelProperty partially in Regular System, partially in Land Court.
HARPTAHawaii Real Property Tax Act. Currently 7.25% withholding on non-resident seller proceeds at closing.
FIRPTAFederal Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act. 15% federal withholding on foreign sellers.
GETGeneral Excise Tax. Hawaii's gross-receipts business tax. Applies to commissions and rents.
GET visible pass-onCommon practice of itemizing GET as a separate line item passed to the consumer.
Conveyance taxHawaii state tax on real property transfers. Tiered rate based on price + buyer status.
Owner-occupant rateLower conveyance tax rate when buyer will occupy property as primary residence.
HRS 508DMandatory Seller Disclosures statute for residential resales (1-4 units).
Seller's Property Disclosure StatementWritten disclosure of known material facts. Required under HRS 508D.
HRS 514ETime share and leasehold disclosures for condominium properties.
Leasehold disclosureMandatory disclosure of remaining term, rent, step-ups, reversion.
Material factAnything reasonable buyer would consider important. Disclose if known.
Lava-zone disclosureHawaii County requires disclosure of lava-flow hazard zones (1–9). Affects insurance and value.
Tsunami evacuation zoneCoastal-area disclosure where applicable.
Flood zoneFEMA-designated flood hazard zone. Affects insurance requirements.
TMK (Tax Map Key)Hawaii's parcel identifier: Zone-Section-Plat-Parcel(-CPR).
Termite inspection reportStandard pre-closing inspection in Hawaii. Often required by lender.
Kuleana rightsNative Hawaiian descendants' continued access for cultivation, gathering, or burial.
Hawaiian Home Lands (HHCA)Lands leased only to qualifying Native Hawaiians under federal Hawaiian Homes Commission Act.
Mahele of 1848Transition from communal to fee ownership. Origin of many chain-of-title issues.
Land Commission AwardOriginal grant from Hawaiian government, traceable in old chain of title.
Royal Patent GrantTitle from Hawaiian Kingdom era. Sometimes appears in chain.
Distressed Property DisclosureRequired when seller is in foreclosure, short sale, or similar.
Condominium Public ReportDeveloper disclosure required for new condo sales.

Q 12.1 A seller from California sells a Maui house to a Hawaii resident. The buyer is responsible for withholding under:
A. GET
B. FIRPTA
C. RESPA
D. HARPTA ✓
Answer: D. Non-Hawaii-resident seller triggers HARPTA withholding (currently 7.25% of sale price).
Q 12.1·v1 An out-of-state seller conveys residential property in Hawaii to a local buyer. Which withholding requirement applies to this transaction?
A. HARPTA withholding on the gross proceeds ✓
B. FIRPTA withholding by the escrow agent
C. RESPA withholding at point of sale
D. GET exemption for non-residents
Answer: A. HARPTA (Hawaii Real Property Tax Act) requires withholding when a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii real property, regardless of the buyer's residency status.
Q 12.1·v2 A mainland investor sells a Honolulu condominium to a Hawaii resident buyer. The escrow officer must ensure compliance with which state withholding statute?
A. General Excise Tax (GET) collection duties
B. Hawaii HARPTA withholding obligations ✓
C. Federal FIRPTA requirements only
D. Interstate Commerce Act provisions
Answer: B. HARPTA is Hawaii's residential property transfer withholding law that applies when a non-resident seller transfers residential property located in Hawaii, requiring the buyer or escrow to withhold a percentage of sale proceeds.
Q 12.1·v3 During a real estate closing in Maui, the listing agent discovers the seller is a non-resident of Hawaii. What withholding requirement must the buyer or settlement agent address?
A. HARPTA withholding based on the sale price ✓
B. RESPA escrow disclosure and withholding
C. Property transfer tax under county ordinance
D. FIRPTA withholding of 10% of purchase price
Answer: A. HARPTA applies to non-resident sellers of Hawaii residential property and requires withholding of the statutory percentage from the gross sale proceeds at closing.
Q 12.1·v4 A buyer in Hawaii is purchasing a single-family home from a seller residing in Nevada. Which of the following withholding requirements must the buyer or closing agent satisfy?
A. FIRPTA federal withholding of 15%
B. RESPA federal escrow account rules
C. General Excise Tax pass-through payment
D. Hawaii HARPTA withholding on the transaction ✓
Answer: D. HARPTA mandates withholding when a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii residential real property, with the buyer or escrow agent responsible for remitting the withheld amount to the Hawaii Department of Taxation.
Q 12.1·v5 A mainland investor from Oregon completes the purchase of a condominium on Oahu. Which withholding statute applies to this transaction?
A. FIRPTA
B. HARPTA ✓
C. HRS Chapter 507
D. GET
Answer: B. HARPTA (Hawaii Real Property Tax Act) requires withholding when a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii real property; the buyer is typically responsible for compliance.
Q 12.1·v6 During the closing of a Big Island property sale, the escrow agent discovers the seller is a foreign national residing outside Hawaii. What withholding requirement must the buyer's agent address?
A. Conveyance tax under HRS 247
B. HARPTA withholding obligation ✓
C. FIRPTA withholding on the net proceeds
D. RESPA withholding at settlement
Answer: B. HARPTA applies to sales of Hawaii real property by non-Hawaii residents; the buyer or escrow agent must withhold a percentage of the purchase price.
Q 12.1·v7 A broker assists with the sale of a Kauai home where the seller is a Washington state resident. The buyer asks which federal or state withholding law governs the transaction. What is the correct response?
A. GET applies at the county assessor level
B. HARPTA, because Hawaii imposes withholding on non-resident sellers ✓
C. FIRPTA, because the seller is out-of-state
D. No withholding applies—only federal income tax reporting
Answer: B. HARPTA is Hawaii's real property transfer withholding statute that applies when a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii property; it is separate from federal FIRPTA requirements.
Q 12.1·v8 At the settlement table, the title company's closing attorney notes the seller transferred to Hawaii only three years ago and is still a Nevada resident. Which withholding obligation takes precedence in this Hawaii real estate transaction?
A. HARPTA withholding (currently 7.25% of the purchase price) ✓
B. Passive Activity Loss (PAL) withholding
C. No withholding because the seller has already paid state income taxes
D. FIRPTA withholding of 15% of the sale price
Answer: A. HARPTA requires withholding by the buyer or escrow agent on sales by non-Hawaii residents; residency status, not length of time in Hawaii, determines the withholding obligation.
Q 12.1·v9 When a mainland seller transfers residential property in Hawaii to a local buyer, which withholding requirement typically applies to the transaction?
A. HARPTA ✓
B. GET (General Excise Tax)
C. FIRPTA
D. Hawaii Resident Property Tax Act
Answer: A. HARPTA requires withholding when a non-Hawaii resident sells Hawaii real property, with the buyer/escrow agent responsible for withholding approximately 7.25% of the sale price.
Q 12.2 Hawaii's Torrens-style registered title system is called:
A. Land Court ✓
B. TMK
C. CPR
D. BOC
Answer: A. Land Court issues a TCT (Transfer Certificate of Title) — conclusive.
Q 12.2·v1 Which Hawaii administrative body operates a system similar to the Torrens title registration model, issuing conclusive certificates of title?
A. The Bureau of Conveyances
B. The County Tax Assessor's Office
C. Land Court ✓
D. The Real Estate Commission
Answer: C. Land Court administers Hawaii's Torrens-style registered title system and issues a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) that is conclusive proof of ownership.
Q 12.2·v2 In Hawaii, which institution provides registered title with conclusive legal protection through a Torrens-style system?
A. TMK Registry
B. Bureau of Conveyances
C. Department of Transportation
D. Land Court ✓
Answer: D. Land Court is Hawaii's Torrens system authority, issuing a TCT that provides conclusive registered title protection to property owners.
Q 12.2·v3 What is the name of Hawaii's registered title system that issues conclusive Transfer Certificates of Title?
A. Torrens-Based Land Court System ✓
B. Tax Map Key System
C. CPR Title Registry
D. Conventional Recording System
Answer: A. Land Court operates Hawaii's Torrens-style registered title system, issuing conclusive TCTs rather than relying on a conventional recording system.
Q 12.2·v4 A property owner in Hawaii receives a conclusive Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) from which entity?
A. The Bureau of Conveyances
B. County Recorder's Office
C. The Real Estate Commission
D. Land Court ✓
Answer: D. Land Court issues the TCT under Hawaii's Torrens-style registered title system, providing conclusive proof of ownership superior to conventional recording.
Q 12.2·v5 Which Hawaii system provides conclusive title through a judicial process similar to the Torrens model used in other jurisdictions?
A. Bureau of Conveyances filing
B. Land Court certification ✓
C. Tax Map Key assignment
D. CPR registration
Answer: B. Land Court is Hawaii's Torrens-style system that issues a conclusive Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) after judicial examination of ownership.
Q 12.2·v6 In Hawaii, when a property owner obtains a TCT (Transfer Certificate of Title) through judicial process, they have gone through which system?
A. The Land Court process ✓
B. The Bureau of Conveyances recording
C. The CPR (Condominium Property Regime)
D. The TMK (Tax Map Key) classification
Answer: A. The Land Court system issues Transfer Certificates of Title as the conclusive proof of ownership, modeled after the Torrens title system.

Q 12.2·v8 A buyer who receives a court-issued certificate of title showing conclusive ownership in Hawaii has obtained this document from which system?
A. TMK

C. Real Estate Commission

A. The state's General Excise Tax on business receipts ✓

Answer: A. The TMK is Hawaii's official tax parcel identification system using zone-section-plat-parcel numbering to uniquely identify every property for tax and administrative purposes.
Q 12.4·v3 A real estate professional needs to locate a specific property in Hawaii's property records system. What does the TMK number provide?

B. The mortgage lender's key for accessing deed of trust documents

Answer: A. TMK (Tax Map Key) uniquely identifies a property parcel in Hawaii using a structured format of zone-section-plat-parcel numbers to organize and locate properties in government records.

Q 12.4·v5 When a Hawaii real estate agent needs to locate a specific residential lot in a subdivision, which document or identifier would contain the TMK?

Q 12.4·v6 A licensee is preparing a CMA and needs to reference comparable properties by their unique parcel identifiers in Hawaii. What system would use the format Zone-Section-Plat-Parcel?
A. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission's licensing database

Q 12.4·v7 Which of the following best describes what TMK stands for and its primary use in Hawaii real estate transactions?

Q 12.4·v9 When a Hawaii real estate professional needs to locate and reference a specific property on the tax assessor's records, which designation would they use?

Q 12.5 A foreign national selling Hawaii real estate triggers withholding under:
A. Neither
B. HARPTA only
C. FIRPTA only
D. Both HARPTA and FIRPTA ✓
Answer: D. Foreign + non-Hawaii-resident — both can apply to the same transaction.
Q 12.5·v1 When a non-U.S. citizen sells residential property in Hawaii, which withholding requirement(s) must the escrow agent consider?
A. Federal FIRPTA withholding only
B. State HARPTA withholding and federal FIRPTA withholding ✓
C. No withholding if the buyer assumes the mortgage
D. State HARPTA withholding only
Answer: B. Both HARPTA (Hawaii state law) and FIRPTA (federal law) can independently apply when a foreign national sells Hawaii real estate, requiring dual withholding compliance.
Q 12.5·v2 An alien investor disposes of a Honolulu condominium. Which of the following correctly identifies the applicable withholding laws?
A. Neither statute applies if the property is mortgaged
B. HARPTA applies; FIRPTA does not apply to residential transfers
C. Both HARPTA and FIRPTA may apply to the same transaction ✓
D. FIRPTA applies; HARPTA applies only to commercial property
Answer: C. Foreign nationals selling Hawaii property are subject to overlapping state (HARPTA) and federal (FIRPTA) withholding obligations simultaneously, not alternatively.
Q 12.5·v3 A real estate licensee is closing a sale where the seller is a foreign entity. What withholding compliance issue should the licensee flag?
A. Only federal tax withholding under FIRPTA is mandatory
B. Both federal FIRPTA and Hawaii HARPTA withholding requirements may be triggered ✓
C. Withholding applies only if the property is located in Honolulu County
D. Only Hawaii state withholding under HARPTA is mandatory
Answer: B. A foreign seller in Hawaii creates potential dual withholding obligations under both state and federal law, and the licensee must ensure compliance with both statutes.
Q 12.5·v4 Which statement most accurately describes the withholding requirements for an international corporation selling agricultural land in Hawaii?
A. No withholding is required if the buyer is a Hawaii resident
B. FIRPTA withholding is required; HARPTA does not apply to corporate sellers
C. Both HARPTA and FIRPTA withholding provisions may be required in the same transaction ✓
D. HARPTA withholding is required; FIRPTA does not apply to foreign corporations
Answer: C. Hawaii's HARPTA and the federal FIRPTA statute both independently govern withholding for foreign entity sales of Hawaii property and can apply concurrently.
Q 12.5·v5 An individual from Japan sells a condominium in Honolulu. Which withholding requirement(s) apply to this transaction?
A. State HARPTA withholding only
B. No withholding is required for foreign nationals
C. Federal FIRPTA withholding only
D. Federal FIRPTA and state HARPTA withholding ✓
Answer: D. A foreign national (non-U.S. citizen) selling Hawaii real property is subject to both federal FIRPTA withholding and Hawaii's parallel state withholding requirement (HARPTA), which operate independently.
Q 12.5·v6 When a non-citizen resident of another country conveys real property located in Hawaii, the escrow agent must withhold funds under:
A. HARPTA exclusively
B. FIRPTA and HARPTA concurrently ✓
C. State income tax only
D. FIRPTA exclusively
Answer: B. Foreign persons disposing of Hawaii real estate must comply with both the federal FIRPTA withholding requirement and Hawaii's HARPTA withholding requirement, which are separate obligations.
Q 12.5·v7 A seller who is a foreign corporation liquidates its Maui property holdings. Withholding obligations include:
A. Both FIRPTA at the federal level and HARPTA at the state level ✓
B. Neither, as corporate sales are exempt from withholding
C. FIRPTA only, as state law defers to federal withholding
D. HARPTA, but only if the seller is also a nonresident
Answer: A. Foreign persons and entities selling Hawaii real property are subject to concurrent federal FIRPTA withholding and state HARPTA withholding; these are separate statutory requirements that both apply.
Q 12.5·v8 During closing of a Hawaii real estate sale, the title company identifies that the seller is a foreign national. This triggers withholding compliance under:
A. State HARPTA only
B. Both federal FIRPTA and state HARPTA requirements ✓
C. Federal FIRPTA only
D. Neither requirement applies to foreign nationals
Answer: B. Foreign nationals selling Hawaii real property must satisfy both the federal Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act (FIRPTA) and Hawaii's Real Property Tax Act (HARPTA), which operate as parallel withholding obligations.
Q 12.5·v9 When a nonresident alien disposes of Hawaii real property, which withholding requirement(s) apply?
A. Federal FIRPTA withholding applies, but Hawaii HARPTA does not apply to foreign nationals
B. Neither withholding applies if the seller has a valid Hawaii driver's license
C. Both federal FIRPTA and Hawaii HARPTA withholding may be required on the same sale ✓
D. Hawaii HARPTA withholding applies, but federal FIRPTA does not apply to nonresidents
Answer: C. A nonresident alien selling Hawaii real estate is subject to both FIRPTA (federal) and HARPTA (Hawaii state) withholding obligations simultaneously, as they address different statutory frameworks.
Q 12.6 The Hawaii Mandatory Seller Disclosures statute is:

Q 12.6·v3 The statutory law requiring Hawaii sellers to reveal known material defects in residential property is:

B. HRS 508D ✓

A. HRS 508D pertaining to residential property disclosures ✓
B. HRS 514B concerning condominium associations

Q 12.6·v7 Under Hawaii law, the statute that establishes seller disclosure obligations for property condition is:
A. HRS 467
B. HRS 508D ✓

Q 12.6·v8 Which of the following HRS sections contains Hawaii's residential seller disclosure requirements?

Q 12.6·v9 Under Hawaii law, which statute specifically requires residential sellers to provide property condition disclosures to prospective buyers?
A. HRS 514B

C. HRS 508D ✓
