Q 12.7 A buyer does not know they're buying leasehold. The seller failed to disclose. The buyer may:
A. Force a fee conversion
B. Have no remedy
C. Have rescission rights under leasehold disclosure law ✓
D. Only sue for cosmetic damages
Answer: C. Failure to disclose leasehold is actionable; buyer has rescission rights.
Q 12.7·v1 A seller omits material information that the property is held under a leasehold estate rather than fee simple. Upon discovery, the buyer's available remedies include:
A. Accepting the property with no legal recourse
B. Filing a complaint for breach of warranty of habitability only
C. Demanding immediate fee simple conversion at seller's expense
D. Rescission of the transaction under leasehold disclosure requirements ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires disclosure of leasehold status; non-disclosure gives the buyer rescission rights as a remedy.
Q 12.7·v2 During closing, a buyer discovers the property is leasehold, not fee simple as represented in marketing materials. The seller claims they were unaware of the disclosure requirement. The buyer can:
A. Sue only for specific performance on lease extension
B. Require the seller to purchase a property protection endorsement
C. Recover damages limited to title insurance premiums
D. Exercise rescission rights based on the leasehold disclosure violation ✓
Answer: D. Failure to disclose leasehold status is a material defect; rescission is the appropriate remedy available to the buyer.
Q 12.7·v3 A buyer relies on representations that the property is owned in fee and later learns it is actually leasehold. The seller failed to provide required disclosures. Which statement is accurate regarding the buyer's legal position?
A. The buyer can force a lease buyout at the seller's cost
B. The buyer may only negotiate a rent reduction with the lessor
C. The buyer has rescission rights due to non-disclosure of leasehold status ✓
D. The buyer must accept the property under the doctrine of caveat emptor
Answer: C. Leasehold disclosure is mandatory in Hawaii; failure to disclose provides the buyer with rescission rights as a statutory remedy.
Q 12.7·v4 Prior to final signing, a buyer learns their property interest is leasehold rather than fee simple—information the seller never disclosed. The buyer's position includes:
A. Liability for the seller's legal costs in defending non-disclosure
B. No recourse unless the lease term is under 20 years
C. The right to rescind the purchase agreement based on leasehold disclosure requirements ✓
D. An obligation to accept the transaction but seek damages later
Answer: C. Non-disclosure of leasehold status is a material violation; the buyer has the statutory right to rescind the transaction.
Q 12.7·v5 A property transaction closes without the buyer being informed of the leasehold nature of the property. The seller omitted this material fact. What legal recourse is available to the buyer?
A. Accept the property with no legal remedies available
B. File a complaint limited to cosmetic defect claims
C. Seek rescission under Hawaii leasehold disclosure requirements ✓
D. Demand immediate fee-simple conversion at seller's expense
Answer: C. Non-disclosure of leasehold status is a material misrepresentation; Hawaii law provides rescission rights to the uninformed buyer.
Q 12.7·v6 During escrow, a licensee fails to reveal that the property operates under a lease rather than fee ownership. Upon discovery after closing, the buyer:
A. Is limited to claiming damages for missing disclosures only
B. Can only pursue damages if the lease term is under 10 years
C. May rescind the transaction based on leasehold non-disclosure ✓
D. Must accept the property as-is with no recourse
Answer: C. Failure to disclose leasehold status constitutes a material omission giving the buyer rescission rights under Hawaii leasehold disclosure law.
Q 12.7·v7 A buyer unknowingly purchases a leasehold property because the seller concealed this essential term. Which of the following best describes the buyer's rights?
A. Rights to sue for breach of warranty of habitability
B. Rights limited to recovering inspection costs only
C. Rescission rights due to material non-disclosure of leasehold status ✓
D. No rights; the buyer should have investigated independently
Answer: C. Material non-disclosure of leasehold creates a duty to remedy; rescission is the primary remedy available to the deceived buyer.
Q 12.7·v8 A seller deliberately omits leasehold information from the property disclosures. The buyer closes unaware and later discovers the truth. The buyer's primary legal remedy is:
A. Forced renegotiation of the lease terms with the lessor
B. Right of rescission under leasehold disclosure statutes ✓
C. Specific performance forcing the seller to obtain fee ownership
D. Damages limited to the cost of title insurance
Answer: B. Intentional or negligent failure to disclose leasehold status enables the buyer to rescind under Hawaii's leasehold disclosure requirements.
Q 12.7·v9 A purchaser enters into a contract expecting to own a property in fee simple, but discovers at closing that the property is actually leasehold and the seller never disclosed this material fact. Which of the following remedies is likely available to the buyer?
A. A claim for specific performance to convert the lease to fee ownership
B. Damages limited to the cost of property inspections
C. The right to cancel the transaction and recover earnest money under leasehold nondisclosure laws ✓
D. Mandatory acceptance of the property with a price reduction negotiated at closing
Answer: C. Failure to disclose leasehold status is a material nondisclosure that triggers rescission rights, allowing the buyer to unwind the transaction and recover their earnest money.
Q 12.8 Hawaii's state-level real estate transfer tax is:
A. HARPTA
B. FIRPTA
C. GET
D. Conveyance tax ✓
Answer: D. Conveyance tax is the transfer tax. Tiered rates.
Q 12.8·v1 When a property changes ownership in Hawaii, which tax applies specifically to the real estate transaction itself?
A. Hawaii Alternative Minimum Tax
B. Federal withholding tax on foreign persons
C. General Excise Tax on the transfer amount
D. Conveyance tax ✓
Answer: D. Conveyance tax is Hawaii's state-level tax on real estate transfers, assessed at tiered rates based on sale price. The other options are different types of taxes that do not apply to property transfers in the same manner.
Q 12.8·v2 A homebuyer in Honolulu purchases a residential property for $750,000. Which Hawaii state tax directly applies to this real estate conveyance?
A. GET on the purchase price
B. Conveyance tax ✓
C. HARPTA tax
D. State capital gains tax
Answer: B. Hawaii imposes a conveyance tax on real estate transfers using a tiered rate structure. GET applies to most transactions but operates differently; HARPTA is a federal withholding requirement; Hawaii has no separate capital gains tax on real estate.
Q 12.8·v3 Which of the following best describes Hawaii's primary transfer tax on real estate transactions?
A. The conveyance tax, imposed on deeds and assessed at progressive rates ✓
B. A documentary stamp tax equivalent to the federal FIRPTA
C. A transactional fee collected by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. An excise tax that replaces all property-related state fees
Answer: A. The conveyance tax is Hawaii's state-level transfer tax on real estate, structured with tiered rates based on the purchase price or value. FIRPTA is federal; the REC does not collect transfer taxes; and Hawaii's conveyance tax operates alongside other fees, not as a replacement.
Q 12.8·v4 A real estate agent assists a client selling land in Maui. The seller must pay a state-mandated tax on the transfer of the real property. What is this tax called?
A. Conveyance tax ✓
B. HARPTA obligation
C. Property transfer surcharge
D. Recording fee tax
Answer: A. Hawaii's conveyance tax is the official state transfer tax on real estate transactions, imposed on the sale and calculated using tiered rates. Recording fees are separate administrative costs; property transfer surcharge and HARPTA are not the correct names for Hawaii's state transfer tax.
Q 12.8·v5 When a property sells in Hawaii, which tax is imposed on the transfer of ownership?
A. Conveyance tax ✓
B. General Excise Tax (GET)
C. Hawaii Real Property Tax Act (HARPTA)
D. Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act (FIRPTA)
Answer: A. Conveyance tax is Hawaii's state-level real estate transfer tax, applied to the deed or instrument transferring property. GET, HARPTA, and FIRPTA are different taxes or acts that do not serve as Hawaii's transfer tax mechanism.
Q 12.8·v6 Which of the following best describes Hawaii's real estate transfer tax?
A. A tiered tax based on the sale price of real property ✓
B. The General Excise Tax imposed on all commercial transactions
C. A federal withholding tax on non-resident sellers
D. FIRPTA compliance requirement for foreign buyers
Answer: A. Hawaii's conveyance tax is applied to real estate transfers with tiered rates based on purchase price. FIRPTA is federal, GET is a general sales tax, and the fourth option describes federal withholding requirements.
Q 12.8·v7 A residential property in Honolulu closes for $800,000. Which state tax specifically applies to this transaction?
A. Hawaii Real Property Tax Act surcharge
B. Conveyance tax ✓
C. Real Estate Commission transfer fee
D. General Excise Tax exclusion
Answer: B. The conveyance tax is the state-level transfer tax on real property sales in Hawaii, calculated based on the sale price. The other options either do not apply to the transfer itself or are not the correct state transfer tax.
Q 12.8·v8 A licensee explains to a buyer that when purchasing property in Hawaii, a certain tax is due based on the property's transfer. This tax is called:
A. Conveyance tax ✓
B. Hawaii transfer withholding tax
C. Property acquisition tax (PAT)
D. Deed recording surcharge
Answer: A. Conveyance tax is Hawaii's designated state transfer tax on real estate transactions. The other options are not actual Hawaii transfer taxes or are misnamed instruments.
Q 12.8·v9 When a property changes ownership in Hawaii, what is the name of the state tax imposed on the transaction?
A. General Excise Tax (GET)
B. HARPTA compliance fee
C. Conveyance tax ✓
D. FIRPTA withholding tax
Answer: C. Conveyance tax is Hawaii's state-level real estate transfer tax applied to property sales. It operates on a tiered rate structure based on the purchase price.
Q 12.9 A property described in chain of title as deriving from a "Land Commission Award" is:
A. A modern grant
B. A condo
C. A relic of the Mahele period requiring careful chain analysis ✓
D. Federal land
Answer: C. Land Commission Awards date from the Mahele era.
Q 12.9·v1 When examining a Hawaii property's deed history, you encounter a reference to a 'Land Commission Award' as the original source of title. What does this indicate about the property?
A. The property originates from the Mahele division and requires thorough historical chain review ✓
B. The property is held in condominium regime under state law
C. The property was recently granted by the Hawaii Land Commission
D. The property was awarded by the federal government during territorial statehood
Answer: A. Land Commission Awards are historical documents from the Mahele era (1848) when Hawaiian lands were divided, making them significant historical anchors requiring careful chain of title analysis.
Q 12.9·v2 A title search reveals that a parcel's origin traces back to a Land Commission Award. Which statement best characterizes this finding?

B. It is a historical grant from Hawaii's Mahele period that necessitates careful examination of the subsequent chain ✓
C. It is a contemporary conveyance that must comply with modern subdivision rules
D. It is evidence the property was part of a corporate condo development
Answer: B. Land Commission Awards are nineteenth-century grants from the Great Mahele (1848) that serve as critical historical reference points and require meticulous chain of title review.
Q 12.9·v3 In Hawaii real estate practice, if you discover that a property's root of title stems from a 'Land Commission Award,' you should understand this as:
A. Proof of direct federal ownership with state management
B. A recent administrative decision by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
C. A time-share interest issued under state condominium law
D. A nineteenth-century claim originating from the Mahele that demands careful historical title analysis ✓
Answer: D. Land Commission Awards date from the Mahele period (1848) when Hawaiian lands were initially divided and distributed, establishing important historical chain-of-title origins requiring expert examination.
Q 12.9·v4 A Hawaii property's title document references an original Land Commission Award. What is the professional implication of this finding?
A. The property must be registered as state-owned trust land
B. The property is automatically exempt from current zoning regulations
C. The property's chain of title requires detailed historical analysis rooted in the Mahele era grants ✓
D. The property was recently subdivided and must meet modern platting standards
Answer: C. Land Commission Awards are historical grants from the 1848 Mahele period that serve as foundational title documents requiring careful and thorough chain of title examination.
Q 12.9·v5 When examining a deed that references a 'Land Commission Award' as the original source of title, a Hawaii real estate licensee should recognize this as:
A. A nineteenth-century Hawaiian Kingdom distribution requiring thorough title investigation ✓
B. A contemporary conveyance method still in use today
C. A U.S. government patent issued under federal homestead law
D. A timeshare or fractional ownership instrument
Answer: A. Land Commission Awards originated during the Mahele period in 1848 and represent a unique aspect of Hawaiian land history requiring careful examination of title records.
Q 12.9·v6 A seller's abstract of title shows the property's lineage beginning with an LCA (Land Commission Award). This historical designation indicates:
A. Title derives from the Hawaiian Kingdom's 1848 division of lands and demands thorough chain-of-title analysis ✓
B. The property was subdivided from a larger modern development
C. The property is held in common ownership by multiple parties

Hawaii: Types of Ownership
State portion6 PSI items25 key concepts10 base questions

Hawaii is condo-heavy and leasehold-rich. The state portion tests these structures more than typical state exams.

Chapter Overview

Condominiums in Hawaii are governed by HRS 514B (the modern Condominium Property Act enacted in 2006) for new and most existing projects, with HRS 514A (the older statute) still applicable to many pre-2006 condos that haven't opted into 514B. Every condo project has a recorded Declaration (the foundational document creating the project), Bylaws (governance procedures), and House Rules (day-to-day rules adoptable and amendable by the board). The Association of Apartment Owners (AOAO) is the governing body — Hawaii's term for what mainland calls the condo HOA. Owners pay maintenance fees ("monthly common element assessments"); the AOAO can place liens on units for unpaid fees, with priority typically following recording rules.

CPRs (Condominium Property Regimes) are a uniquely Hawaiian use of condominium law. A single house lot is carved into two or more "units" (typically two stand-alone houses on one parcel, or a primary + ohana unit) under a CPR declaration. Each unit gets its own TMK and can be sold separately. CPRs let two owners share a parcel without a partition action and without the higher cost of subdivision. They're common in older neighborhoods being incrementally densified, but they create complexity around maintenance allocation and lender willingness to finance.

Leasehold is far more common in Hawaii than in mainland markets. Buyers acquire only the leasehold interest; the underlying land remains owned by the lessor (often a major Hawaiian-history landowner like Kamehameha Schools/Bishop Estate, the State of Hawaii, or other large trusts). Lease terms run 30-75+ years with renegotiation provisions. The most critical agent disclosures: (1) remaining lease term, (2) current lease rent, (3) lease rent renegotiation dates and how new rent is determined (often a percentage of land value), (4) what happens to improvements at lease end (do they revert to the lessor, or is there a buyout). A leaseholder approaching renegotiation faces possible dramatic rent increases — an unprepared buyer may suddenly owe multiples of prior lease rent.

Time share plans are governed by HRS 514E with extensive disclosure requirements. Buyers must receive a public report and have a 7-day right of rescission from contract signing — the buyer may cancel for any reason within seven days and receive a full refund. Hawaii has a separate Time Share Plan Manager license requirement. Aggressive time share marketing is heavily regulated. Resale of time shares is notoriously difficult — secondary market prices are often a tiny fraction of original purchase.

Cooperatives are rare in Hawaii compared to condos. A few exist in Honolulu but the structure (own shares + proprietary lease, financing complications) hasn't taken hold here as it did in New York. Planned Unit Developments (PUDs) exist but are less common than condos because Hawaii's land scarcity and historic plantation patterns favored condo development.

Land trusts exist in Hawaii for various purposes — affordable housing trusts, conservation trusts, family trusts holding ancestral land. The "hui" structure, traditional Hawaiian co-ownership often family-held across many heirs, can lead to partition complications when even one heir wants to sell.

Common-interest community governance: The AOAO board has duties to all owners, must hold annual meetings, must keep records open to owners, and must act consistently with declaration and bylaws. Many disputes arise from board decisions on common-element repairs, special assessments, and house rule enforcement. Hawaii has detailed statutory protections for owners against board overreach.

Buyer due diligence on common-interest property: review the project's budget and reserves, recent meeting minutes, special assessment history, pending litigation, current and projected maintenance fees, rules on rentals (some projects ban short-term, vacation rentals, or pets), and the project's Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac warrantability status (affects financing options). A "non-warrantable" condo is harder to finance because GSE-backed loans are unavailable.

Key Concepts & Definitions
HRS 514BHawaii's modern Condominium Property Act (post-2006). Governs declarations, AOAO, owner rights.
HRS 514AOlder condo act (pre-2006). Some legacy projects still operate under it.
AOAOAssociation of Apartment Owners. The condo HOA equivalent. Manages common elements.
Declaration / Bylaws / House RulesThe three governing documents recorded against the project.
Common elementsProject property shared by all unit owners — lobby, pool, roof, grounds.
Limited common elementsCommon elements assigned to specific units — assigned parking, lanai, storage.
Maintenance feeMonthly common element assessment paid by each unit owner.
Special assessmentOne-time charge for major capital expense not covered by reserves.
Reserve studyEngineering analysis of long-term capital needs. Funded by reserves.
CPRCondominium Property Regime. Uniquely Hawaiian. Two or more units on one lot, each with own TMK.
Leasehold interestTenant's long-term right to occupy land owned by a lessor. Common in Hawaii.
LessorLand owner under a lease. Often a major Hawaiian-history trust.
Lessee / leaseholderHolds the leasehold interest. Pays lease rent. May own improvements.
Fee simpleOutright land ownership. Often distinguished sharply from leasehold here.
Lease rentPeriodic payment from leaseholder to fee-owner.
Lease step-up / renegotiationScheduled date when lease rent is reset upward, often dramatically.
Reversion of improvementsAt lease end, the building/structures may revert to the lessor without payment.
Time shareRight to occupy a unit for set period each year. HRS 514E governs disclosure.
7-day rescission (time share)Buyer's statutory right to cancel a time share contract for any reason within seven days.
Time Share Plan ManagerLicensed individual responsible for time share plan operations.
HuiTraditional Hawaiian co-ownership of land. Often family-held across many heirs. Partition complications.
Warrantable condoProject meeting Fannie/Freddie standards. Eligible for conventional financing.
Non-warrantable condoProject failing Fannie/Freddie standards (excessive rentals, litigation, deferred maintenance, etc.).
CooperativeOwn shares in corporation owning the building + proprietary lease. Rare in Hawaii.
PUDPlanned Unit Development. Lot ownership + common areas. Less common in Hawaii than condo.

Q 13.1 A "CPR" in Hawaii most commonly means:
A. Continuous Property Recording

Q 13.1·v1 In Hawaii real estate terminology, what does the acronym CPR stand for?

Answer: D. CPR stands for Condominium Property Regime and is the Hawaii legal structure enabling individual unit ownership on a shared parcel of land.
Q 13.1·v4 A developer is creating a building with 20 separate residential units on one lot in Hawaii. This type of ownership structure is regulated under which acronym?

Q 13.1·v6 A real estate professional in Hawaii encounters a property described as being under CPR. This most likely refers to:

Q 13.1·v7 When reviewing a Hawaii property listing, an agent sees "CPR" noted in the legal description. The agent should understand this indicates:

Q 13.1·v9 When a Hawaii real estate professional encounters the acronym CPR on property documents, what does it refer to in the context of residential units?

Q 13.2 A buyer acquires a 50-year leasehold condo. They own:

B. The fee + lease
C. Stock in the AOAO
D. The leasehold interest in the unit only ✓
Answer: D. Leasehold = right to occupy. Land remains with lessor.
Q 13.2·v1 When a purchaser closes on a 50-year leasehold condominium unit in Hawaii, what property right is actually conveyed?

B. Equitable title to the land with the lessor retaining legal title

Answer: A. A leasehold conveys only the right to possess and occupy the unit for the lease term; the underlying land and fee simple title remain with the lessor or fee owner.
Q 13.2·v2 A buyer takes title to a leasehold condominium unit. Which of the following best describes their ownership interest?

Q 13.2·v3 In a Hawaii leasehold condominium transaction, the purchaser receives ownership of which of the following?

Answer: A. Leasehold means the buyer obtains only occupancy rights in the unit; the land beneath remains owned by the lessor or fee holder.
Q 13.2·v4 A buyer purchases a 50-year leasehold condominium. What does this buyer NOT own?
A. The underlying fee simple interest in the land ✓
B. An interest in the condominium unit itself

Answer: A. In a leasehold, the buyer does not own the fee or land; they own only a temporary right of occupancy while the lessor retains the underlying fee simple title.
Q 13.2·v5 In Hawaii, when a condominium owner purchases a 50-year leasehold unit, what property interest do they actually own?

Answer: B. Leasehold ownership grants only use and occupancy rights during the lease term; the underlying fee interest in the land remains with the lessor.

Answer: C. Leasehold conveys only the right to occupy for the lease term; the lessor retains ownership of the underlying land and legal title.
Q 13.2·v9 When a condominium buyer takes title to a 50-year leasehold unit in Hawaii, what property right has been transferred to the buyer?

D. Only the right to occupy and use the unit for the lease term ✓

Q 13.5·v1 Which of the following best describes a step-up provision in a commercial lease?

D. Rent amounts will increase at predetermined times during the lease period ✓
Answer: D. Step-up provisions establish scheduled rent increases at defined intervals; they do not affect subletting rights, tenancy type conversion, or tax responsibility allocation.
Q 13.5·v3 A property manager explains that the five-year lease has a step-up component. This means:
A. The tenant receives tax credits for property improvements
B. Rent payments increase at fixed dates as outlined in the lease agreement ✓
C. The tenant has the option to extend the lease by one additional year
D. The landlord may terminate the lease if market rents decline
Answer: B. Step-up refers to scheduled rent increases at specific times in the lease; it does not grant renewal options, termination rights based on market conditions, or tax benefits.
Q 13.5·v4 In Hawaii real estate, a lease with step-up terms typically involves:
A. Sequentially higher rent payments triggered at predetermined lease milestones ✓
B. Rent indexed entirely to the Hawaii median home price index
C. The lessee's right to purchase the fee simple interest
D. An automatic abatement clause if the property is damaged
Answer: A. Step-up provisions establish planned rent increases at set times; they are distinct from purchase options, abatement clauses, or index-based escalations.
Q 13.5·v5 A commercial lease includes a rent step-up provision. What does this term typically describe?
A. The lease automatically converts to a month-to-month tenancy
B. The lessor must maintain and repair all structural elements
C. Rent increases at predetermined intervals, commonly escalating over the lease term ✓
D. The tenant has the right to purchase the underlying property
Answer: C. Rent step-up refers to scheduled rent increases at fixed dates during the lease term, often growing progressively higher.
Q 13.5·v6 Which of the following best defines a step-up rent clause in a lease agreement?
A. A requirement that the tenant improve the leased premises
B. An option for the tenant to extend the lease at the current rent rate
C. A clause allowing the tenant to terminate early without penalty
D. A provision for periodic rent adjustments on specified dates, typically increasing ✓
Answer: D. Step-up rent is a structured rent adjustment mechanism where rental payments increase on predetermined dates throughout the lease period.
Q 13.5·v7 In lease terminology, a step-up structure primarily refers to:
A. The lessee's right to assume the lessor's position in the agreement
B. Physical improvements required to the rental property's entrance
C. An acceleration clause triggered by late payment
D. Scheduled increases in rental payments at designated renewal points ✓
Answer: D. Step-up is a rental escalation mechanism where rent payments increase according to a predetermined schedule, typically at higher amounts.
Q 13.5·v8 A landlord and tenant negotiate a lease with a step-up provision. This means the lease includes:
A. Predetermined rent increases that take effect on specified dates during the tenancy ✓
B. A graduated property tax adjustment passed to the lessee
C. An automatic buyout option favoring the tenant after five years
D. Mandatory tenant-funded capital improvements
Answer: A. A step-up provision establishes a schedule of increasing rent payments at fixed intervals, a common strategy to phase in market-rate adjustments.
Q 13.5·v9 In a commercial lease, a step-up provision typically refers to:
A. The landlord's obligation to maintain and upgrade the property
B. A clause permitting early lease termination without penalty
C. The tenant's right to purchase the underlying fee simple
D. An automatic increase in rental payments at predetermined intervals ✓

Q 13.6 Specific parking stalls assigned to specific units in a condo project are:

B. Fee parcels

D. Limited common elements ✓

B. Personal property of the unit owner

Q 13.6·v2 Which of the following best describes designated parking spaces in a condominium project that serve specific units?
A. Limited common elements restricted to particular units ✓
B. Fixtures that may be removed by the unit owner

Q 13.6·v5 In a Hawaii condominium, a parking space that is designated for use by residents of Unit 405 only would be classified as a:

Hawaii: Property Management
State portion3 PSI items18 key concepts9 base questions

HRS 521 (Residential Landlord-Tenant Code) controls every long-term rental in Hawaii.

Chapter Overview

HRS 521 (the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code) covers most residential rentals in Hawaii — residential premises rented for dwelling purposes. Key tenant protections: a written rental agreement is required for terms over a year (Statute of Frauds), security deposit is capped at one month's rent (with separate allowance for pet deposits), security deposit must be returned within 14 days of move-out with itemized deductions (or full refund), notice for periodic-tenancy termination, and prohibitions against retaliatory eviction.

Specific notice periods to memorize: 5-day notice for non-payment of rent (gives tenant 5 days to pay or vacate), 10-day notice for material breach that's curable (tenant has 10 days to cure or vacate), 28-day notice from tenant to terminate month-to-month (most common tenant exit), 45-day notice from landlord to terminate month-to-month or to raise rent, 5-day notice for landlord termination after non-payment notice expires, longer notices for fixed-term ends without breach.

Eviction (called "summary possession" in Hawaii) requires court order. Self-help eviction — changing locks, removing belongings, cutting utilities, threats to vacate — is illegal and creates statutory damages payable to the tenant (often actual damages plus a multiple plus attorney fees). Landlord must follow the formal process: serve proper notice → file complaint in district court → obtain judgment → engage sheriff for actual removal if tenant doesn't vacate.

Disclosures and required practices: lead-paint disclosure (federal, pre-1978 housing), security-deposit accounting at move-out, written notice of contact information for landlord/agent, written notice of rent increases (45 days for month-to-month). Landlord must maintain habitable premises (HRS 521 includes warranty of habitability), make timely repairs after notice from tenant, and comply with building codes. Tenant has rights including to repair-and-deduct in some situations and to terminate for landlord's material breach of habitability.

A property manager managing rental property for compensation must hold a Hawaii real estate broker license. Salespersons may assist under broker supervision but cannot independently manage. Trust account rules from HRS 467 + HAR Title 16 Chapter 99 apply rigorously to property managers: tenant security deposits must be held in a separate trust account, separate from the broker's operating funds, properly identified, reconciled regularly. Mishandling deposits is one of the top three license-revocation triggers.

Commercial property management (governed by lease contract more than statute) typically follows different rules. HRS 521 generally does not apply to commercial leases. Commercial tenants have less statutory protection and greater contract freedom. PMs handling commercial property should clearly distinguish residential from commercial accounting and disclosure practices.

Vacation rental and short-term rental (STR) regulation is increasingly significant. Each Hawaii county has its own STR rules — Honolulu has some of the strictest, requiring registration, limiting locations, and capping rental terms. Operating an unregistered STR can trigger fines and permit denial. Property managers must verify legal status before listing or managing any vacation rental.

Key Concepts & Definitions
HRS 521Hawaii Residential Landlord-Tenant Code. Governs nearly all residential leases.
Rental agreementRequired in writing for terms over one year (Statute of Frauds).
Security deposit capOne month's rent (separate pet deposit allowed for some pets).
Deposit return14 days after move-out, with itemized deductions or full return.
Summary possessionHawaii's formal eviction process. Court-supervised. Self-help eviction is illegal.
Self-help evictionChanging locks, removing belongings, cutting utilities. Illegal under HRS 521.
Retaliatory evictionEviction in response to tenant's lawful action. Illegal under HRS 521.
5-day noticeNon-payment of rent. Tenant has 5 days to pay or vacate.
10-day noticeMaterial breach (curable). Tenant has 10 days to cure or vacate.
28-day noticeStandard tenant termination of periodic tenancy.
45-day noticeLandlord termination of periodic tenancy or rent increase.
Warranty of habitabilityImplied warranty that premises are fit for human habitation.
Repair and deductTenant remedy in some circumstances when landlord fails to repair.
Trust account (PM)Tenant deposits held separately from broker funds. HRS 467 + admin rules apply.
Property management licenseCompensated PM management requires Hawaii broker license.
Short-term rental (STR)Rentals under set duration (varies by county). Heavy regulation.
Vacation rentalSpecific license/permit required in many Hawaii counties.
Commercial leaseGenerally outside HRS 521. Governed by lease contract.

Q 14.1 A landlord must return the security deposit within how many days of move-out?
A. 14 ✓

Q 14.1·v1 Under Hawaii Revised Statutes, if a tenant vacates a rental unit, the property owner is required to refund any security deposit by what deadline?
A. Within 10 days if the tenant provides a forwarding address
B. Within 21 days, unless written notice is provided
C. Within 14 days, with an itemized accounting of any deductions ✓
D. Within 30 days, regardless of any damages claimed
Answer: C. HRS 521-44 requires landlords to return security deposits within 14 days of move-out, and if deductions are made, an itemized statement must accompany the return.
Q 14.1·v2 A tenant has just moved out of a residential lease in Hawaii. The landlord is holding the security deposit and plans to make deductions for cleaning and minor repairs. What is the maximum timeframe for the landlord to return the remaining balance?
A. 30 days from the date the unit is inspected
B. 60 days if repairs exceed $500
C. 45 days from the date the unit is re-rented
D. 14 days from move-out, along with a detailed list of deductions ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law mandates a 14-day return period for security deposits measured from the tenant's move-out date, and any deductions must be itemized and documented.
Q 14.1·v3 When must a Hawaii landlord deliver the security deposit refund to a former tenant after the tenant has vacated the premises?
A. Within 21 days if the tenant has not provided a forwarding address
B. Immediately upon move-out if no damages are claimed
C. Within 14 days, with written justification for any amounts withheld ✓
D. Within 60 days or within 30 days of lease termination, whichever is longer
Answer: C. HRS 521 establishes a 14-day deadline for security deposit return from move-out, and landlords must provide written itemization if any deductions are made.
Q 14.1·v4 A property manager in Hawaii is processing security deposit returns for three units that were vacated this month. What is the statutory timeframe for returning these deposits to comply with state law?
A. Within one month if the property manager is coordinating repairs
B. 14 calendar days from the tenant's move-out date, with itemized deductions if applicable ✓
C. 7 business days from when the landlord approves the move-out inspection
D. 30 days from the date the lease officially terminates
Answer: B. HRS 521-44 specifies that security deposits must be returned within 14 calendar days of move-out, and any deductions must be itemized and provided to the tenant.
Q 14.1·v5 Under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 521, what is the maximum timeframe a property owner has to refund a tenant's security deposit following the tenant's vacating the rental unit?
A. Within 21 days, with written notice of any deductions
B. Within 45 days, provided the landlord submits a formal inspection report
C. Within 14 days, with an itemized accounting of deductions if applicable ✓
D. Within 30 days, regardless of whether deductions are claimed
Answer: C. HRS 521-44 requires landlords to return security deposits within 14 days of move-out, and if deductions are made, they must provide an itemized statement of those deductions.
Q 14.1·v6 A tenant in Honolulu moves out of an apartment on the first of the month. By what date must the landlord return the full security deposit or provide a detailed accounting of deductions?
A. By the 8th of the same month
B. By the 15th of the same month ✓
C. By the end of the following month
D. By the 21st of the same month
Answer: B. Hawaii law (HRS 521) establishes a 14-day deadline from move-out for return of security deposits; if the deposit cannot be fully returned, the landlord must provide an itemized breakdown of deductions within this period.
Q 14.1·v7 If a Hawaii rental property manager receives a move-out notice from a tenant, what is the statutory deadline for either returning the security deposit in full or submitting written documentation of any claimed deductions?
A. Two weeks from the date of move-out ✓
B. One full month from the lease termination date
C. Within 30 calendar days, with optional supplemental notice
D. 10 business days after the tenant vacates
Answer: A. HRS 521-44 mandates that landlords return security deposits within 14 days (two weeks) of move-out; any deductions must be itemized and documented within this same 14-day window.
Q 14.1·v8 A landlord in Hawaii intends to make deductions from a tenant's security deposit for damages. What is the deadline for returning the remaining balance and providing the tenant with an itemized list of deductions?
A. 7 days from move-out
B. 45 days from move-out, pending inspection completion
C. 60 days from move-out, pending insurance claim resolution
D. 14 days from move-out ✓
Answer: D. Under HRS 521, landlords must return the security deposit (or remaining balance after itemized deductions) and provide written documentation of any deductions within 14 days of the tenant's move-out date.
Q 14.1·v9 Under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 521, if a tenant vacates a rental unit, by what deadline must the landlord deliver the security deposit refund or provide a written accounting of deductions?
A. Within 10 business days of the move-out date
B. Within 21 days of the move-out date
C. Within 14 days of the move-out date ✓
D. Within 30 days of the move-out date
Answer: C. HRS 521-44 requires landlords to return the security deposit within 14 days, or provide an itemized statement of any lawful deductions within that timeframe.
Q 14.2 The maximum security deposit allowed in Hawaii is:
A. ½ month's rent
B. 3 months' rent
C. 2 months' rent
D. 1 month's rent ✓
Answer: D. Capped at one month's rent (separate pet deposit allowed).
Q 14.2·v1 Under Hawaii rental law, what is the legal ceiling for a landlord to collect as a security deposit from a tenant?
A. Whatever amount the lease agreement specifies
B. No more than one month's rent ✓
C. Up to two months' rent plus a pet fee
D. Up to 45 days' rent
Answer: B. Hawaii law caps security deposits at one month's rent, with pet deposits treated separately from this limit.
Q 14.2·v2 A landlord in Honolulu is preparing a lease and wants to know the maximum security deposit permissible. What amount should the rental agreement reflect?
A. 1 month's rent as the statutory maximum ✓
B. 2 months' rent if the unit is furnished
C. ½ month's rent plus an additional damage deposit
D. 3 months' rent to cover potential damages
Answer: A. Hawaii's statutory limit for security deposits is one month's rent regardless of furnishings or property condition.
Q 14.2·v3 If a Hawaii rental property has an annual rent of $24,000, what is the maximum security deposit a landlord may lawfully retain at lease signing?
A. $6,000
B. $2,000 ✓
C. $4,000
D. $2,500
Answer: B. One month's rent is the legal maximum; $24,000 ÷ 12 months = $2,000 maximum security deposit allowed.
Q 14.2·v4 Which statement correctly describes Hawaii's security deposit regulations for residential leases?
A. The security deposit limit is one month's rent, though pet deposits can be collected separately ✓
B. Security deposits are unlimited if specified in a written lease agreement
C. Security deposits may equal up to 3 months' rent in high-value properties
D. Landlords may collect 1.5 months' rent as a standard security deposit
Answer: A. Hawaii law strictly limits security deposits to one month's rent, with pet deposits as a separate permissible charge.
Q 14.2·v5 Under Hawaii rental law, what is the legal limit on the initial security deposit a landlord may collect from a tenant?
A. Not to exceed one month's rent ✓
B. Whatever amount the lease agreement specifies
C. Two months' rent if the unit is furnished
D. Up to 60 days' rent plus a pet fee
Answer: A. Hawaii law caps security deposits at one month's rent; any additional deposits for pets must be handled separately and are not counted toward this limit.
Q 14.2·v6 A property manager in Hawaii is preparing a lease for a residential rental unit. How much can the landlord legally require as a security deposit at move-in?
A. Two months' rent for a multi-year lease
B. One month's rent maximum ✓
C. Three months' rent if the property is in a high-demand area
D. Half a month's rent plus a damage reserve
Answer: B. Hawaii REC regulations limit security deposits to one month's rent regardless of location, lease term, or market conditions.
Q 14.2·v7 When a tenant applies for a rental property in Hawaii, the landlord may collect a security deposit not to exceed:
A. One month of rent plus an additional pet deposit fee
B. Two full months of rent
C. 45 days of monthly rent
D. One full month of rent ✓
Answer: D. The statutory cap is one month's rent; pet deposits are separate and allowed in addition, but the base security deposit is limited to one month.
Q 14.2·v8 Which statement correctly describes Hawaii's security deposit requirements for residential leases?
A. Deposits can total up to three months' rent when combined with all optional fees
B. The maximum deposit is limited to one month's rent ✓
C. Hawaii allows unlimited deposits if documented in writing by both parties
D. Deposits may be increased to two months' rent if the property has a pool or ocean view
Answer: B. Hawaii law strictly caps the security deposit at one month's rent; other terms or conditions cannot override this statutory maximum.
Q 14.2·v9 Under Hawaii residential tenancy law, what is the statutory limit a landlord may collect as a security deposit from a tenant at lease signing?
A. Two months' rent if the property is furnished
B. Up to 60 days' rent plus a pet deposit
C. Not to exceed one month's rent, with pet deposits handled separately ✓
D. A maximum of 45 days' rent regardless of lease duration
Answer: C. Hawaii law caps residential security deposits at one month's rent; any pet deposit is a separate, additional charge and does not count toward this limit.
Q 14.3 Self-help eviction (changing locks) is:
A. Allowed in Hawaii
B. Allowed after 5-day notice
C. Allowed only for non-payment
D. Illegal — must use summary possession ✓
Answer: D. Court order required; self-help is illegal.
Q 14.3·v1 A property manager in Honolulu wants to remove a tenant for lease violation. Which action is prohibited under Hawaii law?
A. Obtaining a court order before lock-out
B. Providing proper notice before eviction proceedings
C. Filing for summary possession in District Court
D. Changing the locks without judicial process ✓
Answer: D. Self-help eviction via lock-out is illegal in Hawaii; landlords must obtain a court order through formal summary possession proceedings.
Q 14.3·v2 A landlord discovers a tenant has abandoned the property. The landlord considers changing the locks immediately. Is this permitted in Hawaii?
A. Yes, if the rent is 30 days past due
B. No, a court order must be obtained first ✓
C. Yes, if the property appears vacant
D. Yes, after written notice only
Answer: B. Hawaii law prohibits self-help eviction; landlords must pursue judicial eviction through summary possession regardless of circumstances.
Q 14.3·v3 Which of the following best describes the legal requirement for removing a tenant from a residential property in Hawaii?
A. Lock-out is permitted for serious breaches
B. Landlord may use self-help remedies after reasonable notice
C. Verbal notice followed by immediate removal is acceptable
D. Summary possession action in court is mandatory ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii requires landlords to use the judicial process of summary possession; self-help eviction methods are strictly prohibited.
Q 14.3·v4 A tenant stops paying rent. The landlord decides to remove the tenant's belongings and change the locks to regain possession. Under Hawaii law, this is:
A. Lawful if documented in writing
B. Permitted only after 10 days of non-payment
C. Acceptable when combined with proper notice
D. Illegal and subjects the landlord to liability ✓
Answer: D. Self-help eviction through lock-out or removal of belongings is illegal in Hawaii; the landlord must obtain a court order through summary possession.
Q 14.3·v5 A landlord in Hawaii wants to remove a tenant immediately by installing new locks and changing the door codes. What is the legal status of this action?
A. Permitted if the landlord provides written notice 24 hours in advance
B. Valid as long as the landlord compensates the tenant for inconvenience
C. Allowed only when the tenant has violated lease terms
D. Prohibited; the landlord must obtain a court order through summary possession proceedings ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law prohibits self-help eviction; landlords must follow judicial eviction procedures and obtain a court order for summary possession to legally remove a tenant.
Q 14.3·v6 Which statement correctly describes Hawaii's position on landlords using self-help remedies such as removing a tenant's belongings or locking them out?
A. Self-help remedies are permitted without court involvement in cases of lease violations
B. Self-help eviction methods are illegal; formal summary possession through the courts is required ✓
C. Self-help is legal if conducted during business hours
D. Self-help is allowed if the tenant is more than 30 days behind on rent
Answer: B. Hawaii law strictly prohibits self-help eviction and requires landlords to pursue the formal summary possession judicial process to legally evict a tenant.
Q 14.3·v7 A landlord in Honolulu changes the locks on a rental unit to force out a non-paying tenant. Is this action lawful in Hawaii?
A. Yes, if the landlord has given the tenant a 3-day notice to vacate
B. Yes, provided the landlord files for eviction within 10 days of the lock change
C. No; this is an illegal self-help eviction and violates Hawaii landlord-tenant law ✓
D. Yes, because non-payment of rent justifies immediate self-help removal
Answer: C. Changing locks without a court order is illegal self-help eviction in Hawaii; landlords must use the legal summary possession process through the courts regardless of the reason for eviction.
Q 14.3·v8 Under Hawaii real estate law, can a property manager lawfully exclude a tenant by removing locks and personal property without going to court?
A. Yes, after providing a 5-day cure period
B. Yes, in cases where the lease contains a self-help eviction clause
C. No; summary possession through judicial proceedings is the only legal eviction method in Hawaii ✓
D. Yes, if the property manager acts on behalf of the owner
Answer: C. Hawaii law prohibits all forms of self-help eviction, including by property managers; courts must order the eviction through summary possession proceedings.
Q 14.3·v9 A Hawaii property manager discovers a tenant has abandoned the rental unit. The manager changes the locks and removes the tenant's belongings to regain possession. This action is:
A. Permissible under Hawaii's self-help remedy doctrine
B. A violation of law requiring court-ordered summary possession instead ✓
C. Allowed as long as written notice was provided beforehand
D. Valid only if the tenant owes rent
Answer: B. Hawaii law prohibits self-help eviction regardless of circumstances; landlords must obtain a court judgment through summary possession proceedings to lawfully regain possession.
Q 14.4 For a month-to-month rent increase, landlord must give:
A. 60 days notice
B. 45 days notice ✓
C. 14 days notice
D. 28 days notice
Answer: B. 45 days advance written notice required.
Q 14.4·v1 A landlord in Hawaii intends to increase rent on a month-to-month tenancy. What is the minimum notice period required before the increase takes effect?
A. 90 days written notice
B. 30 days written notice
C. 60 days written notice
D. 45 days written notice ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires 45 days advance written notice for rent increases on month-to-month leases.
Q 14.4·v2 If a property manager needs to raise rent on a periodic tenancy (month-to-month), how much advance notice must be provided?
A. 45 days in writing ✓
B. 14 days in writing
C. 21 days in writing
D. 60 days orally or in writing
Answer: A. Month-to-month tenancies in Hawaii require 45 days advance written notice before a rent increase becomes effective.
Q 14.4·v3 A landlord wants to implement a rent increase on a month-to-month lease. What notice requirement applies?
A. Written notice 7 days before the next rental period
B. Oral notification 30 days prior
C. Written notice 28 days before the effective date
D. Written notice 45 days before the increase takes effect ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii requires 45 days advance written notice for any rent increase on month-to-month rental agreements.
Q 14.4·v4 Under Hawaii real estate law, when a landlord modifies the rental rate for a month-to-month tenancy, the notice requirement is:
A. 3 weeks advance written notice
B. 1 month oral notice followed by written confirmation
C. 2 weeks written notice before the next rent due date
D. 45 days advance written notice ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law mandates 45 days advance written notice as the minimum period for rent increases on month-to-month leases.
Q 14.4·v5 Under Hawaii law, how much advance notice must a landlord provide before implementing a rent increase on a month-to-month tenancy?
A. 21 days written notice
B. 30 days written notice
C. 60 days written notice
D. 45 days written notice ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires 45 days advance written notice for any rent increase on a month-to-month lease agreement.
Q 14.4·v6 A landlord in Hawaii wants to raise rent on a tenant with a month-to-month agreement. What notice period applies?
A. 90 calendar days
B. 10 business days
C. 45 calendar days ✓
D. 30 calendar days
Answer: C. 45 days advance written notice is the statutory requirement for rent increases on month-to-month tenancies in Hawaii.
Q 14.4·v7 Which notice requirement applies when a landlord seeks to increase monthly rent on a periodic tenancy in Hawaii?
A. 14 days verbal notice allowed
B. 60 days notice with 30-day cure period
C. 45 days written notice required ✓
D. 30 days notice to vacate required
Answer: C. Hawaii landlord-tenant law mandates 45 days advance written notice before any rent increase takes effect on a month-to-month lease.
Q 14.4·v8 A property manager represents a landlord with a month-to-month tenant. Before notifying the tenant of a rent increase, how far in advance must written notice be delivered?
A. At least 28 days before the increase effective date
B. At least 45 days before the increase effective date ✓
C. At least 14 days before the increase effective date
D. At least 60 days before the increase effective date
Answer: B. 45 days advance written notice is required by Hawaii law before a rent increase on a month-to-month tenancy can become effective.
Q 14.4·v9 A landlord in Hawaii wishes to modify the rental rate on a month-to-month tenancy. What advance notice period must be provided to the tenant in writing?
A. 45 days prior to the effective date ✓
B. 30 days prior to the effective date
C. 60 days prior to the effective date
D. 21 days prior to the effective date
Answer: A. Hawaii law requires 45 days advance written notice for any rent increase on a month-to-month lease. This longer notice period protects tenants from sudden rent changes.
Q 14.5 Hawaii's formal eviction process is called:
A. Suit for ejectment
B. Summary possession ✓
C. Forcible detainer
D. Quiet title
Answer: B. Hawaii term is "summary possession."
Q 14.5·v1 When a Hawaii landlord needs to remove a tenant through the courts, the legal proceeding is formally known as:
A. Eviction in ejectment
B. Distress for rent
C. Forcible detainer action
D. Summary possession ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's statutory term for the formal court process to remove a tenant is 'summary possession,' not the terms used in other jurisdictions.
Q 14.5·v2 Which of the following is the correct Hawaii legal terminology for a formal landlord-initiated removal action against a tenant?
A. Forcible detainer
B. Summary possession ✓
C. Replevin proceeding
D. Suit for ejectment
Answer: B. Hawaii law specifically uses the term 'summary possession' to describe the formal eviction process, distinguishing it from mainland jurisdictions that use other terminology.
Q 14.5·v3 A landlord in Hawaii who seeks court authorization to remove a non-paying tenant would file a:
A. Forcible detainer complaint
B. Quiet title action
C. Summary possession action ✓
D. Partition suit
Answer: C. 'Summary possession' is Hawaii's official court procedure for evicting a tenant, regardless of the cause (non-payment, lease violation, holdover, etc.).
Q 14.5·v4 Under Hawaii law, the proper judicial remedy available to a property owner to regain possession of property from an occupant is called:
A. Suit for ejectment
B. Summary possession ✓
C. Action for unlawful detainer
D. Forcible detainer
Answer: B. Hawaii uses the specific statutory term 'summary possession' for its formal eviction process, which is the state's designated procedure under Hawaii Revised Statutes.
Q 14.5·v5 Under Hawaii law, when a landlord seeks to remove a tenant through the court system, the legal action is known as:
A. Summary possession ✓
B. Forcible detainer
C. Unlawful detainer action
D. Suit for ejectment
Answer: A. Hawaii's statutory eviction procedure is termed "summary possession," which is the formal court process for removing a tenant from rental property.
Q 14.5·v6 A Hawaii property owner who needs judicial relief to recover possession of a rental unit from a non-paying tenant would file an action for:
A. Declaratory judgment
B. Quiet title action
C. Forcible detainer
D. Summary possession ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii uses the term "summary possession" to describe the statutory eviction remedy available to landlords seeking court-ordered removal of tenants.
Q 14.5·v7 Which of the following correctly identifies Hawaii's primary statutory mechanism for evicting a tenant through the courts?
A. Suit for ejectment
B. Forcible detainer
C. Replevin action
D. Summary possession ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's formal eviction procedure is called "summary possession," which is the established legal term used in Hawaii eviction statutes and court practice.
Q 14.5·v8 A landlord in Hawaii who wishes to initiate a court-ordered eviction of a defaulting tenant would pursue what type of legal action?
A. Unlawful detainer
B. Summary possession ✓
C. Forcible detainer
D. Suit for specific performance
Answer: B. "Summary possession" is Hawaii's specific legal term for the formal eviction proceeding that allows a landlord to recover rental property through judicial action.
Q 14.5·v9 Which of the following legal actions is the proper Hawaii term for initiating a landlord's formal court proceeding to remove a tenant?
A. Unlawful detainer action
B. Suit for ejectment
C. Summary possession ✓
D. Forcible detainer
Answer: C. Hawaii uses the term "summary possession" as the formal eviction procedure under Hawaii law, rather than the terms used in other states.
Q 14.6 A tenant must give what notice to terminate month-to-month?
A. 7 days
B. 45 days
C. 28 days ✓
D. 14 days
Answer: C. 28-day tenant notice for month-to-month termination.
Q 14.6·v1 Under Hawaii law, how many days advance notice must a month-to-month tenant provide before ending their tenancy?
A. 14 days prior to the end of any rental period
B. 28 days prior to the end of any rental period ✓
C. 21 days prior to the end of any rental period
D. 30 days prior to the end of any rental period
Answer: B. Hawaii requires a month-to-month tenant to provide 28 days' written notice before the end of any rental period to lawfully terminate the lease.
Q 14.6·v2 If a residential tenant on a month-to-month lease wishes to vacate the property, what is the minimum notice period required by Hawaii law?
A. 60 days from the date of written notice
B. Two weeks before lease expiration
C. Four weeks before the end of the current rental month ✓
D. 10 days before the first of the month
Answer: C. A month-to-month tenant in Hawaii must give 28 days' notice (four weeks) before the end of the current rental period to properly terminate the tenancy.
Q 14.6·v3 A property manager receives written notice from a month-to-month tenant on the 5th of the month. If the tenant complies with Hawaii notice requirements, what is the earliest the tenancy can lawfully end?
A. The last day of the current month
B. The last day of the following month ✓
C. 14 days from the date of notice
D. 45 days from the date of notice
Answer: B. Since Hawaii requires 28 days' notice before the end of any rental period, notice given on the 5th of one month allows termination at the end of the following month (more than 28 days later).
Q 14.6·v4 Which statement correctly describes the notice requirement for a tenant seeking to terminate a month-to-month tenancy in Hawaii?
A. The tenant must provide at least two weeks' notice, which may be given at any time during the month
B. The tenant must provide notice 45 days before the intended move-out date
C. The tenant may terminate immediately upon oral notice to the landlord
D. The tenant must provide at least 28 days' notice before the end of the rental period ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law mandates that a month-to-month tenant provide written notice of at least 28 days before the end of any rental period to effect a lawful termination.
Q 14.6·v5 Under Hawaii law, how much advance notice must a month-to-month tenant provide to the landlord when ending the tenancy?
A. 14 days prior to the end of the rental period
B. 21 days prior to the end of the rental period
C. 28 days prior to the end of the rental period ✓
D. 30 days prior to the end of the rental period
Answer: C. Hawaii law requires a month-to-month tenant to provide 28 days' written notice to terminate the lease, which must be given prior to the end of the rental period.
Q 14.6·v6 A landlord receives notice from a month-to-month tenant on the 1st of the month requesting to vacate. What is the minimum notice period the tenant must provide?
A. The tenant must vacate by the 15th of that month
B. The tenant must vacate by the 29th of that month ✓
C. The tenant must vacate by the last day of the following month
D. The tenant must vacate within 14 days of notice
Answer: B. A month-to-month tenant must give at least 28 days’ written notice (HRS §521-71(a)). Notice on the 1st permits termination about the 29th of the same month.
Q 14.6·v7 Which statement accurately describes the notice requirement for terminating a month-to-month residential lease in Hawaii?
A. The tenant must provide at least 28 days' written notice ✓
B. A verbal notice of 30 days is sufficient for termination
C. The tenant may terminate immediately if 14 days' written notice is given
D. Either party may terminate with 7 days' written notice
Answer: A. Hawaii law mandates that a month-to-month tenant provide at least 28 days' written notice before the tenancy will terminate.
Q 14.6·v8 A property manager in Hawaii is managing a month-to-month rental property. A tenant submits written notice on June 1st to end the tenancy. Assuming no special lease provisions, when is the earliest date the tenant's occupancy will terminate?
A. June 29 ✓
B. July 1
C. June 30
D. June 14
Answer: A. A month-to-month tenant must give at least 28 days’ notice (HRS §521-71(a)). Notice given June 1 permits the earliest termination on June 29 (June 1 + 28 days).
Q 14.6·v9 Under Hawaii law, how many days' written notice must a month-to-month tenant provide to their landlord to end the tenancy?
A. 14 days before the end of the rental period
B. 21 days before the end of the rental period
C. 28 days before the end of the rental period ✓
D. 30 days before the end of the rental period
Answer: C. Hawaii law requires a month-to-month tenant to provide 28 days' written notice to terminate the lease; this is the statutory requirement for tenancy termination in month-to-month agreements.
Q 14.7 Compensated property management requires:
A. A broker license ✓
B. A general business license only
C. No license
D. A salesperson license only
Answer: A. Property management for compensation requires a broker license in Hawaii.
Q 14.7·v1 A real estate professional who manages rental properties for a fee in Hawaii must hold what type of license?
A. A salesperson license with broker supervision
B. A property management certificate
C. A broker license ✓
D. A general contractor license
Answer: C. Property management for compensation requires a broker license in Hawaii; a salesperson license is insufficient and no certificate alone qualifies.
Q 14.7·v2 Which licensing requirement applies to an individual who receives payment to manage residential rental units?
A. Broker license only ✓
B. Real estate transaction coordinator certification
C. A notary public endorsement
D. Salesperson license under a broker
Answer: A. Hawaii law requires a broker license to perform property management services for compensation; salesperson licenses do not authorize independent property management.
Q 14.7·v3 An individual acting as a paid property manager in Hawaii is required to possess:
A. A real estate sales license only
B. A business tax permit
C. A broker license ✓
D. A condominium management license
Answer: C. Compensated property management in Hawaii requires a broker license; other credentials like sales licenses or business permits do not satisfy the statutory requirement.
Q 14.7·v4 To legally charge fees for managing another person's real property in Hawaii, a licensee must have:
A. A broker license ✓
B. An affiliation with a property management association
C. A salesperson license issued by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
D. A trust account authorization only
Answer: A. Property management for compensation is a broker function in Hawaii and cannot be performed under a salesperson license or through association affiliation alone.
Q 14.7·v5 A real estate professional accepts a fee to manage rental properties on behalf of an owner. What licensing requirement must be satisfied?
A. A salesperson license with property management endorsement
B. No real estate license if the manager is an employee of the owner
C. Registration with the Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs only
D. A broker license ✓
Answer: D. Property management services provided for compensation require a broker license under Hawaii real estate law, regardless of employment status or other registrations.
Q 14.7·v6 Which licensing credential is mandatory for an individual who charges fees to oversee tenant relations, collect rents, and maintain rental properties?
A. Salesperson license
B. Broker license ✓
C. Business tax license only
D. Property manager certificate from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
Answer: B. In Hawaii, any person receiving compensation for property management must hold a broker license; a salesperson license or business tax license alone is insufficient.
Q 14.7·v7 A property owner hires a professional to handle leasing, maintenance coordination, and rent collection for multiple residential units in exchange for a monthly management fee. What is required?
A. No real estate license if the owner provides written authorization
B. A broker license ✓
C. An escrow account license
D. A general real estate salesperson license
Answer: B. Property management for compensation in Hawaii requires a broker license; written owner authorization does not exempt the manager from licensing requirements.
Q 14.7·v8 Under Hawaii real estate law, if a property manager receives compensation for managing residential or commercial properties, which licensing requirement applies?
A. Broker license only ✓
B. Salesperson license only
C. Either a broker or salesperson license at the manager's discretion
D. No real estate license is required if the manager is bonded
Answer: A. Hawaii REC regulations mandate that paid property managers must hold a broker license; a salesperson license or bonding does not satisfy this requirement.
Q 14.7·v9 A property manager in Hawaii who receives a fee for managing rental properties on behalf of an owner must hold which type of license?
A. Only a general business permit from the city
B. A salesperson license with property management endorsement
C. No real estate license if bonded and insured
D. A broker license ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law requires a broker license to engage in property management for compensation; a salesperson license is insufficient, and general business permits do not satisfy real estate licensing requirements.
Q 14.8 A 10-day notice is for:
A. Annual inspection
B. Lease end
C. Non-payment of rent ✓
D. Routine maintenance
Answer: C. 10-day = non-payment of rent.
Q 14.8·v1 Under Hawaii residential tenancy law, when a landlord issues a 10-day notice to the tenant, what breach is being addressed?
A. Violation of lease terms regarding occupancy limits
B. Unauthorized alterations to the rental unit
C. Failure to pay rent when due ✓
D. Failure to maintain the premises in habitable condition
Answer: C. A 10-day notice in Hawaii is specifically for non-payment of rent, giving the tenant 10 days to cure or vacate before eviction proceedings begin.
Q 14.8·v2 A landlord in Hawaii provides written notice giving a tenant 10 days to remedy the situation or face lease termination. Which tenant default triggered this notice?
A. Late submission of a lease renewal application
B. Request for a lease modification
C. Complaint about unit temperature control

Hawaii: Land Utilization
State portion2 PSI items19 key concepts6 base questions

Hawaii has a unique two-tier land-use system: state district + county zoning.

Chapter Overview

The State Land Use Commission (LUC) classifies all Hawaii land into four districts: Urban, Rural, Agricultural, and Conservation. This is the primary classification — county zoning operates within state districts. Urban district allows the highest density development; Conservation is the most restrictive. Boundary changes require petition to LUC, public hearings, and substantial justification.

Conservation district is the most heavily restricted, with development requiring a Conservation District Use Permit (CDUP) from the Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR). Most ordinary residential or commercial development is forbidden in Conservation. Forest reserves, mountain wilderness, watershed areas typically fall here. Reclassification to allow development is rare and politically contested.

Agricultural district covers the largest land area in Hawaii (former plantation lands, ranches, etc.). Residential development on Ag is permitted but with significant restrictions: typically one dwelling per minimum lot area (varies by county), use must be agriculturally compatible, often a "farm dwelling" requirement requiring genuine agricultural activity. Buyers of "ag" homes should verify they aren't living in violation of agricultural-use requirements.

County zoning is the second tier. Each of Hawaii's four counties (Honolulu/Oahu, Hawaii/Big Island, Maui, Kauai) has its own zoning ordinance. Honolulu uses the Land Use Ordinance (LUO). Each county has standard residential, commercial, industrial, mixed-use, and special districts, with detailed standards on density, setbacks, height, parking, lot coverage. Variances and special permits are issued by county boards.

Special Management Areas (SMAs) are coastal-zone areas where development is heavily regulated under the Coastal Zone Management Act (CZMA). Any "development" within an SMA — broadly defined to include construction, demolition, grading, change of use, even some additions — requires an SMA permit from the county planning department. The line between minor and major SMA permits depends on scale and impact. SMAs typically extend roughly to the 350-foot setback from the high tide line, but boundaries vary.

Restrictive covenants (CC&Rs) and HOA rules layer on top of county zoning. Many older neighborhoods (especially planned developments from the 1970s-90s) have strict architectural rules, paint colors, fence heights, and landscaping requirements. Race-restrictive covenants from earlier eras are unenforceable but often still appear in title chains — Hawaii recognizes them as void but agents should know the issue.

Subdivision in Hawaii follows county subdivision ordinances. Major subdivisions require formal platting, infrastructure dedication, environmental review, often public hearings. Minor subdivisions and consolidations are simpler. CPR can sometimes accomplish similar densification goals without formal subdivision.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Land Use Commission (LUC)State body that classifies all land into four districts.
State land-use districtsUrban, Rural, Agricultural, Conservation.
Urban districtHighest-density development. Most cities and towns.
Rural districtLower density, residential + light agricultural mix.
Agricultural districtLargest land area. Ag-compatible uses; residential restrictions.
Conservation districtMost restrictive. CDUP required for development. Mountain, forest, watershed.
CDUPConservation District Use Permit. Required for development in Conservation district.
County zoningSecond tier within state districts. Each of 4 counties has own ordinance.
Land Use Ordinance (LUO)Honolulu (Oahu) county zoning code.
Special Management Area (SMA)Coastal-zone heavy regulation. Permits required for most development.
SMA permitCoastal development permit. Major or minor depending on scale.
CZMACoastal Zone Management Act. Federal/state coastal regulation framework.
Lava zonesHawaii County 1-9 hazard rating. Disclose; affects insurance.
Tsunami evacuation zoneCoastal disclosure required where applicable.
Flood zoneFEMA zone affecting insurance + development.
VarianceCounty-level exception to zoning for unique hardship.
Special use permitCounty-level permission for use allowed under conditions.
SubdivisionDivision of land into lots. Major and minor procedures.
Farm dwelling requirementSome Ag-district dwellings require genuine agricultural activity.

Hawaii: Title & Conveyances
State portion4 PSI items17 key concepts7 base questions

Two title systems, leasehold dominance, and unique Hawaiian estates.

Chapter Overview

Title in Hawaii lives in two systems. Regular System uses the Bureau of Conveyances chain-of-title model — recording protects subsequent purchasers, chain is searched back to a marketable starting point, and clouds are resolved through ordinary title actions. Land Court uses the Torrens model: a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) is conclusive against the world. Once a parcel is registered in Land Court, ownership cannot be challenged outside the registration system except in narrow statutory exceptions. Most older Hawaii title work involves checking which system the parcel is in.

Tenancies in Hawaii follow standard categories with some local nuances. Tenancy in common — separate, inheritable, often unequal shares; default form when intent is unclear. Joint tenancy with right of survivorship — must use the express language "as joint tenants with right of survivorship" or substantially equivalent words; survivorship eliminates probate of that interest. Tenancy by the entirety — only available to married couples (and same-sex married couples), with both survivorship and protection from individual-spouse creditors on the marital home.

Liens in Hawaii: real property tax liens take priority over almost everything except prior recorded mortgages on Land Court parcels (Land Court rules differ slightly). Mechanic's liens (HRS 507) protect contractors, suppliers, architects, and design professionals for unpaid work or materials — must be filed within statutory time limits. AOAO liens for unpaid maintenance fees in condos take their priority based on recording. State and federal tax liens follow recording priority within their classes. Judgment liens attach when a judgment is recorded.

Foreclosure in Hawaii has two paths. Judicial foreclosure is court-supervised: lender files complaint, court issues judgment, property sold at court-confirmed auction. Slower (often 12-18 months) but with more borrower protections. Non-judicial (power-of-sale) foreclosure — used when the security instrument contains a power-of-sale clause — is faster, governed by the Mortgage Foreclosure Act's notice and auction procedures (HRS 667). Hawaii also has alternate Mortgage Foreclosure Dispute Resolution (MFDR) for owner-occupied homes, requiring the lender to engage in dispute resolution before non-judicial foreclosure.

Quiet title actions are court proceedings to resolve title clouds and confirm ownership. Common in Hawaii where chain-of-title issues from the Mahele era, undocumented family transfers in older neighborhoods, or unrecorded deeds create disputes. Adverse possession is recognized in Hawaii but the requirements are stringent: open, notorious, hostile, exclusive, continuous occupation for the statutory period (varies; 20 years is a common figure for Hawaii but verify current).

Estates in Hawaii: standard fee simple, life estate (can be created in deed or will), leasehold (40-65 year residential leases common, longer for commercial), Hawaiian Home Lands (federal HHCA-restricted), and special homestead exemptions for primary residence. The state's old "ahupuaʻa" land divisions occasionally surface in older deeds and modern conservation/Native Hawaiian rights cases.

Recording fees and conveyance tax. Conveyance tax is paid by the seller (typically) at closing, calculated as a tiered rate on sale price with reduced rates for owner-occupant buyers and homestead exemptions. Recording fees at BOC or Land Court are charged per page; clean documents save money. Closing escrow handles recording and tax payment as part of the closing settlement.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Regular SystemStandard recorded chain-of-title at Bureau of Conveyances.
Land CourtHawaii's Torrens system. TCT is conclusive.
TCTTransfer Certificate of Title issued by Land Court.
Tenancy in commonDefault co-ownership in Hawaii. Separate inheritable shares.
Joint tenancyCo-ownership with survivorship. Express language required.
Tenancy by the entiretySpousal co-ownership with survivorship + creditor protection on marital home.
Mechanic's lien (HRS 507)Contractor/supplier lien for unpaid work or materials. Strict filing deadlines.
AOAO lienCondo association lien for unpaid maintenance fees.
Judicial foreclosureCourt-supervised. Slower but more protections.
Non-judicial foreclosurePower-of-sale. Faster. Governed by HRS 667.
MFDRMortgage Foreclosure Dispute Resolution. Alternative for owner-occupied homes.
Quiet title actionCourt proceeding to resolve title clouds and confirm ownership.
Adverse possessionAcquiring title by open, notorious, hostile, continuous occupation for statutory period.
Homestead exemptionProperty tax + creditor protection for primary residence.
Conveyance taxHawaii state transfer tax. Tiered by price + owner-occupant status.
Recording feeBOC or Land Court charge per page. Paid at closing.
AhupuaʻaTraditional Hawaiian land division (mountain to sea). Occasionally referenced in deeds.

Q 16.7·v8 When a property has multiple parties claiming ownership rights or unresolved liens, a real estate attorney typically recommends filing:
