Hawaii: Contracts & Addenda
State portion6 PSI items15 key concepts7 base questions

Hawaii uses standardized purchase forms with required addenda. Know which addendum attaches when.

Chapter Overview

The Hawaii Association of REALTORS® (HAR) publishes the most-used standard residential purchase contract — the Deposit Receipt Offer and Acceptance ("DROA"). Every Hawaii agent should be able to read it cold and identify each section: parties, property, price, deposit, financing, closing date, contingencies (inspection, financing, appraisal, condo docs review), prorations, conveyance tax, escrow, signatures. The DROA is a starting template — modifications require careful drafting and ideally attorney review for non-standard terms.

Required addenda by transaction type. Lead-based paint addendum for pre-1978 housing (federal). Seller's Real Property Disclosure Statement under HRS 508D. Condominium Public Report addendum for new condo sales (developer disclosure). HAR's lead-based paint addendum, often combined with the federal form. As-is addendum if applicable. Various contingency addenda — inspection, appraisal, financing, sale-of-buyer's-current-home. Counter-offer forms when responses change material terms.

Listing agreements in Hawaii follow standard categories: Exclusive Right to Sell (most common), Exclusive Agency, Open Listing. The HAR listing agreement form covers commission rate, term, listing price, agent obligations, seller obligations, MLS authorization, and dispute resolution. Net listings are generally avoided due to conflict-of-interest concerns.

Dual-agency consent forms (Form RR105C or current equivalent) are mandatory in Hawaii before any dual representation begins. The form explains the consumer's options: representation by seller's agent, representation by buyer's agent, dual agency (with informed consent), or customer status (no representation). The form must be delivered "before any substantive interaction" — practically, before showings or any negotiation. Designated-agency arrangements within a brokerage are also typical and require their own disclosure.

Common contract pitfalls: failing to specify whether contingencies are passive ("expires unless objected to within X days") or active ("requires written notice to remove or contract terminates"); failing to state whether closing date is "time of the essence"; ambiguity on who pays which closing costs (some traditional Hawaii allocations differ from mainland); missing addenda that void disclosure protection; failing to identify the proper TMK including any CPR designation.

Counter-offers on the standard HAR form preserve all unchanged terms. Multiple counters can occur. Each counter resets prior offers — the most recent counter is the live one. "Acceptance" of a counter must be unconditional; a further change is itself a new counter. Time to respond is governed by the form's terms (often 24-72 hours).

Earnest money deposit handling: typically held in the listing brokerage's trust account or by the escrow company. Hawaii custom is to deposit with escrow rather than the listing brokerage in most resale transactions. Failure to deposit promptly can void the contract and creates broker liability.

Distressed property and short-sale contracts add layers: lender approval contingencies, additional disclosures, longer timelines, often "subject to lender approval" language. Hawaii also has Distressed Property Conveyance (DPC) protections under HRS 480E for certain transactions involving residences in default.

Key Concepts & Definitions
DROADeposit Receipt Offer and Acceptance — Hawaii's standard residential purchase form (HAR-published).
Hawaii Association of REALTORS® (HAR)Statewide REALTOR® organization. Publishes standard forms.
Lead-paint addendumFederal mandate for pre-1978 housing. Buyer 10-day inspection right.
HRS 508D disclosureSeller's Real Property Disclosure Statement. Required for residential resales.
Condominium Public ReportRequired developer disclosure for new condo sales.
As-is addendumBuyer accepts current condition. Doesn't override mandatory disclosures.
RR105C / Mandatory Agency DisclosureRequired form delivered before substantive interaction.
Dual agency consentWritten consent from both parties. Required before dual representation.
Designated agencyDifferent agents in same firm represent opposite sides.
Counter-offerConditional acceptance with changed terms. Cancels prior offer.
Earnest money handlingTypically held in escrow; deposited promptly.
Distressed Property Conveyance Act (HRS 480E)Protections for residences in default during sale.
Inspection contingencyBuyer's right to inspect and request repairs or terminate.
Financing contingencyBuyer must obtain financing within X days.
Condo document review contingencyBuyer's right to review AOAO documents and terminate if unacceptable.

Q 17.3·v1 When a Hawaii real estate licensee represents both the buyer and seller in the same transaction, what documentation is legally required?

Q 17.3·v2 A broker in Hawaii wants to represent both parties in a residential sale. Which of the following correctly describes the legal requirement?

Q 17.3·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, if a licensee intends to represent both the buyer and seller, what must occur before entering into dual agency?

Q 17.3·v4 A Hawaii real estate agent discovers mid-transaction that she can represent the buyer, even though she listed the property. What step must the agent take to legally proceed as a dual agent?

Answer: B. Written informed consent from both parties is a prerequisite to dual agency; proceeding without documented consent violates Hawaii's fiduciary standards.
Q 17.3·v5 Under Hawaii real estate law, when a broker intends to represent both the buyer and seller in the same transaction, what documentation is legally required?

C. It requires mutual written consent to be withdrawn
D. It continues in force until the counter-offer is fully negotiated
Answer: A. Once the seller counters with different terms, the original offer is dead; only the counter-offer remains for the buyer to accept or reject.
Q 17.5·v4 During offer negotiations, a seller presents a counter-offer with adjusted price and closing date. From a contract law perspective, this counter-offer:
A. Constitutes a rejection of the buyer's offer and creates a new offer from the seller ✓
B. Requires the buyer's broker to approve before it becomes effective
C. Accepts the buyer's offer in substance but modifies non-material terms
D. Suspends the buyer's offer while the parties continue informal negotiations
Answer: A. A counter-offer is both a rejection of the original offer and a new offer made by the counter-offering party; the original offer is no longer available for acceptance.
Q 17.5·v5 When a seller presents a counter-offer to a buyer's initial proposal, what is the legal effect on the original offer?
A. The original offer is suspended but can be revived if the counter is rejected
B. The original offer is terminated and superseded by the counter-offer ✓
C. Both offers exist simultaneously and the buyer must choose one
D. The original offer remains active until the counter-offer is signed
Answer: B. A counter-offer extinguishes the original offer by operation of law; only the counter becomes the active, live offer on the table.
Q 17.5·v6 During contract negotiations, the buyer's agent submits a revised offer with different terms than the seller's initial proposal. This revised offer:
A. Constitutes a rejection of the original offer and creates a new offer ✓
B. Maintains both the original and new terms in a combined contract
C. Modifies the original terms while keeping the offer alive
D. Requires written approval from the listing agent before it terminates the original
Answer: A. A counteroffer is a rejection of the original offer and the presentation of new terms; the original offer ceases to exist once the counter is communicated.
Q 17.5·v7 In Hawaii real estate negotiations, when a seller responds to a purchase offer with modified terms, the original offer's status becomes:
A. Dead—it no longer exists and is replaced by the counter-offer ✓
B. Held in escrow until both parties agree on final terms
C. Binding on the buyer unless they formally withdraw within 24 hours
D. Accepted conditionally pending the buyer's review
Answer: A. Counter-offers automatically terminate the prior offer; the prior offer cannot be accepted once a counter has been made because it no longer exists as a live option.
Q 17.5·v8 A seller receives an offer from a buyer and provides a written response with revised price and closing terms. Regarding the buyer's initial offer, it is now:
A. Valid and may be accepted by the seller at any time during the transaction
B. Enforceable as a backup in case the counter-offer fails
C. Extinguished and replaced by the seller's counter-proposal ✓
D. Temporarily suspended while the counter-offer is negotiated
Answer: C. The counter-offer legally destroys the original offer; once made, the original cannot be revived or accepted because it no longer exists as a valid offer.
Q 17.5·v9 When a seller presents a counter-offer to a buyer's original proposal, what is the legal effect on the buyer's initial offer?
A. It is terminated and superseded by the counter-offer as the new negotiating position ✓
B. It remains active and binding until the seller formally withdraws it in writing
C. It becomes part of a binding contract once acknowledged by either party
D. It is suspended but can be revived if the counter-offer is rejected within 24 hours
Answer: A. A counter-offer operates as a rejection of the original offer and creates a new offer from the seller; the original buyer offer no longer exists as a live proposition.

Q 17.6·v5 When a developer offers a newly constructed condominium unit for sale in Hawaii, what document must be delivered to prospective purchasers?

Q 17.6·v6 A buyer is interested in purchasing a brand-new condominium unit from the developer. Which of the following disclosures is specifically mandated by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission for this transaction?

Q 17.7·v4 A homeowner facing foreclosure in Hawaii wants to know which statute protects them during a distressed property sale. The correct statutory reference is:

Q 17.7·v6 A real estate licensee in Hawaii must be familiar with distressed property conveyance rules. These statutory protections are codified in:

A. HRS 521

A. HRS 508D (Mortgage Servicer Regulations)

Hawaii: Financing
State portion4 PSI items11 key concepts5 base questions

Beyond standard mortgages, Hawaii sees more agreement-of-sale financing and unique lender quirks.

Chapter Overview

Agreement of Sale ("AOS") is a Hawaii-flavored installment land contract. The buyer takes possession but legal title stays with seller until purchase price is paid. Common when a buyer can't qualify for conventional financing, in leasehold-conversion deals where lender financing is unusual, or for unique properties. AOS is recordable and creates an equitable interest in the buyer. Default remedies typically follow the contract terms but generally require notice and a cure period; harsh forfeiture is disfavored.

Purchase Money Mortgage (PMM) is seller financing where the seller takes back a mortgage instead of all-cash. Common in Hawaii for high-end and unique properties where conventional lenders are slow or skeptical. The PMM is junior to any senior institutional financing and creates a recorded lien against the property. Common terms: 30-year amortization, 5-15 year balloon, market interest rate.

Hawaii institutional lenders include local credit unions (HSFCU, Aloha Pacific FCU, others), Bank of Hawaii, First Hawaiian Bank, Central Pacific Bank, plus mainland-headquartered banks and online lenders. Local lenders often have better insight into leasehold deals, condo project warrantability, and CPR quirks. Many condo projects are non-warrantable for Fannie/Freddie and require a portfolio lender.

Hawaii has a usury statute (HRS 478) capping consumer loan interest. Most institutional loans are exempt from the statutory cap (federal preemption + statutory exemption), but the cap matters mostly in private lending and seller financing. Verify the current cap and exemption rules; statutes update.

FHA, VA, and USDA loans are available in Hawaii but with state-specific caveats. FHA condo project approval is required — many Hawaii condos are not FHA-approved. VA loans work in Hawaii but the VA appraisal can be conservative on leasehold properties. USDA rural housing applies to specific eligible areas, more limited in Hawaii than mainland.

Closing costs in Hawaii: conveyance tax (state), recording fees, escrow fee, title insurance, lender fees, prorated taxes and condo fees, prepaid insurance and interest. Some allocations differ from mainland custom — agents should reference HAR's standard closing-cost allocation for guidance and customize per contract.

Lease conversion: the process of buying out the underlying fee on a leasehold property. Often complex, requiring lessor cooperation (sometimes legally compelled under certain statutes), professional appraisal of fee value, financing arrangement for the fee purchase, and recording of the deed-in-fee. Major lessors (Bishop Estate/Kamehameha Schools, others) have established processes for many of their leases.

Key Concepts & Definitions
Agreement of Sale (AOS)Hawaii installment land contract. Buyer occupies; seller holds title until paid.
Purchase Money Mortgage (PMM)Seller-financed mortgage taken back at sale.
Wraparound mortgageNew larger loan "wraps" existing senior loan. Seller financing structure.
HRS 478Hawaii usury statute. Caps interest on certain non-institutional loans.
Warrantable condoCondo project meeting Fannie/Freddie standards. Easier to finance.
Non-warrantable condoProject failing Fannie/Freddie standards. Requires portfolio lender.
FHA condo approvalRequired for FHA financing on condos. Many Hawaii projects not approved.
Lease conversionBuying out underlying fee on leasehold property.
Bishop Estate / Kamehameha SchoolsMajor Hawaiian-history landowner. Many lease properties.
Portfolio lenderLender holding loans on own books rather than selling to GSEs.
Equitable interestBuyer's interest in property under AOS or contract for deed.
Question Bank — Hawaii: Financing
Q 18.1 In an Agreement of Sale, legal title:
A. Passes to escrow
B. Passes to buyer immediately
C. Passes to lender
D. Stays with seller until paid in full ✓
Answer: D. AOS = installment land contract; title held by seller pending full payment.
Q 18.1·v1 Under a land contract (Agreement of Sale), when does the seller relinquish legal title to the buyer?
A. Upon recording the contract with the Bureau of Conveyances
B. Upon execution of the contract
C. When the buyer makes the first down payment
D. Only after the buyer has paid the full purchase price ✓
Answer: D. In a land contract, the seller retains legal title as security until the buyer completes all payments; title transfers only upon full satisfaction of the agreement.
Q 18.1·v2 Which statement correctly describes title ownership during an installment land contract transaction?
A. The buyer receives equitable title and the lender holds legal title
B. Title is split equally between buyer and seller until closing
C. The seller maintains legal title until the entire purchase price is paid ✓
D. Escrow holds legal title on behalf of both parties
Answer: C. In an installment land contract, the seller holds legal title as collateral; the buyer obtains equitable title and legal title transfers only upon final payment.
Q 18.1·v3 In Hawaii, when a buyer and seller enter into an Agreement of Sale (land contract), what is the status of legal title?
A. Seller retains legal title until the purchase obligation is fully satisfied ✓
B. Title is transferred to a trustee to hold in escrow
C. Buyer obtains legal title subject to a mortgage lien
D. Legal title vests jointly with the buyer and seller as tenants in common
Answer: A. The Agreement of Sale is an installment contract where the seller retains legal title as security interest until the buyer completes all required payments.
Q 18.1·v4 A buyer enters into an Agreement of Sale with a seller to purchase land on installment. At the time of signing the contract, legal title belongs to:
A. The buyer, subject to a seller's lien
B. The seller, contingent on receipt of full payment ✓
C. Both parties equally as co-owners
D. The title company holding it in trust
Answer: B. Under an Agreement of Sale, the seller retains legal title throughout the installment payment period as security; title transfers to the buyer only after full payment is made.
Q 18.1·v5 Under a Hawaii Agreement of Sale (land contract), who retains ownership of the property during the payment period?
A. The seller maintains legal title until final payment is made ✓
B. The buyer receives equitable title only, not legal title
C. The title company holds the deed in trust
D. The buyer holds legal title subject to a mortgage
Answer: A. In an Agreement of Sale, the seller retains legal title as security until the buyer completes all payments; the buyer has equitable title and possession rights.
Q 18.1·v6 Which statement correctly describes title ownership in an installment land contract?
A. Both buyer and seller hold joint legal title during the contract period
B. Legal title remains with the seller until all payments are received ✓
C. Title transfers to the buyer upon signing the contract
D. The buyer receives full legal title when the first payment is made
Answer: B. An installment land contract (Agreement of Sale) is structured so the seller keeps legal title as security and only transfers it upon final payment by the buyer.
Q 18.1·v7 A buyer enters into an Agreement of Sale to purchase raw land in Hawaii. Before the buyer makes the final payment, legal title is held by:
A. A neutral third-party escrow agent on behalf of the buyer
B. The buyer, who has both legal and equitable title
C. The primary lender as security for the purchase loan
D. The seller, pending full satisfaction of the contract terms ✓
Answer: D. In an Agreement of Sale, the seller retains legal title until the buyer completes all contractual obligations and full payment is made.
Q 18.1·v8 Under a typical Agreement of Sale in Hawaii, what is the status of legal title while the buyer is making installment payments?
A. Title is held by the Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources
B. Title remains vested in the seller as security for payment ✓
C. Title transfers gradually to the buyer with each payment made
D. Title is held by the buyer with a lien in favor of the seller
Answer: B. The seller retains legal title throughout the payment period as a security mechanism; title passes to the buyer only upon satisfaction of all contract obligations.
Q 18.1·v9 Under a Hawaii installment land contract, when does the seller's equitable interest in the property terminate?
A. When the buyer obtains financing from a lender
B. Upon execution of the contract by both parties
C. Immediately when the buyer takes possession of the property
D. Only after the buyer completes all payments and the deed is delivered ✓
Answer: D. In an installment land contract (Agreement of Sale), the seller retains legal title as security until the buyer fulfills all payment obligations; title passes only upon final payment and delivery of the deed.
Q 18.2 A PMM is typically:
A. Identical to a HELOC
B. Required by FHA
C. Senior to institutional financing
D. Junior to senior institutional liens ✓
Answer: D. PMMs typically sit junior to existing senior loans.
Q 18.2·v1 When a buyer obtains a PMM to bridge a down payment gap, what is its typical lien position relative to the primary mortgage?
A. It ranks subordinate to the primary institutional mortgage ✓
B. It functions as an unsecured personal loan with no lien
C. It must be paid off before the first mortgage can be recorded
D. It holds first lien position ahead of the institutional loan
Answer: A. PMMs are structured as junior liens, sitting behind (subordinate to) the senior institutional first mortgage in lien priority.
Q 18.2·v2 A piggyback mortgage arrangement is BEST characterized as:
A. A form of equity line of credit required by Fannie Mae
B. A subordinate lien that exists in second or lower lien position ✓
C. An alternative to title insurance on investment properties
D. A bridge loan that eliminates the need for homeowner's insurance
Answer: B. PMMs (piggyback mortgages) are characteristically junior liens positioned below senior institutional mortgages in the lien hierarchy.
Q 18.2·v3 From a lender's risk perspective, a PMM differs from a first mortgage primarily because the PMM holder:
A. Assumes a riskier position due to subordination to the senior loan ✓
B. Is not required to file a promissory note
C. Is guaranteed repayment by the state of Hawaii
D. Receives payment before the institutional lender in case of default
Answer: A. Because PMMs are junior to institutional liens, the PMM lender bears greater default risk and recovery risk should the property be foreclosed.
Q 18.2·v4 If a property has an existing first mortgage and the buyer needs additional financing via a PMM, the PMM will likely be:
A. Exempt from recording requirements under Hawaii real property law
B. Recorded in first lien position with the original mortgage subordinated
C. Combined with the first mortgage into a single unified loan document
D. Recorded as a second or lower lien subject to the existing senior mortgage ✓
Answer: D. PMMs are recorded as subordinate liens, meaning they are junior to and recorded after the senior institutional mortgage in the chain of title.
Q 18.2·v5 In a transaction with an existing first mortgage, where would a PMM typically be positioned in the lien hierarchy?
A. In place of the original mortgage as a replacement loan
B. Behind the senior institutional mortgage ✓
C. With equal priority to any VA or FHA loan
D. Ahead of all other encumbrances on the property
Answer: B. PMMs are subordinate instruments that sit junior to existing first mortgages and other senior liens on the property.
Q 18.2·v6 When comparing a piggyback mortgage to a first mortgage, the piggyback loan is best characterized as:
A. Subordinate to the primary institutional lender's security interest ✓
B. A refinancing tool that replaces the original obligation
C. Exempt from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission's oversight
D. Holding primary lien position on the real property
Answer: A. A piggyback mortgage (PMM) is subordinate by nature—it is inferior to the senior lien held by the institutional lender.
Q 18.2·v7 A buyer uses a piggyback mortgage strategy alongside a traditional bank loan. The PMM holder's claim on the property is:
A. Secondary to the primary institutional lender ✓
B. Mandated by state law for all residential purchases
C. Superior to all other secured lenders
D. Interchangeable with a home equity line of credit in function
Answer: A. PMMs occupy a junior position relative to the primary mortgage lender, meaning the primary lender has first claim in case of default.
Q 18.2·v8 Which statement accurately describes the lien position of a piggyback mortgage in relation to a conventional first mortgage?
A. The PMM takes priority and must be satisfied before the first mortgage
B. The PMM is prohibited under Hawaii Real Estate Commission rules
C. The PMM is subordinated to the first mortgage holder's security interest ✓
D. The PMM functions identically to a cash-out refinance on the same property
Answer: C. PMMs are junior liens by definition—they are subordinate to the senior institutional lender's first mortgage position.
Q 18.2·v9 In the lien priority structure of a Hawaii property, where does a piggyback mortgage (PMM) typically rank?
A. Above all other mortgages and trust deeds on the property
B. In parity with the primary institutional mortgage
C. As the sole security instrument, replacing conventional financing
D. Behind the first mortgage but ahead of any home equity lines of credit ✓
Answer: D. A PMM is subordinate to the senior first mortgage but typically takes priority over subsequent liens like HELOCs; it holds a junior position in the lien hierarchy.
Q 18.3 A non-warrantable condo means:
A. It's tax-exempt
B. Conventional financing through Fannie/Freddie is unavailable ✓
C. It cannot be sold
D. It's illegal
Answer: B. Non-warrantable = doesn't meet GSE standards; portfolio loan needed.
Q 18.3·v1 What is the primary financing challenge a buyer faces when purchasing a non-warrantable condominium?
A. The property cannot be transferred to a new owner
B. The buyer must pay a higher property tax rate
C. Government-sponsored enterprises will not purchase the mortgage in the secondary market ✓
D. The homeowners association must approve all financing arrangements
Answer: C. Non-warrantable condos fail GSE (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) underwriting standards, making conventional loans unavailable; buyers typically need portfolio loans from private lenders.
Q 18.3·v2 A condo building is deemed non-warrantable primarily because:
A. It has outstanding code violations that prevent occupancy
B. It is located in an area designated for commercial development
C. It does not comply with state building codes
D. It does not meet the lending standards established by secondary mortgage market investors ✓
Answer: D. Non-warrantable status refers specifically to failing GSE (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) approval criteria, which restricts conventional financing options available to buyers.
Q 18.3·v3 Which statement best describes the financing implication of a property being classified as non-warrantable?
A. Mortgages cannot be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac in the secondary market ✓
B. The property owner forfeits all mortgage tax deductions
C. VA and USDA loans become the only financing options
D. Federal Housing Administration loans are prohibited
Answer: A. Non-warrantable means the property fails GSE guidelines, so conventional mortgages cannot be sold to Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac; lenders must hold the loan in portfolio.
Q 18.3·v4 When a condominium is identified as non-warrantable, a real estate licensee should inform buyers that:
A. Traditional mortgage programs offered through major lenders may not be available ✓
B. The Hawaii Department of Commerce will need to issue a special waiver
C. The condominium can only be purchased through cash transactions
D. The condominium must undergo remediation before any sale can close
Answer: A. Non-warrantable condos fall outside GSE standards, eliminating access to conventional financing through traditional lenders, though portfolio and niche loan products may still exist.
Q 18.3·v5 Why would a condominium project receive a non-warrantable classification from lenders?
A. The project does not satisfy Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac underwriting requirements ✓
B. The developer never recorded the master deed
C. The building fails to meet structural safety codes
D. The homeowners association has unpaid property taxes
Answer: A. Non-warrantable condos fail GSE (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) standards, requiring portfolio or alternative financing rather than conventional loans.
Q 18.3·v6 A buyer interested in purchasing a unit in a non-warrantable condominium should understand that:
A. The property cannot legally be mortgaged under any circumstances
B. Financing options will be restricted to portfolio lenders or non-GSE sources ✓
C. VA and FHA financing are the only options available
D. Standard conventional mortgages from major lenders will likely be available
Answer: B. Non-warrantable condos cannot use GSE-backed conventional financing, forcing buyers toward portfolio lenders or alternative financing sources.
Q 18.3·v7 When a condominium is labeled non-warrantable, what is the primary lending consequence?
A. The unit cannot be used as a primary residence
B. Property taxes increase by 15% annually
C. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will not purchase or guarantee the mortgage ✓
D. All construction defects become the buyer's liability
Answer: C. Non-warrantable status means the property does not comply with GSE standards, so Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will not guarantee conventional loans on the unit.
Q 18.3·v8 A broker explains to a client that their desired condo unit is non-warrantable. This designation primarily affects:
A. Whether conventional financing from GSE-backed lenders is obtainable ✓
B. The unit's eligibility for property tax exemptions
C. The requirement to maintain flood insurance coverage
D. The ability to claim depreciation on rental income
Answer: A. Non-warrantable means the condo does not meet GSE (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) standards, eliminating access to conventional mortgage products backed by these entities.
Q 18.3·v9 When a condominium project fails to meet Government-Sponsored Enterprise underwriting criteria, what financing restriction typically results?
A. Property tax assessments are increased by the county
B. Borrowers must seek portfolio loans or non-conforming lenders instead of traditional mortgage companies ✓
C. The homeowners association is dissolved by the state
D. The property cannot legally be listed for sale
Answer: B. Non-warrantable condos don't qualify for Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans, forcing buyers to use portfolio lenders, FHA, or other alternative financing rather than conventional mortgages.
Q 18.4 Hawaii's usury statute is at:
A. HRS 478 ✓
B. HRS 521
C. HRS 467
D. HRS 514B
Answer: A. HRS 478 governs interest rate caps.
Q 18.4·v1 Which Hawaii Revised Statute specifically addresses maximum allowable interest rates and lending restrictions?
A. HRS 478 ✓
B. HRS 467
C. HRS 521
D. HRS 514B
Answer: A. HRS 478 is Hawaii's usury statute that establishes caps on interest rates and protects borrowers from excessive lending charges.
Q 18.4·v2 A real estate licensee needs to understand Hawaii's usury law to advise clients on financing terms. Where should they locate this statute?
A. HRS 478 (usury and interest rate limits) ✓
B. HRS 514B (condominium property regime)
C. HRS 467 (professional licensing)
D. HRS 521 (residential tenancies)
Answer: A. HRS 478 contains Hawaii's usury provisions governing the maximum interest rates lenders may charge on loans.
Q 18.4·v3 When educating clients about predatory lending practices and legal interest rate ceilings in Hawaii, which statute applies?
A. HRS 521
B. HRS 514B
C. HRS 478 ✓
D. HRS 467
Answer: C. HRS 478 is Hawaii's usury law that establishes legal limits on interest rates and prevents usurious lending practices.
Q 18.4·v4 A mortgage lender's interest rate proposal must comply with Hawaii law. The relevant statutory authority is:
A. HRS 478 ✓
B. HRS 521
C. HRS 467
D. HRS 514B
Answer: A. HRS 478 governs interest rate caps and usury restrictions that all lenders in Hawaii must follow when structuring loan terms.
Q 18.4·v5 Under Hawaii Revised Statutes, which chapter specifically addresses maximum allowable interest rates that lenders may charge on loans?
A. HRS 467 (Real Estate Commission)
B. HRS 514B (Condominium Property Regimes)
C. HRS 521 (Residential Tenancies)
D. HRS 478 (Interest Rate Limitations) ✓
Answer: D. HRS 478 is Hawaii's usury statute that establishes the legal caps on interest rates charged by lenders on consumer loans and mortgages.
Q 18.4·v6 A borrower in Hawaii wants to understand what state law prohibits excessive interest charges on their mortgage. Which statute should they consult?
A. HRS 514B
B. HRS 478 ✓
C. HRS 467
D. HRS 521
Answer: B. HRS 478 is Hawaii's usury law that protects borrowers by limiting the maximum interest rates lenders are permitted to charge on loans.
Q 18.4·v7 Which of the following Hawaii statutes contains provisions protecting borrowers from usurious lending practices?

Hawaii: Escrow Process & Closing
State portion3 PSI items14 key concepts5 base questions

Hawaii is an "escrow state" — a neutral escrow holds everything and disburses on closing.

Chapter Overview

In Hawaii, virtually all residential real estate transactions go through escrow. The escrow agent (a licensed escrow company under HRS 449 — Hawaii Escrow Depositories statute) is a neutral third party holding funds, deeds, and instructions. Escrow opens with the executed purchase contract and earnest money deposit. Escrow closes only when all conditions are satisfied: inspection waivers or repair completions, financing commitments, title clearance, signed deed, buyer's funds, payoff of seller's loans, and any required disclosures, releases, and approvals.

The escrow agent's duties are strictly defined by escrow instructions agreed by both parties. The agent is NOT a party advocate — it's neutral. It cannot disburse funds without proper authority, cannot release the deed without payment, and cannot waive contract conditions. Escrow officers handle title searches, prepare closing documents, calculate prorations, coordinate with lenders and title insurers, and ultimately fund and record the transaction.

Closing statements summarize every credit and debit. Modern closings use the federal Closing Disclosure form for residential mortgage loans (replaces HUD-1 for TRID-covered loans). Items include sales price, deposits, loan proceeds, prorations (taxes, condo fees, lease rent), conveyance tax (often Hawaii line item), GET on commissions, escrow fee, title insurance premiums, recording fees, lender fees, and net to seller.

Conveyance tax: Hawaii imposes a state-level transfer tax based on sale price and buyer category. Owner-occupant rates are lower than investor rates. The current schedule is tiered (rate per $100 of sale price, increasing at higher price brackets). Verify the current rate schedule annually — they update. The seller typically pays unless contract specifies otherwise. Failure to pay conveyance tax can void recording of the deed.

Common Hawaii prorations: real property taxes (semiannual; July 1 to December 31 is one billing period), condo maintenance fees (monthly), lease rent (varies by lease — often quarterly or annually), tenant rents on income property. Hawaii contracts typically prorate using actual day count (365-day year), though contracts may specify 360-day banker's year. Confirm in contract.

Title insurance in Hawaii: standard policies cover the typical risks. Owner's policy is a one-time premium protecting buyer for as long as they own. Lender's policy is required by lender, covers loan amount, decreases as loan balance drops. Hawaii title insurance carriers commonly include Title Guaranty, First American, Old Republic, others. Special endorsements address Hawaii-specific issues like leasehold and AOAO.

Common closing-day issues: missing signatures or notarizations, last-minute lender conditions, failed wire transfers, undisclosed liens discovered at title pull, AOAO estoppel showing back fees owed. Smooth closings come from thorough pre-closing review and proactive communication among agents, escrow, lender, and title insurer.

Key Concepts & Definitions
EscrowNeutral third party holding funds + documents until conditions met.
HRS 449Hawaii Escrow Depositories statute. Governs escrow companies.
Escrow instructionsWritten agreement from both parties directing escrow agent's actions.
Closing DisclosureFederal CD form replacing HUD-1 for most residential loans.
HUD-1 Settlement StatementOlder closing form. Still used for some non-TRID loans.
Conveyance taxHawaii state transfer tax. Tiered rates by price + buyer status.
Owner-occupant rateLower conveyance tax rate for primary-residence buyers.
Recording feesBureau of Conveyances or Land Court charges per page recorded.
Net to sellerSale price minus all seller debits; the wire-out at closing.
Estoppel certificateAOAO statement of fees owed. Required at closing for condos.
365-day prorationHawaii contracts usually prorate on actual day count. Verify in contract.
Title insuranceProtects against title defects existing at closing. Owner's + lender's policies.
Wire transferStandard method for closing-day funding. Subject to fraud risk; verify wire instructions.
Wire fraudIncreasing risk. Always verify wire instructions by phone with known number.

Hawaii: Professional Practices & Conduct
State portion14 PSI items27 key concepts16 base questions

HRS 467 + HAR Title 16 Chapter 99 are the bedrock of Hawaii license law. This section is the largest weight on the state portion (14 items).

Chapter Overview

Hawaii has two real estate license categories regulated under HRS 467: Salesperson and Broker. A Salesperson must be 18+, have a valid Social Security number, complete the 60-hour Salesperson Pre-Licensing Course at a REC-approved school, pass the PSI examination (national + state portions, 70%+ on each), be sponsored by a Hawaii-licensed real estate broker (an "employing" or "sponsoring" broker), and pay the licensing fees. A criminal background check applies; certain criminal histories can disqualify or require explanation. Salespersons may not collect fees directly from a customer — fees flow through their employing broker.

A Broker must hold a current valid Salesperson license, have at least three years of active full-time experience as a salesperson within the prior five years (the experience requirement) along with a minimum number of completed transactions, complete the 80-hour Broker Pre-Licensing Course, pass the broker examination, provide additional documentation including evidence of experience, and pay the broker license fees. Brokers can practice independently as a sole-broker firm, supervise salespersons, or operate under a brokerage entity.

Continuing education (CE) requirements: 20 hours every 2-year license cycle (the cycle ends on the last day of December of even-numbered years for individual licensees on the standard cycle; verify current). The 20 hours must include the state-mandated Core Course (typically 6 hours, updated each cycle to reflect law changes). The remaining hours come from approved electives. Late renewal incurs fees and possible inactive status. CE must be completed at REC-approved providers.

Trust account rules under HRS 467 + HAR §16-99: client funds must be held in a Hawaii bank or savings institution, separate from the broker's operating account, properly identified ("Trust Account" or similar). Funds must be deposited promptly (typically 2 business days). Records must be retained for the period state rules require (commonly 3 years). Monthly reconciliation is standard. Audits by REC are unannounced. The penalties for trust-fund violations are severe — typically license revocation, sometimes felony charges.

Disciplinary grounds under HRS 467: misrepresentation or fraud in transactions, commingling, conversion, undisclosed dual agency or other conflicts of interest, discrimination violating state or federal law, failure to supervise (broker), advertising violations, paying or receiving undisclosed referral fees in violation of RESPA, conviction of crime involving moral turpitude, drug or alcohol abuse impairing practice, and violation of any other duty imposed on licensees. The Real Estate Commission may revoke, suspend, fine, place on probation, require additional education, or impose other discipline. Civil and criminal liability layer on top of license discipline.

Mandatory Agency Disclosure: Hawaii requires written agency disclosure to consumers before any "substantive interaction" — meaning before any showing, listing presentation, or detailed negotiation. The form (commonly known by its current code, historically RR105C; verify current form name) explains the consumer's representation options: Seller's Agent, Buyer's Agent, Dual Agent (with informed consent), or Customer (no representation). Failure to deliver the form on time is a license-law violation.

Advertising rules under HAR §16-99: every ad must include the firm name as licensed (not just the agent's name). Out-of-state advertising for Hawaii property must comply. Internet advertising follows the same standards as print and broadcast. Cannot advertise as the listing broker on a property under another broker's exclusive listing. Cannot use misleading terms or imply qualifications not held. Team or group names are permitted only if certain disclosure rules are met. Photos and information must accurately represent the property and licensee.

Procuring cause and commission disputes are common. Hawaii follows general principles: the agent who initiated the unbroken chain leading to the sale is typically the procuring cause. Disputes between cooperating brokers are often resolved through the listing broker's offer of cooperation in MLS. Hawaii REALTORS® can use NAR's arbitration process. Non-REALTORS® rely on contract terms and possibly civil litigation.

Practicing within scope: salespersons cannot operate independently of their broker; cannot sign listing agreements in their own name; cannot accept fees directly. Broker liability is broad — the broker is responsible for all licensees affiliated with the firm, including independent contractors. Switching brokers requires release from the prior broker or appropriate procedures under HRS 467 and REC rules. Inactive licensees (those without an employing broker, or who haven't paid renewal) cannot list, show, negotiate, or be paid for real estate services.

Key Concepts & Definitions
HRS 467Hawaii Real Estate Brokers and Salespersons statute. Foundation of license law.
HAR Title 16 Chapter 99Real Estate Commission administrative rules. Implements HRS 467.
Salesperson license18+, 60-hour course, PSI exam, sponsoring broker, fees, background check.
Broker licenseActive salesperson + 3 years experience + 80-hour broker course + broker exam.
Sponsoring / employing brokerBroker who employs/supervises a salesperson.
CE: 20 hours / 2 yearsIncludes mandatory Core Course; balance is electives.
Core CourseState-mandated 6-hour CE update each cycle. Reflects law changes.
License renewalBiennial. Late renewal carries fees + possible inactive status.
Trust accountClient funds in Hawaii bank, separate, identified, reconciled, records 3+ years.
ComminglingMixing personal and trust funds. Per se license violation.
ConversionUsing trust funds for own benefit. Felony in many cases.
RR105C / Mandatory Agency DisclosureRequired form delivered to consumer before substantive interaction. Verify current form name.
Real Estate Commission (REC)Hawaii regulator. Sets rules, investigates, disciplines. Under DCCA.
DCCAHawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs. Oversees REC.
PVLProfessional and Vocational Licensing Division within DCCA.
Inactive licenseLicensee not currently practicing. Cannot list, show, negotiate.
Discrimination (HRS 515)Hawaii Fair Housing — adds classes beyond federal: ancestry, age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, HIV/AIDS, source of income.
Procuring causeOrigin of unbroken chain producing a sale. Determines commission entitlement.
Advertising rules (HAR §16-99)Must include firm name. Cannot mislead. Cannot solicit currently-listed property.
Failure to superviseBroker liability for licensee's violations. Can revoke broker license.
Suspension / revocationLicense sanctions for serious violations. May be stayed with probation.
FineMonetary penalty. Levied separately or with other discipline.
ProbationLicense continuance under conditions (additional education, supervision, audits).
Background checkRequired at licensure. Certain convictions require explanation or disqualify.
Moral turpitudeCrime involving baseness, vileness, or depravity. Disciplinary trigger.
NAR arbitrationVoluntary dispute resolution for REALTOR® member commission disputes.
License switchingSalesperson moving to new broker — requires proper release/transfer procedure.

Q 20.3 Mixing client trust funds with broker's operating funds is:
A. Conversion only
B. Allowed if reconciled
C. Allowed for under-$1,000 amounts
D. Commingling — license violation ✓
Answer: D. Any mixing is commingling, regardless of amount.
Q 20.3·v1 A Hawaii real estate broker deposits earnest money from a buyer into the same account used for the broker's own business expenses. This practice is:
A. Acceptable for transactions under 30 days
B. A violation of commingling requirements ✓
C. Only prohibited if the funds are later misappropriated
D. Permissible if the broker maintains separate ledgers
Answer: B. Commingling occurs the moment client funds are mixed with broker operating funds, regardless of accounting methods or time frame—it is a license violation by definition.
Q 20.3·v2 When a broker combines client trust account funds with the brokerage's general operating account, what violation has occurred?
A. Commingling ✓
B. Negligent custody of funds
C. Conversion and theft
D. Breach of fiduciary duty only
Answer: A. The act of mixing client money with broker operating funds is commingling itself—a direct license violation under Hawaii real estate law.
Q 20.3·v3 A Hawaii broker receives client earnest money and deposits it into an account that also contains the broker's payroll and overhead expenses. Which statement is accurate?
A. This is permissible if monthly reconciliations are performed
B. This is only a violation if the broker fails to return the funds on time
C. This constitutes commingling and violates licensing regulations ✓
D. This is allowed if client funds can be identified separately within the account
Answer: C. Commingling is the prohibited mixing of client funds with broker funds—the violation exists at the moment of deposit, regardless of accounting controls or intent.
Q 20.3·v4 A broker pools client trust funds with company operating funds in a single bank account for convenience. What licensing violation has the broker committed?
A. Failure to maintain errors and omissions insurance
B. Improper disclosure of account ownership
C. Commingling of client funds ✓
D. Unauthorized practice of real estate
Answer: C. Commingling—the unlawful combining of client trust money with broker business funds—is a per se violation of Hawaii licensing law.
Q 20.3·v5 A broker deposits earnest money and security deposits into the same account used for paying office rent and salaries. This practice violates which principle?
A. Commingling — client funds must remain separate ✓
B. Requirements for notarizing escrow agreements
C. Proper reconciliation procedures under HRS 467-14
D. The statute of limitations on trust account audits
Answer: A. Commingling occurs when fiduciary funds are mixed with a broker's personal or operating accounts, regardless of accounting practices. This is a fundamental license violation under Hawaii REC rules.
Q 20.3·v6 Which situation describes a commingling violation?
A. A broker places client trust funds and broker commission in the same financial institution but separate accounts
B. A broker records client funds in the trust ledger but reconciles monthly instead of weekly
C. A broker holds client earnest money in a trust account but fails to deposit it within 5 business days
D. A broker temporarily deposits client funds into an operating account before transferring to the trust account ✓
Answer: D. Commingling is the unauthorized mixing of client fiduciary funds with the broker's own funds, even temporarily. Separate accounts at the same institution or accounting delays do not constitute commingling.
Q 20.3·v7 Under Hawaii real estate law, what is the consequence of a broker combining client trust account funds with broker operating funds, even if the amounts are small?
A. Misappropriation charges only if the funds cannot be located
B. Commingling — a direct license violation regardless of amount ✓
C. A fine of up to $500 per violation
D. Suspension of trust account privileges for 30 days
Answer: B. Commingling is a per se violation of trust account requirements; the dollar amount is irrelevant. Any unauthorized mixing of fiduciary and operating funds is a license violation.
Q 20.3·v8 A salesperson advises the broker that it's more efficient to deposit all incoming funds (client escrow, earnest money, and commissions) into one master account and then distribute them later. The broker should:
A. Implement it for transactions under $5,000 only
B. Reject this proposal because it constitutes commingling ✓
C. Require the salesperson to obtain REC approval in advance
D. Allow this practice only if the salesperson reconciles weekly
Answer: B. Commingling is prohibited regardless of accounting procedures, efficiency arguments, or transaction size. Client trust funds must be maintained in separate accounts from broker operating funds.
Q 20.3·v9 A broker deposits earnest money checks from multiple transactions into a single bank account that also contains the broker's payroll and office expenses. This practice is known as:
A. Conversion of client property
B. Trust account management
C. Commingling of funds — a violation ✓
D. Proper reconciliation procedure
Answer: C. Commingling occurs when client trust funds are mixed with broker operating or personal funds in any amount or manner, regardless of whether accounts are later reconciled.

Q 20.7 A licensee's required minimum age is:
A. 21
B. 25
C. 16
D. 18 ✓
Answer: D. 18 years old to apply for salesperson license.
Q 20.7·v1 Under Hawaii real estate law, what is the minimum age requirement to qualify for a salesperson license?
A. 18 years old ✓
B. 16 years old
C. 21 years old
D. 25 years old
Answer: A. Hawaii REC requires applicants for a salesperson license to be at least 18 years of age at the time of application.
Q 20.7·v2 A person seeking to obtain a real estate salesperson license in Hawaii must be:
A. at least 18 years of age ✓
B. at least 16 years of age with parental consent
C. at least 25 years of age with prior sales experience
D. at least 21 years of age and a permanent resident
Answer: A. The minimum age requirement for a salesperson license in Hawaii is 18 years old; no additional conditions such as residency status or prior experience alter this basic age requirement.
Q 20.7·v3 Which statement accurately reflects Hawaii's age requirement for real estate salesperson licensure?
A. Applicants must be at least 21 years of age
B. Applicants must have reached their 25th birthday
C. Applicants must be at least 16 years of age
D. Applicants must be at least 18 years of age ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law establishes 18 years as the minimum age for salesperson license applicants, which is lower than some other professional licenses but higher than minors.
Q 20.7·v4 If a prospective licensee is 17 years old and otherwise meets all qualifications, can they apply for a Hawaii real estate salesperson license?
A. No, they must be at least 18 years old ✓
B. Yes, if they have written parental consent
C. Yes, if they pass the salesperson exam first
D. No, they must be at least 21 years old
Answer: A. Age 18 is a mandatory minimum requirement; parental consent or exam passage does not waive the age requirement for salesperson licensure.
Q 20.7·v5 Under Hawaii real estate licensing laws, what is the minimum age requirement to qualify for a salesperson license?
A. 25 years old
B. 21 years old
C. 17 years old
D. 18 years old ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC requires applicants for a salesperson license to be at least 18 years of age at the time of application.
Q 20.7·v6 To be eligible to apply for a real estate salesperson license in Hawaii, an applicant must meet a minimum age of:
A. 20 years
B. 16 years
C. 19 years
D. 18 years ✓
Answer: D. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission mandates that salesperson applicants must be at least 18 years old to meet licensing eligibility requirements.
Q 20.7·v7 Which of the following correctly states the age requirement for obtaining a Hawaii real estate salesperson license?
A. Applicants must be at least 18 years old ✓
B. Applicants must be at least 21 years old
C. Applicants must be at least 16 years old
D. Applicants must be at least 25 years old
Answer: A. Hawaii law requires prospective salesperson licensees to be a minimum of 18 years of age to satisfy the basic eligibility criteria.
Q 20.7·v8 A person interested in becoming a real estate salesperson in Hawaii should know that the minimum age requirement is:
A. 25 years of age or older
B. 17 years of age or older
C. 21 years of age or older
D. 18 years of age or older ✓
Answer: D. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission establishes 18 years old as the minimum age threshold for salesperson license applicants.
Q 20.7·v9 Under Hawaii real estate law, what is the minimum age requirement to obtain a salesperson license?
A. 19 years old
B. 21 years old
C. 17 years old
D. 18 years old ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC requires applicants for a salesperson license to be at least 18 years of age to meet the basic eligibility requirements.
Q 20.8 A salesperson can practice while holding an "inactive" license:
A. Yes, with broker permission
B. Only for past clients
C. No — inactive licensees cannot practice ✓
D. Only as a referral agent
Answer: C. Inactive license = cannot list, show, negotiate, or be paid.
Q 20.8·v1 An individual holding an inactive real estate license in Hawaii may engage in which of the following activities?
A. Assist with contract negotiations as a non-compensated volunteer
B. List properties and collect commissions with broker consent
C. Show properties to prospective buyers only
D. None—an inactive license prohibits all real estate practice ✓
Answer: D. An inactive license status means the licensee cannot perform any real estate services, including listing, showing, negotiating, or earning compensation, regardless of broker permission or client relationship.
Q 20.8·v2 If a real estate salesperson allows their license to become inactive, what activities remain legally permissible?
A. Real estate activities of any kind
B. No real estate practice activities whatsoever ✓
C. Advising referral sources about properties in exchange for fees
D. Representing clients in transactions if the broker signs off
Answer: B. Inactive status suspends all real estate authority; the licensee cannot list, show, negotiate, or earn compensation until the license is reactivated.
Q 20.8·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, which statement accurately describes the scope of practice for a person with an inactive license?
A. They possess no authority to engage in any licensed real estate activities ✓
B. They may perform transaction management but not client solicitation
C. They may practice only for existing clients under a broker's supervision
D. They may accept compensation if approved by the Real Estate Commission
Answer: A. An inactive license removes all rights to practice real estate; no exceptions exist for broker permission, client relationships, or specific transaction types.
Q 20.8·v4 A salesperson's license becomes inactive due to non-renewal. Can this person immediately resume showing properties to qualified buyers?
A. Yes, but only as a licensed assistant under a broker's direct supervision
B. Yes, provided the broker authorizes the activity in writing
C. No—the inactive status automatically prohibits all real estate practice ✓
D. Yes, as long as no compensation is accepted for those services
Answer: C. Inactive licensees cannot perform any real estate services—listing, showing, negotiating, or earning compensation—until their license is reactivated through proper REC procedures.
Q 20.8·v5 Which statement best describes what an inactive Hawaii real estate licensee is permitted to do?
A. Market properties to former clients without listing them publicly
B. Perform transaction coordination duties without a valid license
C. Accept commissions and conduct transactions with explicit broker consent
D. Engage in no real estate brokerage activities whatsoever ✓
Answer: D. An inactive license suspends all real estate practice rights; the licensee cannot list, show, negotiate, or receive compensation regardless of circumstances or relationships.
Q 20.8·v6 A salesperson places their license on inactive status. During this period, can they legally conduct any real estate transactions?
A. Yes, provided the broker authorizes it in writing
B. Yes, but only for investment properties they personally own
C. No, an inactive status prohibits all transactional activity ✓
D. Yes, as long as no compensation is involved
Answer: C. Inactive status means the licensee cannot practice real estate at all—no listing, showing, negotiating, or transaction involvement is permitted under Hawaii REC rules.
Q 20.8·v7 While holding an inactive real estate license, a salesperson is asked to negotiate a deal for a friend. What is the correct course of action?
A. They must decline because inactive licensees are prohibited from practicing ✓
B. They may proceed if the broker approves the arrangement
C. They may handle it if documented as a favor with no commission
D. They may assist as a consultant without formal brokerage duties
Answer: A. Inactive licensees cannot engage in any real estate practice, including negotiation or transaction facilitation, regardless of compensation status or broker permission.
Q 20.8·v8 An agent's license is converted to inactive status. Which of the following activities would constitute a violation?
A. Maintaining an office desk and email with company contact information
B. Answering general real estate questions from acquaintances
C. Attending broker meetings and reviewing market trends
D. Listing property, negotiating on behalf of clients, or receiving transaction-based compensation ✓
Answer: D. Inactive licensees are barred from all brokerage activities including listing, showing, negotiating, and compensation; only status-neutral activities like learning are permitted.
Q 20.8·v9 An individual holding an inactive real estate license in Hawaii is permitted to engage in which of the following activities?
A. Accept referral fees from active agents in their former office
B. Show properties to friends and family without compensation
C. No real estate practice activities whatsoever ✓
D. Negotiate commissions on behalf of a broker with written authorization
Answer: C. An inactive license holder is prohibited from all real estate practice activities including listing, showing, negotiating, or accepting compensation of any kind; the inactive status means no practice is permitted.
Q 20.9 A broker license requires how many hours of pre-licensing education in addition to active salesperson experience?
A. 60
B. 80 ✓
C. 120
D. 40
Answer: B. 80-hour Broker Pre-Licensing Course on top of salesperson licensure + experience.
Q 20.9·v1 After obtaining an active salesperson license, how many classroom hours must a candidate complete to qualify for a broker license in Hawaii?
A. 40 hours
B. 120 hours
C. 60 hours
D. 80 hours ✓
Answer: D. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission requires 80 hours of broker pre-licensing education for candidates who already hold an active salesperson license.
Q 20.9·v2 An experienced real estate salesperson in Hawaii wants to transition to broker status. What is the mandatory pre-licensing course requirement?
A. 45 hours of broker instruction
B. 120 hours of broker instruction
C. 100 hours of broker instruction
D. 80 hours of broker instruction ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC mandates an 80-hour broker pre-licensing course for licensed salespersons seeking broker licensure.
Q 20.9·v3 To become a broker in Hawaii after holding a current salesperson license, a candidate must complete a pre-licensing course of:
A. 80 hours minimum ✓
B. 40 hours minimum
C. 100 hours minimum
D. 60 hours minimum
Answer: A. The broker pre-licensing requirement in Hawaii is 80 hours of classroom instruction for applicants with active salesperson experience.
Q 20.9·v4 A licensed Hawaii salesperson applies for broker licensure. Beyond the experience requirement, the REC stipulates a pre-licensing education component of how many hours?
A. 80 hours ✓
B. 90 hours
C. 70 hours
D. 75 hours
Answer: A. Hawaii requires 80 hours of broker pre-licensing education in addition to qualifying salesperson experience for broker license applicants.
Q 20.9·v5 To transition from an active salesperson license to a broker license in Hawaii, what is the required classroom hour commitment for the broker pre-licensing course?
A. 60 hours
B. 100 hours
C. 120 hours
D. 80 hours ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii requires 80 hours of broker pre-licensing education as a prerequisite for obtaining a broker license, in addition to holding an active salesperson license and meeting experience requirements.
Q 20.9·v6 A salesperson with 2 years of active experience is applying for a broker license. Besides meeting the experience requirement, how many instructional hours must they complete?
A. 40 hours of broker training
B. 80 hours of broker training ✓
C. 70 hours of broker training
D. 110 hours of broker training
Answer: B. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission mandates an 80-hour broker pre-licensing course for all broker applicants, regardless of their salesperson experience level.
Q 20.9·v7 Which of the following correctly describes the classroom education requirement for obtaining a broker license in Hawaii?
A. 90 hours of approved broker education plus 3 years active salesperson experience
B. 50 hours of approved broker education plus 2 years active salesperson experience
C. 120 hours of approved broker education plus 5 years active salesperson experience
D. 80 hours of approved broker education plus active salesperson licensure ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's broker pre-licensing requirement is 80 hours of classroom instruction, which must be completed in addition to holding an active salesperson license and meeting experience qualifications.
Q 20.9·v8 If a salesperson completes all other broker license requirements, how many hours of pre-licensing education coursework must still be fulfilled?
A. 60 hours minimum
B. 80 hours minimum ✓
C. 30 hours minimum
D. 100 hours minimum
Answer: B. The 80-hour broker pre-licensing course is a mandatory education component that all applicants must complete before they can qualify for a broker license in Hawaii.
Q 20.9·v9 After obtaining an active Hawaii salesperson license and meeting experience requirements, how many classroom instruction hours must a candidate complete to qualify for a broker license?
A. 40 hours
B. 60 hours
C. 120 hours
D. 80 hours ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii requires 80 hours of broker pre-licensing education as a prerequisite, separate from and in addition to the salesperson license and experience requirement.
Q 20.10 A broker is responsible for the acts of:
A. Only employees
B. All licensees affiliated with the firm, including independent contractors ✓
C. Only licensees in writing
D. Only their own personal transactions
Answer: B. Broker liability extends to all affiliated licensees.
Q 20.10·v1 Under Hawaii real estate law, a broker's supervisory responsibility applies to which group of licensees?
A. Licensees under the broker's supervision only during business hours
B. Only those licensees who have signed an exclusivity agreement
C. All affiliated licensees, whether employees or independent contractors ✓
D. Only salespersons employed full-time at the brokerage
Answer: C. Broker responsibility encompasses all affiliated licensees regardless of employment classification or contractual arrangements; supervision applies at all times.
Q 20.10·v2 A broker can be held liable for violations committed by:
A. Unlicensed assistants working under direct broker supervision
B. Associated salespersons and independent contractors affiliated with the brokerage ✓
C. Only salespersons directly employed on the payroll
D. Licensees they have explicitly authorized in writing to act independently
Answer: B. Broker liability extends to all affiliated licensees including both employees and independent contractors without exception.
Q 20.10·v3 Which statement correctly describes a broker's fiduciary and supervisory obligations?
A. Brokers are liable only for violations by licensees who have signed non-compete agreements
B. Brokers can delegate all supervisory responsibility to a designated managing broker
C. Brokers are only responsible for violations occurring within the broker's personal office
D. Brokers bear responsibility for the professional conduct of all licensees affiliated with their firm ✓
Answer: D. A broker's responsibility is nondelegable and encompasses all affiliated licensees regardless of employment status or office location.
Q 20.10·v4 When determining broker liability for licensee misconduct, the scope includes:
A. All licensees currently holding a license issued by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
B. All licensees affiliated with the broker's firm, including both employees and independent contractor associates ✓
C. Licensees only during the time they are actively showing property
D. Only licensees who have completed the broker's mandatory training program
Answer: B. Broker accountability extends to all licensees affiliated with the firm regardless of their employment classification or training status.
Q 20.10·v5 Under Hawaii real estate law, which parties' conduct can create liability for a broker's firm?
A. All associated licensees, whether employed or operating as independent contractors ✓
B. Only salespersons who are W-2 employees on payroll
C. Exclusively the broker's personal transactions and those directly supervised
D. Only those licensees with written employment agreements signed before listing property
Answer: A. A broker is responsible for all affiliated licensees—including both employees and independent contractors—under Hawaii REC regulations and agency law principles.
Q 20.10·v6 A broker faces potential disciplinary action for the misconduct of which licensees?
A. Only licensees who report directly to the broker in an office location
B. Salespersons and associates who have signed restrictive covenants
C. Only those classified as employees in the company's payroll system
D. All licensees affiliated with the brokerage, regardless of employment classification ✓
Answer: D. Broker responsibility encompasses all affiliated licensees—employees and independent contractors alike—making the broker liable for their acts within the scope of their license.
Q 20.10·v7 Which of the following best describes a broker's scope of responsibility regarding licensee conduct?
A. Limited to transactions personally negotiated by the broker
B. Restricted to employees who work exclusively at the broker's main office
C. Applicable only when the licensee's misconduct is documented in writing beforehand
D. Extends to all licensees affiliated with the brokerage firm, including independent contractors ✓
Answer: D. A broker's supervisory and vicarious liability extends to all affiliated licensees—both employees and independent contractors—under Hawaii real estate licensing law.
Q 20.10·v8 A salesperson working as an independent contractor at a brokerage commits a violation. Which entity bears responsibility?
A. The broker and brokerage firm are responsible for all affiliated licensees' conduct ✓
B. Only the broker if the violation occurred during office business hours
C. Only the individual salesperson, since they are an independent contractor
D. The sponsoring broker, but only if the salesperson signed an agency agreement
Answer: A. Broker liability is not limited to employees; brokers are responsible for the conduct of all affiliated licensees, including independent contractors, under Hawaii REC regulations.
Q 20.10·v9 Under Hawaii real estate law, a broker's supervisory responsibility covers which of the following groups?
A. Only salespersons who are direct employees of the brokerage
B. Licensees who have signed an exclusive representation agreement
C. All associated licensees, whether employees or independent contractors operating under the firm's license ✓
D. Only transactions personally closed by the broker
Answer: C. A broker is responsible for supervising and controlling the conduct of all licensees affiliated with their firm, including both employees and independent contractor agents, regardless of employment classification.
Q 20.11 Salespersons cannot:
A. Provide CMA
B. Sign listing agreements in their own name or accept fees directly from customers ✓
C. Show property
D. Negotiate offers
Answer: B. Salesperson activities flow through and are paid through the employing broker.
Q 20.11·v1 Which of the following is prohibited for a Hawaii real estate salesperson?
A. Showing properties to prospective purchasers
B. Preparing market analysis reports for clients
C. Accepting compensation directly from a buyer without broker involvement ✓
D. Presenting counteroffers on behalf of clients
Answer: C. All salesperson compensation and client fee agreements must be processed through the employing broker; salespersons cannot contract independently with the public.
Q 20.11·v2 A salesperson may NOT:
A. Conduct comparative market analysis
B. Show occupied and vacant properties
C. Assist with offer preparation and negotiation
D. Enter into a listing agreement as the principal party and collect fees directly ✓
Answer: D. Salespersons operate under their broker's license and must conduct all business through the broker; they cannot bind clients directly or receive fees independently.
Q 20.11·v3 Under Hawaii real estate law, which activity is outside the scope of salesperson authority?
A. Listing properties and marketing them
B. Receiving a direct payment from a customer for services rendered ✓
C. Facilitating negotiations between buyer and seller
D. Preparing CMAs and property evaluations
Answer: B. Salespersons must work exclusively through their broker; any fees or payments from customers must flow through the broker-salesperson relationship, never directly.
Q 20.11·v4 A salesperson's employment arrangement requires that they:
A. Must have all client agreements and compensation routed through their sponsoring broker ✓
B. May provide appraisals and CMAs directly to the public
C. Are permitted to show properties without broker authorization
D. Can independently sign contracts and receive client fees as long as they split commissions with the broker
Answer: A. The broker-salesperson relationship mandates that all client contracts, agreements, and fee collection occur through the broker; salespersons cannot contract or accept payment independently.
Q 20.11·v5 Which of the following is prohibited for a salesperson under Hawaii real estate law?
A. Showing listed properties during business hours
B. Accepting compensation directly from a buyer without broker involvement ✓
C. Preparing a market analysis for a prospective seller
D. Presenting an offer to purchase on behalf of a client
Answer: B. All salesperson compensation and contractual agreements must flow through their employing broker; direct payment from clients violates the agency relationship and licensing requirements.
Q 20.11·v6 A salesperson violates Hawaii licensing law if they:
A. Enter into a listing contract in their own name and collect fees directly ✓
B. Schedule property showings for interested parties
C. Conduct a comparative market analysis
D. Assist in negotiating purchase terms
Answer: A. Salespersons act as agents of their broker and cannot independently sign contracts or accept client fees; all such transactions must be conducted through and compensated by the broker.
Q 20.11·v7 Under Hawaii real estate regulations, which activity is NOT permitted for a licensed salesperson?
A. Establishing a direct financial arrangement with clients for services rendered ✓
B. Negotiating lease or purchase terms with interested parties
C. Showing properties on behalf of their brokerage firm
D. Providing property valuations and market comparisons
Answer: A. Salespersons must operate exclusively under their broker's supervision and cannot create independent fee arrangements; all compensation must be processed by and distributed through the broker.
Q 20.11·v8 A salesperson's employment restrictions include the inability to:
A. Prepare or present comparative market analyses
B. Coordinate showings and open houses
C. Discuss property features and financing options with buyers
D. Sign listing agreements independently and receive payment directly from customers ✓
Answer: D. Salespersons lack independent authority to bind clients through contracts or collect compensation; all client relationships and payments must be facilitated by their employing broker.
Q 20.11·v9 Which of the following activities is prohibited for a Hawaii real estate salesperson?
A. Accepting commission payments directly from a client outside the broker's trust account ✓
B. Preparing comparative market analyses for prospective buyers
C. Assisting in contract negotiations between parties
D. Showing properties to qualified interested parties
Answer: A. All compensation and fee arrangements for salespersons must flow through their employing broker; direct acceptance of fees from customers violates Hawaii REC requirements and the employment relationship.
Q 20.12 Trust account records must be retained for at least:
A. 3 years (commonly) ✓
B. 5 years
C. Forever
D. 1 year
Answer: A. Hawaii rules typically require 3 years; verify current.
Q 20.12·v1 How long should a Hawaii real estate broker maintain client trust account documentation?
A. A minimum of 3 years ✓
B. 2 years from the date of deposit
C. Only during the license renewal period
D. Until the transaction closes
Answer: A. Hawaii Commission rules require brokers to retain trust account records for at least 3 years to ensure compliance and facilitate audits or dispute resolution.
Q 20.12·v2 Under Hawaii real estate regulations, what is the required retention period for escrow account ledgers and transaction records?
A. 6 months after transaction settlement
B. 18 months from the date of final disbursement
C. 3 years minimum ✓
D. Indefinitely, or until the broker retires
Answer: C. Hawaii REC standards mandate that trust and escrow account records be kept for no less than 3 years to support regulatory oversight and client protection.
Q 20.12·v3 A broker receives a client complaint regarding a transaction from 4 years ago. The broker claims the trust account records were discarded after 2 years. What violation has likely occurred?
A. No violation—2 years exceeds the standard federal requirement
B. The broker failed to maintain records for the standard 3-year minimum period ✓
C. The broker violated the 1-year retention rule for all escrow documents
D. The broker should have retained records only for 18 months
Answer: B. Hawaii regulations require a 3-year minimum retention period for trust account records; discarding them after 2 years violates this requirement and exposes the broker to disciplinary action.
Q 20.12·v4 Which statement best reflects Hawaii's trust account record-keeping requirements?
A. Records should be retained for at least 3 years as a standard practice ✓
B. Records need only be kept while the license is active
C. Records must be kept for 1 year and then may be destroyed
D. Records must be archived permanently in a bonded vault
Answer: A. Hawaii Commission rules establish a 3-year minimum retention period for trust account documents to ensure adequate documentation for compliance reviews and consumer protection.
Q 20.12·v5 A Hawaii broker maintains a client trust account. How long must detailed records of all deposits and withdrawals be kept on file?
A. A minimum of 3 years from the date of transaction ✓
B. Until the client relationship terminates
C. 6 months following final reconciliation
D. 2 years for active accounts, 1 year after closure
Answer: A. Hawaii real estate regulations require trust account records to be retained for at least 3 years to ensure audit compliance and regulatory oversight.
Q 20.12·v6 What is the standard retention period for broker trust account documentation under Hawaii real estate law?
A. Indefinitely, without exception
B. 2 years
C. 1 year per transaction
D. 3 years as a general requirement ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's regulatory framework establishes a 3-year record-retention standard for all trust account transactions and supporting documentation.
Q 20.12·v7 If a broker receives earnest money deposits in a trust account, the transaction records and bank statements must be preserved for no less than:
A. 3 years ✓
B. 5 years after property sale closing
C. 18 months
D. The duration of any subsequent disputes
Answer: A. Hawaii requires brokers to maintain trust account records, including earnest money documentation, for a minimum of 3 years to satisfy regulatory and audit requirements.
Q 20.12·v8 During a routine audit, a Hawaii real estate commission investigator asks to review trust account ledgers. What timeframe of records must a broker be able to produce?
A. The preceding 3 years ✓
B. A rolling 24-month period
C. All records since the broker's license inception
D. Current year only
Answer: A. Hawaii regulatory standards require brokers to maintain and produce trust account records covering at least the preceding 3 years for compliance verification.
Q 20.12·v9 When a Hawaii real estate licensee maintains a client trust account, what is the standard minimum period for which transaction records and account documentation must be preserved?
A. Until the transaction closes and all funds are disbursed
B. Two years, unless the property is in litigation
C. Seven years, consistent with federal tax requirements
D. Three years from the date of the transaction ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's regulatory standards require trust account records to be retained for a minimum of three years; this aligns with Hawaii Real Estate Commission rules for broker accountability and audit purposes.
Q 20.13 The Mandatory Agency Disclosure must be delivered:
A. After offer signed
B. Only if asked
C. Before any substantive interaction ✓
D. At closing
Answer: C. Before showing/negotiation/listing presentation — substantive interaction.
Q 20.13·v1 When must a licensee present the Mandatory Agency Disclosure form to a prospective buyer or seller?
A. During the listing appointment or initial buyer consultation, before discussing property details ✓
B. At the time the purchase agreement is executed
C. Within three business days after the first showing
D. Only upon written request by the consumer
Answer: A. The disclosure must be delivered before any substantive interaction—including listing presentations, buyer consultations, or property discussions—to ensure informed consent before the relationship develops.
Q 20.13·v2 A licensee may delay providing the Mandatory Agency Disclosure until:
A. The parties sign the purchase contract
B. The transaction closes
C. Never—it must precede any substantive business discussion ✓
D. The consumer requests it in writing
Answer: C. The disclosure cannot be delayed and must be given before substantive interaction begins; delaying until request, signing, or closing violates the agency disclosure requirement.
Q 20.13·v3 At what point in the transaction must the Mandatory Agency Disclosure be given to ensure compliance with Hawaii real estate law?
A. Once the earnest money deposit is received
B. After the consumer has selected the agent
C. Before the licensee engages in any negotiation, representation, or listing discussion ✓
D. Before the closing attorney reviews documents
Answer: C. Compliance requires disclosure before substantive interaction begins, including negotiations, property showings, and listing presentations, not after consumer selection or during closing stages.
Q 20.13·v4 Which statement regarding the timing of the Mandatory Agency Disclosure is correct?
A. It should be given at the initial showing as a courtesy
B. It satisfies requirements if provided with the purchase agreement
