C. It must be delivered prior to any substantive business communication or representation ✓
D. It may be omitted if the consumer is a repeat client
Answer: C. The disclosure must precede substantive interaction—before showings, negotiations, or listing discussions—regardless of client history or transaction stage.
Q 20.13·v5 When must a licensee provide the Mandatory Agency Disclosure form to a prospective buyer or seller?
A. Immediately after the purchase agreement is executed
B. Prior to engaging in any substantive discussions about a transaction ✓
C. During the final walkthrough before closing
D. Only when the client requests information about agency relationships
Answer: B. The Mandatory Agency Disclosure must be delivered before substantive interaction begins, which includes showing property, discussing terms, or conducting a listing presentation.
Q 20.13·v6 A real estate licensee is about to meet with a prospective seller to discuss listing their home. At what point should the Mandatory Agency Disclosure be given?
A. Only if the seller indicates they do not understand agency
B. After the seller signs the listing agreement
C. At the time of the closing appointment
D. Before beginning substantive discussions about representation ✓
Answer: D. Substantive interaction includes listing presentations and negotiations, so the disclosure must be delivered before these conversations begin.
Q 20.13·v7 Which statement correctly describes when the Mandatory Agency Disclosure requirement applies?
A. It is only required if the transaction involves a multiple listing service
B. It applies whenever a licensee engages in substantive representation discussions with a client or customer ✓
C. It must be provided to all parties at the closing table
D. It becomes effective only after an offer to purchase is presented
Answer: B. The disclosure is required before substantive interaction occurs, meaning before showings, negotiations, listing presentations, or any meaningful discussion about representation.
Q 20.13·v8 A licensee is working with a buyer who calls to discuss a property seen online. When must the Mandatory Agency Disclosure be delivered in this scenario?
A. Only if the buyer requests to work exclusively with the licensee
B. Before discussing the buyer's needs and property preferences ✓
C. After the buyer submits an offer on the property
D. At the time of the inspections
Answer: B. Discussing the buyer's needs and property preferences constitutes substantive interaction, which requires prior delivery of the Mandatory Agency Disclosure.
Q 20.13·v9 When is a licensee required to present the Mandatory Agency Disclosure form to a prospective buyer or seller?
A. Prior to commencing any substantive dealings or discussions ✓
B. At the time of final walkthrough inspection
C. Upon receipt of a signed purchase agreement
D. Only upon the client's written request for disclosure
Answer: A. The Mandatory Agency Disclosure must be delivered before substantive interaction begins, including before property showings, listing consultations, or negotiations occur.
Q 20.14 A "Core Course" in Hawaii CE is:
A. A test, not training
B. A national course
C. A state-mandated update reflecting recent law changes ✓
D. Optional elective
Answer: C. Core Course is mandatory portion of CE updated each cycle.
Q 20.14·v1 Under Hawaii's continuing education requirements, what is the primary purpose of a Core Course?
A. To ensure all licensees receive current training on Hawaii-specific regulatory updates and legal changes ✓
B. To allow licensees to choose only topics they find interesting
C. To serve as an examination that replaces classroom instruction
D. To fulfill the same requirement across all U.S. states without variation
Answer: A. Core Courses are mandatory Hawaii CE components designed to keep licensees current on state law changes and regulatory updates each renewal cycle.
Q 20.14·v2 Which statement accurately describes a Core Course requirement in Hawaii real estate licensing?
A. It is a voluntary supplemental course that licensees may take for additional credit
B. It is a proctored exam given in place of attending live training
C. It is a national standardized course administered by the National Association of REALTORS®
D. It is a required component of Hawaii's CE program that addresses recent statutory amendments and rule changes ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii's Core Course is a mandatory CE requirement updated regularly to reflect current state laws and regulatory developments affecting licensees.
Q 20.14·v3 What role does a Core Course play in Hawaii's CE renewal structure?
A. It is a compulsory course segment reflecting Hawaii's most recent legislative and regulatory changes ✓
B. It provides an alternative pathway so licensees can skip other required courses
C. It is an elective option available only to brokers, not salespersons
D. It functions as a standardized national requirement identical across all states
Answer: A. Core Courses are a non-optional part of Hawaii CE designed to update all licensees on newly enacted laws and regulatory modifications each renewal period.
Q 20.14·v4 A Hawaii licensee renewing their license must understand that a Core Course is best defined as:
A. A testing mechanism that substitutes for formal classroom training hours
B. A self-study optional module available through the Hawaii Real Estate Commission website
C. A continuing education requirement that meets the same standard in every U.S. jurisdiction
D. A mandatory education component covering current Hawaii law changes and regulatory updates ✓
Answer: D. Core Courses are required portions of Hawaii's CE curriculum specifically designed to keep licensees informed of changes in Hawaii real estate law and commission rules.
Q 20.14·v5 Which of the following best describes Hawaii's Core Course requirement for license renewal?
A. A required biennial update addressing current Hawaii real estate law and regulatory changes ✓
B. A proctored examination that counts toward CE hours upon passing
C. An online national standardized course administered by NAR
D. A voluntary training module agents may take for continuing education credits
Answer: A. Core Course is a mandatory component of Hawaii's CE cycle that updates licensees on recent state law changes and regulatory updates specific to Hawaii.
Q 20.14·v6 When Hawaii real estate agents complete their continuing education, the Core Course portion is:
A. Satisfied by passing a written exam instead of attending classroom training
B. An elective topic chosen by the agent based on personal interest
C. Designed by the National Association of REALTORS® and applies nationwide
D. A compulsory segment of the CE requirement that addresses Hawaii-specific legal updates ✓
Answer: D. Core Course is a mandatory part of Hawaii's CE that must be completed and covers state-mandated content reflecting recent changes in Hawaii real estate law.
Q 20.14·v7 Under Hawaii's continuing education rules, what role does the Core Course play?
A. It serves as an optional supplement for agents who want advanced training
B. It is a national reciprocal course recognized across all states
C. It fulfills the mandatory continuing education requirement with content on recent Hawaii law modifications ✓
D. It replaces the need for licensees to take an examination to renew
Answer: C. Core Course is the required, state-mandated portion of Hawaii CE that ensures agents receive updates on current Hawaii real estate laws and regulatory changes.
Q 20.14·v8 A licensee renewing their Hawaii real estate license must complete a Core Course because it is:
A. A specialized elective covering topics like commercial or residential practices
B. An internationally recognized course standard for real estate professionals
C. Part of the mandatory CE curriculum reflecting the latest Hawaii legal and regulatory developments ✓
D. A practical skills assessment rather than a formal instructional requirement
Answer: C. Core Course is a non-negotiable component of Hawaii's CE cycle designed to keep licensees current with recent changes in Hawaii real estate law and regulations.
Q 20.14·v9 Which of the following best describes Hawaii's Core Course requirement for license renewal?
A. A mandatory education component that addresses current statutory and regulatory changes ✓
B. A nationally standardized course applicable to all U.S. real estate professionals
C. An examination administered instead of traditional classroom instruction
D. A voluntary advanced training program offered by the Real Estate Commission
Answer: A. Core Course is a required, state-specific CE component that updates licensees on new laws and regulations affecting Hawaii real estate practice each renewal cycle.
Q 20.15 A licensee paying an undisclosed referral fee to a settlement service provider may violate:
A. Both RESPA and HRS 467 ✓
B. Only RESPA
C. Only HRS 467
D. Neither
Answer: A. RESPA Section 8 + HRS 467 prohibitions on undisclosed referral fees.
Q 20.15·v1 Which of the following statements best describes the legal exposure a Hawaii real estate agent faces when accepting an undisclosed referral fee from a title company?
A. No violation, as referral fees are permitted if documented internally
B. Violation of Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 467 only
C. Potential violation of both federal RESPA and Hawaii state law ✓
D. Violation of federal RESPA requirements only
Answer: C. RESPA Section 8 and HRS §467-14(14) both explicitly prohibit undisclosed referral fees to settlement service providers; violation of either or both statutes is possible.
Q 20.15·v2 A broker receives an undisclosed referral payment from an escrow company for directing clients to their services. This conduct would most likely constitute a violation of:
A. RESPA but not HRS 467, which allows referral arrangements
B. Neither statute, provided the referral fee is reasonable in amount
C. HRS 467 but not RESPA, since Hawaii law is more stringent
D. Both RESPA and HRS 467 provisions on referral fee prohibitions ✓
Answer: D. Both RESPA Section 8 and HRS §467-14(14) prohibit undisclosed referral fees to settlement service providers regardless of the fee's reasonableness or amount.
Q 20.15·v3 When a Hawaii licensee accepts payment from a mortgage lender in exchange for steering clients to that lender without proper disclosure, potential violations may include:
A. RESPA violations exclusively
B. Violations under both RESPA and HRS 467 ✓
C. Violations under neither if the licensee discloses the arrangement to the lender
D. HRS 467 violations exclusively
Answer: B. Undisclosed steering payments violate both RESPA Section 8 (federal) and HRS §467-14(14) (Hawaii state); disclosure must be to clients, not merely to the settlement service provider.
Q 20.15·v4 A salesperson receives a hidden referral fee from a home inspection company. Which regulatory violations could result from this arrangement?
A. Violation of both RESPA and Hawaii state law under HRS 467 ✓
B. Violation of HRS 467 alone
C. No violation if the fee is clearly marked on the HUD-1 settlement statement
D. Violation of RESPA alone
Answer: A. Undisclosed (hidden) referral fees breach both RESPA Section 8 and HRS §467-14(14), regardless of later disclosure on closing documents; the prohibition applies to the lack of upfront disclosure.
Q 20.15·v5 A Hawaii real estate agent receives a fee from a title company in exchange for client referrals but fails to disclose this arrangement to the referring party. This conduct most likely violates:
A. HRS 467 exclusively
B. Both federal RESPA regulations and Hawaii state law under HRS 467 ✓
C. Neither statute, as referral fees between licensees and settlement providers are permitted
D. RESPA Section 8 exclusively
Answer: B. Undisclosed referral fees to settlement service providers trigger both RESPA Section 8 (federal prohibition) and HRS 467 (Hawaii's mirror prohibition on unlawful kickbacks).
Q 20.15·v6 Which of the following scenarios would create a potential violation for a Hawaii licensee?
A. Accepting an undisclosed payment from an escrow agent for steering business their way ✓
B. Refusing referral fees from any settlement service provider
C. Charging clients a documented transaction fee based on property value
D. Disclosing all referral fee arrangements with closing attorneys to clients in writing
Answer: A. Accepting undisclosed payments from settlement service providers violates both RESPA Section 8 and HRS 467, regardless of whether the licensee intended harm.
Q 20.15·v7 A settlement service provider offers a licensee a concealed kickback arrangement. Under Hawaii and federal law, what is the regulatory status of this proposal?
A. Legal as long as the consumer ultimately receives a competitive rate
B. Prohibited by both RESPA and HRS 467 ✓
C. Violates RESPA but not Hawaii state regulations
D. Permissible under HRS 467 if properly documented
Answer: B. Both RESPA Section 8 and HRS 467 explicitly prohibit undisclosed referral fees or kickbacks to settlement service providers, regardless of documentation or consumer benefit claims.
Q 20.15·v8 If a Hawaii licensee secretly receives compensation from a mortgage lender for referrals, which legal framework(s) would likely be implicated?
A. Licensing law only; no violation occurs absent consumer injury
B. Federal RESPA requirements and Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 467 ✓
C. Only the Real Estate Commission's ethical rules, not statutory law
D. Only Hawaii state law; RESPA does not apply to residential transactions
Answer: B. Secret referral payments to settlement service providers breach both RESPA Section 8 (federal) and HRS 467 (state), creating dual statutory violations.
Q 20.15·v9 A Hawaii real estate agent receives a fee from a title company in exchange for steering clients to that company's services without disclosing the arrangement to the clients. Which regulatory requirements has the agent potentially violated?
A. Neither, because referral fees are permissible if documented internally
B. Both federal RESPA regulations and Hawaii's HRS 467 statute ✓
C. HRS 467 only, since it is Hawaii state law
D. RESPA only, since federal law always supersedes state law
Answer: B. Undisclosed referral fees violate both RESPA Section 8 (federal) and HRS 467 (Hawaii state law), which independently prohibit such arrangements regardless of internal documentation.
Q 20.16 Failure to supervise a licensee:
A. Is only a tort
B. Can result in broker license discipline ✓
C. Only applies to employees
D. Cannot affect the broker's license
Answer: B. Broker license can be sanctioned for failure to supervise.
Q 20.16·v1 Under Hawaii real estate law, what is a potential consequence to a broker who neglects to properly oversee the conduct of their licensees?
A. The broker faces civil liability only, with no regulatory sanctions
B. Only the individual licensee's license is subject to discipline
C. The broker must file a notice of noncompliance but cannot lose their license
D. Disciplinary action may be taken against the broker's license ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC regulations hold brokers accountable through license discipline when they fail to supervise licensees under their management.
Q 20.16·v2 A broker's inadequate supervision of licensed agents could potentially result in:
A. A requirement to attend continuing education with no other penalties
B. Automatic reinstatement after a six-month waiting period
C. Sanctions against the broker's license by the Hawaii REC ✓
D. A complaint that only affects the agent's license status
Answer: C. Brokers can face license discipline, including suspension or revocation, for failing to maintain proper supervision over their licensees' activities.
Q 20.16·v3 Which statement correctly describes the regulatory implications of a broker's failure to supervise?
A. It cannot result in adverse actions against the broker's license
B. It applies exclusively to brokers managing independent contractors
C. The broker's license is subject to disciplinary action by the REC ✓
D. It is a violation enforceable only through civil court proceedings
Answer: C. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission can discipline a broker's license for inadequate supervision, regardless of the licensee's employment status.
Q 20.16·v4 A licensee's violation of real estate law while working under a broker could expose the broker to:
A. Liability limited to restitution paid directly to the consumer
B. Fines payable to the licensee personally
C. Criminal charges only, with no administrative sanctions
D. Potential license discipline for insufficient oversight ✓
Answer: D. Brokers bear responsibility through potential REC license sanctions when they fail to properly supervise licensees' compliance with real estate laws.
Q 20.16·v5 A Hawaii broker fails to adequately supervise one of her associate licensees. What is a possible consequence for the broker?
A. The broker's license remains unaffected as supervisory liability is the agent's responsibility
B. The broker can only be held liable in civil court, not administratively
C. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission may impose discipline against the broker's license ✓
D. Supervision requirements apply only to unlicensed office staff
Answer: C. The REC holds brokers accountable for supervising licensees and can discipline the broker's license for failure to do so; this is an administrative sanction, not merely a civil remedy.
Q 20.16·v6 Which statement correctly describes the regulatory consequence of a broker's inadequate supervision of affiliated licensees?
A. Supervision duties apply only to brokers in offices with more than five agents
B. The broker is protected from any license action if a single licensee violates the law
C. Disciplinary action may be taken against the broker's license by the Hawaii REC ✓
D. Failure to supervise constitutes a contractual breach but not a regulatory violation
Answer: C. The Hawaii REC can discipline a broker's license for failure to properly supervise licensees under their control, making it a direct regulatory matter.
Q 20.16·v7 A broker in Hawaii receives a complaint about an associate licensee's conduct. The broker did not monitor the agent's transaction files or review compliance procedures. What risk does the broker face?
A. The complaint is automatically dismissed because it targets the associate, not the broker
B. Regulatory liability applies only if the licensee was an independent contractor, not an employee
C. Risk of civil lawsuit only, with no regulatory impact
D. Potential disciplinary action against the broker's own license ✓
Answer: D. A broker's failure to supervise is grounds for the REC to take disciplinary action against the broker's license independently of action taken against the associate licensee.
Q 20.16·v8 Under Hawaii real estate law, a broker's license may be subject to discipline if the broker:
A. Delegates all supervisory tasks to a designated broker representative without retaining oversight responsibility
B. Fails to exercise adequate supervision over the business activities of licensed associates ✓
C. Does not document social interactions with staff but maintains transaction file reviews
D. Employs only salaried brokers rather than commissioned sales associates
Answer: B. The Hawaii REC requires brokers to maintain active supervision of their licensees, and inadequate supervision can result in disciplinary sanctions against the broker's license.
Q 20.16·v9 A broker who fails to adequately oversee the activities of a sponsored salesperson may face which consequence?
A. Automatic license revocation without any hearing process
B. Penalties limited to fines paid by the individual licensee, not the broker
C. Administrative discipline or suspension of the broker's license by the Hawaii Real Estate Commission ✓
D. A civil lawsuit only, with no regulatory action possible
Answer: C. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission has authority to discipline a broker's license for inadequate supervision of sponsored licensees, including warnings, fines, or license suspension/revocation.
Appendix B

Elevated-Difficulty Examination Bank

The following items comprise the Academy's complete elevated-difficulty pool used to assemble the Hard and Gnarly mock examinations — longer scenarios, two-correct-but-one-best constructions, and the trickier financing, proration, and agency edge cases. Every item and every variant is reproduced with its answer and rationale.

Tough 1 A buyer's agent learns during a transaction that the buyer plans to default on their mortgage within six months to force a short sale and walk away with cash from a side arrangement. The agent's PRIMARY duty in this moment is to:
A. Disclose the buyer's intent to the listing agent and seller
B. Withdraw from the transaction; the buyer's plan constitutes fraud the agent cannot facilitate ✓
C. Report the buyer to the lender to protect the lender's interest
D. Continue representing the buyer because all communications are confidential
Answer: B. Confidentiality protects lawful confidences only. Knowing participation in mortgage fraud violates the agent's duty of legality and exposes the licensee. The correct course is to withdraw and document — not unilaterally disclose private information, and not "report" the buyer to a non-client lender.
Tough 2 Of the fiduciary duties owed by an agent to a principal, which one survives the termination of the agency relationship?
A. Loyalty
B. Confidentiality ✓
C. Obedience
D. Accountability
Answer: B. Confidentiality persists indefinitely after the agency ends — an agent cannot disclose a former principal's lowest acceptable price years later. Obedience, accountability, and loyalty terminate with the relationship.
Tough 3 A buyer is qualified for a $720,000 loan at 6.5% on a 30-year fixed. Two discount points are paid by the buyer at closing. Approximately how much do the points cost the buyer?
A. $28,800
B. $14,400 ✓
C. $1,440
D. $7,200
Answer: B. One discount point equals 1% of the loan amount. Two points on $720,000 = 0.02 × $720,000 = $14,400. Note the trap: the question gives the rate and term to make you reach for a payment calculation that isn't asked.
Tough 4 Three recent sales of comparable Kailua homes net to: $1,420,000 (after $40K of adjustments), $1,460,000 (after $20K of adjustments), and $1,490,000 (after $80K of adjustments). For valuation purposes the BEST indicator of market value among these comps is:
A. $1,490,000 — closest to current market trend
B. $1,420,000 — the lowest adjusted figure is the most conservative
C. The arithmetic average of all three
D. $1,460,000 — required the fewest adjustments and is therefore the most reliable ✓
Answer: D. In the sales comparison approach, the comp requiring the FEWEST adjustments is the most reliable indicator — its similarity to the subject is doing the work, not your adjustments. Averaging masks data quality differences.
Tough 5 Under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 467, a real estate licensee who knowingly handles trust funds in violation of REC rules is MOST exposed to:
A. A criminal misdemeanor charge only
B. Both REC disciplinary action AND potential criminal liability ✓
C. Only a fine, since trust fund mishandling is administrative in Hawaii
D. A civil suit by the client only
Answer: B. Hawaii REC disciplinary powers and criminal statutes are not mutually exclusive. Knowing mishandling of trust funds can trigger both administrative discipline (suspension, revocation, fines) AND, depending on facts, criminal prosecution.
Tough 6 Under HRS 514B, a condominium developer must deliver the Public Report to a prospective purchaser:
A. Before the purchaser signs a binding contract ✓
B. Only upon written request from the purchaser
C. After the contract is signed but before closing
D. Within 30 days of association turnover
Answer: A. HRS 514B requires the developer to deliver the Public Report BEFORE a purchaser becomes contractually bound — so the buyer can make an informed decision. Post-signing delivery defeats the disclosure purpose.
Tough 7 A non-resident seller closes on a $950,000 Hawaii investment property. Assuming no exemption applies, the HARPTA withholding due at closing is:
A. $28,500
B. $95,000
C. $68,875 ✓
D. $47,500
Answer: C. HARPTA withholding is 7.25% of the gross sales price for non-resident sellers (not 3% — that was the old rate). 0.0725 × $950,000 = $68,875. Watch for distractors using outdated rates.
Tough 8 Which of the following is NOT a required disclosure to a buyer of leasehold residential property in Hawaii?
A. Lease rent reopening / renegotiation dates
B. The ground lease term remaining
C. The fee owner's asking price to convert to fee simple ✓
D. The lease rent amount and adjustment schedule
Answer: C. Lease term, lease rent, and reopening dates are required disclosures because they materially affect the buyer's long-term cost. The fee owner's asking conversion price is not a disclosure obligation — that price may not even exist or be public.
Tough 9 A buyer signs an offer on Monday at 3 PM with an expiration of "Wednesday at 5 PM." The seller signs and delivers acceptance Wednesday at 6:15 PM. The legal result is:
A. No contract — a late acceptance is a counteroffer that the buyer can accept or reject ✓
B. A contract pending court determination of "reasonable time"
C. A valid contract — the 5 PM deadline applies only to revocation
D. A valid contract — the seller still accepted in writing
Answer: A. An offer dies at its stated expiration. A "late acceptance" is legally a counteroffer back to the original offeror, who may accept it, reject it, or counter again. There is no automatic contract.
Tough 10 A licensee acts as a dual agent for both buyer and seller in a transaction with informed written consent from both parties. Which duty is MOST diminished by dual agency?
A. Disclosure
B. Accountability
C. Loyalty ✓
D. Care
Answer: C. Loyalty (putting one principal's interests above the other's) cannot be fully delivered to two parties with opposing economic interests. Care, disclosure, and accountability remain enforceable, but loyalty is the structural casualty of dual agency.
Tough 11 An out-of-state licensee meets a Hawaii buyer at a mainland trade show and discusses a Big Island property for sale. Under Hawaii law, the out-of-state licensee:
A. May negotiate the Hawaii portion of the transaction under reciprocity
B. May complete the transaction if both parties consent
C. Must be a Hawaii broker; Hawaii has no licensing-recognition provisions of any kind
D. May refer the buyer to a Hawaii-licensed broker for a referral fee, but cannot perform Hawaii real estate brokerage acts ✓
Answer: D. A non-licensed-in-Hawaii agent cannot lawfully perform Hawaii brokerage acts even if they originated the lead. The lawful path is a referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker for a referral fee. Hawaii does not have full reciprocity with most states.
Tough 12 A property assessed at $1,200,000 has a tax rate of $11.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. The annual property tax is approximately:
A. $1,332
B. $132,000
C. $13,320 ✓
D. $11,100
Answer: C. ($1,200,000 / $1,000) × $11.10 = 1,200 × 11.10 = $13,320. Decimal-place errors are the most common trap here — practice unit math, not just calculator math.
Tough 13 A seller of a fee-simple Oahu single-family home knows the property had a violent crime occur in the master bedroom three years ago. The seller asks the listing agent whether they have to disclose this to buyers. The agent's BEST response is:
A. Hawaii requires disclosure of all stigmatizing events; you must list it on the Seller Real Property Disclosure Statement
B. Federal Fair Housing law prohibits any disclosure of crimes that could "blockbust" the neighborhood
C. The agent must disclose it whether or not the seller agrees, under the agent's duty of disclosure to third parties
D. Hawaii law does not require disclosure of stigmatizing events such as past crimes that did not affect the physical property; but a direct buyer question would require a truthful answer ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii follows the general rule: stigmatizing events (crimes not affecting physical condition, deaths from natural causes, etc.) are not required disclosures on the Seller Disclosure Statement. However, if a buyer asks directly, an agent cannot answer falsely — that crosses into misrepresentation. The "best" answer threads both rules.
Tough 14 A seller tells the listing agent in confidence that she will accept any offer above $1.4M. The listing agent then meets with a prospective buyer who is unrepresented. The buyer asks, "What's the lowest the seller will accept?" The agent's correct response is:
A. Disclose the figure but only after the buyer signs a buyer-broker agreement
B. Disclose the figure if the buyer offers to pay the agent a commission
C. Truthfully disclose the $1.4M figure — the buyer asked directly
D. Decline to disclose; recommend the buyer submit their best offer ✓
Answer: D. The seller is the principal. Disclosing the seller's confidential reservation price to a buyer — whether the buyer is represented or not — violates the duty of loyalty and confidentiality. The agent must decline, regardless of whether a buyer-broker relationship is later established.
Tough 15 A seller resides in California year-round but owns a Kihei condo she rents out and visits twice a year. She sells the condo for $785,000. At closing, the listing agent's buyer mentions the seller "should be HARPTA-exempt because she's a U.S. citizen." The agent should:
A. Disagree — HARPTA applies based on Hawaii residency status, not citizenship; the seller appears to be a non-resident and likely subject to 7.25% withholding ✓
B. Apply only the FIRPTA federal rules, since HARPTA was repealed in 2020
C. Agree — U.S. citizens are exempt from HARPTA
D. Defer to the escrow agent and decline to comment
Answer: A. HARPTA (HRS 235-68) keys on whether the seller is a Hawaii RESIDENT for state income tax purposes, not on citizenship. A California-domiciled owner is a non-resident regardless of citizenship. FIRPTA is the separate federal counterpart and was not repealed. The agent shouldn't parrot the buyer's incorrect statement.
Tough 16 Consider four loans, each on a $600,000 home with 10% down. Which loan has the LOWEST total interest paid over its life?
A. 30-year fixed at 5.95% with one discount point
B. 15-year fixed at 5.75% ✓
C. 30-year fixed at 6.25%
D. 20-year fixed at 6.00%
Answer: B. A 15-year fixed at 5.75% pays the least total interest by far — shorter term dominates rate differences for total-interest math. The 30-year-with-point option may have a lower stated rate, but it still amortizes over 30 years with the point added to upfront cost.
Tough 17 A condo board on the windward side of Oahu wants to ban short-term rentals (under 30 days) building-wide. Under HRS 514B and recent Hawaii court guidance, the board's action is MOST LIKELY:
A. Invalid because the federal Fair Housing Act protects vacation use
B. Automatically valid as a routine board policy under the board's general rule-making authority
C. Valid only if the original developer's declaration permits the restriction or a supermajority of owners amends the declaration ✓
D. Invalid because Hawaii state law preempts all local short-term-rental regulation
Answer: C. Use restrictions of this scope generally require an amendment to the condominium declaration — not a simple board policy — under HRS 514B. The supermajority threshold and developer original-declaration language control. Boards routinely overreach here, and Hawaii courts have struck down board-only bans.
Tough 18 A listing agent receives two simultaneous offers: one at full asking price from a buyer the seller dislikes personally, and one at $30,000 below asking from a buyer the seller "really likes." The agent should:
A. Recommend the seller accept the higher offer because failing to maximize price would violate the agent's duty of loyalty
B. Present only the higher offer, since the seller's economic interest is paramount
C. Present both offers truthfully and let the seller choose; the seller can lawfully select either offer for any non-protected-class reason ✓
D. Present both, but advise the seller that taking the lower offer creates a legal risk under fair housing law
Answer: C. The agent must present all offers and respect the seller's right to choose. The seller is free to take a lower offer for personal preference — UNLESS the preference is based on a protected class (race, religion, etc.). "Personal dislike" alone is not unlawful. The agent's loyalty does not override the principal's decision.
Tough 19 Under the Hawaii Association of Realtors Standard Purchase Contract, the time period within which the buyer must complete due diligence and either approve or terminate is GENERALLY governed by:
A. The contract's contingency timeline as negotiated and inserted by the parties ✓
B. The Hawaii REC default of 14 calendar days
C. A statutory 30-day window per HRS 484A
D. The "as is" clause, which eliminates any due-diligence period
Answer: A. There is no fixed statutory window. The Hawaii Standard Purchase Contract provides default fields the parties fill in (often 10–17 days for inspection, financing, etc.). The negotiated timeline governs, and an "as is" sale does not eliminate a buyer's right to inspect — it shifts cost-of-repair allocation.
Tough 20 A property sells for $1,850,000. Closing is on April 14. Annual property tax of $9,600 has not yet been paid by the seller for the current tax year (assume calendar-year tax cycle, 360-day year for proration). At closing, the seller will be CREDITED or DEBITED for taxes in the amount of:
A. Credited $9,600
B. Debited $6,826.67
C. Credited $2,746.67
D. Debited $2,746.67 ✓
Answer: D. The seller owes tax for days owned. Jan 1 – Apr 13 = 103 days (3×30 + 13). 103/360 × $9,600 = $2,746.67. The seller is DEBITED that amount and the buyer is credited.
Tough 21 A Hawaii salesperson licensee owns 60% of a corporation and wants the corporation to purchase a property listed by another agent at the licensee's brokerage. Under Hawaii license law, the licensee MUST:
A. Resign from active licensure before the purchase
B. Disclose to the seller in writing that they hold a real estate license and have a principal interest in the buying entity ✓
C. Have their broker sign the purchase contract on their behalf
D. Refrain from the purchase; licensee-as-principal transactions are prohibited
Answer: B. Hawaii license law requires written disclosure when a licensee acts as a principal (buyer or seller, including through entities they control). Disclosure — not abstention — is the rule. The broker doesn't sign on their behalf; the licensee discloses and proceeds.
Tough 22 A property owner refuses to rent a unit to a family with two young children, stating "the unit isn't safe for kids" because there are stairs. Under the federal Fair Housing Act, this refusal is:
A. Permissible if the owner offers to rent a different unit on the ground floor
B. A violation of fair housing law — familial status is a protected class and "safety" pretexts based on age of children are unlawful ✓
C. Permissible — safety concerns are a legitimate business reason
D. Permissible because the federal Fair Housing Act does not protect against age discrimination
Answer: B. Familial status (presence of children under 18) is a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act amendments of 1988. An owner cannot refuse to rent based on the presence of children, even framed as a safety concern. "I'll offer you a different unit" is steering, also unlawful. The exception applies only to legitimate senior housing.
Tough 23 A buyer is purchasing a property in the Land Court system. Compared with property in the Regular System, the Land Court system provides which of the following PRIMARY advantages?
A. Automatic clearance of all liens upon transfer
B. The Certificate of Title is itself the conclusive evidence of ownership, eliminating the need for separate chain-of-title research ✓
C. Exemption from the conveyance tax
D. Lower title insurance premiums and faster closings
Answer: B. Hawaii operates a dual recording system: the Regular System (chain-of-title research required) and the Land Court system (Torrens-style — the Certificate of Title is conclusive). Liens still attach in Land Court, and conveyance tax applies regardless. The primary advantage is title certainty.
Tough 24 A buyer's purchase contract for a $2.1M Oahu home contains a financing contingency. The buyer's lender denies the loan in writing on Day 18 of a 21-day financing contingency window. The buyer wants to terminate and recover the deposit. The CORRECT analysis is:
A. The contingency cannot be invoked unless the buyer applies to at least three lenders
B. The buyer is in default; once the seller accepted, the buyer is locked in
C. The seller may keep the deposit because the buyer "caused" the denial by their financial profile
D. The buyer may terminate within the contingency window upon proof of good-faith denial and is entitled to the deposit back ✓
Answer: D. A financing contingency entitles the buyer to terminate and recover the deposit if the lender denies the loan in good faith within the contingency window — even on Day 18. There is no "three lenders" rule. The seller cannot retain the deposit for a contingency-protected denial.
Tough·v1 A residential property changes hands on June 20 for $1,850,000. The seller has not paid the annual property tax bill of $9,600 for the current calendar year (use 360-day year for proration purposes). How will unpaid property taxes be settled at closing?
A. Seller receives a credit of $9,600
B. Seller receives a credit of $4,507
C. Seller receives a debit of $4,507 ✓
D. Buyer assumes full $9,600 liability
Answer: C. The seller owned Jan 1 – June 19 = 169 days (5×30 + 19). 169/360 × $9,600 = $4,506.67 ≈ $4,507. The seller is DEBITED their share and the buyer is credited the same amount.
Tough·v2 At closing on September 5, a property sells for $2,100,000. Annual property taxes of $12,000 remain unpaid for the current tax year (calendar-year tax basis, 360-day proration method). The settlement of unpaid taxes will result in:
A. A debit to seller and credit to buyer for approximately $8,133 ✓
B. A debit to buyer and credit to seller for $3,650
C. A debit to seller only; buyer pays nothing
D. A credit to seller equal to full annual tax amount
Answer: A. Jan 1 – Sept 4 = 244 days (8×30 + 4). 244/360 × $12,000 = $8,133.33. The seller is DEBITED this amount and the buyer is credited the same.
Tough·v3 A commercial property closes on March 10 with a purchase price of $3,500,000. The seller has not yet remitted the current year's property taxes of $18,000 (assume 360-day year and calendar-year tax year). At settlement, the unpaid tax proration will be handled by:
A. Debiting the seller approximately $3,450 ✓
B. Charging the buyer an additional $18,000 at closing
C. Crediting the seller $3,450
D. Crediting the buyer and debiting the seller $9,000
Answer: A. Jan 1 – Mar 9 = 69 days (2×30 + 9). 69/360 × $18,000 = $3,450 owed by the seller. The seller is DEBITED $3,450 and the buyer is credited the same.
Tough·v4 A residential property transfers on June 21. The seller has not paid the annual property tax bill of $7,200 (calendar-year tax period, 360-day proration year). What entry appears on the seller's side of the closing statement for property tax adjustment?
A. Debit of $3,400 ✓
B. Debit of $1,800
C. Credit of $7,200
D. Credit of $3,400
Answer: A. The seller owned Jan 1 – June 20 = 170 days (5×30 + 20). 170/360 × $7,200 = $3,400. The seller is DEBITED their tax obligation and the buyer is credited.
Tough·v5 At closing on March 3, a buyer takes title to a home. The seller has not remitted the current year's property tax of $8,400 (assume 30-day months, 360-day year). Regarding property tax proration, the seller will receive which adjustment?
A. A credit of $8,400
B. A debit of $1,447 ✓
C. A credit of $1,447
D. A debit of $7,140
Answer: B. Jan 1 – Mar 2 = 62 days (2×30 + 2). 62/360 × $8,400 = $1,446.67 ≈ $1,447. The seller is DEBITED and the buyer receives the corresponding credit.
Tough·v6 A commercial office building sells on August 5. Annual property tax of $14,400 remains unpaid for the year (360-day year, 30-day month calculation). How is the unpaid tax adjustment recorded on the seller's closing settlement?
A. Credit $14,400
B. Credit $10,920
C. Debit $8,560 ✓
D. Debit $3,600
Answer: C. The seller owned Jan 1 – Aug 4 = 214 days (7×30 + 4). 214/360 × $14,400 = $8,560. The seller is DEBITED this amount and the buyer is credited the same.
Tough·v7 A residential property closes on March 22 with a purchase price of $2,100,000. The current property tax bill for the year totals $8,400 and remains unpaid by the seller at closing time. Using a 360-day proration method (30-day months), which entry appears on the closing statement?
A. Seller debit of $1,890 ✓
B. Seller credit of $1,890
C. Seller credit of $8,400
D. Seller debit of $5,600
Answer: A. The seller owns Jan 1 – Mar 21 = 81 days (30+30+21). 81/360 × $8,400 = $1,890. The seller is DEBITED their share for the days owned; the buyer is credited the same.
Tough·v8 At a closing on July 9, a property exchanges hands with a sales price of $1,620,000. Annual property taxes of $7,200 for the year have not been paid. The seller must be shown on the closing statement as receiving a debit or credit for property tax in the approximate amount of (using 360-day year):
A. Credit $3,600
B. Debit $7,200
C. Credit $3,300
D. Debit $3,747 ✓
Answer: D. Jan 1 – July 8 = 188 days (6×30 + 8). 188/360 × $7,200 = $3,746.67 ≈ $3,747. The seller is DEBITED their prorated tax obligation; the buyer is credited the same.
Tough·v9 A closing occurs on May 18 on a $1,950,000 purchase. The annual property tax of $10,800 remains outstanding as of the closing date. Assuming a 360-day year and standard 30-day monthly proration, the closing statement will show a tax adjustment that is:
A. A buyer debit of approximately $6,900
B. A seller debit of approximately $4,050 ✓
C. A buyer credit of approximately $4,050
D. A seller credit of $10,800
Answer: B. From Jan 1 through May 17 = 137 days (Jan 30 + Feb 30 + Mar 30 + Apr 30 + May 17 = 137). The seller's tax liability for days owned is 137/360 × $10,800 = $4,116.67, approximately $4,050. A seller debit indicates the seller must pay (or credit the buyer with) their prorated share of the unpaid annual tax obligation.
Tough·v10 A seller agrees to pay 2.5 discount points on behalf of the buyer to facilitate a $720,000 mortgage loan origination. What is the approximate cost in dollars that the seller will credit at closing?
A. $9,000
B. $14,400
C. $18,000 ✓
D. $7,200
Answer: C. One discount point = 1% of loan amount. 2.5 points on $720,000 = 0.025 × $720,000 = $18,000. The question tests whether the candidate understands that points are calculated as a percentage of principal regardless of rate or term.
Tough·v11 During underwriting, a borrower negotiates to buy down the interest rate by paying 3 discount points upfront on a $720,000 loan. Assuming standard point calculation, approximately what amount will appear as a credit to the buyer's closing statement?
A. $28,800
B. $14,400
C. $10,800
D. $21,600 ✓
Answer: D. Three discount points on $720,000 = 0.03 × $720,000 = $21,600. This variant shifts focus to 'buying down the rate' to test whether the student relies on memorized calculation mechanics rather than understanding the rate-adjustment narrative.
Tough·v12 A lender offers a 30-year fixed loan for $720,000 and quotes a rate of 5.9% with an estimated 1.5 discount points charged to the buyer. What is the approximate out-of-pocket cost for the points at closing?
A. $7,200
B. $10,800 ✓
C. $5,400
D. $14,400
Answer: B. One discount point = 1% of the loan principal. 1.5 points on $720,000 = 0.015 × $720,000 = $10,800. The quoted rate of 5.9% is a classic red herring—points depend only on loan amount, not the interest rate itself.
Tough·v13 A lender quotes a borrower on a $720,000 mortgage at 6.5% interest over 30 years. The borrower elects to buy down the rate by purchasing two discount points at origination. What is the approximate out-of-pocket cost to the borrower for those points?
A. $7,200
B. $2,880
C. $14,400 ✓
D. $28,800
Answer: C. One discount point = 1% of loan amount. Two points = 2% of $720,000 = $14,400. The rate and term are red herrings meant to distract from the straightforward point calculation.
Tough·v14 A buyer finances $720,000 and agrees to pay 2 discount points to reduce the interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage. Ignoring the interest rate itself, what does the buyer pay upfront for the points?
A. $10,800
B. $36,000
C. $14,400 ✓
D. $21,600
Answer: C. Discount points are calculated as a percentage of the principal loan amount, not the payment or rate. Two points = 0.02 × $720,000 = $14,400 paid at closing.
Tough·v15 A buyer obtains approval for a $720,000 loan at 6.5% interest on a 30-year term. To secure a lower rate, the buyer pays 2 origination discount points. Approximately how much cash does the buyer need at closing for the points alone?
A. $7,200
B. $21,600
C. $43,200
D. $14,400 ✓
Answer: D. Each discount point costs 1% of the loan principal. Two points on $720,000 = $14,400. The interest rate and amortization period are extraneous information.
Tough·v16 A seller agrees to pay 1.5 discount points on behalf of the buyer to facilitate the sale. The purchase price is $720,000 and financing covers 100% of value. What is the approximate cost of those points?
A. $21,600
B. $43,200
C. $14,400
D. $10,800 ✓
Answer: D. Discount points are a percentage of the loan amount. With 100% financing the loan equals the $720,000 price. 1.5 points = 0.015 × $720,000 = $10,800.
Tough·v17 A borrower obtains pre-approval for a $720,000 mortgage at 5.75% interest over 30 years. At closing, the lender discloses that the buyer will pay 2 points to buy down the rate. Approximately what dollar amount should the buyer expect to pay for these points?
A. $7,200
B. $28,800
C. $14,400 ✓
D. $36,000
Answer: C. One discount point = 1% of the loan amount. Two points = 2% of $720,000 = 0.02 × $720,000 = $14,400. The rate and term are provided as distractors; calculating a monthly payment would yield a much larger wrong answer.
Tough·v18 In a Hawaii residential transaction, a buyer finances $720,000 and negotiates to pay discount points to lower the interest rate from 6.8% to 6.2%. The lender charges 2 points for this rate adjustment. What is the approximate upfront cost in points?
A. $21,600
B. $72,000
C. $14,400 ✓
D. $4,320
Answer: C. Discount points are always calculated as 1% of the loan amount per point. Two points on a $720,000 loan = 2 × (0.01 × $720,000) = $14,400. The rate reduction and loan-to-value context are red herrings meant to trigger incorrect payment or equity calculations.
Tough·v19 A Hawaii appraiser is reconciling three comparable sales for a Honolulu property. Sale A required $35,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,550,000 adjusted; Sale B required $85,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,505,000 adjusted; Sale C required $60,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,480,000 adjusted. Which adjusted sale price should carry the MOST weight in the final value opinion?
A. $1,550,000 because it required the smallest dollar amount of adjustments ✓
B. $1,505,000 because it falls in the middle of the three values
C. All three equally, weighted by their proximity to the subject property's age
D. $1,480,000 because it represents the lowest price point in the market
Answer: A. The comparable requiring the fewest adjustments is most reliable because its inherent similarity to the subject requires minimal modification, meaning the actual market data carries greater credibility than the appraiser's subjective estimates.
Tough·v20 When using the sales comparison approach to value a Windward Oahu home, an appraiser identifies three recent sales. Comp 1 sold for $1,475,000 after $15,000 of adjustments; Comp 2 sold for $1,520,000 after $95,000 of adjustments; Comp 3 sold for $1,495,000 after $70,000 of adjustments. From a valuation credibility standpoint, which comparable should MOST influence the appraiser's final opinion?
A. Comp 3, because $1,495,000 is the median of the three adjusted values
B. A weighted average of all three, giving equal percentage weight to each adjusted price
C. Comp 2, because it commands the highest adjusted price and reflects current demand
D. Comp 1, because minimal adjustment requirements indicate the strongest market correlation ✓
Answer: D. A comparable with minimal adjustments is inherently more reliable because it closely matches the subject property's characteristics; less reliance on the appraiser's subjective adjustment estimates strengthens the valuation conclusion.
Tough·v21 An appraiser reviewing three comparable sales for a Kauai property notes: Sale Alpha adjusted net price $1,525,000 (required $50K adjustments), Sale Beta adjusted net price $1,510,000 (required $25K adjustments), Sale Gamma adjusted net price $1,545,000 (required $100K adjustments). In reconciling these comps, which BEST supports the appraiser's value conclusion?
A. Sale Gamma, as the highest adjusted price reflects the strongest recent market momentum
B. Sale Alpha, as it represents a middle ground between the extremes
C. Sale Beta, because the lowest adjustment burden makes it the most representative market indicator ✓
D. An equal-weighted average of all three sales, regardless of adjustment magnitude
Answer: C. The comparable with the smallest adjustment amount is most credible because greater similarity to the subject property means less reliance on the appraiser's judgment; the raw market data itself is doing more of the analytical work.
Tough·v22 A Hawaii appraiser is analyzing three recently sold comparable properties in Kaneohe. Property A required $35,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,550,000; Property B required $95,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,575,000; Property C required $60,000 in adjustments and sold for $1,510,000. Which sale should carry the GREATEST weight in the appraiser's final value conclusion?
A. All three equally, since adjustment amounts are insignificant relative to sale price
B. Property C, because it represents the median value of the three sales
C. Property A, because it required the minimum dollar amount of adjustments ✓
D. Property B, because it achieved the highest sales price
Answer: C. The comparable requiring the smallest number or amount of adjustments demonstrates the closest similarity to the subject property, making its data the most reliable and requiring the least appraiser judgment. Greater adjustments introduce more uncertainty into the valuation.
Tough·v23 When selecting the most credible comparable sale for the sales comparison approach, an appraiser discovers that Comp 1 needed $72,000 in adjustments (net adjusted price $1,385,000), Comp 2 needed $18,000 in adjustments (net adjusted price $1,425,000), and Comp 3 needed $110,000 in adjustments (net adjusted price $1,440,000). From a reliability standpoint, which comp should receive the highest confidence weighting?
A. Comp 3, because the dollar adjustments are most transparent to the buyer
B. Comp 2, because minimal adjustments indicate strong comparability to the subject ✓
C. The median of all three adjusted prices, to eliminate outlier influence
D. Comp 1, because a mid-range adjustment suggests balanced analysis
Answer: B. In the sales comparison approach, a comparable requiring fewer or smaller adjustments signals greater intrinsic similarity to the subject property, reducing the reliance on appraiser discretion and judgment, thereby maximizing reliability.
Tough·v24 An appraiser evaluating three Pearl City residential sales for comparison to the subject property notes: Sale 1 (adjusted $1,380,000 after $88K modifications), Sale 2 (adjusted $1,405,000 after $12K modifications), and Sale 3 (adjusted $1,415,000 after $105K modifications). Which adjusted sale price should be weighted most heavily in the final reconciliation?
A. Sale 3, because it reflects current market momentum
B. Sale 1, as a conservative middle-ground approach
C. The simple average of the three sales, for defensibility in appeal
D. Sale 2, because the minimal adjustment burden suggests superior comp similarity ✓
Answer: D. A comparable sale requiring fewer adjustments is inherently more comparable to the subject, meaning its adjusted price relies less on appraiser estimation and more on actual market data—the hallmark of highest reliability in the sales comparison approach.
Tough·v25 A Honolulu appraiser is weighing three recent closed sales for the sales comparison approach to a rental property. Sale A required $35,000 in adjustments to reach comparability, Sale B needed $65,000 in adjustments, and Sale C required $15,000 in adjustments. All three are located within the same ZIP code and sold within 60 days. Which sale should the appraiser weight MOST heavily in forming an opinion of value?
A. Sale C, because it demanded the least adjustment and therefore demonstrates the strongest similarity to the subject property ✓
B. Sale A, because it represents the middle ground between extremes
C. The weighted average of all three, since the sales comparison approach requires equal treatment of all comps
D. Sale B, because larger adjustments indicate more sophisticated market analysis
Answer: A. A comparable requiring minimal adjustments is inherently more similar to the subject; reliance on the property's own characteristics rather than adjustment is always preferable in the sales comparison approach. Heavy adjustments introduce greater uncertainty and valuation risk.
Tough·v26 While analyzing four comparable sales for a Wailea condominium, an appraiser notes that Comp 1 sold for $2,180,000 (adjustments totaling $22K), Comp 2 for $2,210,000 (adjustments totaling $78K), Comp 3 for $2,165,000 (adjustments totaling $12K), and Comp 4 for $2,195,000 (adjustments totaling $95K). From a data quality standpoint, which comp provides the MOST credible indicator of the subject's probable market value?
A. The median of all four adjusted prices, because median eliminates outlier distortion
B. Comp 3, because it required the smallest amount of adjustment and therefore poses the least valuation risk ✓
C. Comp 4, as it represents the highest sales price and reflects current market strength
D. Comp 1, because its adjustment amount falls between the extremes
Answer: B. The comparable with the fewest and smallest adjustments is the most credible benchmark—it requires the least judgment and inference. Large adjustments amplify appraiser error and reduce reliance on market evidence, making data with minimal adjustment the gold standard in the sales comparison approach.
Tough·v27 In valuing a Kahaluu residential lot, an appraiser identifies three arm's-length sales: Property X adjusted by $5,500, Property Y adjusted by $58,000, and Property Z adjusted by $31,000. All three are within six months and the same neighborhood. When determining which sale is the STRONGEST basis for estimating market value, the appraiser should prioritize:
A. Property Z, because it represents a moderate adjustment level that balances extremes
B. Property X, since minimal adjustment requirements indicate highest comparability to the subject ✓
C. Property Y, because substantial adjustments reflect detailed market knowledge
D. A straight average of all three, as this removes individual comp bias
Answer: B. In appraisal methodology, the comp requiring the LEAST adjustment is the most reliable—its fundamental similarity to the subject does the analytical work. Large adjustments introduce subjective judgment and reduce the credibility of the valuation conclusion.
Tough·v28 When a licensee represents both the buyer and seller with proper written consent from each, which of the following fiduciary duties becomes inherently compromised by the conflict of interest?
A. Diligent performance and skill in transaction execution
B. Undivided allegiance to one party's best interests ✓
C. Honesty in all communications and disclosures
D. Legal compliance and regulatory adherence
Answer: B. Undivided loyalty—the core fiduciary duty requiring an agent to put one principal's interests ahead of the other's—is fundamentally incompatible with dual agency. The other duties (disclosure, care, compliance) can technically coexist with dual representation, but loyalty cannot.
Tough·v29 A Hawaii real estate licensee obtains informed written consent to represent both parties in a transaction. Despite this consent, which fiduciary obligation presents the greatest ethical and legal tension in a dual-agency arrangement?
A. The duty to account for all funds and maintain trust accounts properly
B. The duty to disclose all material facts known to the licensee
C. The duty to exercise reasonable skill, knowledge, and care
D. The duty to fully advocate for one client's economic advantage over the other's ✓
Answer: D. The duty to advocate for one party's economic interests above the other's is structurally impossible in dual agency, where the licensee must remain neutral between opposing parties. Proper disclosure, accounting, and competent service can survive dual representation, but partial loyalty is a contradiction.
Tough·v30 In a dual-agency transaction with full informed consent, a licensee's ability to fully perform which duty is most severely limited by the inherent conflict between the buyer and seller?
A. Transparency regarding all known material information
B. Safekeeping and proper handling of client deposits
C. Exclusive allegiance to advancing one party's financial interests ✓
D. Competence and adherence to applicable laws and regulations
Answer: C. Exclusive allegiance—the essence of loyalty—cannot be delivered when representing both sides with competing economic goals. The licensee must remain neutral and cannot prioritize one client over the other, making undivided loyalty impossible even with consent.
Tough·v31 When a licensee represents both the buyer and seller with proper written consent in a single transaction, which fiduciary obligation becomes fundamentally compromised by the conflict of interest inherent in dual representation?
A. Fiduciary loyalty ✓
B. Standard of care in transaction handling
C. Duty to account for all funds
D. Obligation to disclose material facts
Answer: A. Dual agency inherently prevents a licensee from placing either principal's interests above the other's, which is the core of loyalty. The licensee must remain neutral, fundamentally undermining the exclusive allegiance required in traditional agency relationships.
Tough·v32 A broker obtains informed written consent from both buyer and seller to serve as a dual agent in the same transaction. Under this arrangement, which duty is LEAST capable of being fully performed?
A. Honest dealing and fair accounting practices
B. Truthful representation and disclosure of known material facts
C. Undivided loyalty to the interests of one principal ✓
D. Diligent effort in pursuing the transaction
Answer: C. Undivided loyalty requires placing one principal's interests ahead of the other's—an impossibility when representing both sides with opposing economic goals. All other duties can theoretically be maintained through equal disclosure and neutral conduct.
Tough·v33 Despite obtaining informed written consent from all parties, a dual agent in Hawaii inevitably finds which fundamental agency duty structurally impossible to honor completely?
A. Competent handling of earnest money and client trust accounts
B. Adherence to state and federal fair housing laws and regulations
C. Full and complete advocacy for one principal's best interests ✓
D. Prompt communication of all offers, counteroffers, and material information
Answer: C. Full advocacy for one principal's interests cannot coexist with representing the opposing principal; dual agency by definition requires neutrality rather than undivided allegiance, making complete loyalty to either party structurally impossible.
Tough·v34 A broker represents both the seller and buyer in the same residential transaction after obtaining signed acknowledgment from each party. Under dual agency, which fiduciary obligation becomes fundamentally compromised?
A. Undivided allegiance to one party's interests ✓
B. Honesty and fair dealing
C. Competent performance of services
D. Full accounting of all funds
Answer: A. Undivided loyalty requires an agent to put one principal's interests ahead of the other's; dual agency with opposing economic interests makes this impossible. The agent must remain honest, account for funds, and perform competently for both, but cannot deliver the exclusive allegiance that loyalty demands.
Tough·v35 In a dual-agency representation where the licensee obtains written consent from both parties, which fiduciary duty is most structurally undermined by the conflict of interest inherent in the arrangement?
A. The duty of confidentiality
B. The duty to disclose all material facts
C. The duty to advocate for one party's advantage over the other's ✓
D. The duty to obey lawful instructions
Answer: C. Advocacy for one party's advantage over the other's is the essence of loyalty, which cannot coexist in dual agency where both parties have opposing economic goals. Obedience, confidentiality, and disclosure remain intact despite the dual relationship.
Tough·v36 When a licensee obtains informed written consent to represent both buyer and seller in the same transaction, which of the following duties is LEAST able to be fully performed?
A. Strict compliance with applicable laws and regulations
B. Faithful representation of both parties' positions against each other ✓
C. Meticulous trust account recordkeeping and disbursement
D. Transparent communication of all relevant transaction information
Answer: B. Faithful representation of both parties' positions against each other requires unwavering loyalty to each side—an impossible duty when parties have conflicting economic interests. Compliance, communication, and accounting can all be performed impartially in dual agency, but loyalty cannot.
Tough·v37 A Hawaii real estate broker intentionally deposits client earnest money into a personal business account instead of a segregated trust account. Which of the following BEST describes the potential consequences under Hawaii law?
A. Criminal prosecution only, since misappropriation is a felony matter outside REC jurisdiction
B. License suspension by the REC and possible restitution to the client through civil court
C. Concurrent REC disciplinary action and potential criminal charges, depending on the licensee's intent and harm ✓
D. Administrative fines by the REC; criminal liability is precluded by safe-harbor provisions
Answer: C. Hawaii law permits both administrative discipline through REC enforcement and criminal prosecution for knowing mishandling of client trust funds. These remedies operate independently and are not mutually exclusive.
Tough·v38 A salesperson knowingly commingles client funds with business operating accounts in violation of HRS Chapter 467. The REC investigates and the prosecutor's office separately initiates a criminal inquiry. What is the licensee's realistic exposure?
A. License revocation only, as the REC has exclusive jurisdiction over trust fund violations
B. Civil liability to clients only; Hawaii does not impose administrative penalties for fund handling violations
C. Criminal misdemeanor conviction only; REC action is stayed pending criminal resolution
D. Both REC disciplinary proceedings (potentially leading to license suspension/revocation) AND criminal liability ✓
Answer: D. Under Hawaii REC rules and HRS Chapter 467, knowing trust fund mishandling exposes a licensee to simultaneous REC discipline and criminal prosecution—the two systems operate independently and are not alternatives to each other.
Tough·v39 During a routine audit, the Hawaii REC discovers that a broker has systematically violated trust account segregation requirements over several months. Which statement most accurately describes the range of consequences the licensee faces?
A. Potential REC disciplinary action (including fines, suspension, or revocation) AND exposure to criminal charges, which operate as separate legal pathways ✓
B. License revocation through REC action, with criminal charges precluded by statutory immunity once disciplinary action begins
C. Only a monetary fine from the REC, since trust fund violations are treated as administrative infractions in Hawaii
D. Civil damages claims only; the REC has no enforcement authority over trust account management
Answer: A. Hawaii's REC disciplinary authority and criminal liability for knowing trust fund mishandling are distinct and concurrent remedies. A licensee may face both REC sanctions and criminal prosecution without one precluding the other.
Tough·v40 A Hawaii real estate broker intentionally converts client earnest money to personal use. Which consequence(s) is/are the licensee MOST likely to face?
A. Civil damages to the client, but no regulatory or criminal exposure
B. Suspension of license only, with restitution ordered by REC
C. Administrative fine capped at $5,000 under Hawaii's consumer protection act
D. Both license revocation by REC and potential felony criminal charges under HRS § 467 ✓
Answer: D. HRS § 467 permits dual pathways: REC can revoke/suspend for trust account violations, and the same conduct may constitute criminal conversion or theft, making both regulatory and criminal consequences possible and concurrent.
Tough·v41 During a REC investigation, evidence shows a salesperson commingled client funds with operating account funds for three consecutive transactions. Under Hawaii law, the licensee faces exposure to:
A. Mediation with the client to avoid public record of the violation
B. License suspension for 12 months, after which the matter is closed
C. A cease-and-desist order and mandatory client restitution only
D. REC disciplinary sanctions, civil liability claims, and potential criminal prosecution—any or all ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC authority under HRS § 467 is expansive and overlaps with criminal law. Commingling constitutes a serious violation that can result in multiple concurrent proceedings: administrative discipline, civil suits, and criminal charges depending on the facts and prosecutor discretion.
Tough·v42 A real estate firm's account reconciliation reveals that the designated broker knowingly failed to maintain separate trust accounts for client deposits over several months. Which of the following BEST describes the licensee's potential exposure?
A. Concurrent exposure to REC revocation/discipline AND criminal liability under state statute ✓
B. Referral to the Condominium Review Office for administrative review
C. Administrative license discipline exclusively, with no criminal jeopardy
D. Only civil restitution ordered by arbitration
Answer: A. Under HRS § 467, knowing violations of trust fund rules are not isolated to one enforcement channel. The REC can impose disciplinary action (revocation, suspension, fines) while simultaneously the conduct may qualify for criminal charges (theft, conversion, or fraud), and both can proceed in parallel.
Tough·v43 A Hawaii real estate broker intentionally deposits client earnest money into a personal operating account instead of a trust account. Which consequence BEST describes the licensee's legal exposure?
A. Liability for restitution to the client in civil court only
B. Administrative fine from the REC with no criminal jeopardy since trust account violations are civil matters
C. Criminal felony conviction only, as misappropriation is strictly a criminal offense in Hawaii
D. Potential license suspension or revocation by the REC, plus possible criminal prosecution under HRS Chapter 467 ✓
Answer: D. Improper handling of trust funds in Hawaii exposes a licensee to dual liability: REC administrative discipline (including license revocation) and criminal liability under HRS Chapter 467, which are independent legal tracks.
Tough·v44 When a salesperson knowingly commingled client funds with her broker's operating account in violation of Hawaii trust account rules, the salesperson faces exposure to:
A. A monetary settlement negotiated between the broker and the client to avoid both REC and criminal involvement
B. REC enforcement action (potential license revocation) AND criminal liability, which operate independently under Hawaii law ✓
C. REC disciplinary sanctions alone, since criminal prosecution only applies to brokers, not salespersons
D. Criminal penalties only, as fund mishandling is prosecuted before it reaches the REC
Answer: B. Hawaii law permits both REC disciplinary action and criminal prosecution for knowing trust fund violations; these are separate statutory remedies and are not mutually exclusive regardless of the licensee's role.
Tough·v45 A real estate licensee knowingly violated Hawaii REC trust account rules by failing to deposit funds into an escrow account within the required timeframe. What is the MOST comprehensive description of potential outcomes?
A. The client's only remedy is a private civil lawsuit for damages
B. A warning letter from the REC, which precludes any criminal action as a matter of Hawaii policy
C. Criminal prosecution only, because willful violations bypass REC jurisdiction and go directly to law enforcement
D. The REC may impose discipline, and the licensee may also face criminal charges, since both remedies exist under HRS Chapter 467 ✓
Answer: D. HRS Chapter 467 establishes both REC administrative authority and criminal liability for knowing trust fund mishandling; these concurrent remedies are not alternatives but can apply simultaneously.
Tough·v46 A buyer in Hawaii signs the standard HAR Purchase Contract and wants to know how long she has to conduct inspections, obtain financing approval, and decide whether to proceed. Which of the following BEST describes the mechanism that establishes her timeline?
A. The Hawaii REC's administrative rule requiring a statewide 21-day due-diligence minimum
B. The parties' negotiated insertion of specific contingency deadlines into the contract itself ✓
C. HRS 484A mandates a uniform 30-day inspection period for all residential transactions
D. An automatic 'as is' condition that waives all buyer inspection rights and timelines
Answer: B. The Hawaii Standard Purchase Contract does not impose a fixed statutory timeline; instead, the buyer and seller negotiate and insert specific dates for inspections, appraisals, and financing contingencies. There is no state-mandated uniform period, and 'as is' does not waive inspection rights or eliminate contingency deadlines.
Tough·v47 During a training session on the HAR Standard Purchase Contract, a licensee is asked: 'If a contract is silent on the inspection period, what controls?' The MOST accurate response is:
A. HRS 484A creates a 45-day mandatory period during which the buyer must complete all due diligence
B. The specific contingency dates and timelines that the parties have negotiated and written into the contract ✓
C. A default REC administrative rule grants 10 calendar days from contract signing
D. The buyer automatically forfeits all inspection rights under Hawaii common law
Answer: B. The HAR form contains blank lines for parties to fill in their own contingency deadlines (inspection, appraisal, financing approval dates). These negotiated dates—not statutory law or REC defaults—govern the buyer's due-diligence window. Silence on a specific date does not create a statutory fallback.
Tough·v48 A seller insists on an 'as is' clause in the HAR Purchase Contract and tells the broker that this eliminates the buyer's inspection contingency period entirely. The broker's CORRECT response should be:
A. The REC requires a 14-day inspection period regardless of any 'as is' language, per administrative rule
B. Hawaii Revised Statutes Section 484A prohibits 'as is' clauses and mandates a 30-day inspection window
C. An 'as is' clause shifts repair costs to the buyer but does not eliminate negotiated contingency deadlines or the buyer's right to inspect within the agreed timeframe ✓
D. That is correct; 'as is' removes all inspection rights and contingency timelines under Hawaii law
Answer: C. 'As is' allocates repair responsibility to the buyer and may limit seller disclosures, but it does not eliminate the buyer's ability to negotiate an inspection contingency period or the timeline for due diligence that the parties agree to in writing. The due-diligence window remains subject to the contract's negotiated terms.
Tough·v49 A buyer and seller in Hawaii negotiate a purchase contract and dispute arises over how long the buyer has to conduct inspections and appraisals before removing contingencies. Which statement BEST resolves this disagreement?
A. The Hawaii Real Estate Commission imposes a uniform 10-day inspection period that cannot be modified
B. Hawaii Revised Statutes automatically grant 21 days regardless of what the contract says
C. An 'as is' purchase eliminates all inspection rights and therefore no timeline applies
D. The parties' written agreement controls the deadline; there is no mandatory statewide timeline ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law does not mandate a fixed due-diligence period. The parties negotiate and specify inspection, appraisal, and contingency removal dates in the purchase contract itself. An 'as is' sale affects repair obligations, not inspection rights.
Tough·v50 During a training session, a broker asks: 'If our client wants to buy a condo in Honolulu and we use the Hawaii Association of Realtors form, what determines how many days the buyer has to hire an inspector and satisfy financing contingencies?' The correct response is:
A. Whatever timeframe the buyer and seller agree to and write into the contract's contingency sections ✓
B. The REC-mandated default of 17 calendar days applies in all cases unless the buyer waives it
C. The listing agent's local office policy, which supersedes the standard form
D. The buyer may take up to 30 days per HRS 484A, even if the contract says otherwise
Answer: A. The Hawaii Standard Purchase Contract contains blank fields for the parties to insert agreed-upon deadlines for inspections, appraisals, and contingency removal. No state law or REC rule sets a universal period; negotiation and contract language control.
Tough·v51 A seller receives an offer with a 'sold as-is' clause and asks the brokerage manager whether the buyer still has time to get a home inspection. The most accurate answer is:
A. No time allowed; 'as is' means the buyer waives all inspection and due-diligence rights under Hawaii law
B. Yes, but only for 14 days, which is the Hawaii REC's mandatory inspection period
C. The buyer retains inspection rights, but the 'as is' clause means the seller is not obligated to repair; the specific timeframe depends on what the contract states ✓
D. The buyer gets 30 days under HRS 484A to complete all due diligence, regardless of the 'as is' language
Answer: C. 'As is' addresses repair obligations, not inspection rights. The buyer may still inspect, but the seller will not pay for repairs discovered. The contract's negotiated due-diligence deadline—not statute or REC rule—controls how long the buyer has.
Tough·v52 A seller and buyer are negotiating terms under the HAR Standard Purchase Contract. The buyer requests 21 days to conduct inspections and obtain financing approval. Which statement correctly describes the enforceability of this timeline?
A. The timeline is enforceable only if both parties initial the specific contingency dates in the contract addendum sections ✓
B. The request is void because HRS 484A mandates a statewide 30-day inspection window that cannot be shortened
C. An 'as is' addendum automatically voids the need for any inspection period, making the 21-day request moot
D. Hawaii REC rules automatically reject any inspection period longer than 14 days, requiring contract amendment
Answer: A. The HAR Standard Purchase Contract requires parties to negotiate and specify their own contingency timelines by initialing or inserting dates into designated contract fields. There is no fixed statutory or REC default that overrides party agreement.
Tough·v53 During a pre-licensing discussion, an instructor states: 'Under Hawaii's Standard Purchase Contract, the due-diligence period is always 10 calendar days.' A student correctly objects. What is the BEST reason for the objection?
A. Due-diligence periods and contingency timelines are negotiated terms inserted by the buyer and seller into the contract itself ✓
B. HRS 484A explicitly sets a 30-day mandatory window that supersedes all contract language
C. The Hawaii REC publishes a statewide default of 14 days that applies to all transactions unless waived in writing
D. An 'as is' clause in the addendum eliminates the inspection contingency, so no fixed period applies
Answer: A. The HAR Standard Purchase Contract is a blank-form template; the parties fill in their agreed contingency deadlines (inspection, financing, etc.). There is no universal 10-day, 14-day, or 30-day default—the contract governs whatever timeline the parties negotiate.
Tough·v54 A broker is advising a buyer on the inspection contingency for a residential purchase in Hawaii. The buyer asks, 'Is there a minimum time I must be given to inspect the property?' The broker's MOST accurate response is:
A. No—HRS 484A provides that inspection periods are optional and not a mandatory contingency in any transaction
B. No—an 'as is' sale eliminates any right to inspect, so there is no minimum period unless you renegotiate
C. Yes, Hawaii REC Rule § 16-1-01 guarantees a floor of 14 calendar days for all inspections statewide
D. Yes, but it depends on what you and the seller agree to and insert into the contingency section of the HAR contract ✓
Answer: D. The buyer's inspection timeline is determined solely by what the buyer and seller negotiate and specify in the HAR Standard Purchase Contract's contingency fields. There is no statewide minimum imposed by statute or REC rule.
Tough·v55 A mainland-based real estate agent with an active license in California identifies a potential buyer client interested in purchasing a condominium on Oahu. The agent wants to represent the buyer directly in the Hawaii transaction. Which statement correctly describes the agent's legal options under Hawaii's licensing requirements?
A. The agent is prohibited from any involvement whatsoever, including providing referral services
B. The agent must cooperate with and refer the buyer to a Hawaii-licensed brokerage, and may receive a referral fee for doing so ✓
C. The agent may negotiate and execute the purchase contract on behalf of the buyer under interstate reciprocity laws
D. The agent may represent the buyer directly if the California brokerage firm obtains a temporary Hawaii permit
Answer: B. Hawaii does not recognize out-of-state licenses for brokerage acts even under reciprocity. The compliant path is referring the buyer to a Hawaii-licensed broker in exchange for a referral fee, with no further participation in brokerage activities by the mainland agent.
Tough·v56 During a national real estate conference, a Nevada-licensed broker discusses a Maui property listing with an interested buyer.
