The Nevada broker believes the buyer is a strong client and wants to coordinate the purchase agreement directly. Under Hawaii law, what is the broker's proper course of action?
A. Partner with any Hawaii brokerage firm and split the commission without additional licensing
B. Refer the client to a Hawaii-licensed broker and accept a referral fee; the Nevada broker cannot perform brokerage services in Hawaii ✓
C. Obtain a temporary license extension from Hawaii's Real Estate Commission valid for the single transaction
D. Conduct the transaction as long as all parties acknowledge the Nevada broker's status in writing
Answer: B. Out-of-state brokers cannot legally perform Hawaii brokerage acts regardless of the transaction size, client consent, or written disclosures. The only lawful option is a formal referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker, who then handles all brokerage responsibilities while the referring broker receives a referral fee.
Tough·v57 A broker licensed in Oregon contacts a Hawaii brokerage about a listing on the Big Island. The Oregon broker has generated significant buyer interest online and wants to submit offers and negotiate terms directly with the seller's agent. Which of the following correctly states the Oregon broker's legal position in Hawaii?
A. The Oregon broker cannot engage in Hawaii brokerage acts; the proper method is to refer the buyer to a Hawaii licensee and receive a referral fee ✓
B. The Oregon broker must apply for a nonresident broker license, which Hawaii approves within 30 days of application
C. The Oregon broker may perform all transaction work provided the buyer signs a notice acknowledging out-of-state representation
D. The Oregon broker may handle offer submission and negotiations under the national reciprocity agreement for interstate transactions
Answer: A. Hawaii law does not permit out-of-state brokers to perform brokerage services, including negotiation and offer submission, even with buyer consent or disclosure. The compliant approach is referring the buyer to a Hawaii-licensed broker and accepting a referral fee for the lead.
Tough·v58 A mainland real estate agent with an active license in California contacts a Hawaii seller about listing a Maui condominium. The California licensee wants to represent both parties and split commission with a local broker. Which statement best reflects Hawaii law?
A. The California licensee may handle the transaction under mainland-Hawaii reciprocal licensing agreements if the property is a residential unit
B. The California licensee cannot perform brokerage acts in Hawaii and must route the transaction through a Hawaii-licensed broker, who may pay a referral fee for the lead ✓
C. The California licensee may proceed if the Hawaii broker agrees to co-list and both parties waive their right to dual representation disclosures
D. Full compensation is permissible if the California licensee obtains a temporary work permit from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission
Answer: B. An out-of-state licensee cannot perform Hawaii real estate acts regardless of their home-state credentials or reciprocity status. The only compliant path is referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker, who may compensate the out-of-state agent for the referral under Hawaii law.
Tough·v59 During a national real estate conference in Las Vegas, a Washington state agent discusses a potential Oahu deal with a Hawaii buyer who initiated contact. The Washington licensee secured the buyer but is not licensed in Hawaii. What is the lawful course of action?
A. Refer the buyer directly to the seller with no involvement of any licensed party
B. Obtain temporary authority from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission to handle transactions originating outside Hawaii
C. Negotiate and draft the purchase agreement if both parties consent in writing to the out-of-state representation
D. Partner with a Hawaii broker to close the deal, with the Washington agent receiving referral compensation only and performing no Hawaii brokerage functions ✓
Answer: D. An out-of-state licensee who sourced a buyer cannot legally perform Hawaii real estate brokerage acts, even with consent. The compliant structure is referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker who takes over all brokerage functions, while the originating agent receives a referral fee.
Tough·v60 An Oregon licensee attends a Hawaii property seminar and a local owner asks them to help sell a Kona residential home. The Oregon agent has significant Hawaii sales experience but is not currently licensed there. Under Hawaii administrative code, the Oregon licensee:
A. May serve as transaction coordinator and handle administrative tasks so long as a Hawaii broker provides legal oversight
B. Requires only a temporary single-transaction license issued by the Hawaii REC commissioner
C. May list and market the property under Oregon reciprocity if the seller executes a non-representation agreement
D. Must refer the listing engagement to a Hawaii broker and may receive a referral fee without engaging in any Hawaii real estate acts ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii law does not permit out-of-state licensees to perform brokerage acts on Hawaii properties, regardless of experience or reciprocity arrangements. The compliant solution is a referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker with a referral fee to the out-of-state agent for sourcing the engagement.
Tough·v61 A licensed real estate agent from California establishes contact with a prospective buyer at a national real estate conference. The buyer is interested in purchasing residential property on Maui. What is the California agent's proper course of action under Hawaii's licensing requirements?
A. Directly negotiate and close the transaction, provided written consent is obtained from the Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
B. Obtain a temporary Hawaii permit valid for 90 days to facilitate the transaction
C. Apply for Hawaii reciprocal status, which allows mainland agents to practice in Hawaii without additional licensing
D. Coordinate with a Hawaii-licensed broker, who may accept a referral fee while the California agent steps back from further brokerage activity ✓
Answer: D. The out-of-state licensee cannot perform Hawaii brokerage functions. The compliant method is to refer the buyer to a Hawaii-licensed broker in exchange for a referral fee, allowing the out-of-state agent to exit the transaction.
Tough·v62 During a national broker convention, an Oregon-licensed agent and a Hawaii-based buyer discuss a condominium deal in Honolulu. The Oregon broker wants to represent the buyer and earn commission. Which statement correctly describes Hawaii law on this scenario?
A. The Oregon broker must partner with a Hawaii broker who holds the brokerage responsibility and may share compensation, while the Oregon broker relinquishes direct brokerage authority ✓
B. The Oregon broker is exempt from Hawaii licensing rules under interstate commerce provisions of the Fair Housing Act
C. The Oregon broker may operate under an umbrella agreement with any national franchise that has Hawaii offices
D. The Oregon broker may close the sale independently if the buyer signs a full disclosure acknowledging out-of-state licensure
Answer: A. An out-of-state licensee cannot lawfully perform Hawaii brokerage acts. The correct approach is engaging a Hawaii-licensed broker who controls the transaction, with the out-of-state agent receiving a referral fee for originating the lead.
Tough·v63 A Washington state real estate professional generates a buyer lead for a Kauai property while attending a real estate symposium. The buyer wants the Washington agent to handle the transaction directly. Under Hawaii real estate law, the Washington agent:
A. May conduct the full transaction as long as they maintain E&O insurance and register with the Hawaii Department of Commerce
B. Must obtain a temporary license from Hawaii within 10 days of first client contact or face disciplinary action
C. Violates Hawaii statute if they perform brokerage acts, but may legally introduce the buyer to a Hawaii broker for a referral commission and step aside ✓
D. Is permitted to co-broker with any Hawaii agent without formal broker supervision or referral-fee arrangement
Answer: C. Hawaii law prohibits non-Hawaii-licensed agents from performing brokerage acts in the state. The lawful alternative is a referral to a Hawaii-licensed broker for a referral fee, where the out-of-state agent's role ends.
Tough·v64 A seller's agent receives three competing offers simultaneously: Offer A at list price from Buyer A, Offer B at 95% of list from Buyer B (whom the seller knows and trusts), and Offer C at 98% of list from Buyer C (whom the seller has never met). The agent's obligation is to:
A. Recommend Offer C as the best compromise between price and the seller's potential comfort level with the buyer
B. Submit only Offer A and Offer C, since Offer B is below asking and does not serve the seller's financial interest
C. Present all three offers with their material terms, allowing the seller to rank them according to the seller's own preferences, provided those preferences do not violate fair housing laws ✓
D. Advise the seller to reject Offer B immediately because accepting a lower offer from a familiar party could imply discriminatory intent
Answer: C. The agent's fiduciary duty requires disclosure of all offers with material terms so the seller can make an informed decision. The seller may lawfully choose any offer for personal, business, or non-protected-class reasons—familiarity and rapport are legitimate preferences, not violations of fair housing law.
Tough·v65 During a multiple-offer scenario, a listing agent learns that the seller intends to reject the highest-priced offer because the buyer's ethnic background differs from the seller's own. The agent should:
A. Accept the seller's decision silently, since personal preference in selecting a buyer is protected under state real estate law
B. Submit all offers as received, then counsel the seller privately that the stated reason violates fair housing law and could expose the seller to liability ✓
C. Present only the lower offers that align with the seller's apparent preferences to minimize legal exposure for both parties
D. Refuse to submit the rejected offer, as presenting it would facilitate discrimination
Answer: B. The agent must present all offers and has a duty to advise the seller when the seller's stated reason for rejection is based on a protected class characteristic, which violates fair housing law. The agent cannot facilitate discrimination by withholding offers or endorsing unlawful selection criteria.
Tough·v66 A seller receives two identical cash offers on the same day: one from a buyer the seller played college sports with, and one from a stranger. The seller prefers the friend's offer despite it being $25,000 lower. The listing agent should:
A. Contact the higher bidder and encourage them to increase their offer to compete with the lower bid that the seller favors
B. Present both offers but suggest the seller reconsider, since the agent's fiduciary duty requires the seller to choose the highest price
C. Present both offers clearly and accurately; the seller's decision based on personal relationship is lawful and the agent must respect the seller's autonomous choice ✓
D. Recommend the higher offer in writing to create documentation that the agent upheld professional standards, regardless of the seller's final decision
Answer: C. An agent's duty of loyalty includes presenting all offers and allowing the principal (seller) to make decisions based on their own preferences, including personal relationships. Taking a lower offer for non-discriminatory reasons is entirely within the seller's rights, and the agent must not coerce or override that decision.
Tough·v67 A seller receives three competing offers simultaneously: Offer A at $520,000 from a buyer whose profile the seller finds objectionable on a personal level, Offer B at $490,000 from a buyer the seller has known socially for years, and Offer C at $515,000 from a neutral third party. The listing agent's obligation is to:
A. Present all three offers with a written recommendation that the seller accept Offer A to satisfy fiduciary duty to maximize proceeds
B. Present Offers B and C only, since Offer A is so significantly lower that presenting it would be a disservice
C. Present all three offers completely and accurately, allowing the seller to select based on personal preference as long as the decision is not discriminatory under fair housing law ✓
D. Advise the seller that accepting Offer B would expose them to litigation under Hawaii's antidiscrimination statutes because the motivation involves personal relationship
Answer: C. The agent must present all legitimate offers without filtering based on price or the agent's judgment of the seller's preferences. The seller may lawfully choose Offer B (lower price, known buyer) for personal reasons, provided those reasons do not involve protected-class discrimination. The agent cannot ethically withhold or rank offers.
Tough·v68 During a multiple-offer situation, a seller tells their agent: "I prefer the offer from the out-of-state buyer even though it's $25,000 lower, because I trust them more than the local buyer." The agent believes the higher local offer is in the seller's financial best interest. The agent should:
A. Decline to present the lower offer and instead counsel the seller that personal trust is not a legitimate basis for rejecting a higher bid
B. Present both offers but add a disclaimer that the seller's choice of the lower offer may violate Hawaii fair housing rules
C. Present only the higher offer, noting that the agent's fiduciary duty overrides the seller's subjective preferences regarding buyer character
D. Present both offers in full, explain the price difference, and allow the seller to make the final decision since personal preference (absent protected-class bias) is a lawful basis for choosing ✓
Answer: D. The agent's duty is to present all offers truthfully and facilitate the seller's informed choice, not to impose economic optimization. The seller's personal trust in a buyer is a lawful, non-discriminatory reason to prefer a lower offer. The agent may advise but cannot override the principal's decision.
Tough·v69 A listing agent obtains two offers concurrently: $475,000 from Buyer X (whom the seller has stated he 'cannot stand') and $465,000 from Buyer Y (a childhood friend of the seller). The agent is concerned about potential liability. What is the agent's legally correct course of action?
A. Present both offers but recommend in writing that the seller accept the higher offer to document that the agent acted in the seller's economic interest
B. Present only Buyer Y's offer, since the seller's stated personal animosity toward Buyer X suggests the transaction will close more smoothly
C. Inform the seller that choosing the lower offer based on personal preference could constitute discrimination and advise refusal of both until a neutral buyer emerges
D. Present both offers in writing with equal clarity and allow the seller to decide, provided the seller's choice is not rooted in the buyer's protected characteristics ✓
Answer: D. The agent must present all bona fide offers equally and transparently. The seller's personal dislike of a buyer—standing alone—is not an unlawful basis for rejection under fair housing law. Liability exposure is minimized by presenting all offers and documenting the seller's own decision-making, not by filtering offers.
Tough·v70 A seller's agent obtains three competing offers simultaneously: Offer A at list price from Buyer A; Offer B at 5% below list from Buyer B, whom the seller has known socially for years and "would prefer to work with"; Offer C at list price plus $15,000 from Buyer C. What is the agent's fiduciary obligation?
A. Present Offers A and C only, since personal relationships should not cloud the seller's economic decision
B. Present all three offers with equal transparency and allow the seller to rank or select based on the seller's own criteria, provided no protected-class bias is involved ✓
C. Withhold Offer B and recommend the seller accept Offer C to satisfy the duty of loyalty and maximize net proceeds
D. Present all three but explicitly warn that choosing Offer B on personal grounds may expose the seller to discrimination liability
Answer: B. The agent must present all offers and let the seller decide. The seller's preference for a known buyer is lawful personal discretion unless rooted in a protected class. The agent's loyalty duty is owed to the principal's chosen objectives, not to overriding the principal's preferences for non-discriminatory personal reasons.
Tough·v71 During a multiple-offer situation, a listing agent learns the seller wants to reject the highest offer ($600,000) in favor of a lower offer ($575,000) from a buyer the seller finds 'more trustworthy.' The agent believes this is financially unwise. What should the agent do?
A. Present both offers but require the seller to sign a liability waiver acknowledging the lost proceeds and potential fair housing exposure
B. Present both offers in full detail, counsel the seller on the financial difference, but ultimately honor the seller's right to choose either offer so long as the preference is not based on protected-class status ✓
C. Present only the $600,000 offer, since the agent cannot ethically facilitate a decision that breaches the seller's own duty to maximize value
D. Refuse to present the lower offer and insist the seller accept the highest bidder to fulfill fiduciary duties
Answer: B. The agent must present all offers transparently and can advise on financial consequences, but the seller retains the right to choose based on personal judgment—including 'trustworthiness' or comfort—so long as that judgment does not rest on a protected class. The agent's loyalty is to the principal's decision-making authority, not to overriding it.
Tough·v72 A seller instructs the listing agent: 'I have two offers—one for the full asking price from someone I don't know, and one for $40,000 less from my neighbor. I want to accept my neighbor's offer.' The agent has concerns about the seller 'leaving money on the table.' What is the agent's proper course of action under Hawaii law and ethical standards?
A. Present both offers with clear financial comparison, provide counsel on the opportunity cost, but then facilitate the seller's choice without further pressure, since neighborly preference is a lawful personal reason absent protected-class considerations ✓
B. Advise the seller in writing that accepting the lower offer violates the seller's fiduciary duty to maximize proceeds and recommend rejection
C. Present only the higher offer and explain that accepting a lower offer from a known party creates legal liability under state anti-discrimination law
D. Require the seller to obtain independent counsel before accepting the lower offer to shield the agent from potential complaints
Answer: A. The agent must present all offers and may advise on the financial gap, but the seller is free to choose the lower offer based on personal relationship or preference, as long as the preference is not motivated by a protected class. The agent's role is to inform and facilitate, not to override the principal's business judgment on non-protected grounds.
Tough·v73 During a listing consultation, a seller privately confides to the agent that $1.35M is their absolute minimum acceptable price. Three days later, an unrepresented buyer calls the listing office and asks, "What is your seller truly willing to take?" The listing agent should:
A. Share the information in writing so there is a record of full transparency
B. Disclose the figure because the buyer initiated the conversation without representation
C. Provide the minimum price only if it will accelerate a sale and benefit the seller
D. Refuse to reveal the seller's reservation price and encourage the buyer to submit an offer ✓
Answer: D. A seller's confidential bottom-line price is privileged information protected by the fiduciary duty of loyalty. The listing agent may not disclose it to any buyer, represented or unrepresented, regardless of who asked or how the conversation began.
Tough·v74 A listing agent receives a written offer of $1.5M on a property. Before presenting it, the agent recalls that the seller mentioned in private—off the record—that she would accept $1.45M. A prospective unrepresented buyer appears at an open house and casually asks, "What price would make your seller happy?" The agent's best course of action is to:
A. Withhold the seller's reservation price and advise the buyer to submit an offer reflecting their true value proposition ✓
B. Tell the buyer the seller's bottom line only after confirming the buyer will work exclusively with the agent
C. Reveal both figures so the buyer can make an informed negotiating decision
D. Disclose only the lower amount ($1.45M) since it was already communicated in writing elsewhere
Answer: A. Even though an offer above the seller's reservation price has been received, the agent's fiduciary duty prevents disclosing the seller's confidential minimum acceptable price. The agent must protect the seller's negotiating position by declining to share this privileged information.
Tough·v75 A seller lists her home with an agent and states confidentially, "Don't tell anyone, but I'll take $1.28M." Two weeks later, a buyer without representation contacts the listing agent directly and states, "I'm ready to make an offer, but I need to know the rock-bottom price or I'm walking away." The listing agent should:
A. Disclose the price contingent on the buyer agreeing to pay a portion of the listing agent's commission
B. Politely decline to share the seller's confidential price and recommend the buyer submit their strongest offer ✓
C. Disclose the $1.28M figure because the buyer's ultimatum creates a practical necessity to negotiate
D. Provide the information since no buyer-broker agreement exists and therefore no fiduciary duty to the buyer is owed
Answer: B. The seller's confidential reservation price is privileged information protected by fiduciary duty, regardless of buyer pressure, ultimatums, or the absence of a buyer-broker agreement. The agent's allegiance is to the seller and must remain confidential.
Tough·v76 During a listing appointment, the seller confides to the agent that $1.3M is the absolute minimum she needs to net after closing costs. An hour later, a self-represented buyer calls the agent directly and says, "I want to make a strong offer, but I need to know the seller's rock-bottom price." What should the agent do?
A. Share the figure only if the buyer agrees to work with the agent as a buyer's representative going forward
B. Disclose it in writing to protect both parties and create a clear audit trail
C. Provide the $1.3M figure since the buyer is motivated and will likely make a competitive offer
D. Withhold the information and encourage the buyer to submit their highest and best offer without that guidance ✓
Answer: D. The seller's confidential reservation price is privileged information belonging to the principal (seller). Disclosing it to any buyer—represented or unrepresented—breaches the fiduciary duty of confidentiality and loyalty, regardless of the buyer's motivation or the agent's intent to facilitate a transaction.
Tough·v77 A listing agent receives a phone inquiry from an unrepresented investor who asks, "Can you tell me the lowest offer your seller would seriously consider?" The agent knows from the listing meeting that the seller has a minimum acceptable price. The agent's legally sound course of action is:
A. Decline to reveal the seller's reservation price; instruct the buyer to make an offer based on the property's market value and their own analysis ✓
B. Share the information only if the caller provides proof of financial pre-qualification
C. Provide a range instead of a specific figure to soften the breach of confidence
D. Disclose the seller's minimum and then seek signed buyer-broker representation from the caller
Answer: A. A seller's private reservation price or minimum acceptable offer is confidential client information. The agent's fiduciary duty to the seller prohibits disclosure of this strategic information to any buyer, regardless of the buyer's status, credentials, or timing. The buyer should always submit offers based on independent market analysis.
Tough·v78 At an open house, a prospective buyer approaches the agent and says, "I overheard you mention to another agent that the seller is motivated. What's the absolute lowest they'd go?" The agent knows the seller has stated a firm minimum in private. The most professionally and ethically correct response is:
A. Refuse to divulge the seller's confidential threshold; redirect the buyer to submit their best and final offer ✓
B. Disclose the minimum only if the buyer commits to viewing the property again within 48 hours
C. Provide the information because the buyer claims they overheard it being discussed already
D. Clarify that the seller is indeed motivated, then disclose the private minimum to prove good faith
Answer: A. The seller's private reservation price is confidential regardless of what the buyer may have overheard or assumed. The listing agent's duty of confidentiality and loyalty to the seller (the principal) is absolute and cannot be waived by the buyer's persistence, claimed familiarity with the seller's position, or unrepresented status.
Tough·v79 During a private listing consultation, a seller confides in her agent that she is motivated to sell and would accept $950K even though the asking price is $1.1M. Later that week, an unrepresented buyer visits the property and casually asks the agent, "Is there any flexibility on price?" What should the agent do?
A. Disclose the figure only if the buyer agrees to work exclusively with the agent going forward
B. Refrain from disclosing the seller's private reservation price and encourage the buyer to submit an offer ✓
C. Provide the seller's minimum acceptable price in writing to protect both parties legally
D. Share the seller's confidential bottom line since the buyer asked an open-ended question about flexibility
Answer: B. The agent's fiduciary duty to the seller prohibits disclosure of confidential negotiating parameters, including reservation prices, regardless of how the buyer's question is framed. Recommending the buyer submit their best offer respects the seller's confidence while allowing fair negotiation.
Tough·v80 A listing agent learns from the seller in a closed-door meeting that the owner will consider any serious offer at $2.2M or above. The next day, a walk-in buyer (without representation) corners the agent at the property and demands to know the seller's minimum acceptable price. The agent should:
A. Decline to reveal the threshold and suggest the buyer's offer will speak for itself ✓
B. Refer the buyer to a sub-agent who can disclose the information without breaching loyalty
C. Share the figure but require written acknowledgment that it is confidential
D. Disclose the amount because the buyer is unrepresented and therefore more vulnerable
Answer: A. Confidentiality and loyalty to the seller are non-waivable duties. The agent must decline to disclose the seller's reservation price regardless of the buyer's representation status or persistence. Suggesting the buyer submit an offer protects the seller's bargaining position.
Tough·v81 At the listing presentation, a seller explicitly tells her agent, "I need at least $575K to make this sale worthwhile—don't tell anyone." Two weeks later, an unrepresented buyer approaches the agent and states, "I'm ready to make an offer, but I need to know your absolute rock-bottom number first." The agent's best response is:
A. Disclose the threshold after obtaining the buyer's email confirmation of receipt
B. Agree to share it only if the buyer commits to representation with the agent's brokerage
C. Provide the $575K figure because the buyer explicitly asked for the 'rock-bottom' price
D. Withhold the seller's private minimum and direct the buyer to submit their highest and best offer without that information ✓
Answer: D. The agent's fiduciary obligation to the seller includes keeping negotiating parameters confidential. Disclosing the seller's walk-away price would compromise the seller's leverage and violate the duty of loyalty, even when directly requested by an unrepresented buyer.
Tough·v82 A seller accepts an offer on a $1.8M Kailua property with a 30-day financing contingency. On Day 25, the buyer's lender issues a written conditional commitment but imposes a cash-out refinance requirement the buyer cannot meet. The buyer formally notifies the seller of the loan denial and demands return of earnest money. What is the seller's legal position?
A. The buyer must reapply with a different lender before invoking the contingency
B. The seller may claim the buyer failed to disclose financial problems and forfeit the deposit
C. The seller must return the deposit because a loan contingency failure within the window is a protected termination right ✓
D. The seller can enforce the sale because Day 25 is past the contingency period
Answer: C. A financing contingency protects the buyer's right to terminate and recover the deposit if the lender denies or imposes unreasonable conditions within the contingency window. Day 25 of a 30-day period is still within the window. The seller has no legal basis to retain funds for a bona fide lender denial.
Tough·v83 During escrow on a $2.4M Honolulu condo, the buyer's institutional lender rejects the final loan approval due to a property defect found in the appraisal. The financing contingency expires in two days. The buyer provides the lender's written denial to the escrow officer and requests return of the deposit. Which statement correctly applies Hawaii financing contingency law?
A. The contingency is void because the lender's denial was based on property condition, not creditworthiness
B. The buyer may withdraw and recover the deposit if the denial is documented and timely, regardless of whether the defect is material to the purchase ✓
C. The buyer forfeited contingency protection by not addressing the appraisal issue earlier in escrow
D. The seller can keep the deposit unless the buyer can prove the lender acted in bad faith
Answer: B. A financing contingency triggered by a written lender denial—whether due to property, credit, or appraisal issues—entitles the buyer to terminate and recover the deposit if invoked within the contingency period. The reason for denial does not eliminate the contingency right.
Tough·v84 An offer on a $3.2M Big Island estate includes a 28-day financing contingency. On Day 22, the buyer's lender issues a formal notice stating the loan cannot be approved in the current rate environment but suggests the buyer reapply in 60 days. The buyer immediately notifies the seller and demands the earnest money be released. The seller argues the denial was not final. What is the correct outcome?
A. The buyer's deposit must be returned because a written lender denial—even if conditional or temporary—triggers the contingency protection within the window ✓
B. The seller may retain the deposit pending the 60-day reapplication period
C. The buyer forfeited the contingency by not waiting the full 28 days to allow the market to change
D. The contingency only applies to rejections based on the buyer's credit, not market conditions
Answer: A. A written loan denial communicated within the contingency period entitles the buyer to terminate and recover the deposit, even if the lender suggests a future reapplication or cites external conditions. The contingency right does not depend on the permanence or reason for the denial.
Tough·v85 A seller accepted a buyer's offer on a $1.8M Maui property with a standard 21-day financing contingency. On Day 19, the buyer receives a written loan denial from their primary lender citing insufficient reserves. The buyer submits the denial notice and requests deposit return. What is the correct legal outcome?
A. The buyer must appeal the denial and reapply with a different lender to preserve contingency rights
B. The buyer forfeits the deposit because they failed to secure financing within the contingency period
C. The buyer may withdraw and recover the deposit if the denial is documented as a good-faith lender decision made within the contingency window ✓
D. The seller may retain the deposit as liquidated damages since the buyer did not satisfy the financing condition
Answer: C. A financing contingency allows the buyer to terminate and recover the deposit upon receipt of a bona fide loan denial during the contingency period. Day 19 is still within the window, and the written denial satisfies the burden of proof. No reapplication requirement exists.
Tough·v86 During a purchase agreement on a $2.3M Big Island residence, the buyer invokes a financing contingency after the lender delivers a written conditional denial on Day 20 of a 20-day window. The seller argues the contingency expired at midnight Day 20 and asserts a right to the earnest money deposit. Under Hawaii real estate law, who prevails?
A. Neither party may claim the deposit; it must go to escrow pending litigation
B. The buyer prevails only if they can prove they applied to multiple lenders and all denied the loan
C. The buyer prevails if the denial was delivered by the lender in writing before the contingency deadline and the buyer acts to terminate promptly ✓
D. The seller prevails; the contingency window closed and the buyer is now in default
Answer: C. Timing for a financing contingency is measured by when the lender's written denial is received, not by application date. A Day 20 denial within a 20-day window allows the buyer to terminate and recover the deposit without penalty, provided the denial is legitimate and documented.
Tough·v87 A buyer made an offer on a $1.95M Honolulu condo with a financing contingency set to expire on Day 21. The seller accepted. The buyer's lender issued a formal written loan denial on Day 18 citing the property's appraisal coming in $150K below purchase price. The buyer wants out and to recover earnest money. The seller claims the buyer should have waived the appraisal contingency. What is the controlling principle?
A. The financing contingency is void if the buyer's down payment offer was less than 20 percent
B. The buyer may terminate and recover the deposit because a legitimate lender denial, supported in writing and received within the contingency window, permits withdrawal without forfeiture ✓
C. The buyer forfeited contingency rights by not addressing the appraisal issue before Day 18
D. The seller is correct; an appraisal shortfall is the buyer's responsibility and the financing contingency does not apply
Answer: B. A financing contingency protects the buyer when the lender issues a good-faith denial within the contingency period, regardless of the reason (appraisal, income, debt ratio, etc.). An appraisal-based denial is a legitimate basis for contingency invocation and deposit return.
Tough·v88 A buyer enters into a purchase agreement for a $2.1M Oahu residential property with a 21-day financing contingency clause. On Day 19, the buyer receives a written loan denial from their institutional lender citing insufficient debt-to-income ratio. The buyer immediately notifies the seller of the denial and requests release of the earnest money deposit. What is the proper outcome?
A. The seller is entitled to retain the deposit as compensation for the buyer's failure to qualify, regardless of the contingency clause
B. The buyer must continue seeking financing from alternative lenders and cannot invoke the contingency until all reasonable sources are exhausted
C. The buyer may terminate the contract and recover the deposit provided the loan denial is documented and occurred within the contingency timeframe ✓
D. The buyer forfeits the deposit because the denial occurred after the midpoint of the contingency period
Answer: C. A financing contingency protects the buyer's deposit if a lender denies the loan in good faith within the contingency window — timing within that window (Day 19 of 21) does not negate the protection. The contingency is satisfied upon documented denial; no exhaustion requirement exists.
Tough·v89 During a $2.1M Oahu property transaction, the buyer's mortgage lender issues a formal written denial on Day 17 of the financing contingency period (set for 21 days). The seller argues the buyer should have chosen a more favorable lender and refuses to release the earnest money. Under Hawaii purchase agreement law, which statement correctly describes the buyer's position?
A. The buyer must request the seller's permission to shop for a new lender or lose contingency protection
B. The buyer is protected by the financing contingency and may terminate while recovering the deposit, provided the denial is genuine and timely ✓
C. The buyer has waived the contingency by not pre-qualifying with multiple lenders before signing
D. The seller may keep the deposit because the buyer bears liability for lender discretion and underwriting decisions
Answer: B. A financing contingency provides unconditional protection to the buyer upon receipt of a good-faith written loan denial within the contingency window. The buyer's lender choice, qualification efforts, or the seller's subjective satisfaction are irrelevant—the contingency is a contractual safety net.
Tough·v90 A $2.1M purchase agreement for an Oahu home includes a 21-day financing contingency. The buyer's conventional loan is formally denied in writing on Day 20 due to appraisal shortfall. The buyer notifies the seller that same day and demands the earnest money be returned. The seller contends the denial is the buyer's fault because they chose an overpriced property. Is the buyer entitled to recover the deposit?
A. Yes, because a documented lender denial within the contingency period entitles the buyer to deposit recovery, regardless of the denial reason ✓
B. Yes, but only if the buyer can prove the appraisal was conducted improperly by the lender's appraiser
C. No, because an appraisal-based denial is attributed to the buyer's selection and does not trigger contingency protection
D. No, because the denial occurred on Day 20, which is beyond the middle of the contingency window and constitutes waiver
Answer: A. Financing contingencies protect the buyer upon any good-faith lender denial within the window — the cause (appraisal, income, credit, etc.) is immaterial. Day 20 of 21 is still within the contingency period, and the seller's opinion of property value does not override the contractual contingency protection.
Tough·v91 A mainland corporation sells a commercial building in Honolulu for $1,200,000. The seller is not a Hawaii resident. What amount must be withheld and remitted to the Hawaii Department of Revenue at closing under HARPTA, absent any qualifying exemptions?
A. $60,000
B. $36,000
C. $87,000 ✓
D. $120,000
Answer: C. HARPTA requires 7.25% withholding on non-resident seller transactions. 0.0725 × $1,200,000 = $87,000. Distractors include 3% (outdated rate), 5% (common withholding confusion), and 10% (excessive estimate).
Tough·v92 At closing, a non-resident alien transfers a residential condominium in Maui valued at $575,000. No valid exemption certificate has been filed. The title company must withhold and pay to Hawaii:
A. $57,500
B. $41,688 ✓
C. $17,250
D. $28,875
Answer: B. Non-resident HARPTA withholding is 7.25% of sales price, not 3%. 0.0725 × $575,000 = $41,687.50, rounded to $41,688. The 3% rate ($17,250) is an old/incorrect threshold; other amounts mix dates or use wrong percentages.
Tough·v93 A foreign investor closes on the purchase of a $680,000 Hawaii vacation rental property and immediately resells it three months later for $720,000 as a non-resident. Ignoring any exemptions, how much HARPTA must be remitted on the resale transaction?
A. $51,480
B. $52,200 ✓
C. $21,600
D. $43,200
Answer: B. HARPTA withholding applies to the sale proceeds at 7.25% of the gross sale price. 0.0725 × $720,000 = $52,200. The distractors include 3% of sale price ($21,600), 7.25% of the lower purchase price ($49,300 area), and incorrect percentages applied to sale price.
Tough·v94 A mainland developer sells a Honolulu commercial property for $1,200,000. The developer is a non-resident of Hawaii and no withholding exemption has been granted. What amount must be withheld under HARPTA at the time of closing?
A. $87,000 ✓
B. $60,000
C. $36,000
D. $120,000
Answer: A. HARPTA requires 7.25% withholding on the full purchase price for non-resident sellers. 0.0725 × $1,200,000 = $87,000. The 3% and 6% distractors represent outdated or incorrect tax rates.
Tough·v95 At closing, a foreign national who owns real property in Hawaii as an investment sells the property for $875,000. No applicable exemption exists. The HARPTA withholding obligation equals:
A. $63,438 ✓
B. $70,000
C. $52,500
D. $43,750
Answer: A. Non-resident sellers must remit 7.25% of gross sales price as HARPTA withholding. 0.0725 × $875,000 = $63,438. Distractors include 6% and 5% rates, which do not apply to HARPTA.
Tough·v96 A non-Hawaiian resident closes the sale of a rental property valued at $650,000. The escrow officer must calculate the mandatory HARPTA withholding. Assuming the sale qualifies for no exemption, the required withholding is:
A. $32,500
B. $19,500
C. $58,500
D. $47,125 ✓
Answer: D. HARPTA withholding is calculated at 7.25% of the sales price for non-resident sellers. 0.0725 × $650,000 = $47,125. Common errors involve applying 3%, 5%, or 9% rates, which are incorrect under current Hawaii law.
Tough·v97 A mainland investor sells a Honolulu condominium for $950,000. The property was held as a rental. What amount must the closing agent withhold under Hawaii's non-resident seller rules, assuming no statutory exemption is claimed?
A. $47,500
B. $95,000
C. $28,500
D. $68,875 ✓
Answer: D. HARPTA imposes a 7.25% withholding obligation on non-resident sellers of Hawaii real property. 0.0725 × $950,000 = $68,875. The 3% rate and 10% rate are common distractors but do not apply to HARPTA withholding calculations.
Tough·v98 At closing of a $950,000 sale, the title company confirms the seller is a non-resident of Hawaii with no applicable exemption under HARPTA. How much must be withheld from the seller's proceeds?
A. $47,500
B. $28,500
C. $95,000
D. $68,875 ✓
Answer: D. Non-resident seller withholding under HARPTA is 7.25% of the gross sales price. $950,000 × 0.0725 = $68,875. Common errors include confusing HARPTA withholding with conveyance tax (2.5%) or using the superseded 3% rate.
Tough·v99 A California resident completes a $950,000 purchase of a Hawaii commercial building from a non-resident owner. The escrow officer must calculate HARPTA withholding. Assuming no exemptions apply, the required withholding is:
A. $47,500
B. $68,875 ✓
C. $95,000
D. $23,750
Answer: B. HARPTA withholding for non-resident sellers is 7.25% of the purchase price, regardless of property type or buyer residency. $950,000 × 0.0725 = $68,875. Distractors reflect outdated percentages and incorrect multiples of the price.
Tough·v100 A landlord advertises a rental property and tells an interested applicant with a 6-year-old child that "we prefer tenants without kids because children tend to damage the property and create noise complaints." Under the Fair Housing Act, the landlord's statement is:
A. Legal, because property damage and noise are legitimate concerns that apply equally to all tenants
B. Illegal — familial status is a protected class and discrimination based on the presence of children violates federal law regardless of the stated reason ✓
C. Permissible if the landlord discloses this policy in writing before showing the property
D. Legal if the landlord applies the same exclusion uniformly to all families with children
Answer: B. The Fair Housing Act protects familial status (presence of children under 18). A landlord cannot refuse to rent or set different terms based on children, even when citing property damage or noise concerns. These rationales are pretexts for familial status discrimination and violate federal law.
Tough·v101 During a showing, a property manager tells prospective tenants with a toddler that the building's pool and balcony features make it unsuitable for young children and suggests they look at a different property in the portfolio. This action most likely constitutes:
A. Legitimate risk management by the property manager to prevent liability claims
B. A violation only if the manager refused to rent to them outright rather than suggesting alternatives
C. Permissible guidance that actually protects the family's welfare
D. Steering and familial status discrimination under the Fair Housing Act ✓
Answer: D. Directing or discouraging applicants with children from viewing or renting certain properties (steering) while offering them other properties is a form of familial status discrimination. The Fair Housing Act prohibits this conduct regardless of the stated safety or welfare justification, and offering alternatives does not cure the violation.
Tough·v102 A real estate investor excludes families with children from renting a two-story townhome, citing building code requirements for handrails and the fact that young children cannot independently use stairs safely. Under federal fair housing law, this exclusion is:
A. Permissible if the investor proves the property lacks essential safety features required by local fire codes
B. Permissible because building codes and safety regulations override Fair Housing Act protections
C. Illegal — familial status is protected, and safety-based pretexts cannot justify refusing to rent to families with children ✓
D. Legal only if the investor documents a prior incident involving a child on the stairs
Answer: C. Familial status protection under the Fair Housing Act cannot be circumvented by citing safety codes or features inherent to the property. The presence of stairs or other design elements does not justify blanket exclusion of families; parental responsibility and customization are not the landlord's burden. This reasoning constitutes a pretext for unlawful discrimination.
Tough·v103 A landlord denies a rental application from a couple with a 6-year-old child, explaining that "families with young children create excessive noise and wear-and-tear on the property." Under federal fair housing standards, this denial is most likely:
A. Unlawful because familial status is a protected class and generalized assumptions about children violate the Fair Housing Act ✓
B. Lawful if the landlord applies the same reasoning consistently to all applicants with children
C. Lawful provided the landlord documents a legitimate business purpose related to property maintenance
D. Unlawful only if the landlord has a prior history of rental violations
Answer: A. Familial status is a federally protected class under the 1988 Fair Housing Act amendments. Denying housing based on the presence of children, regardless of the stated reasoning (noise, wear, safety), constitutes discrimination. Consistent application or documented business concerns do not override this protection.
Tough·v104 An owner of a multi-unit residential building refuses to show a one-bedroom apartment to a single mother with two minor children, claiming "the unit layout is unsuitable for families." When the mother asks if she can view it anyway, the owner declines. This conduct most likely violates fair housing law because:
A. The refusal is based on familial status, a protected class, and steering applicants away from units based on family composition is prohibited ✓
B. The owner failed to provide reasonable accommodations for the applicant's disability status
C. The unit's size makes it objectively unsuitable for occupancy by more than one person
D. Federal law requires owners to actively advertise properties as family-friendly if children are likely to occupy them
Answer: A. The owner's refusal to allow viewing and the claim that the unit is unsuitable for families constitutes both direct discrimination and steering based on familial status. Familial status protection under the Fair Housing Act prohibits denying, limiting, or otherwise making housing unavailable based on the presence of children under 18.
Tough·v105 During a showing, a property manager tells prospective tenants with a 5-year-old child that the building's community pool poses "too much liability" and suggests they consider a different property "more appropriate for families." Under the federal Fair Housing Act, the manager's conduct is:
A. Unlawful only if the manager made a similar statement to applicants without children
B. Permissible because liability concerns are legitimate business considerations that override fair housing protections
C. A violation of fair housing law—the suggestion to look elsewhere and the implication that the property is unsuitable for families constitutes illegal steering based on familial status ✓
D. Permissible if the property has a documented history of accidents involving children
Answer: C. Steering—directing applicants toward or away from properties or areas based on protected characteristics—is a per se violation of fair housing law. Suggesting that families with children look elsewhere based on safety or suitability concerns is textbook steering on the basis of familial status, a federally protected class.
Tough·v106 A landlord advertises a rental property and tells an applicant family with a 7-year-old child that the building's narrow hallways and proximity to a busy street make it "unsuitable for families with young children." The applicant is denied tenancy based on this statement. Under the Fair Housing Act, the landlord's action is:
A. Legal only if the landlord offers alternative properties specifically designed for families
B. Legal because landlords have a fiduciary duty to protect all tenants from environmental risks
C. Legal if the landlord documents the safety hazards in writing and applies the policy uniformly
D. Illegal because familial status is a protected class and safety-based pretexts cannot be used to exclude families with children ✓
Answer: D. Familial status (presence of children under 18) is protected under the Fair Housing Act. A landlord cannot use paternalistic safety arguments—regardless of how legitimate they sound—to exclude families with children from housing. This is a classic pretext violation, and offering alternatives constitutes illegal steering.
Tough·v107 During a showing, a property manager tells prospective tenants with two children that the unit has a loft bedroom accessible only by a steep ladder, and therefore "we cannot rent to families with kids for liability reasons." The manager then suggests the applicants view a different property without children in the building. Which statement most accurately reflects fair housing compliance?
A. The manager's disclosure of physical features is permissible, but steering the family to another property violates fair housing law
B. Both the refusal and the suggestion of an alternative are permissible risk-management practices
C. The practice is legal if the manager applies the same policy to all families with children consistently
D. The refusal based on a child safety concern and the steering together constitute a violation of the Fair Housing Act's protection of familial status ✓
Answer: D. Refusing tenancy based on the presence of children—framed as a safety concern—violates familial status protection. Adding steering (offering a "safer" alternative property) compounds the violation. Consistent application of an unlawful policy does not cure the fundamental violation of protected-class rights.
Tough·v108 A property owner in Hawaii tells an interested renter with three children under age 10 that the two-story townhouse "poses fall hazards and isn't appropriate for young kids." The owner states this is a firm policy to minimize property liability. The owner does not explicitly refuse to rent, but indicates the family should "consider units specifically marketed to families." Under Hawaii and federal fair housing law, this conduct is:
A. Permissible because the owner's liability concerns override familial status protections in Hawaii
B. Legal if the property has documented code violations or safety deficiencies related to child access
C. Permissible if the owner applies this screening consistently to all families regardless of income
D. Unlawful discrimination based on familial status, including both the safety-based discouragement and the steering practice ✓
Answer: D. Familial status is protected under both the federal Fair Housing Act and Hawaii's fair housing statute. Using safety pretexts and steering families with children to different properties—even indirectly—constitutes unlawful discrimination. Hawaii law mirrors federal protections; liability concerns do not override these statutory protections.
Tough·v109 A buyer is financing $540,000 (10% down on a $600,000 property). She is deciding between four loan products. Which option will result in the LEAST amount of interest paid in total?
A. 20-year fixed at 6.10%
B. 30-year fixed at 6.25%
C. 15-year fixed at 5.75% ✓
D. 30-year fixed at 5.95% plus 0.75 discount points
Answer: C. The 15-year fixed at 5.75% produces the lowest total interest because the substantially shorter amortization period more than compensates for a slightly higher rate compared to some alternatives. Total interest is driven primarily by loan term length; reducing 15 years saves far more in interest than marginal rate differences over 20 or 30 years.
Tough·v110 A licensee presents four loan scenarios to a client purchasing a $600,000 home with 10% down payment. The client wants to minimize lifetime interest cost. Which loan structure achieves this?
A. 30-year fixed at 6.25%
B. 20-year fixed at 5.80% with two discount points
C. 7/1 ARM starting at 5.50% then adjusting to market rate
D. 15-year fixed at 5.75% ✓
Answer: D. The 15-year fixed at 5.75% delivers the lowest total interest paid over the loan's life. Although the 20-year option with points has a competitive rate, the 15-year term's accelerated payoff window eliminates far more interest accrual than either longer-term or adjustable products can achieve.
Tough·v111 An investor analyzing debt service on a $600,000 purchase (10% down) reviews loan proposals from three lenders plus an in-house portfolio product. From a total-interest perspective, which is the most efficient?
A. Lender A: 30-year fixed at 6.00%
B. Lender B: 30-year fixed at 5.95% after paying 1 point upfront
C. Lender C: 20-year fixed at 6.05%
D. Portfolio product: 15-year fixed at 5.75% ✓
Answer: D. The 15-year fixed at 5.75% minimizes total lifetime interest because the 15-year amortization schedule creates substantially less cumulative interest expense than 20- or 30-year products, regardless of initial rate or discount points applied to the longer-term loans.
Tough·v112 A buyer is financing $540,000 (10% down on a $600,000 property) and comparing four loan structures. Which option results in the MINIMUM cumulative interest expense over the full loan term?
A. 15-year fixed at 5.80% ✓
B. 30-year fixed at 6.20% with two discount points
C. 20-year fixed at 6.10%
D. 30-year fixed at 5.90%
Answer: A. The 15-year fixed at 5.80% generates the lowest total interest paid because the shorter amortization period substantially outweighs modest rate differences. Although the 30-year options carry lower rates, the extended 15-year advantage in principal reduction more than compensates.
Tough·v113 Four financing scenarios exist for a $540,000 loan balance (10% down payment on $600,000 purchase price). Assume all loans are conventional fixed-rate mortgages. Which scenario minimizes the total amount of interest paid through payoff?
A. 15-year fixed at 5.70% ✓
B. 20-year fixed at 5.95%
C. 30-year fixed at 6.00% plus one origination point
D. 30-year fixed at 5.85%
Answer: A. The 15-year fixed at 5.70% produces the lowest total interest despite a slightly lower rate on the 30-year options, because the term reduction significantly decreases cumulative interest accrual. Discount points on longer-term loans do not overcome the fundamental mathematics of extended amortization.
Tough·v114 A homebuyer financing $540,000 (after 10% down on a $600,000 home) receives four loan quotes. Which loan structure will cost the LEAST in total interest dollars paid from origination through final payoff?
A. 15-year fixed at 5.75% ✓
B. 30-year fixed at 5.80%
C. 25-year fixed at 5.95%
D. 30-year fixed at 6.15% with one discount point buydown
Answer: A. The 15-year fixed at 5.75% incurs the lowest total interest because shortening the amortization term by half dramatically reduces the principal-times-time component of interest calculation. Longer-term loans, even with lower rates or point buydowns, still accumulate substantially more cumulative interest over their extended lives.
Tough·v115 A buyer is financing $540,000 on a $600,000 property (10% down). She is deciding between four 30-year options: (A) 6.50% with no points, (B) 6.25% with two discount points, (C) a 20-year fixed at 6.10%, or (D) a 15-year fixed at 5.80%. Over the entire loan life, which option will result in the smallest cumulative interest expense?
A. 30-year fixed at 6.25% with two discount points
B. 15-year fixed at 5.80% ✓
C. 20-year fixed at 6.10%
D. 30-year fixed at 6.50% with no points
Answer: B. The 15-year fixed at 5.80% has the shortest amortization period, which overwhelms the modest rate advantage of the longer-term loans. Even though the point-adjusted 30-year option lowers the rate, stretching payments over 30 years generates substantially more total interest than a 15-year payoff.
Tough·v116 An investor comparing total lifetime interest costs on a $540,000 loan amount (10% down on $600,000) examines: (1) 30-year at 6.10%, (2) 20-year at 5.95%, (3) 15-year at 5.70%, and (4) 30-year at 5.85% with 1.5 discount points. Which loan structure minimizes the total dollars paid in interest across its full term?
A. 30-year fixed at 5.85% with 1.5 discount points
B. 30-year fixed at 6.10%
C. 20-year fixed at 5.95%
D. 15-year fixed at 5.70% ✓
Answer: D. The 15-year fixed at 5.70% produces the lowest total interest paid because loan duration is the dominant factor in interest accumulation. Although the 30-year option with discount points appears attractive, the loan's 30-year life results in far greater cumulative interest than the 15-year term.
Tough·v117 A borrower financing 90% of a $600,000 home ($540,000 loan) wants to minimize total interest paid over the loan's life. The four options are: (A) 30-year at 6.30%, (B) 15-year at 5.75%, (C) 25-year at 6.05%, or (D) 30-year at 6.00% with two discount points and a 2/1 buydown. Which loan results in the lowest total interest expense?
A. 15-year at 5.75% ✓
B. 30-year at 6.00% with two discount points and a 2/1 buydown
C. 30-year at 6.30%
D. 25-year at 6.05%
Answer: A. The 15-year at 5.75% yields the minimum total interest because compressing the amortization period to 15 years significantly outweighs the marginal rate savings from discount points or buydown features on 25- and 30-year loans.
Tough·v118 A residential property in Hawaii carries an assessed value of $850,000 and is subject to a millage rate of $12.50 per $1,000 of assessed valuation. What is the approximate annual property tax obligation?
A. $1,062,500
B. $10,625 ✓
C. $68,000
D. $106,250
Answer: B. ($850,000 / $1,000) × $12.50 = 850 × $12.50 = $10,625. Students often misplace the decimal or forget to divide the assessed value by 1,000 before multiplying the rate.
Tough·v119 An investor acquires commercial real estate appraised at $2,500,000. The local tax authority applies a rate of $8.80 per thousand dollars of assessed value. Approximately what annual property tax should the investor budget?
A. $22,000 ✓
B. $28,600
C. $2,200
D. $220,000
Answer: A. ($2,500,000 / $1,000) × $8.80 = 2,500 × $8.80 = $22,000. Common errors include multiplying the rate by the full property value without dividing by 1,000, or confusing the per-thousand divisor with per-hundred.
Tough·v120 A Hawaii homeowner's property carries an assessed valuation of $575,000 subject to a property tax mill rate of $13.20 per $1,000 of assessed value. The owner's approximate annual tax liability is:
A. $7,590 ✓
B. $75,900
C. $43,656
D. $759,000
Answer: A. A mill rate of $13.20 per $1,000 of assessed value: ($575,000 ÷ $1,000) × $13.20 = 575 × $13.20 = $7,590.
Tough·v121 A commercial parcel in Honolulu is assessed at $850,000. The municipality applies a property tax rate of $11.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. What is the owner's annual property tax liability?
A. $850
B. $9,435 ✓
C. $94,350
D. $11,100
Answer: B. ($850,000 / $1,000) × $11.10 = 850 × $11.10 = $9,435. The key is dividing the total assessed value by the $1,000 base unit before multiplying by the rate per unit.
Tough·v122 A residential property carries an assessed value of $2,500,000 and is subject to a tax rate of $11.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. The annual property tax obligation is most nearly:
A. $27,750 ✓
B. $2,775
C. $110,000
D. $225,900
Answer: A. ($2,500,000 / $1,000) × $11.10 = 2,500 × $11.10 = $27,750. Failing to divide assessed value by $1,000 first leads to incorrect answers that are 10 times too large or too small.
Tough·v123 An investor acquires land assessed at $600,000 in a jurisdiction with a property tax rate of $11.10 per $1,000 of assessed value. Approximately how much annual property tax will the investor owe?
A. $66,000
B. $6,600 ✓
C. $1,110
D. $11,100
Answer: B. ($600,000 / $1,000) × $11.10 = 600 × $11.10 = $6,600. This unit-rate calculation is fundamental to property tax estimation and appears frequently on licensing exams.
Tough·v124 A parcel valued at $850,000 for tax purposes carries a millage rate of $9.80 per $1,000 of assessed value. What is the estimated annual property tax liability?
A. $9,800
B. $98,000
C. $833
D. $8,330 ✓
Answer: D. ($850,000 / $1,000) × $9.80 = 850 × $9.80 = $8,330. The correct approach divides the total assessed value by 1,000, then multiplies by the per-thousand rate—a critical unit-conversion step.
Tough·v125 An investor purchases a commercial property assessed at $2,500,000. The local tax rate is $12.50 per thousand dollars of assessed value. Calculate the annual property tax obligation.
A. $312,500
B. $1,250
C. $3,125
D. $31,250 ✓
Answer: D. ($2,500,000 / $1,000) × $12.50 = 2,500 × $12.50 = $31,250. Mishandling the 'per thousand' conversion—multiplying by the full rate instead of dividing the principal first—leads to the most common errors on this calculation type.
Tough·v126 A homeowner's property is assessed at $675,000. The county mill rate stands at $14.40 per $1,000 of assessed value. What annual property tax should the owner expect to pay?
A. $972
B. $14,400
C. $97,200
D. $9,720 ✓
Answer: D. ($675,000 / $1,000) × $14.40 = 675 × $14.40 = $9,720. The 'per $1,000' unit requires dividing the assessed value first; failure to convert to the correct denominator is the primary source of calculation mistakes on licensing exams.
Tough·v127 A Hawaii real estate salesperson holds a 60% ownership stake in an LLC that intends to acquire a property from a listing within their own brokerage firm. What action must the salesperson take to comply with Hawaii license law?
A. Request that their broker's designated broker execute all documents in place of the licensee-controlled entity
B. Immediately notify the Hawaii Real Estate Commission and wait for written approval before proceeding
C. Provide written disclosure to the seller that the salesperson holds an active real estate license and has a material ownership interest in the purchasing entity ✓
D. Transfer their license to another broker to avoid a conflict of interest
Answer: C. Hawaii license law mandates written disclosure when a licensee acts as principal—whether directly or through an entity they substantially control. Disclosure is the compliance mechanism; abstention or broker substitution is unnecessary.
Tough·v128 A salesperson licensed under a Hawaii brokerage is the beneficial owner of 60% of a corporation seeking to buy property listed by a different agent at that same brokerage. Under Hawaii law, the salesperson's obligation is to:
A. Require the broker to file a conflict-of-interest waiver with the Commission prior to offer submission
B. Obtain a separate limited broker license to represent the corporate buyer independently
C. Withdraw from the transaction and have an unlicensed party assume the buyer role
D. Provide clear written disclosure to the seller of their licensee status and principal interest in the buying corporation before contract execution ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii real estate law requires written disclosure when a licensee has a principal interest in a transaction—even when acting through a controlled entity. Disclosure, not license withdrawal or separate licensing, satisfies the regulatory requirement.
Tough·v129 A Hawaii salesperson who owns a controlling interest in a corporate buyer wishes to purchase a property that another agent in the salesperson's brokerage has listed for sale. Which statement correctly describes the salesperson's legal duty?
A. The salesperson must furnish written disclosure to the seller revealing their real estate license status and controlling ownership interest in the purchasing corporation ✓
B. The salesperson may not participate in the transaction in any capacity and must sit out completely
C. The salesperson's broker may represent the transaction on behalf of both parties if the broker is not the listing agent
D. The salesperson must resign from licensure for the transaction duration and rejoin after closing
Answer: A. Hawaii license law requires written disclosure of licensee principal status—including principal interest through controlled entities. Disclosure enables the transaction to proceed lawfully; resignation or complete abstention is not mandated.
Tough·v130 A Hawaii real estate licensee holds a 60% ownership stake in a development LLC. The LLC intends to acquire property that is listed through the licensee's own brokerage firm. Which statement accurately reflects the licensee's obligations?
A. The licensee's broker must act as intermediary and sign all documents to shield the licensee from liability
B. The licensee is prohibited from participating in any transaction where an entity they own is involved
C. The licensee must immediately terminate their license to avoid conflict of interest
D. The licensee may proceed with the transaction provided they deliver written disclosure to the seller that they are licensed and have a controlling interest in the buyer ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii REC rules require written disclosure when a licensee acts as principal through a controlled entity, but do not prohibit the transaction. Disclosure is the mandatory mechanism; the licensee may proceed after proper disclosure.
Tough·v131 A salesperson who is a majority shareholder in a corporation wants that corporation to bid on a property listed by a competing agent at the same brokerage. What is the salesperson's primary statutory duty?
A. Withdraw from the transaction and allow the broker to handle all communications with the seller
B. Relinquish their real estate license for the duration of the transaction
C. Require the seller's agent to disclose the salesperson's involvement on the MLS
D. Provide written notification to the seller disclosing licensee status and beneficial ownership in the purchasing corporation ✓
Answer: D. Hawaii license law mandates written disclosure by the licensee when they have a principal interest in the transaction, even if acting through an entity. This disclosure—naming the licensee and their ownership stake—is the compliance requirement, not prohibition or license suspension.
Tough·v132 A Hawaii licensee owns a controlling interest in a real estate investment company. That company wishes to purchase property listed by another licensee at the same brokerage. The licensee is considering their options. Which approach complies with state regulations?
A. Abstain from the transaction entirely; principal transactions by in-house licensees are categorically forbidden
B. Obtain written consent from the broker before making any disclosure to the seller
C. Furnish the seller with a written statement that the licensee holds an active real estate license and maintains principal ownership in the buyer entity ✓
D. Execute the purchase agreement through the company without involvement from the licensee to avoid dual agency issues
Answer: C. Hawaii law requires the licensee to disclose in writing their licensee status and principal interest to the seller. Disclosure is mandatory and permissible; the transaction is not prohibited as long as proper written notice is provided before execution.
Tough·v133 A real estate salesperson in Hawaii holds a 60% ownership stake in an LLC that intends to acquire property listed through the salesperson's own brokerage. Which action MUST the salesperson take to comply with Hawaii license law?
A. Transfer the listing to a different brokerage to avoid any appearance of self-dealing
B. Declare the transaction void ab initio because licensees cannot purchase through their own listings
C. Provide written disclosure to the seller that the salesperson holds a real estate license and has a material interest in the purchasing entity ✓
D. Obtain written approval from the Hawaii Real Estate Commission before the LLC makes an offer
Answer: C. Hawaii REC rules require written disclosure of the licensee's license status and principal interest when a licensee (or entity controlled by the licensee) acts as buyer or seller. Disclosure is the remedy, not prohibition or transfer.
Tough·v134 A Hawaii-licensed salesperson is the controlling member of a partnership that wants to buy a property listed by a colleague at the same brokerage. Under state law, the salesperson's PRIMARY obligation is to:
A. Make written disclosure to the seller identifying the salesperson's license and principal stake in the buying entity ✓
B. Immediately terminate the salesperson's license to eliminate conflicts of interest
C. Ensure the broker never becomes aware of the principal interest to preserve client confidentiality
D. Request that the listing agent's broker consent in writing before negotiations commence
Answer: A. Hawaii license law mandates written disclosure when a licensee has a principal (ownership or beneficial) interest in a transaction. The disclosure must reach the other party (here, the seller) regardless of broker knowledge.
Tough·v135 A Hawaii salesperson owns a controlling interest in an entity seeking to purchase a property listed by that salesperson's brokerage. Failure to comply with disclosure requirements in this scenario could result in:
A. License discipline, including potential revocation, for acting as an undisclosed principal in a real estate transaction ✓
B. A void contract that cannot be enforced against the seller under any circumstances
C. Mandatory forfeiture of all earnest money deposits by the buying entity
D. Automatic license suspension pending a cure period of 90 days
Answer: A. Hawaii REC violations involving undisclosed principal interests by licensees can lead to license discipline up to and including revocation. The requirement to disclose is mandatory; failure is a disciplinary matter, not automatically a contract issue.
Tough·v136 A Hawaii condominium developer is showing a unit to a qualified buyer who expresses serious interest. At what point in the transaction must the developer provide the Public Report per HRS 514B?
A. Only if the buyer submits a formal information request in writing
B. Immediately after the buyer submits a written offer to purchase
C. Prior to the buyer committing to a purchase agreement ✓
D. At the time of closing, along with other closing documents
Answer: C. HRS 514B mandates pre-contractual delivery of the Public Report so that prospective purchasers receive full disclosure before becoming legally bound. Delivery after an offer or contract is signed violates the statute's protective intent.
Tough·v137 Which statement most accurately describes the timing requirement for Public Report delivery under Hawaii's Condominium Property Regime law (HRS 514B)?
A. The developer may provide the Public Report up to 30 days after the purchaser executes the purchase agreement
B. The Public Report is required only when specifically demanded by the purchaser's attorney
C. The developer must furnish the Public Report before the purchaser is obligated by a binding contract ✓
D. The developer shall deliver the Public Report concurrent with the deed at closing
Answer: C. HRS 514B's disclosure requirement is front-loaded: the Public Report must reach the buyer before they sign any binding agreement. This ensures informed consent prior to contractual obligation, not after.
Tough·v138 A developer in Hawaii is negotiating with a potential condo buyer who has viewed the model units and is ready to move forward. When must the developer satisfy the Public Report delivery obligation under HRS 514B?
A. Before the prospect becomes party to a binding purchase contract ✓
B. No later than the date of closing, as part of the title company's document package
C. Within ten business days of the buyer submitting a purchase offer
D. Upon the buyer's request, but only if the request is in writing and notarized
Answer: A. HRS 514B requires pre-contractual delivery to protect the buyer's right to make an informed decision without being legally bound. Any post-contract delivery or conditional delivery undermines the statute's disclosure mandate.
Tough·v139 A condominium developer in Hawaii is showing a unit to a buyer who expresses serious interest. When must the developer provide the Public Report as required by HRS 514B?
A. At the time of closing, along with the deed
B. Only if the buyer explicitly asks for it in writing
C. Within 14 days after the buyer's offer is accepted
D. Prior to the buyer becoming legally obligated by a purchase agreement ✓
Answer: D. HRS 514B mandates delivery of the Public Report before the purchaser enters into a binding contract to allow informed decision-making. Timing after contractual obligation eliminates the protective purpose of the disclosure.
Tough·v140 Which statement correctly describes the timing requirement for Public Report delivery under Hawaii's condominium law (HRS 514B)?
A. The developer may provide the Public Report up to 10 days before settlement
B. Delivery is required within 30 days of the initial showing
C. The report satisfies disclosure only if given during escrow
D. The purchaser must receive the Public Report before being bound to purchase ✓
Answer: D. HRS 514B requires pre-contractual delivery to protect the purchaser's right to make an informed decision before taking on legal obligations. Post-contractual or conditional delivery does not satisfy the statute's disclosure mandate.
Tough·v141 A prospective condo buyer in Hawaii signs a purchase offer on Tuesday. The developer provides the Public Report on Thursday before closing. Under HRS 514B, has the developer complied with disclosure requirements?
A. No, unless the buyer waived the requirement in writing at the time of offer
B. Yes, because the report was delivered before the scheduled closing date
C. No, because the Public Report must be furnished before the buyer becomes contractually bound ✓
D. Yes, as long as the report is provided within 30 days of contract execution
Answer: C. HRS 514B requires the Public Report to be delivered before the purchaser signs a binding contract; delivery after contract formation violates the statute regardless of how soon before closing it occurs. The disclosure is meaningless once the buyer is already legally committed.
Tough·v142 A condominium developer in Hawaii is showing a unit to a buyer who expresses serious interest. At what point must the developer ensure the prospect receives the Public Report under HRS 514B?
A. Simultaneously with delivery of the deed at closing
B. Within 10 business days following the buyer's initial site visit
C. Before the buyer is legally obligated by signing a purchase contract ✓
D. Only if the buyer explicitly demands it in writing
Answer: C. HRS 514B mandates pre-contractual delivery of the Public Report so the buyer has full disclosure before becoming bound. Delivery after signature, upon demand, or at closing all violate the statute's protective timing requirement.
Tough·v143 Which statement correctly describes the timing requirement for Public Report delivery under HRS 514B in Hawaii condominium transactions?
A. The developer is required to deliver it no later than the date of the homeowners association transition
B. The developer may deliver it during the rescission period if the buyer waives the requirement in writing
C. The developer may withhold it until the buyer submits a formal written application for financing
D. The developer must provide it before the purchaser executes a binding sales contract ✓
Answer: D. HRS 514B requires pre-contractual disclosure specifically to allow the purchaser to make an informed decision before incurring contractual liability. Any delay—whether post-signing, conditional on written request, or tied to association turnover—violates this protective standard.
Tough·v144 A prospective condo buyer in Hawaii tells the developer's agent, 'Just send me the Public Report after I sign the contract so I can review it during my rescission period.' Under HRS 514B, what should the agent do?
A. Provide the Public Report before the buyer signs any binding contract, regardless of the buyer's preference ✓
B. Deliver the report only if the buyer submits a formal written demand within 5 days of signing
C. Wait until the developer receives loan approval documentation before distributing the Public Report
D. Accommodate the buyer's request and deliver the report within the rescission window
Answer: A. HRS 514B mandates pre-contractual delivery as a matter of law, not negotiable preference. The timing exists specifically to prevent buyers from being bound before accessing critical disclosure information, even if the buyer requests otherwise.
Tough·v145 During a listing presentation, a seller's agent overhears the seller state that they intend to misrepresent the property's flood history to potential buyers to expedite the sale. The agent's most appropriate response is to:
A. Advise the seller to disclose only to the buyer's agent, not to all parties
B. Proceed with marketing but insert a disclaimer in all advertising to protect the brokerage
C. Immediately notify the Hawaii Real Estate Commission and local building department
D. Withdraw representation and document the conversation; continuing would make the agent complicit in fraud ✓
Answer: D. An agent cannot knowingly facilitate fraud. Confidentiality does not shield illegal conduct. The agent must withdraw from representation and create documentation of the basis for withdrawal—neither unilaterally disclosing the seller's private statements nor remaining in a transaction that would involve fraud.
